Camp Jubilee was named after the fiftieth anniversary of the YMCA and was located on several islands in Lake Saint-Joseph with a landing area on shore.

Concordia Archives hold Camp Jubilee records including: fishing rights on Lake St. Joseph (1893-1902), a promotional letter (1895), land purchase correspondence (1897-1901), photographs (1898), and brochures (1898-1900).
YMCA Camp Pine Crest was founded in 1910 in Torrance, Ontario (Muskoka), and is now part of the YMCA of Greater Toronto. It is one of Canada's earliest overnight camps.
YMCA John Island Camp was established in 1954 on an island in the North Channel of Lake Huron, south of Spanish, Ontario. It is the overnight camp of the YMCA of Northeastern Ontario.
Big Cove YMCA Camp in Merigomish, Nova Scotia, founded in 1889, is the oldest residential camp in Canada. Camp Kanawana (1894) is the oldest in Quebec and the second oldest in Canada.

The Canadian Camping Association (CCA) was founded in 1936. The first meeting was held on May 20, 1936 at the Central YMCA, Toronto. Taylor Statten was first president; Mary Edgar was first vice-president.
The Ontario Camping Association archives at Trent University include a file for Camp Kanawana dated 1940.

Stuart McLean worked as a counsellor at Camp Kanawana beginning in 1969, serving five summers in the late 1960s and early 1970s, starting in the senior boys' section and eventually becoming assistant summer camp director.

Stuart McLean said of Camp Kanawana: 'I began pulling my adult self together at Camp Kanawana, and I benefited greatly from my camp experiences' and called it 'the first place I ever felt I truly belonged.'

After Stuart McLean's death in February 2017, his family established the Stuart McLean Camp Kanawana Fund, requesting donations in lieu of flowers to help children without financial means attend Camp YMCA Kanawana.

Stuart McLean attended Sir George Williams University (now Concordia University). He once passed up a chance to study journalism at Carleton University to return to Camp Kanawana as assistant director.

A 1993 documentary 'Kamp Kanawana: The Experience that lasts a lifetime' (9 min) was produced by Laurentien Productions for the Montreal YMCA, directed by Cathy Reeves. It describes Kanawana as the oldest camp in Quebec and second oldest in Canada.
The YMCA of Quebec ran day camps at Concordia University (Fine Arts Camp, Science and Engineering Camp) alongside Camp Kanawana programs, until discontinuing day camps in fall 2025.
Camp Kanawana's motto is 'Non Nobis Solum' — 'Not for ourselves alone.'
Dave Twynam served as camp director of Kamp Kanawana. Correspondence from 'Camp director Dave Twynam' is dated 1979 in the Concordia YMCA archives (sub-sub-series P0145/12B01).

Ross Bannerman authored a 'Report on Kamp Kanawana' in 1969, listed in Concordia YMCA archives (sub-sub-series P0145/12B01). Role at camp not confirmed but authoring a camp report suggests administrative authority.

Concordia archives contain 'Camping and Outdoor Education Branch Director's Report' for 1972 (5 copies) and 1970, plus 'Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA' from 1974.

David Leduc managed YMCA Camp Kanawana's summer and winter programs per his LinkedIn (profile: davidgleduc), including recruitment/supervision of 75 employees, all programs and operational budgets, safety/security of 800 participants, reporting to Board of Directors, strategic business planning, and development/implementation of an intensive youth leadership program. Exact dates of tenure not specified but must predate his Oxfam-Quebec Lebanon role (Mar 2000-Jun 2002), placing Kanawana service likely in the late 1990s. Education: BA International Development (Dalhousie), MBA (McGill, 2006-2011). Subsequent career: Oxfam-Quebec Lebanon coordinator (2000-2002), McGill ICAN director of operations (~11 years), Executive Director of Development and Peace (2015-~2020), Director of Philanthropy Quebec at Pathways to Education Canada (current). Based in Greater Montreal (Outremont). Languages: English, French, Spanish, functional Arabic.

The anonymous Westmount Magazine commenter who was camp director at Kanawana in 1974-1975 (alongside Stuart McLean as assistant director) also sublet McLean's flat on Dorchester and looked after his piano when McLean moved to Toronto in the late 1970s. The commenter's name is not visible in available web results.

Concordia archives P0145/12B01 contains 'YMCA Kamp Kanawana Facts-timeline 1894-1998' and 'Kanawana Reminiscence (of 1948), by Ben T. Hannah (1989)'. These documents likely contain comprehensive director lists.
'Kanawana, a Place to Grow: A Proposal for the Future of Kanawana, by Kanawana Camping Task Force' report from 1988 is held in Concordia archives P0145/12B01.

Sean Day is described as 'former director of Camp YMCA Kanawana' in recent references (post-2022), indicating he has left the director role. Kate Taylor and Kevin Slezak (Assistant Director) are current leadership.
On September 5, 2014, Camp YMCA Kanawana alumni assembled at Victoria Hall to celebrate the camp's 120th anniversary reunion.
A 1993 documentary about Camp Kanawana was produced, describing it as the oldest camp in Quebec and second oldest in Canada. This was one year before the 1994 centennial.
The Green Triangle camp newsletter dates from 1932-1940 per Concordia finding aid; additional issues (KA-News and Green Triangle) from 1976 and 1978-1982 are also held.
Standardized YMCA Camp Songs Books existed by 1938 (per eBay listing of lot of 7 books from that year), contemporaneous with Kanawana's song books (1941-1945) in the Concordia archives.
The YMCA published a formal Association Hymn Book in 1904, containing sacred hymns for male chorus, unaccompanied, in English. This is the only YMCA collection on IMSLP.
The YMCA published a Service Song Book during WWI, prepared by the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations, for men in military and naval service.

Camp Sloane YMCA organizes village cheers and chants by section/age group (Pioneer Girls, Junior Girls, Senior Girls, Student Girls, LEAD, CIT, Day Camp), confirming the YMCA tradition of section-specific cheers.

The L&V Games at Kanawana are 3 days long (not 2 as at Pine Crest). A former staff member described them as involving 'incredible teamwork, determination, and passion' where 'every person, campers and staff alike, unite with their team.'
Stuart McLean described Camp Kanawana as 'a microcosm of Canada, where English, French, rich, poor, recent immigrants and locals sing together around the camp fire.'

Stuart McLean described himself before camp as 'an utter academic, athletic and social failure' who 'didn't have a lot of confidence.' At camp he found 'a place where I was accepted by others and I was able to contribute to the greater good.'

The Camp Kanawana current sections are: Pioneers (girls 7-12), Woodsmen (boys 7-12), Pathfinders (girls 13-15), Coureurs des Bois (boys 13-15), Mountaineers (gender-neutral 13-15, est. 2022). Specialized programs: Voyageurs (all-gender long canoe trip program), Trailblazers (Leaders-in-Training, age 16), Foresters (canoe trip leader specialization). 'Senior Kanawanians' is not a section name. The section structure dates to at least the early 1980s.
The Mountaineer program was launched at Kanawana as an all-gender tent to provide a safe and welcoming environment for transgender, non-binary, and gender non-conforming campers.

YMCA Camp Waabanaki (previously Camp Wabanaki) changed its name in early 2023 at the recommendation of a local elder as part of reconciliation with the local Indigenous community. The new name means 'a new dawn day.'

Taylor Statten established Camp Ahmek in 1921 at Canoe Lake in Algonquin Park. Statten's camp philosophy was a result of his 1905 role as Boys' Work Secretary for the Toronto YMCA and his role organizing a YMCA summer camp near Orillia.

The Canadian Summer Camp Research Project (CSCRP, 2006-2011) by the CCA and University of Waterloo interviewed over 50 camp directors and identified five common areas of youth development at camps: social connections/integration, environmental awareness, attitudes toward physical activity, emotional intelligence, and personal development/self-confidence.

Over 30 web searches for 'Chopsy' (also 'Chopsey', 'Chopsie') combined with camp, ghost, Quebec, Kanawana, and legend returned zero relevant results. The name does not appear in any indexed folklore archive, academic database, Reddit discussion, blog, or camp ghost story collection as of March 2026.

No web source connects any 'Richard Kerr' to YMCA camp song composition. The prominent Richard Kerr (songwriter, 1944-2023) was an English pop songwriter (co-wrote 'Mandy' for Barry Manilow) with no documented connection to camps or YMCAs. Richard 'Itch/Itche' Kerr, the Kanawana alumnus who composed 'On My Way to Kanawana' and received the inaugural Pip Award c. 2007, has no web presence.

No web source documents any Kanawana-specific lyrics, sheet music, or digital recording of 'On My Way to Kanawana.' The Concordia Archives CD (P145/SR0001) remains the sole known copy as of March 2026.

The Concordia YMCA of Montreal fonds finding aid page confirms holdings include: Green Triangle-Kamp Kanawana Kampers' newsletter (1932-1940), KA-News and Green Triangle issues (1976, 1978-1982), camp brochures, photographs, promotional materials, and t-shirt artwork spanning from the early 1920s through the late 1990s.

Lemuel Cushing Jr. (1842-1881) was president of the Montreal YMCA from 1869 to 1870. He was a McGill-educated lawyer and Liberal MP for Argenteuil (1874-75), married Ellen Myra Macdougall in 1869, published the first Cushing family genealogy in 1877, and died March 1, 1881.

Lemuel Cushing Sr. (1806-1875) had 13 children including 8 sons: Colonel James Brock, Lemuel Jr. (1842-1881), Thomas (founded Montreal Brewing 1876), Francis (hired Olmsted), Charles (notary), Frederick (b. 1851), William Mair (d. 1925), and others.

Since Lemuel Cushing Jr. died in 1881, the 'Lemuel Cushing' who led the 1892 YMCA camping trip to Lake Saint-Joseph must be a third-generation Cushing — either a son of Lemuel Jr. or a grandson of Lemuel Sr. bearing the family name. James Stevenson Cushing (1878-1957), author of the 1905 genealogy update, was born in Quebec and is likely a son or close relative of Lemuel Jr.

The motto 'Non Nobis Solum' derives from Cicero's De Officiis (1:22): 'non nobis solum nati sumus ortusque nostri partem patria vindicat, partem amici' — 'Not for us alone are we born; our country, our friends, have a share in us.' It is itself a translation of a sentiment from Plato.

Lower Canada College (LCC, founded 1909) shares the motto 'Non Nobis Solum' with Camp Kanawana. LCC founder Charles Sanderson Fosbery adopted it from the Fosbery family crest. Whether Kanawana adopted the motto independently or through LCC connection is unknown.

The Pagé family has deep roots in Saint-Sauveur. Boulangerie Pagé was established in 1903; Édouard Pagé acquired it in 1914. 'Domaine-Pagé' is a named locality in Saint-Sauveur. The 'Page family' from whom the YMCA acquired the camp property is almost certainly this Pagé family.

Weredale House (Boys' Home of Montreal) was founded in 1870 by Charles Alexander (1816-1905), a Scottish immigrant confectioner and philanthropist. Alexander built the institution at his own expense on Mountain Street and served as president from 1870 until his death. Over 1,000 boys were housed during his presidency.

Before Camp Weredale (1934), Weredale House boys attended a shared camp in Ste. Marguerite from the 1920s. An earlier 'Camp Boy' was sponsored in 1918, renamed 'Camp Lewis' in 1919 after Major John Lewis, killed in WWI.
Library and Archives Canada holds the Weredale House fonds (1868-1975), containing textual records, graphic material, and architectural drawings.

Dave Twynam (G. David Twynam) was camp director of Kamp Kanawana circa 1979. He later became an academic specializing in outdoor recreation, tourism, and event management — Dean of Faculty of Management at Vancouver Island University and previously at Thompson Rivers University.
A Flickr account under the name 'Kanawana' hosts 4,416 photos. The Instagram account (@ymcakanawana) has 571 posts. Neither has been reviewed for historical content.
Camp Kanawana held a 120th anniversary reunion at Victoria Hall on September 5, 2014.
A Montreal Gazette article from February 24, 1933 titled 'Music and Comedy in Fossils' Revue' reveals an alumni group called 'the Fossils' connected to Camp Kanawana.

A Montreal Gazette article from August 5, 1942 titled 'Y.M.C.A. Boys Stage Parade and Circus' names Camp Director R.H. Hanagan (in Indian garb on horseback) and Resident Director E.E. Smee. Mentions Bantam/Junior/Intermediate/Senior sections.
Ross Bannerman authored a 'Report on Kamp Kanawana' in 1969 (Concordia Archives), suggesting a senior role at the camp — possibly director — during that period.
David Leduc managed all Kanawana summer/winter programs (75 employees, 800 participants) per LinkedIn. Dates of service unknown.
Sean Day confirmed as 'former director' of Camp Kanawana (post-2022). Kate Taylor and Kevin Slezak are current leadership.

E.E. Smee held the role of 'Resident Director' at Camp Kanawana in 1942, distinct from the Camp Director role held by R.H. Hanagan. This documents a two-tier directorship structure during the wartime period.
Sean Day grew up at Camp Kanawana, as stated in a 2017 CBC article about the Stuart McLean Camp Kanawana Fund.
Sean Day held the dual title of 'Regional Director of Camps for the Quebec YMCAs' and 'Director of Camp YMCA Kanawana' simultaneously, as confirmed by multiple CBC News articles (2017-2022).

In 2021, Sean Day decided to close Camp Kanawana's overnight camp due to COVID-19, as offering overnight services to 250+ campers was not feasible. YMCA Quebec instead offered 10 day camps (up from 3 the previous summer).

In May 2022, Sean Day reported Camp Kanawana had only hired 75% of counsellors by end of April (normally fully staffed by then). YMCA made 'huge increases' to salaries to recruit staff. Waiting lists existed at many YMCA camps.
After leaving YMCA Quebec (c. April 2023), Sean Day's LinkedIn title is 'Director of Fund Development', and prior KB notes indicate he moved to the Rossy Foundation.
Sean Day said of Camp Kanawana: 'Helping kids to understand their potential in the context of community and nature is what the camp is all about.' (CBC, 2017)

E.E. Smee's full name was Edgar E. Smee. The McMorris thesis lists him as 'Edgar Smee' (Juvenile section director, 1939) and the 1942 Gazette article uses 'E.E. Smee' (Resident Director). These are the same person.

Edgar E. Smee died on February 7, 2002, at the Glebe Centre in Ottawa, at age 89. He was survived by his wife Frieda, daughters Linda, Susan, Sydney, and Sonia, and brothers Norman and Leonard. Obituary published in The Globe and Mail, February 11, 2002.
Edgar E. Smee was born circa 1912-1913 (age 89 at death in February 2002). His hometown was Hamilton, Ontario, where he grew up swimming in Red Hill Creek as a boy.

Edgar E. Smee returned to Hamilton in 1968 after a 30-year absence (c.1938). He was dismayed by pollution at Red Hill Creek and local beaches, which 'sparked a deep anger' and led to his environmental activism.

Edgar E. Smee was the founding Chair of the Conserver Society of Hamilton & District (originally 'Clear Hamilton of Pollution' / CHOP, founded 1969; incorporated as Conserver Society 1984). He helped create the first action plan for Hamilton Harbour/Burlington Bay.

Edgar E. Smee was named Environmentalist of the Year in 1983 (EOY Awards). The Ed Smee Conserver Society Environmental Fund was established in his honour in 1999, managed by Hamilton Community Foundation.

Edgar Smee's 30-year absence from Hamilton (c.1938-1968) aligns with his documented Kanawana service (1939 Juvenile section director, 1942 Resident Director), suggesting he may have been based in Montreal during that period for YMCA work.

Twynam's academic research on volunteer motivation and special events was conducted at Lakehead University in Thunder Bay, using data from the 1996 Scott Tournament of Hearts (Canadian Women's Curling Championship) and the 1997 Scouts Canada Canadian Jamboree, both held in Thunder Bay.

Twynam's research also includes sustainable tourism (WWF Arctic Tourism Guidelines with M.E. Johnston), marine tourism (HMS Erebus and Terror National Historic Site in Nunavut), and residents' perceptions of sporting event impacts.

The Concordia University Archives YMCA of Montreal fonds (P0145) sub-series 12 covers Camping and Outdoor Programs, with the following camp-specific sub-series: 12A (Committees), 12B (Kamp Kanawana), 12C (Camp Otoreke), 12D (Camp Becsies), 12E (Camp Dorval), 12F (Camp Weredale), 12G (Camp Perrot), 12H (Ski lodge), 12I (Camp Thunderbird), 12J (Wilderness Survival Camp), 12K (Les Voyageurs de la Vérendrye), 12L (Lac St-Joseph/Camp Jubilee), 12M (Day camp), 12N (Camping associations).
Camp Becsies was a YMCA Montreal camp documented in Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12D, with textual records dating from 1929-1936 and 1960-1971 (3 cm of records).
Camp Dorval was a YMCA Montreal camp documented in Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12E, with textual records dating from 1926-1928 (0.5 cm of records).

Camp Perrot was a boys' camp operated by the Montreal YMCA alongside Kamp Kanawana. Concordia Archives hold a 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' (c.1945-46) and a further comparison of Kamp Kanawana and Camp Perrot (1953-54).

Les Voyageurs de la Vérendrye was a YMCA Montreal canoe-tripping program that began with exploratory trip logs from 1958 and a La Vérendrye Park pilot project proposed budget c.1959. The program leased land at Lac Landron in 1962-63, produced brochures by 1963, and maintained camper records from 1967-1980, with a review booklet in 1982.

The modern YMCA Kanawana Voyageurs program descends from the Les Voyageurs de la Vérendrye program (est. 1958-59). Current offerings include: 12-Day Travelers (Voyageurs) paddling the Coulonge, Dumoine, and Noire Rivers; Adventurers Coureurs des Bois (4-6 day introductory canoe trips in La Vérendrye Wildlife Reserve); and 26-Day Voyageurs Ultimate (21-day white water canoe trip).

Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A (Committees) holds a 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' (c.1945-46), a Boys' Camping Committee Survey Committee report (1950), and a 'Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA' (1974).
Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A holds Permanent Camp Committee minutes dating back to 1895-1896, the earliest known YMCA Montreal camping administrative records.
Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A holds a 'journal of the first Montreal YMCA venture to explore the country around St. Agathe with the view of securing a lake for a summer camp' dated 1895.

In 1921, Mabel C. Jamieson and Ferna G. Halliday jointly acquired land from Mr. Leguerrier at what would become Camp Ouareau. At the time, Quebec law prohibited women from buying or owning property without their father's or husband's permission; both women had to fight to get their fathers' permission to purchase.

Ferna G. Halliday was a graduate of Queen's University. From 1918 to 1921, she served as secretary of the Christian Association of Young Women (YWCA) of Montreal and was responsible for young girls at Camp Oolahwan in the Laurentians.

Mabel C. Jamieson was National Student Secretary of the Christian Association of Young Women of Canada in 1915. After completing her studies in 1918 at Pupils College in Richmond, she became secretary general of the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal at least from 1915 to 1920, and was a member of the Committee of the Sixteen in 1919.

Ferna Halliday co-directed Camp Ouareau in 1922 and 1923. In spring 1922, she toured to Sherbrooke to promote the camp's opening. From 1924, Mabel Jamieson directed Camp Ouareau alone while Halliday founded Camp Oconto in Tichborne, Ontario.

Camp Oconto, an all-girls camp on Eagle Lake in Tichborne, Ontario, was founded by Ferna Halliday in 1924. Halliday ran it each year until 1949 when June Kennedy Labbett and Cliff Labbett took over. Halliday Hall, the original dining hall built in 1924, is named in her honour.

Camp Ouareau and Camp Oconto continued to operate on the same mission with similar traditions, including opening and closing rituals featuring candlelight ceremonies with classical music, poetry, and tableaux.
Dorothy Percival became director of Camp Ouareau in 1934 and acquired the site in 1937. She believed in women's education and paid for some campers to attend school.
Joyce Bertram became manager and owner of Camp Ouareau in 1954, having purchased it from Dorothy Percival. She introduced the camp mascot 'Bymph' and composed several camp songs still sung today.

In 1970, Madeleine Allen created the Language Program at Camp Ouareau, bringing together two aspects of Quebec culture. In 1976, the camp began accepting 50% francophone campers, shifting from an English-only camp.

Jacqui Raill became director of Camp Ouareau in 1994 (she had been a counsellor since 1975). She and her husband Don Raill became co-owners in 2002. Their daughter Gabrielle Raill became assistant director in 2004 and co-director since 2011.

Camp Ouareau's Lodge was built in 1922 and is one of the oldest log buildings still in use in Canada. The camp site covers 14.5 hectares including a peninsula on Leguerrier Bay and two islands on Lac Ouareau.
In May 1941, a forest fire south of Lac Ouareau threatened Camp Ouareau's facilities and its summer opening; the camp was ultimately spared.
In 2014, Camp Ouareau changed its team names from Iroquois, Algonquin, and Micmac, and shifted many names and signs on camp to remove Indigenous-themed naming.
Camp Ouareau (est. 1922) is one of the two oldest summer camps exclusively for young girls still in operation in Canada, alongside Glen Bernard Camp in Huntsville, Ontario (also 1922).
Camp Oolahwan was the longest sustained initiative in YWCA Montreal history. Founded in 1917, it operated until 2005 and contributed to the healthy development of thousands of girls and women.

Mary Susanna Edgar founded Camp Oolahwan in 1917 on Lake Walfred in Sainte-Marguerite-du-Lac-Masson in the Laurentian mountains, north of Montreal. It was an English-speaking camp exclusively for young girls.
The Camp Oolahwan centennial reunion was held in 2017 at Camp Ouareau in Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci. Sources disagree on exact dates: YWCA says September 8-10; West Island Blog says August 25-27.
Ferna Halliday was among the founding members of the Ontario Camping Association in 1933, alongside Mary Edgar, Taylor Statten, Ethel Statten, A.L. Cochrane, and Mary Hamilton.

Montreal's Committee of the Sixteen was formed in 1918 to study 'commercialized vice.' Mabel C. Jamieson was a member in 1919, indicating her involvement in Montreal social reform networks alongside her YMCA and camp work.

Camp Ouareau today serves girls and gender minorities aged 6-16, with capacity of 143 campers per 2-week session and nearly 500 campers per summer. It is divided into three age groups: Nova (6-11), Luna (12-13), and Senior (14-16). The camp operates a bilingual French-English linguistic program.

The YWCA Montreal claims Camp Oolahwan (1917) was the first summer camp for girls in Canada. However, Camp Northway in Ontario predates it (founded 1906). The YWCA claim likely refers to the first YWCA-operated girls camp.
An April 17, 1937 report of the nominating committee for the Quebec Camping Association is preserved in the CCA fonds at Trent University Archives.
Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A holds 'History of Camping' notes dated 1936, the same year the CCA was founded.

Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/12A holds a 'Report — trip to St. Agathe' dated 1893 and 1895, described as the 'Journal of the first Montreal YMCA venture to explore the country round about St. Agathe with the view of securing a lake on which to establish a Summer Camp.' The 1893 date places this scouting expedition one year BEFORE Camp Jubilee's founding in 1894.

Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds Permanent Camp Committee records spanning: minutes (1895-96), correspondence/financial records (1899-1901, fragile documents), minutes/correspondence (1908), minute book (1911-1926), minutes (1921), and a Camp Executive meeting from December 12, 1945.
The 120th anniversary reunion of Camp YMCA Kanawana was held at Victoria Hall on September 5, 2014, for alumni (former campers and staff members).
Camp Kanawana's site is 550 acres with 3 lakes, located in the Laurentians 45 minutes from Montreal.

G. David Twynam (PhD) served as Camp Kanawana director c.1979-1980 (confirmed as 'Dave' in Ka-News 1980). He later held academic positions: faculty at Lakehead University School of Outdoor Recreation, Parks & Tourism (late 1990s); Dean of School of Tourism at University College of the Cariboo/Thompson Rivers University (~1999-2009); Dean of Faculty of Management at Vancouver Island University (post-2009). He co-developed the Special Event Volunteer Motivation Scale (SEVMS), his most-cited contribution (10 research works, 723 citations on ResearchGate).

Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/11C holds 'Ross Bannerman's International Branch file' dated 1970, placing Bannerman at the YMCA du Parc (International) branch c.1968-1970, contemporaneous with his 1969 Kanawana report.

Sean Day held the dual title of Regional Director of Camps for the Quebec YMCAs and Director of Camp YMCA Kanawana, serving from 2004 to approximately April 2023 (19 years). He grew up at Camp Kanawana and was Matt Aronson's counsellor. After departing YMCA Quebec, he became Director of Fund Development at the Rossy Foundation.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Sean Day made the decision to close Kanawana's overnight program, citing the impossibility of offering overnight services to 250+ campers. The YMCA pivoted to 10 day camps (up from 3 the previous summer). In 2022, Kanawana had only hired 75% of counsellors by end of April (normally fully staffed by then) due to national staff shortages.

David G. Leduc held a BA in International Development from Dalhousie University and an MBA from McGill (2006-2011). Career sequence: Oxfam-Québec Lebanon coordinator (2000-2002), YMCA Kanawana program manager (dates uncertain, managing 75 employees and 800 participants), McGill ICAN director of operations, Executive Director of Development and Peace (2015-2020), Director of Philanthropy (Quebec) at Pathways to Education.

Mabel C. Jamieson, co-founder of Camp Ouareau (1922), was described as 'secretary general of the YMCA of Montreal' c.1915-1920 in the Camp Ouareau history page. However, this claim could not be independently verified; it may represent a conflation with the YWCA. She was also National Student Secretary of the YWCA of Canada in 1915 and a member of the Committee of the Sixteen (Montreal anti-vice committee) in 1919.

Ferna G. Halliday, co-founder of Camp Ouareau (1922), was a Queen's University graduate and Secretary of YWCA Montreal (1918-1921) responsible for girls at Camp Oolahwan. She co-directed Camp Ouareau 1922-1923, then founded Camp Oconto in Tichborne, Ontario (1924), running it until 1949. She was a founding member of the Ontario Camping Association in 1933 alongside Mary Edgar, Taylor Statten, and Ethel Statten.

Camp Ouareau land was acquired in 1921 from Mr. Leguerrier, under Quebec law requiring fathers' permission for women to buy property. The camp is located at 2464 Route 125, Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci, on 14.5 hectares of Leguerrier Bay, Lac Ouareau, including a peninsula and two islands.
A. Ross Seaman graduated from Sir George Williams University and subsequently offered a colleague a job at the Cornwall YMCA, indicating early career involvement with the Ontario YMCA network.
A. Ross Seaman served as teacher and chairperson of the Community Recreation and Leadership Training (CRLT) Department at Dawson College from 1974 to 1984.
A. Ross Seaman and his wife Margaret developed the Elder Hostel Program at Concordia University's Loyola Campus after his retirement from Dawson College.
A. Ross Seaman served as acting chair of Concordia University Leisure Studies during the 1986-87 school year (more precise than earlier 'during the 1980s' claim).
A. Ross Seaman's home community was Vankleek Hill, Ontario, where he is remembered for church and community involvement. A scholarship is given in his name from Vankleek Hill Collegiate.

The A. Ross Seaman Memorial Leadership Development Fund hosts an annual awards evening with auction — described as possibly the only active Concordia scholarship that raises funds this way. Awards are presented annually at Dawson College. The fund designation code is ES0042.

Five organizations give scholarships in A. Ross Seaman's name: Dawson College, Concordia University, Kamp Kanawana, YMCA, and Vankleek Hill Collegiate. The Dawson CRLT scholarship is $500 to a second-year student displaying leadership, community service, caring, and concern for others.

The Stuart McLean Camp Kanawana Fund was established by Stuart McLean and his family to help children in need attend Camp Kanawana. McLean returned to Camp Kanawana in 2005 for a week and hosted one of his Vinyl Cafe shows there.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Camp Kanawana was closed for overnight camping for two consecutive summers (2020 and 2021). In 2021, YMCA Quebec chose to run 10 day camps instead of reopening overnight operations. Sean Day said offering overnight services to more than 250 campers at once did not seem possible.

Leontyne Hache began attending Camp Kanawana at age eight, joined the overnight camp's leadership training programme, and in summer 2019 became its canoe and kayak program specialist; she was 19 in April 2021. Gaetane Verna, 'growing up in Quebec, attended summer camps from the age of eight, eventually becoming a counsellor and section leader at Camp Kanawana... when she got older' -- the source does NOT say she was a camper at Kanawana itself, only that she was a counsellor and section leader there. Verna was 'now based in Toronto' in April 2021 and has two daughters who attend the camp, one of them 15 that year.
facts.correction: CITATION CORRECTED 2026-08-25. Previously cited src_cbc_2021_kanawana; that record's two CBC articles were re-read in full and contain neither name. Claim also corrected: 'attended as a camper... at Camp Kanawana' was not what the source says.

facts.claim: Camp Kanawana is described as located 90 kilometres north of Montreal (CBC 2017) and 10 minutes from Saint-Sauveur (YMCA website). These distances suggest the camp is near Piedmont/Saint-Sauveur in the Laurentians.

On May 14, 2018, Desjardins contributed $1 million to the YMCAs of Québec, part of the 'Springboard for Life' campaign (Campagne YMCA Tremplin pour la vie) aiming to raise $20 million over five years. A portion was earmarked for a new community pavilion at Camp Kanawana, described as 'the new heart of Kanawana,' to increase capacity and expand environmental awareness programming. The announcement was made by Guy Cormier (President/CEO Mouvement Desjardins) and Stéphane Vaillancourt (President/CEO YMCAs of Québec). Desjardins had supported YMCA Quebec for over 25 years.

The Concordia Archives (YMCA fonds sub-series 12L, Lac St-Joseph/Camp Jubilee) hold photographs of R. H. Dawson and R. L. Charlton, listed together, suggesting they were associates in the early camp movement. Charlton later wrote 'Notes re Early Days of YMCA Camps at Lake St. Joseph and Kanawana' in 1943.

Extensive web searching (March 2026) for 'Ralph Dawson' and 'Ralph H. Dawson' in connection with YMCA Montreal, Montreal obituaries, Montreal genealogy, camp history Quebec, Camp Jubilee, and city directories yielded no biographical details (birth/death dates, profession, family). His online footprint is limited to archival finding aids at Concordia University.

R. H. Hanagan is identified in the Concordia Archives YMCA fonds as 'Montreal YMCA camp director,' but his specific dates of service and relationship to Kanawana vs. other YMCA camps are not specified in the online finding aids.

The 1898 Camp Jubilee photograph in sub-series 12L is labelled 'YMCA Camp - Lac St. Joseph' and names four individuals: W. N. Cunningham, Jim Brown, Frank L. Benedict, and Ralph H. Dawson. A Camp Jubilee promotional letter also exists from 1895, and YMCA camp brochures exist for 1898, 1899, and 1900.

The Grace McMorris MA thesis (Concordia, 2023) 'An Experience That Lasts a Lifetime: Building Modernity, Man, and Nation at the YMCA of Montreal's Kamp Kanawana, 1894-1967' draws from the YMCA of Montreal fonds at Concordia. The full thesis PDF is available at spectrum.library.concordia.ca but direct access was blocked during this research session. The thesis covers religion, colonialism, and national identity at Kanawana across three chapters: active Christian citizenship, playing Indian, and the myth of the voyageur.
Taylor Statten's full name was Emerson Taylor Statten (1882-1956).
Taylor Statten's wife was Ethel Page ('Tonakela'), co-founding director of Camp Wapomeo. Their son Taylor Statten II ('Dr. Tay', 1915-2016) took over as Camp Director in 1954.
Taylor Statten mortgaged his home to fund Camp Ahmek's opening in 1921. The camp opened for six weeks with 60 boys living in tents.

The CSET program was formally launched in October 1918 with two tiers: Trail Rangers (ages 12-14) and TUXIS (ages 15-17). A parallel girls' program, Canadian Girls in Training (CGIT), was also created. Based on a 'fourfold' development philosophy: intellectual, physical, spiritual, and social.
Taylor Statten organized the first Ontario TUXIS and Older Boys' Parliament in 1917.

Hedley Dimock and Charles Hendry conducted their pioneering research at Camp Ahmek starting in 1923, published as 'Camping and Character' (1929/1931). William H. Kilpatrick (progressive educator, colleague of John Dewey) wrote the foreword.

Taylor Statten was elected ACA president in 1942 but resigned due to illness; VP Wes Klusmann assumed responsibilities. (Corrected 2026-07-08 from an earlier misreading of the same ACA presidents page as 1941 -- that year belongs to a separate entry for Esther Waldo of the YWCA. See f_1277 and conflict c_003.)
The Taylor Statten Camps commissioned 42-foot war canoes from the Peterborough Canoe Company in 1926, reportedly still in use.

The Concordia Archives (P0145/12A) place Hanagan's report alongside: 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' (Kanawana and Camp Perrot, c.1945-46), 'Report of the Montreal YMCA Camps for Boys and Girls' (1946), and an ACA Conference report to the Board of Management (1946). This confirms Hanagan's portfolio extended beyond Kanawana.

Howie Langille was Camp Chief/Director in 1941 (48th season, 68 staff, 30+ British wartime evacuees). No director is documented between Langille (1941) and Hanagan (1942), suggesting direct succession.

Dr. Cushing, identified as a pediatrician, visited Kanawana during the 1946 polio outbreak and recommended cancelling canoe trips but keeping the camp open. Three of six cases were discharged by end of summer. This Dr. Cushing is distinct from W.E. Cushing who wrote 'Historical sketches' in 1943.

Derek Walsh (ACQ — Association des camps du Québec) received the CCA Award of Excellence in 1983. The CCA fonds at Trent University Archives associates him with 'Kamp Kanawana, YMCA, Montreal, Quebec.'

According to the Wikipedia article on Camp Ouareau (sourced from Camp Ouareau history): Mabel C. Jamieson was National Student Secretary of the YWCA of Canada in 1915. After completing studies in 1918 at 'Pupils College in Richmond,' she 'became secretary general of the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal at least from 1915 to 1920.' The chronology is inconsistent (YWCA role 1915 precedes 1918 studies), suggesting possible source confusion. She was also a member of the Committee of the Sixteen in 1919 and 'made a career in teaching.'

At least 5 issues of Canadian Camping magazine (CCA, 1949-1988) are digitized on Internet Archive with OCR: Vol. 9/1 (Dec 1956), Vol. 11/2 (Feb 1959), Vol. 13/4 (Jun 1961), Vol. 16/2 (Feb 1964), Vol. 24/2 (Winter 1972). Collection at archive.org/details/canadian-camping-association.

The CCA held an Outdoor Education Conference at La Caleche, Ste-Agathe, Quebec, October 3-6, 1974 — in the Laurentians near Camp Kanawana. Proceedings available as ERIC document ED106010 on Internet Archive.

A 109-page university paper titled 'Mary S. Edgar's Contribution to the Canadian Camping Movement' is held in the Sundridge-Strong Digital Collection (images.ourontario.ca/sunstrong/72744). The Trent University Archives also hold the Mary S. Edgar fonds (82-010). The CCA published 'Legacy to a Camper: The Story of Mary S. Edgar' by Jocelyn Palm.
The earliest known newspaper reference to Camp Kanawana is a Montreal Gazette article from July 7, 1897, titled 'YMCA Summer Camp Kanawana' — three years after the camp's founding in 1894.
A Montreal Gazette article from July 11, 1918 titled 'At Camp Kanawana' reports a record attendance of 110 campers and mentions filming by visiting YMCA representatives from London.

The McCord Stewart Museum in Montreal holds item C387, titled 'Kamp Kanawana', dated approximately 1930. The item is classified as a 'postal card' within the Photography collection. Image is not digitized online ('Image Not Available'). Artefacts Canada identifier: MCCD202639. A related McCord item MCCD198988 is classified as a 'Photograph'. The C387 designation is associated with Bailey Brothers Company Limited (publisher, active before 1898).
The Quebec Camping Association fonds (accession 85-013) is held at Trent University Archives, separate from the CCA and OCA fonds. QCA correspondence also appears in OCA accession 92-005.

The name 'Kanawa' used by Kirk Wipper for his canoe museum derives from Proto-Arawak meaning 'dugout canoe' — a South American/Caribbean word that entered English as 'canoe' via Taino/Spanish. It is unrelated to 'Kanawana', which is likely Algonquian in origin.
Dr. James Orbinski received the Pip Alumni Award in 2024. He is known for his work with Doctors Without Borders (MSF).
Dr. Marina Sharpe received the Pip Alumni Award in 2018. She is a refugee law expert.
Camp Kanawana's official Flickr photostream contains 4,416 photos, primarily documenting modern camp life.
The relevant NTS (National Topographic System) map sheet for Camp Kanawana is 021L13 (Saint-Raymond). Historical editions from 1948 onward are available through Borealis Data and NRCan Toporama.
A CCA photograph from a 1972 Board of Directors meeting at Montreal City Hall is held in the CCA fonds at Trent University Archives.
As of 2026, Camp Kanawana serves ages 7-17 with programs including Pioneers (6-day and 12-day sessions), canoe-tripping, and leadership programs
Kanawana leadership programs require successful completion of Secondary 4/Grade 10 and focus on becoming camp counsellor, canoe trip guide, or program coordinator
As of fall 2025, YMCAs of Quebec no longer offer day camps (including holiday and spring break camps), but Kanawana summer overnight camp continues operating
Camp Kanawana welcomes international campers from the US, UK, Spain, Mexico, Australia, and Zimbabwe, with airport transportation service available from Pierre-Elliot-Trudeau airport
2026 Kanawana Pioneer session dates: June 22-July 3, July 6-17, July 21-31, August 3-14 (12-day sessions)
Kanawana activities (2026) include theatre, music, arts and crafts, nature exploration, dance, survival techniques, woodworking, canoe, archery, general swim, and open program areas
Kanawana changeover weekends include visits to Sommet Saint-Sauveur water park, meals, supervision, laundry service, and opportunity to call home

The 1998 Farrell, Johnston & Twynam paper in Journal of Sport Management (vol.12, no.4, pp.288-300) surveyed 300 volunteers at the Scott Tournament of Hearts (Canadian Women's Curling Championship) in Thunder Bay, March 1996. The SEVMS yielded four factors: purposive, solidary, external traditions, and commitments.

At Lakehead University, Farrell was in the School of Kinesiology, Johnston in the Department of Geography, and Twynam in the School of Outdoor Recreation, Parks & Tourism — confirming three distinct departmental affiliations for the co-authors.
Johnston, Twynam & Farrell (1999) studied motivation and satisfaction of volunteers at the Canadian Jamboree held by Scouts Canada in Thunder Bay in July 1997. Published in Leisure/Loisir 24(1-2).

Mason, Johnston & Twynam (2000) published 'The World Wide Fund for Nature Arctic Tourism Project' in Journal of Sustainable Tourism 8(4): 305-323, and as Chapter 5 in Bramwell & Lane (eds) Tourism Collaboration and Partnerships, Channel View Publications, pp.98-116. Co-author Peter Mason.

The WWF Arctic Tourism Guidelines initiative began in 1995. Workshops held in Longyearbyen, Svalbard in January 1996 and 1997 with 43 invited participants including tour operators, polar scientists, tourism academics, government representatives, and NGO members. Resulted in Ten Principles for Arctic Tourism.

Twynam received the BC Transfer & Articulation Community Leadership Award on November 14, 2014, at a ceremony in Richmond, BC. He was nominated unanimously by his peers on the BC Tourism Management Articulation Committee.

The Heart of Gold Project was initiated in 2004 as a 'mutual learning and research alliance' between Vancouver Island University (formerly Malaspina University College) and the rural Los Santos Region of Costa Rica. Partners included FAALS (Farm & Agro-Tourism Association of Los Santos), Earth University, Cartago University College, Rainforest Alliance of Costa Rica, and Nubotropica Foundation. Project name inspired by a Neil Young song.
Bob Payne, PhD (Lakehead University, Ontario) was also involved in the Heart of Gold Project, connecting Twynam's earlier Lakehead network to his VIU work.

As Dean at TRU, Twynam developed a research partnership with Sun Peaks Resort Corporation, producing five student research studies: Terrain Park, The Beginner Experience, Employee Satisfaction, Resort Shopping, and Research Proposal (reported in InsideTRU, Summer 2006).

Rob Ferguson, Chair for VIU's Department of Recreation and Tourism Management, stated: 'Dr. Twynam's wealth of experience as an educator, administrator and practitioner has been invaluable to the work of the Tourism Management Articulation Committee.'

Twynam's ResearchGate profile lists his affiliation as University of British Columbia (and other places). This may indicate a UBC connection (possibly PhD), but the specific degree-granting institution for his doctorate has not been confirmed in any source.
VIU developed a Graduate Certificate in Business program; Dave Twynam as Dean of the Faculty of Management had a role in its development.
Sungchul Choi succeeded Dave Twynam as Dean of the Faculty of Management at Vancouver Island University.
Terry Mosher's full name is Christopher Terry Mosher, OC. His pen name 'Aislin' is a rendition of his eldest daughter Aislinn's name (without the second 'n').

Terry Mosher attended fourteen different schools in Montreal, Toronto, and Quebec City. He studied art at Toronto's Central Technical School and the Ontario College of Art, then dropped out to hitchhike across North America for two years. He graduated from the École des Beaux-arts (now part of UQAM) in 1967.

Terry Mosher's first published cartoon was a drawing of Charles de Gaulle in Saturday Night magazine (September 1967). His first newspaper cartoon appeared in the Montreal Star on December 10, 1967. He was appointed official cartoonist of the Montreal Star in 1969.
Terry Mosher has produced more than 14,000 editorial cartoons and approximately 52 books. He co-authored 'The Hecklers: A History of Canadian Political Cartooning' (1978) with Peter Desbarats.

Terry Mosher won the National Newspaper Award in 1977 (cartoon of René Lévesque) and 1978 (cartoon of the new Pope). He was the youngest person inducted into the Canadian News Hall of Fame in 1985 (age 43).
In 1993, MP Robert Layton denounced an Aislin cartoon in the House of Commons, making Terry Mosher the first political cartoonist censured in the House of Commons.
The McCord Museum mounted 'Aislin: 50 Years of Cartoons' exhibition in 2017 and holds 6,000 of Terry Mosher's original cartoons in its permanent collection.
Terry Mosher received the Michener-Baxter Award in 2024, 'for his commitment to informing Canadians and lifting their spirits through humour that is cutting, but never cruel.'
Terry Mosher received the Pip Alumni Award on August 3, 2015, in Saint-Sauveur, Quebec, as the eighth recipient of the award.
Canada Post issued a commemorative stamp honouring Terry Mosher (Aislin) on October 8, 2021, as the third in a five-stamp set honouring Canadian editorial cartoonists.

G. David Twynam's career trajectory: YMCA Camp Kanawana director (~1979) → Lakehead University faculty, School of Outdoor Recreation, Parks & Tourism (by late 1990s) → Dean, School of Tourism, University College of the Cariboo / Thompson Rivers University (~1999-2009) → Dean, Faculty of Management, Vancouver Island University (post-2009) → Retired. He developed a research partnership with Sun Peaks Resort at TRU and received the BCCAT Community Leadership Award on November 14, 2014.
Sean Day held the title 'directeur des programmes et du camp Y Kanawana' (Director of Programs and Camp Y Kanawana) in a 2009 Mediaterre press release about Kanawana's revitalization.
Sean Day served as spokesperson for the Quebec Camping Association (Association des camps du Québec / ACQ) during the COVID pandemic, as referenced in 2021 CBC coverage.

Sean Day is now Director of Fund Development at Tyndale St-Georges Community Centre in Little Burgundy, Montreal, as confirmed via LinkedIn. Earlier reports of a Rossy Foundation role appear to be incorrect or reflect a brief interim position.
Sean Day attended Concordia University, per LinkedIn. Specific degree and graduation year not publicly documented.
In 2016, YMCA Quebec provided over $150,000 in financial support for children to attend Camp Kanawana, with a goal of at least one in five campers coming from financially disadvantaged backgrounds.
The Conserver Society of Hamilton & District was incorporated in 1984 (from the earlier CHOP group). Ed Smee served as Founding Chair and initiated its Environmental Trust Fund in 1986.

The Environmentalist of the Year award won by Ed Smee in 1983 is formally named the Dr. Victor Cecilioni Award, given annually since 1979, co-sponsored by the Conserver Society, Hamilton Naturalists' Club, Hamilton Conservation Authority, Environment Hamilton, and the Bay Area Restoration Council.
Ed Smee's memorial gathering was held February 16, 2002, at the Workers Arts and Heritage Centre, 51 Stuart Street, Hamilton.
The Centennial Voyageur Canoe Pageant holds the Guinness World Record (as of 2012) for the longest canoe race in history: 3,283 miles (5,283 km) with 60 miles of portaging across 70 portages.

Gene Rheaume of Flin Flon conceived the Voyageur Canoe Pageant idea in 1963 as a two-man canoe race. Norm Tyson drafted the formal proposal to the Centennial Commission in 1964. Arnie Charbonneau transformed it into a voyageur pageant with larger canoes.

The 10 race canoes for the Voyageur Pageant were built by Moïse Cadorette of St-Jean-de-Piles, Quebec, in fiberglass (~400 lbs each), replacing fragile wood-and-canvas prototypes from Chestnut Canoe Company.

Each Voyageur Pageant canoe was named after an explorer: NWT (Mackenzie), Yukon (Campbell), BC (Fraser), Alberta (Thompson), Saskatchewan (Kelsey), Manitoba (Radisson), Ontario (McGillivray), Quebec (La Vérendrye), NB (Champlain), NS (Cabot).

Team Manitoba captain Norm Crerar and Gib McEachern (both 27) had won the Flin Flon Trout Festival Canoe Derby three times as amateurs and six times as professionals. Nearly the entire team was from Flin Flon.

Bruce Hodgins (1931-2019), Trent University professor and leader of Camp Wanapitei, was an 'extremely active member of the committee that organized the CCA Centenary Journey' in 1967. Hodgins later received the Dorothy Walter Award of Excellence (OCA) and the Jack Pearse Award of Honour (CCA, 2013).

The CCA Centenary Journey was a relay-style educational canoe expedition: campers in every province paddled a section of a cross-Canada route. Planning began April 23, 1964. A book, 'A Log of Canada's Centenary Journey,' was published in 1971.

Several Voyageur Pageant canoes survive: Radisson (Fort Dauphin Museum), Thompson (Rocky Mountain House), Kelsey (Western Development Museum Saskatoon), Champlain (Woodsmen's Museum Boiestown), McGillivray (private, Thunder Bay), Campbell/Mackenzie (BC middle school). Three have been lost.

Misao Dean's 'The Centennial Voyageur Canoe Pageant as Historical Re-enactment' appeared in Journal of Canadian Studies 40:3 (Fall 2006), pp. 43-67, and was later incorporated into her book 'Inheriting a Canoe Paddle' (U of T Press, 2013).

James Orbinski (born 1960, England) received the 2024 Pip Award. Camper and counsellor at Kanawana in 1980s-1990s. Grew up in NDG, Montreal. Dawson CEGEP, BA Psychology Trent (1984), MD McMaster (1990), MA IR U of T (1998). President of MSF International Council 1998; accepted 1999 Nobel Peace Prize on behalf of MSF. Officer of Order of Canada (2009). Currently Principal of Massey College, U of T.

Marina Sharpe received the 2018 Pip Award. Former camper and staff at Kanawana. BA Economics and LLB/BCL (McGill), MSc International Development (LSE), DPhil Law (Oxford, Trudeau Scholar 2011). Currently Associate Professor of International Law at RMC Saint-Jean. Author of 'The Regional Law of Refugee Protection in Africa' (OUP, 2018). Director of Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation.

Chris Adam received the 2017 Pip Award. Former Camp YMCA Kanawana staff member. Director of Sustainability Office and Living Campus at Dawson College, Montreal. Environmental educator who has lectured in multiple countries on sustainability.

Carol Sharman Skinner received the 2016 Pip Award. Counsellor and section director at Camp YMCA Kanawana 1990-1995. Later Director of YMCA Camp Hayward (Cape Cod), school counsellor, and Art Therapist for Canadian Mental Health Association in Ottawa. Diagnosed with ALS in 2013; became ALS Canada advocate. Master's degree in Art Therapy.

Philip 'Pip' Caddell (1913-2004) attended Camp Kanawana as a camper in 1928. He was an officer in the Canadian Army in WWII, a Montreal executive, and a community volunteer. His grandson James Lawrence Caddell (1973-2005) was a camper and counsellor at Kanawana 1983-1991, served in Bosnia (1995), and died of pulmonary edema in Tupiza, Bolivia, on Oct 16 2005 at age 32.

Andrew Caddell (son of Philip, father of James) established the Pip Alumni Award in 2007. He retired from Global Affairs Canada in 2017, is a weekly columnist for the Hill Times, a town councillor in Kamouraska QC, and lectures at McGill's Max Bell School of Public Policy.
The James Caddell Memorial Scholarship for Orphans was established after James Caddell's death, funding education for orphaned and impoverished children in South India.

Stuart McLean's full name was Andrew Stuart McLean, OC. Born April 19, 1948, Montreal West, Quebec. Died February 15, 2017, Toronto, of melanoma, age 68. Parents: Andrew Thompson McLean and Patricia/Margaret (née Godkin), Australian immigrants. Brother Alistair, sister Stephanie. Grew up on Brock Avenue, Montreal West.

Stuart McLean attended Elizabeth Ballantyne School (elementary), Lower Canada College (high school), and Sir George Williams University (BA Applied Social Science, graduated 1971). He received an honorary Doctor of Laws from Concordia University in 2014.

Stuart McLean visited a friend working at Kanawana in summer 1969 and was hired on the spot as a counsellor in the senior boys' section. He worked five summers total, rising to assistant director. A former colleague confirmed McLean was assistant camp director summers of 1974 and 1975.

Stuart McLean on Kanawana: 'When I got to camp, I found a place where I was accepted by others and I was able to contribute to the greater good. It worked its magic on me. Camp is where I found my confidence.' Also: 'It was the first place, as a young person, that I felt I could contribute to the greater good.'

The Vinyl Cafe debuted in 1994 as a summer replacement on CBC Radio; became a weekly staple by 1997. McLean won three Stephen Leacock Medals: Home from the Vinyl Cafe (1999), Vinyl Cafe Unplugged (2001), Secrets from the Vinyl Cafe (2007). Officer of the Order of Canada (2011).
McLean turned down a chance to study journalism at Carleton University one summer in order to return to Kanawana as assistant director.

The YMCA of Montreal was founded November 25, 1851, the first YMCA in North America, predating Boston (December 29, 1851) by about one month. The founding meeting was held at St. Helen Street Baptist Church in Old Montreal.

The YMCA Montreal built purpose-built buildings at: Victoria Square (1873), Dominion Square (1891, reportedly tallest building in the British Empire), and Drummond Street (1912, $540,206 cost). A 500-room residential annex was added to Drummond Street in 1931 during the Great Depression.

Sir George Williams College was organized in 1926 as the education arm of the YMCA of Montreal, named after YMCA founder George Williams. It received a university charter in 1948, becoming Sir George Williams University. On August 24, 1974, SGWU merged with Loyola College to form Concordia University.

The YMCA Montreal was renamed 'Le Y du Québec' around 2009. It now operates as Les YMCA du Québec / The YMCAs of Quebec (ymcaquebec.org). As of 2025 it has 9 centres, 36 service points, serves 120,000+ people, and operates Camp YMCA Kanawana as its sole remaining camp.

The YMCAs of Quebec underwent a major strategic restructuring in November 2019, closing Guy-Favreau and Hochelaga-Maisonneuve centres, shifting toward community programs and away from large fitness facilities. Day camps were discontinued fall 2025; Kanawana summer camp continues.
Pascale Audette was appointed President & CEO of the YMCAs of Quebec in November 2024, the first woman in this role.

J.H. Winn was elected first president of the Montreal YMCA shortly after its 1851 founding. T. James Claxton's father was directly involved in the founding; Claxton chronicled the history in a 1944 letter to G.W. Birks.

The motto 'Non Nobis Solum' is derived from Cicero's De Officiis 1:22 (44 BC), which itself is a Latin translation of a sentiment from Plato's Epistle to Archytas. The full passage reads: 'non nobis solum nati sumus ortusque nostri partem patria vindicat, partem amici' ('Not for us alone are we born; our country, our friends, have a share in us'). Cicero associates the concept with the Stoic ideal of cosmopolitanism.

Camp Kanawana uses the abbreviated form 'Non Nobis Solum' rather than the full Cicero quotation 'Non Nobis Solum Nati Sumus.' The camp presents the motto trilingually: 'Non Nobis Solum — Not for ourselves alone — Pas seulement pour nous-memes.'

The motto 'Each for all and all for each' (Kanawana's earlier English motto, documented 1922 and 1927) is also the current motto of YMCA Hayo-Went-Ha Camps in Michigan, founded 1904. This suggests the English motto may have been a common YMCA camp motto rather than unique to Kanawana.

Lower Canada College founder Charles Sanderson Fosbery (headmaster 1909-1935) adopted 'Non Nobis Solum' from the Fosbery family crest when he founded the school. The Fosbery family crest motto predates LCC. Fosbery was a Trinity College Dublin graduate in classics.

The Pip Alumni Award is named for Philip 'Pip' Caddell (1913-2004), who was a Kanawana camper in 1928, and his grandson James Caddell (1973-2005), a camper and counsellor from 1983 to 1991 who became a UN Peacekeeper and died of altitude sickness in Bolivia. The award was established in 2007.

The 'Non Nobis Solum' motto is NOT a YMCA-wide motto. It is specific to Camp Kanawana within the YMCA. No other YMCA camp was found using this Latin motto. The Wikipedia list of organizations using it includes schools (Massanutten Academy, Walnut Hill School, Pennthorpe School, LCC, University College Durham, Willamette University, Washburn University, Swarthmore College class of 1918), military units (US Army 1st Maintenance Company), and heraldic families (Baron Haden-Guest).
Xavier Maclaren attended Camp Kanawana for six summers before becoming a camp counsellor and canoe tripper.
In 1910, 85 campers registered for the summer session when the YMCA acquired the Saint-Sauveur site.
Camp Kanawana describes itself as an English camp that is accessible to kids who speak many other languages including French, and accommodates campers with different needs and diverse abilities.
Camp Kanawana enforces a no-cellphones and no-Wi-Fi policy, describing itself as an 'unplugged camp.'

Current camp activities (as of 2026) include survival techniques, canoeing, rock climbing, archery, axe throwing, arts and crafts, music, and dance. Activities also include campfires and call-and-response songs in the forest.
Camp Kanawana offers regular, leadership, and expedition programs for kids aged 7 to 17, lasting between 12 and 48 days.
Financial assistance is available for Camp Kanawana through the YMCA's financial assistance program.
Camp Kanawana's address is 673 Saint-Elmire St. in Saint-Sauveur-des-Monts.
Camp Kanawana's contact email is camp.kanawana@ymcaquebec.org and website is campkanawana.org.
The article describes the 1894 founding as motivated by the idea 'to take city youth away from everyday life and teach them about group dynamics, team-building and leadership.'

The Postmedia article (2026) is sponsored content created by Content Works, Postmedia's commercial content division, on behalf of the YMCAs of Québec. It frames Kanawana's programming around addressing 'nature-deficit disorder' (term coined by Richard Louv in 2005).

R. L. Charlton authored "Notes re Early Days of YMCA Camps at Lake St. Joseph and Kanawana" in 1943, held in Concordia Archives P0145/12A.
W. E. Cushing authored "Historical sketches-Lake St. Joseph" in 1943, held in Concordia Archives P0145/12A.
Concordia Archives P0145/12B01 holds Kamp Kanawana Committee meeting records from 1968-1969.
A "Committee report to Metropolitan Board of Directors" regarding Camp Kanawana was produced in 1967, held in P0145/12B01.

A "Report of the Boys and Girls Camping Committee to the Metropolitan Planning and Development Committee of the YMCA of Montreal" was produced in 1967, held in P0145/12A. The committee name confirms both boys and girls camps existed by 1967.
Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds a "Metropolitan Camping Commission" file from 1954-1955.
Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds a "Boys Camping Committee" file from 1956-1958.
Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds a "Special Intercommittee Task Force on Camping" file from 1981-1982.

Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds an "Outdoor Education Branch fall conference" record from 1971.
R. L. Charlton is a previously undocumented individual associated with the YMCA Montreal camping program, authoring historical notes in 1943.
Concordia Archives P0145/12B01 holds a document titled "YMCA Kamp Kanawana Facts-timeline 1894-1998" dated approximately 1998.
Concordia Archives P0145/12B01 holds 4 microfiches titled "Junior Camp Opening Roster" covering 1910-1917 (note: actual date range may be 1916-1923 per finding aid correction).

R. L. Charlton was a Montreal-based independent marine surveyor who maintained his own office. He was elected Treasurer of the Canadian Board of Marine Underwriters (CBMU) at its founding on March 12, 1917.
R. L. Charlton was described as "an ardent YMCA worker" and went to France with the YMCA to render service to Canadian troops during World War I, shortly after the CBMU formation in 1917.

Carol Skinner, Kanawana Pip Alumni Award recipient, described the motto Non Nobis Solum saying: "Never has Non Nobis Solum (Not For Ourselves Alone) meant so much to me. Kamp Kanawana staff and campers have never failed to stand by me."

Stuart McLean attended Lower Canada College for high school, said "LCC was a place where I didn't really fit in," and credited Camp Kanawana with his development: "I began pulling my adult self together at Camp Kanawana, and I benefited greatly from my camp experiences."

The Kanawana "Pip" Alumni Award is a memorial to Philip "Pip" Caddell (1913-2004), a WWII officer, Montreal executive and community volunteer who was a Kanawana camper in 1928, and his grandson James Caddell (1973-2005), a UN Peacekeeper, NGO worker and public servant who was a camper and counsellor in the 1980s and 1990s.
The Pip Award was established in 2007 to recognize the contributions of distinguished Kanawana alumni. The Pip Award Committee is composed of Kanawana alumni. Andrew Caddell is the sponsor.

Richard "Itche" Kerr received the Pip Award for volunteer work with the physically challenged. He is confirmed as the same Richard Kerr who composed "On My Way to Kanawana" (CD P145/SR0001, duration 4 min 30 sec).
Richard Patten, former Ontario cabinet minister, is a Kanawana alumnus and Pip Award recipient.
Bruce Netherwood, YMCA leader and author, is a Kanawana alumnus and Pip Award recipient.
John Cleghorn, former CEO of the Royal Bank of Canada, is a Kanawana alumnus and Pip Award recipient.
Sam Lazarus (deceased), NGO volunteer, and the Lazarus family are Kanawana alumni and Pip Award recipients.
Jeniene Philips Birks, former broadcaster and community volunteer, is a Kanawana alumna and Pip Award recipient.
Carol Sharman Skinner was the 9th Pip Award recipient (2016), recognized as ALS advocate and former Kanawana staff member.
Chris Adam, environmentalist and teacher, received the Pip Award in 2017. Former Kanawana staff member.
Dr. Marina Sharpe, refugee and displacement expert, received the Pip Award in 2018. Former camper and Kanawana staff member.
Dr. James Orbinski, physician and humanitarian, received the Pip Award in 2024.

Camp Kanawana has winterized facilities (Farmhouse and Blockhouse in Front Camp) with fully equipped kitchens, living space, bathrooms, showers and electricity. The site is available for rent year-round (6-250 persons).
Camp Kanawana runs fall camp programs and spring camp programs in addition to summer camp. Staff roles include "Fall Camp Facilitator" and "Spring Camp Facilitator."
Philip "Pip" Caddell was a Kanawana camper in 1928, establishing him as one of the earliest named campers in the record.

Richard Patten (died December 30, 2021, age 79) was a Liberal Ontario MPP for Ottawa Centre (1987-1990, 1995-2007), served as Minister of Government Services and Minister of Correctional Services. He was educated at Sir George Williams University (now Concordia) in Montreal and worked in YMCA summer day camps in Montreal and different Y branches. Pip Award recipient.

Dr. James Orbinski is a Canadian physician and humanitarian who accepted the 1999 Nobel Peace Prize on behalf of Médecins Sans Frontières. He co-founded the Canadian chapter of MSF. He received the 2024 Kanawana Pip Award.
James Caddell (grandson of Pip Caddell) was a McGill graduate in addition to being a UN Peacekeeper, NGO worker, and federal public servant.

Bruce Netherwood has spent more than 30 years in YMCA Camping. He is VP Camping & Social Responsibility at South Shore YMCA (Hanover, Massachusetts), overseeing Camp Burgess & Hayward and day camps at Hale, Emilson, and Science Center branches. He was previously Executive Director at Camp Burgess & Hayward.

An envelope addressed to Bruce Netherwood containing T-shirt design and separation, along with offset colour separation films, is part of the YMCA of Montreal fonds (P0145) at Concordia Archives, confirming his role in Kanawana operations.

Stuart McLean described LCC as a place where he did not fit in: "LCC was a place where I didn't really fit in." He credited Camp Kanawana: "I began pulling my adult self together at Camp Kanawana, and I benefited greatly from my camp experiences." (The Montrealer, 2008)

The word "kanawa" is a widespread Wanderwort in South American and Caribbean languages (Karina kanawa, Trio kanawa, Wayana kanawa, Taino *kanowa) meaning "dugout canoe." This root is widely believed to be the origin of the English word "canoe." Whether the name "Kanawana" derives from this root or from an Algonquian source is unconfirmed.
Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds a "Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA" from 1974, and "Camping and Outdoor Education planning" for 1974-1975.

Camp Kanawana runs school group programs focused on conservation and nature. EMSB students have participated in overnight experiences learning about modern conservation, nature, and team building, then planning community-based conservation action projects.

The YMCA Camp Kanawana site sits on unceded traditional territory. The Laurentians were historically occupied by the Weskarini Algonquin First Nation. Nearby Mohawk communities include Kanesatake and Kahnawake.

Richard Patten (1942-2021) served as Director of International Programs at the Metropolitan YMCA in Montreal from 1971 to 1976, and as Executive Director of YMCA Montreal from 1976 to 1979. As Executive Director during 1976-79, Patten would have been the senior YMCA official overseeing Camp Kanawana during Dave Twynam's directorship (~1979).

Richard Patten worked in summer day camps for the Montreal YMCA as a young person while attending Sir George Williams University in Montreal. He later worked in different branches of the Y. This places him in YMCA Montreal camping programs in the early-to-mid 1960s.

Richard Patten's family rented a cottage at YMCA Geneva Park on Lake Couchiching every summer, indicating lifelong YMCA affiliation. He served as President of the Canadian Council for International Cooperation.

Ben T. Hannah wrote a 'Kanawana Reminiscence (of 1948)' in 1989, held in Concordia Archives (P0145/12B01). The title suggests Hannah was at camp in 1948, potentially as a director, staff member, or senior camper.

John Cleghorn (b. July 7, 1941), former Chairman and CEO of Royal Bank of Canada (1994-2001) and Chancellor of Wilfrid Laurier University (1996-2003), is a Camp Kanawana alumnus. He received the Pip Award in 2012. Born in Montreal, attended Westmount High School and earned B.Com from McGill (1962).

An anonymous commenter on the Westmount Magazine tribute to Stuart McLean (March 2017) wrote: 'He and I worked together at Kanawana; I was the camp director and Stuart was the assistant camp director (summers of 1974 and 1975).' The same person also sublet McLean's flat on Dorchester and looked after his piano. The commenter's identity is unknown.

Concordia Archives P0145/12B01 holds a 'Camping and Outdoor Education Branch Director's Report' from 1972 (5 copies). This report likely names the camping branch director for that year, which could help fill the 1963-1973 gap in the Kanawana directors record.

Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds 'Camping and Outdoor Education Branch of Management minutes' from 1975-1978, and a 'Camping and Outdoor Education Branch budget' from 1979. These records may identify the Branch Director and Kanawana camp director for the mid-to-late 1970s.

Charles "Smillie" Buckland was the first recipient of the Green Triangle award, described as "the coveted Green Triangle awarded to a camper who accomplished a series of feats." He also held the lake swim record.

The Green Triangle award at Camp Kanawana was given to campers who accomplished a series of feats. Charles Buckland was its first recipient circa 1944-1948. The Green Triangle was also the name of the camp newsletter (known issue: July 29, 1938, digitized on Internet Archive).

In 1944, campers traveled to Camp Kanawana by train from Montreal Central Station to Saint-Sauveur, then by bus up a gravel road to the camp. This is a later travel route than the 1922 route via Place Viger Station to Piedmont.

Leigh Evans attended Camp Kanawana for 6 summers: 1 as camper, 1 as Leader-in-Training, and 4 as staff member. She was announced Capitaine for the Voyageur team of the L&V games in 2012. Capitaine is described as "one of the highest honours a staff member can receive."
The L&V (Lumberman and Voyageur) games are described by alumna Leigh Evans as "a 3-day event in which every person, campers and staff alike, unite with their team." Teams are Lumberman and Voyageur.
Camp Kanawana is described with the saying: "If you have never been, you can not understand it and if you have been, you can not explain it." (Leigh Evans blog)

In fall 2025, the YMCAs of Quebec discontinued all day camp programs including Kanawana Adventure (launched 2024) and all holiday/spring break camps. The overnight residential summer camp at Kanawana continues to operate. The decision was described as part of a "simplification process" to "ensure the viability of the organization in the long-term."

Camp Jubilee/Otoreke was located in Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, not in Saint-Sauveur. It was situated on several islands in the middle of a lake with a landing area on the shore. It was renamed from Camp Jubilee to Camp Otoreke in 1909. It closed in 1982 after nearly a century of continuous operation.

The Concordia Archives P0145/12A holds a "Journal of the first Montreal YMCA venture to explore the country round about St. Agathe with the view of securing a lake on which to establish a Summer Camp and journal of Summer Camp 1895" — the earliest documented YMCA camping journal.
The Voyageurs Ultimate program at Camp Kanawana runs from approximately July 20 to August 14 (26 days), for participants aged 15-17.

Kate Taylor is Camp Director of YMCA Camp Kanawana. She appeared on the Go Camp Pro "Beyond Camp" podcast discussing social media advocacy and exploring privilege. She was part of the camp leadership team during COVID-19 alongside Sean Day and Kevin Slezak.

Camp Kanawana was closed for two consecutive summers (2020 and 2021) due to COVID-19. The YMCA statement read: "It is with a heavy heart that we must announce that once again all our Camp YMCA Kanawana programs are cancelled for the summer." The camp normally has about 900 campers per year. YMCA operated day camps in several neighbourhoods as an alternative.

On January 27 (year unspecified, likely 2022), the Camp Kanawana team of Sean Day, Kate Taylor, and Kevin Slezak held a Zoom town hall meeting with families to update them on camp plans. This confirms the leadership structure: Sean Day (Regional Director of Camps), Kate Taylor (Camp Director), Kevin Slezak (role unspecified, possibly Assistant Director).

The Ross & Macdonald fonds at the Canadian Centre for Architecture (CCA) holds architectural drawings for the "Doctor's Cottage for Kamp Kanawana." The fonds dates 1902-1982 (predominantly 1909-1959) and contains 27,893 drawings across approximately 600 documented projects.

YMCA Kanawana offers a winter experience package (January 6 to March 7) that includes snowshoeing adventure adapted to group skill level, outdoor games, a snack on the campfire, and a raclette and fondue dinner in a warm shelter. Available for families, corporate groups, and other groups. Includes all food and snacks with custom menu.

The Rose des Vents Pavilion at Camp Kanawana is available from October 15 to May 20 in 'refuge mode' (without running water), by reservation only. Maximum capacity 16 people. Includes 3 bedrooms, equipped kitchen with cookware and dishes, wood stove, and common area.

Camp Kanawana has five distinct seasonal rental windows: (1) May 21-June 23: full camp package; (2) June 23-August 20: summer camp in session, limited rental 6-26 persons only; (3) August 20-October 14: full camp package; (4) October 15-May 20: Rose des Vents Pavilion in refuge mode; (5) January 6-March 7: winter experience package with snowshoeing and fondue.

YMCA Quebec runs the C-Vert environmental leadership program for ages 14-16, where youth become eco-citizens through bike trips, weekend camping, environmental workshops, and a remunerated July internship creating a community environmental project. Goals include 'reconnecting urban youth with nature to protect them from nature deficit disorder.' Funded by Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions and Secretariat a la jeunesse du Quebec.

Camp Kanawana aspires to be 'Quebec's environmental education leader,' marrying 'its tradition of YMCA value-based camping with leading-edge programming' according to a Program Specialists job posting by Les YMCA Quebec.

Chris Adam, Coordinator of Sustainability Office at Dawson College (Pip Award 2017), has had a 35-year career including 25 years at Dawson in Community Recreation (CRLT department). He is also Executive Director of Earthvalues Institute, a non-profit using 'Nature as Mentor' philosophy. Under his leadership Dawson achieved AASHE Platinum rating (global first for associate-level institution) and International Green Gown Awards Sustainability Institution of the Year.

A 'Familles en nature: 4 saisons de plaisir' program held an activity at Camp Kanawana in Spring 2013, featuring a forest hike exploring spring flora and fauna followed by canoeing and a campfire dinner.
Camp Kanawana is listed on Bonjour Quebec (Quebec tourism portal) as a 'holiday centre' with operating season May 15 to October 15, 2026.

Sam Lazarus's mother Janet Torge is a Montreal broadcaster and writer. His brother Riel Lazarus is an archivist and researcher for film and TV. They established the Sam Lazarus Fund to send children who couldn't otherwise afford camp to Kanawana.

Camp Kanawana corporate retreat packages for groups of 3+ days include: meeting room for up to 16 people, custom food services, Wi-Fi, projector, flip chart, and projection screen, with lodging in Rose des Vents Pavilion and cabins. Price: $643.75 per person per night.

Camp Kanawana's official Flickr account (flickr.com/photos/kanawana/) contains 4,416 photos. Account joined 2010, has 12 followers. Confirmed as official YMCA camp presence via toutMontreal.com listing.

Lac Kanawana participates in Quebec's Reseau de surveillance volontaire des lacs (RSVL) voluntary lake monitoring network. Monitoring includes Secchi disk transparency every two weeks (June-October) and water samples for phosphorus, dissolved organic carbon, and chlorophyll a analyzed by CEAEQ. Water quality data available from at least 2013.
Meal services at Camp Kanawana are only offered for groups of 75 people or more. Reservation for 3 meals per day is required, and food services are invoiced per person.

Jeniene Phillips Birks (also credited as Jeniene Phillips) was a CBC Montreal television journalist who served as fill-in anchor on CBC Montreal's evening newscast (circa 2009, alongside Andrew Chang, Kim Brunhuber, and Nancy Wood filling in for Michel Godbout). She also has IMDB credits as producer/actress on The Art of War (2000) and The Apprentice: Martha Stewart (2005).

Janet Torge, mother of Sam Lazarus, is a Montreal broadcaster, radio talk-show host, traffic reporter, Montreal Gazette columnist, and author of 'Dear Sam.' She is also co-founder of the first Rape Relief Centre in Canada (1973) and founder of Radical Resthomes.

John Cleghorn chaired the Montreal YMCA and was named Officer of YMCA Canada's Fellowship of Honour. He was drafted by the Toronto Argonauts but declined, having played defensive lineman on McGill Redmen's national championship football team. He served as Chancellor of Wilfrid Laurier University (1996-2003) and is a Companion of the Canadian Business Hall of Fame.

Richard Patten had an extensive YMCA career before entering politics: Director of International Programs, Montreal YMCA (1971-76); Executive Director of the YMCA in Montreal (1976-79); Director of International Programs, Canadian National Council of YMCAs, Ottawa (1979-87). He worked with Palestinian youth in refugee camps (Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Gaza) under UNRWA/World Alliance of YMCAs, trained YMCA staff in Guyana (1969-71), and coordinated support for Ugandan Asian refugees expelled by Idi Amin.

Carol Skinner's full name was Carol Sharman Skinner. She was diagnosed with ALS in 2013. She worked as Director of YMCA Camp Hayward in Cape Cod, Massachusetts; earned a Master's in Art Therapy; served as school counsellor for five years; and worked as Art Therapist for the Canadian Mental Health Association in Ottawa.

Chris Adam founded the Sustainable Happiness Certificate at Dawson College. Under his leadership, Dawson College declared itself carbon neutral and won Sustainability Institution of the Year at the International Green Gown Awards (out of 56 finalists from 19 countries).

James Orbinski attended John XXIII High School in Montreal before Dawson CEGEP. He received the Meritorious Service Cross (1997) for his work during the Rwandan genocide. He received the Concordia University Loyola Medal in 2017.

Marina Sharpe previously served as Senior Legal Officer with UNHCR in Addis Ababa, Postdoctoral Fellow at McGill Law, and lawyer at Cravath, Swaine & Moore LLP in New York. She holds a SSHRC Banting Fellowship and is called to the bars of New York and England & Wales.

The 1983 CCA Award of Excellence recipients were: Derek Walsh (ACQ), Rick Ryan (ACQ), Wayne Perkins (ACA — Alberta Camping Association), and Abe Goss (provincial association not confirmed). Two ACQ representatives were honored in the same year.

Janet Torge is a Montreal-based writer and television documentary producer. Her career spans: radio talk-show host, traffic reporter, Montreal Gazette columnist, prenatal teacher and doula, construction site manager, software manual creator, and co-founder of the first Rape Relief Centre in Canada (1973).

Janet Torge is the founder of Radical Resthomes, a co-living housing model for seniors conceived approximately 30 years ago. Inspired by the Baba Yagas feminist community in Paris (heard about in 2011), Radical Resthomes promotes self-directed, affordable housing where residents manage their own community and age in place.

Janet Torge's book 'Dear Sam: Grieving the Death of My Son' was published by iUniverse (ISBN: 9780595423835). The book describes her coping with the death of her son Sam Lazarus through writing letters to him and imagining his responses.
Janet Torge also authored 'I Can't Believe I'm Old: Essays on Aging,' published by Linda Leith Publishing (Montreal).
Janet Torge's television documentary producer credits include: 'Harry Gulkin: Red Dawn on Main Street' (2004), 'The Great War' (2007), and 'The Gig Is Up' (2021).

Janet Torge is a member of the CIHR Institute of Aging Older Adult Advisory Council and is listed as a 'Lived Expertise Advisor' for the Aging in the Right Place (AIRP) initiative at Simon Fraser University.
Janet Torge operates 'Torge Ahead Inc,' a freelance company offering television documentary production, prenatal classes, doula services, and a weekly health radio show.

As of 2015, the Five-Hole Sam Street Hockey Jamboree (Sam Jam) had raised over $260,000 and sent over 70 kids to Camp YMCA Kanawana. The event is organized by Sam's brother Riel Lazarus.
