Sam was known as a legendary street hockey goalie who let goals through 'the five-hole' (between the legs), inspiring the event name.

The Sam Lazarus Fund continues to operate via the Fondation des YMCA du Québec. As of 2024, the fund accepts donations through Zeffy. Over 17 years, dozens of families have been offered camperships for children from diverse backgrounds.
Janet Torge is listed in the QWF Literary Database of Quebec English-Language Authors and has contributed to POV Magazine (Canada's premiere documentary magazine).

When Camp Oolahwan ceased physical operations in 2005, it was replaced by 'Summer Space Day Camp,' an urban day camp sharing the same objectives of empowering young women through self-confidence, healthy habits, and leadership, but in a city environment rather than a residential camp setting.

Camp Oolahwan's programming focused on developing healthy minds and bodies, encouraging self-esteem, building lasting relationships, adopting healthy life habits, leadership roles, nature protection, learning new skills, sports, and campfire singing. The YWCA stated that since 1915 it believed young women must acquire self-confidence and the ability to 'laugh and have fun.'
The Camp Oolahwan centennial celebration in 2017 was organized by a committee of former campers and counselors. Camp Oolahwan has a Twitter account (@campoolahwan) created for the centennial.

Lac Kanawana's RSVL lake number is 573. Additional physical characteristics: volume 1,273,000 m³, mean depth 5.4 m, altitude 318.4 m, watershed area 5.17 km², drainage ratio 22.00. Associated watershed organization: ABRINORD. A 2013 results sheet ('Fiche de résultats 2013') was produced by CRE Laurentides.

A. Ross Seaman died in 1987. The A. Ross Seaman Memorial Fund was established in 1987 to honour his life-long dedication to the communities of Concordia University, Dawson College, Kamp Kanawana, and the YMCA. Five organizations — Dawson, Concordia, Kamp Kanawana, YMCA, and Vankleek Hill Collegiate — give a scholarship in his memory annually.

A. Ross Seaman was Director of Kamp Kanawana for 'many years.' His earlier career was in community work and the camping movement with the YMCA. In 1963, he was a part-time faculty member in Applied Social Science and an active collaborator in the Centre of Human Relations and Community Studies at Concordia University (then Sir George Williams). After retiring from Dawson in 1984, he served as acting chair of Concordia University Leisure Studies during the 1986-87 school year.

The A. Ross Seaman memorial scholarship at Dawson College is a $500 award presented in the CRLT program each year to a second-year student who displays leadership, community service, caring and a genuine concern for others.

A. Ross Seaman had a connection to Vankleek Hill Collegiate (a high school in Vankleek Hill, Ontario), which is one of the five organizations that gives a scholarship in his memory. This suggests a biographical connection to eastern Ontario/Prescott-Russell region.
The Concordia University Archives hold photographs of 'R. H. Dawson' (likely Ralph H. Dawson) and R. L. Charlton (undated) in the YMCA of Montreal fonds P0145/12A.
Camp Kanawana staff receive over 80 hours of training. The camp is described as 'a founding member of the Association des camps du Québec (ACQ)' and 'renowned for its high standards of supervision.'

A Camp Kanawana staff member (unnamed) began in the camp industry in 1996, started integrating the summer camp management team in 2002, and served as director of expeditions at Kanawana from 2007 to 2010.

Camp Kanawana's staff career progression ladder includes: Junior Counsellor → Counsellor → Section Director → Canoe Guide → Camping Programs Coordinator → Summer Camp Assistant Director. A program director role (all Kanawana) was filled in 2024.

Camp Weredale was NOT a YMCA camp. It was established in 1934 by the Rotary Club of Westmount, which bought 260 acres with a mile of shoreline on Lac l'Achigan (55 miles north of Montreal) and gave the property to Weredale House (formerly Boys' Home of Montreal). The camp served orphaned and at-risk boys from Weredale House.

Camp Weredale remains operational today, owned and operated by the Weredale Foundation. Located on Lac l'Achigan in the Laurentians, it welcomes 4 cohorts of 85 campers (340 total) from late June to mid-August, serving boys and girls aged 6-17 receiving youth protected social services or facing family challenges. The camp celebrated its 90th anniversary in 2024.

Weredale House (Boys' Home of Montreal) was founded in 1870 by Charles Alexander, a Montreal confectioner from Dundee, Scotland. In the 1920s the Rotary Club of Montreal raised $289,000 to build a new Boys' Home. Library and Archives Canada hold the Weredale House fonds: bylaws/annual reports (1887-1971), minutes (1868-1971), registers (1881-1975), Camp Lewis/Weredale records (1919-1966). Camp Weredale suffered a fire and was reconstructed in 1965.

A commenter on the Westmount Magazine 2017 Stuart McLean tribute identifies themselves as the Camp Kanawana director who worked with McLean as assistant director in the summers of 1974 and 1975. The commenter also sublet McLean's Dorchester apartment and looked after his piano when McLean moved to Toronto. The commenter's name is not extracted from the search snippet.

Stuart McLean's connection to Camp YMCA Kanawana dates back to the summer of 1969. He spent five summers at camp in the late 60s and early 70s, beginning as a counsellor in the senior boys' section and working up to assistant director. He passed up a chance to study journalism at Carleton University to return to camp as assistant director. He also served as a student services coordinator at Dawson College in Westmount.

Lemuel Cushing Jr. (1842-1881), who was YMCA Montreal president 1869-70, published 'The Genealogy of the Cushing Family' in Montreal in 1877. He died at age 39 in Montreal and could NOT have been the 'Lemuel Cushing' who brought boys to Lake Saint-Joseph in 1892. The 1892 Cushing must be a third-generation Lemuel or a nephew. A supplement to the genealogy covering 1905-1969 was compiled by James Stevenson Cushing (born 1878).

The Cushing genealogy (1905 supplement by James Stevenson Cushing, published in Montreal by Perrault Printing Co.) is digitized on Internet Archive but blocked by proxy. A physical or VPN-accessible copy would identify the 1892 'Lemuel Cushing' who brought boys to Lake Saint-Joseph. The rootsweb.com Cushing genealogy index and seekingmyroots.com files may also contain this information.

H.B. Cushing assisted in the founding of the Children's Memorial Hospital (now Montreal Children's Hospital) in 1902-1904, alongside A.D. Blackader and with encouragement from Sir William Osler. This externally confirms that Harold Beveridge Cushing (b. 1873, M.D. McGill 1898) was the same H.B. Cushing described in the 1905 Cushing genealogy as 'Physician to Children's Hospital.' The Children's Memorial Hospital opened January 30, 1904 on Guy Street in Montreal.

Robertson Macaulay Cushing, son of Charles Cushing and Lily Margaret Macaulay Cushing of Montreal, was killed in WWI and is buried at Nine Elms British Cemetery near Ypres, Belgium. He appears on the McGill Honour Roll 1914-1918 and Page 585 of the First World War Book of Remembrance. His wife was Mabel Louise Dawson Cushing of Montreal. This confirms Charles Cushing (Lemuel Sr.'s son, the notary) had children active in Montreal into the WWI era.

Lydia Maria Cushing, one of Lemuel Sr.'s daughters, married into the Beveridge family (married name: Beveridge). This is the likely origin of the middle name 'Beveridge' given to Harold Beveridge Cushing (b. 1873), son of Lemuel Jr. — named after his aunt's married family.

The YMCA chapter of William Fong's J.W. McConnell biography (2008) is titled 'Keep the Home Fires Burning: Fundraising for the YMCA in Peace and for Canada in the Great War, 1909–19', covering McConnell's YMCA fundraising from 1909 through the First World War.

A Lac Wilson in Sainte-Lucie-des-Laurentides (Commission de toponymie du Québec fiche no_seq 135620) is officially recorded as named for the owner of the lands where the lake is located, a person named Wilson — a documented example of the Quebec pattern of Wilson-named lakes referencing local landowners.
Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs, the municipality adjacent to the Kanawana site, has 96 bodies of water, including lakes Marois, Ouimet, Guindon, Johanne, Suzanne, Parent, and des Seigneurs.

A. Ross Seaman died in October 1987. The Concordia Applied Human Sciences funding page describes his death as 'a loss to countless people from many places where he expended his energies and warmth to help others to become the best they could be.'

Search-engine snippets of the Concordia 12B01 finding aid (retrieved 2026-06-11, two independent queries) describe correspondence from 'Camp director Dave Twynam' dated 1976, which if accurate would extend his directorship back to 1976. An earlier extraction of the same finding aid (f_0752) dated such correspondence to 1979. Whether the finding aid lists two separate correspondence files (1976 and 1979) or one of the datings is an error is unresolved.

Canada's fourth polio epidemic wave ran from 1946 through 1953 and became the country's most serious, ultimately involving all provinces and reaching into parts of the Arctic. During polio outbreaks, summer camps, playgrounds, pools, and youth centres were commonly closed.

Thomas Cushing (entry 881, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 15 April 1843, married Margaret Ellen Cameron of Lachute on 7 January 1874, and was President and Manager of the Montreal Brewing Co. as of 1905. Sons: Thomas Hubert (b. 1877) and Gordon Cameron (b. 1880); first son Archibald Ronald Cameron died in infancy.

Charles Cushing (entry 883, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 1 May 1848, graduated McGill B.C.L. 1869, practised as a Notary-Public in Montreal, married Lily M. Macaulay (daughter of Robertson Macaulay) on 28 January 1883, and was elected a Director of Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada in 1904. His seven children included Robertson Macaulay Cushing (b. 22 June 1884).

William Mair Cushing (entry 884, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 25 October 1853; Captain of the 6th Fusiliers, Montreal (1878) and later Captain of the 11th Argenteuil Rangers; removed to Elkhorn, Manitoba in 1884, serving as Councillor and Reeve for 8 years.

George Cushing (entry 885, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 2 April 1857; travelled the Western States, worked mines at La Trinidad, Otaez, Mexico, and as of 1905 resided in Mexico City as managing director of the Canada Mexico Trading Co.

James Brock Cushing (entry 878, 1905 genealogy) was born in Chatham, Que., 2 October 1839 and died at his residence 'Ingleside', Cushing (Township of Chatham), Que., 22 October 1903. He resided at Cushing until October 1890, when he moved with his family to Montreal; in February 1900 he returned to Chatham as Superintendent of the Carillon and Grenville Canals. For many years he was Colonel of the 11th Battalion (Argenteuil Rangers), retiring as Lieut.-Colonel with the long service and Fenian raid service medals. His son James Wilfred (b. 13 July 1874) died 6 October 1892; son Lemuel (b. 26 November 1875) became a chartered accountant.

Lemuel Cushing Jr. (entry 880, 1905 genealogy): born Chatham, Que., 18 February 1842; McGill B.A. 1865, B.C.L. 1865, M.A. 1867, LL.D. 1879; admitted to the Quebec Bar November 1865; Liberal MP for Argenteuil; President of the Montreal Lacrosse Club and an original member of the Montreal Amateur Athletic Association; 'at one time President' of the Young Men's Christian Association; published the first Genealogy of the Cushing Family in 1877; died in Montreal 1 March 1881.

The 1905 Cushing genealogy gives two different birth dates for Lemuel Cushing Sr.: the child listing under Job Cushing (entry 525 reference) says 29 April 1806, while his full entry says 26 April 1806 (both at Three Rivers). Internal discrepancy in the primary source; possibly an OCR or typesetting error.

In January 2009, the YMCA du Grand Montréal and its 8 regional branches took the name 'Ys du Québec' — the organization now operating as Les YMCA du Québec / The YMCAs of Quebec. The organization was previously named YMCA du Grand Montréal.

Per the Observatoire de l'action humanitaire YMCA history: in 2008 the organization decided to build a new centre in Montreal's Ahuntsic-Cartierville borough, and renovations at Camp Kanawana between 2007 and 2009 were undertaken as part of the YMCA du Québec's commitment to sustainable development and environmental respect.

The Concordia AtoM finding aid lists 'Montreal YMCA Camping Branch Board of Management records — 1969-1970', documenting that by 1969 camping was governed by a dedicated Camping Branch with its own Board of Management (succeeded in records by the Camping and Outdoor Education Branch, 1972-1979).

Camp Y Kanawana's 'virage vert' (green shift) began in 2006. All buildings renovated or constructed at the camp since 2006 were energy-efficient and incorporated educational elements, with the goal of reducing the camp's ecological footprint and making it an outdoor education centre focused on environmental education.

In February 2009, Les Y du Québec announced a new phase of the Camp Y Kanawana revitalization plan involving construction of new accommodation facilities. Environmental features documented in the March 3, 2009 Mediaterre article include green sanitary installations, thermal (heat) exchangers, composting toilets, and an artificial wetland system (marais artificiel) for treating wastewater.
Camp YMCA Kanawana's Facebook page hosted a video titled 'Sean Day against Bullying — Message from our Director Sean Day!', documenting Day's public anti-bullying advocacy as camp director.

The YMCA's proposed Kanawana-Weredale two-site operation (planning documents 1977-1980) coincided exactly with the institutional dissolution of Weredale House: the residence closed in 1977, the year its parent merged with Summerhill Homes, the Girls' Cottage School, and Allencroft Reception Centres to form Youth Horizons. The timing suggests the two-site plan arose from (or was complicated by) this upheaval in Weredale's governance, though no source states why the plan was abandoned.

Per the 1935 camp history, the final week of camp began with an 'eating-out day, when every camper went over to the haunted house and cooked his own supper.' The same day, the dam which had kept the water in Lakes Kanawana and Wilson 'at a desirable height' was let out before the assembled campers. The 'haunted house' was thus an established camp-wide cookout destination within walking distance of camp, not merely a story setting.

The Chopsy legend as told in oral tradition: In the summer of 1945, a kitchen staff member named Charles de Grandprix, a WWI veteran who was very skilled with knives and nicknamed 'Chopsy,' was walking in the woods when he found two Senior boys who had snuck off to practice throwing axes stolen from the Hike and Trip Department's equipment room ('the Cave'). He hid behind the tree they were throwing at, intending to scare them. After hearing two axes hit the tree he jumped out, not realizing there was a third ax, which severed his arm. He grabbed the severed arm, put it in his satchel, and fled into the woods. The camp searched but could not find him and declared him dead.

The Chopsy legend continues: Over the following winter, strange occurrences happened at camp. The next spring, boys on a hike found a makeshift cabin in the woods and a car stolen from a nearby town, parked between trees in a way that it could not be driven out. During the summer, dead animals were found in the woods appearing to have been mauled. A solitary senior boy who had been warned not to go into the woods alone disappeared. A search was launched but nothing was found. A counselor checked the car — the trunk, previously open, was now locked. They broke it open and found the missing boy's body, killed with an ax. The body was still warm. Chopsy was never seen again, but for years people claimed to hear chopping sounds deep in the woods late at night.
The full Chopsy legend takes approximately one hour to tell in complete detail. The story was known to campers in the early 2000s era (Matt Aronson's time).
Chopsy's real name in the legend is Charles de Grandprix. He was described as a WWI veteran and kitchen staff member who was very skilled with knives, which is how he earned the nickname 'Chopsy.'
The Hike and Trip Department at Camp Kanawana had an equipment room known as 'the Cave.' In the Chopsy legend, axes were stolen from this room by senior boys.

The Chopsy legend shares several elements with the American 'Cropsey' camp-legend archetype (a disfigured figure haunting the woods near camp, an origin story involving an accident, a weapon) but is a distinct, fully developed narrative with named characters, a specific year (1945), a three-act structure, and details unique to Kanawana (the Cave, kitchen staff, WWI veteran backstory, the locked car trunk, the warm body, the chopping-sounds coda).

The Chopsy legend was traditionally told at the wreckage of an old car in the woods near an abandoned cabin. The car is known as 'Chopsy's Car' and the cabin was known as 'Chopsy's Cabin.' The cabin has since been destroyed. The physical car and cabin served as both the setting of the story's climax and the venue for its telling.

The Chopsy legend traditionally opens with an oral tradition chain formula: 'I'm going to tell you a story my counsellor told me, and that he said his counsellor told him, his counsellor's counsellor told his counsellor, and that they say has been passed down just like this since the summer it happened, right here, at Camp Kanawana... It began in the summer of 1945...' This framing explicitly presents the story as an inherited tradition passed counsellor-to-counsellor, anchors it to the physical camp site, and positions the listener within the chain of transmission.

At least one teller of the Chopsy legend (Matt Aronson, 2000s era) added to the opening formula: 'and I've looked it up in the Kanawana archives at Concordia, and it's all documented there... you can go check and see for yourself...' This embellishment references the real Concordia University Archives (YMCA of Montreal fonds P0145) to lend verisimilitude to the legend.

The dining hall Grace at Camp Kanawana was not a single fixed prayer but rotated among several sung graces. Two identified graces are: (1) 'Johnny Appleseed' (the folk grace 'Oh, the Lord is good to me, and so I thank the Lord...'), and (2) the lyrics of 'Joy to the World' by Three Dog Night ('Jeremiah was a bullfrog...') adapted as a grace. Multiple graces were used rather than the same one at every meal.

The Kanawana Marching Song/Cheer as performed in the 2000s era opens with a call-and-response: the Chief shushes the crowd ('Shhh, shhh, shhh...'), calls 'Kamp Kanawana, are you ready?!', the camp responds 'We are!', and the Chief says 'Then let's go!' The main body begins with 'Hail, Hail, the gang's all here / What the heck do we care, what the heck? / We're the guys from Kanawana / We're gonna sing our marching song-a!' followed by 'We're gonna shout, shout, shout like anything / And through the woods we're gonna yell...' It ends with a coda: 'Ringle, wrangle, jingle, jangle / What's the matter with the Green Triangle? / Sis-boom-ba-ha, Sis-boom-ba-ha / Kanawana, Kanawana, Rah-rah-rah! / K-A-N-A-W-A-N-A / K-A-N-A-W-A-N-A / YEAH!'

The Kanawana Marching Song/Cheer references the 'Green Triangle' in the coda ('What's the matter with the Green Triangle?'). The Green Triangle was the camp's identity symbol and the name of its newsletter (1932–1940). The cheer also opens with 'Hail, Hail, the gang's all here,' borrowing from the 1917 popular song of that title (melody from Gilbert & Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance).

Grand Portage was one of the oldest cabins at Camp Kanawana, built sometime after the Lookout (a pre-existing structure on site before Kanawana was founded), the Dining Hall (1911), and the Infirmary (1920s?). It was situated just north of the Senior Parking Lot, to the west of the dining hall.
Grand Portage served as the CIT (Counsellor-in-Training) director's cabin in the 1980s and 1990s.
According to oral history, the end of World War II was heard on the radio at Grand Portage cabin at Camp Kanawana.
The Lookout is a structure at Camp Kanawana that pre-existed the camp's founding — it was on the site before Kanawana was established. It is described as the oldest structure on the property.

Grand Portage cabin was demolished around 2006 to make way for the new washroom buildings constructed as part of the green shift / Clivus Multrum composting toilet installation. The new washroom buildings bear the Grand Portage name.

The Longhouse was a large 2- or 3-story pavilion/boathouse on the Boating Waterfront (due south of the Dining Hall), right at the shoreline of Lake Kanawana. It was used for large group gatherings and dances. The Boating Director (at one point called 'the Admiral') had their living quarters in it.
The Longhouse was demolished by controlled fire around 1979 because it was in an irreparable condition.
The Boating Director at Camp Kanawana was at one point known by the title 'the Admiral.'

According to oral history, 'Lac Desjardins' was the original name of the lake that became Lake Wilson. It was renamed after being bought and donated to the camp (by J.W. McConnell, per earlier oral history). This would explain why no 'Lac Desjardins' appears in current toponymy records — the name was replaced.

According to oral history, Lake Kanawana was originally called 'Lac St Joseph.' The informant subsequently agreed this is most likely a conflation with the 1894 founding site — Camp Jubilee was established at Lake Saint-Joseph near Quebec City in 1894, a different location from the current Saint-Sauveur site (acquired 1910). This claim is likely erroneous.

No building was known as 'the haunted house' in the 2000s era at Camp Kanawana. The identity of the 1935 'haunted house' is unknown to the informant. Other minor ghost stories besides Chopsy circulated but have not yet been documented.

Matt Aronson (2000s-era counsellor) wrote an elaborate creative backstory for the Chopsy character, expanding the legend with historically grounded fiction. In this backstory, Charles de Grandprix's father Louis came from Kahnawake ('Khanawake') and his grandfather was a voyageur for the Hudson's Bay Company. Charles grew up destitute in Montreal's Old Port after his mother died in childbirth and his father drank himself to death (New Year's Day, 1910). He enlisted in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces in August 1914, lying about his age. At the Second Battle of Ypres, his Ross Mark II rifle jammed and he killed enemy soldiers with a hatchet. He became feared for hand-to-hand combat in No Man's Land patrols, wielding first a bayonet, then a kitchen knife. The Germans called him 'Der Hirsch Schlachter' (the Stag Slaughterer), but it was his fellow troops who gave him the nickname 'Chopsy.' He was eventually captured and spent the rest of the war as a POW.

The Chopsy backstory written by Matt Aronson represents a modern creative elaboration of the camp legend by an active teller — a piece of camp cultural production that demonstrates how the legend continued to develop through individual storytellers adding historically grounded fiction (CEF enlistment, Second Battle of Ypres, the Ross rifle, No Man's Land patrols) and tying the character's origins to Kahnawake, echoing the documented Kanawana/Kahnawá:ke name connection.
Jay Netherwood was Director of Camp Kanawana in 1986 and 1987. He is the brother of Bruce Netherwood, who succeeded him.
Bruce Netherwood was Director of Camp Kanawana from 1988 to 1994. He is the brother of Jay Netherwood, who preceded him as director.
Joanna AA Hode was Director of Camp Kanawana from 1995 to 2000.
Morgan Carter was Director of Camp Kanawana in 2001 and 2002.
Dave Leduc was Director of Camp Kanawana in 2003.

Peter Goddard was Director of Camp Kanawana before Jay Netherwood (1986). His exact years are uncertain, but he served sometime in the early-to-mid 1980s, between Dave Twynam (~1980) and Jay Netherwood (1986).

The dam ceremony (opening the dam between Lakes Kanawana and Wilson) was no longer practiced by the mid-1980s. An informant whose camp experience began around 1985 was not aware of the tradition, establishing a terminus ante quem: the ceremony ended sometime between 1935 (last documented) and ~1985.

The Council Ring is located in the far west end of the camp, a 10-15 minute walk past the Senior Boys section. It remains an important ceremonial site in the 2000s era. It hosts the Opening Campfire for each session, the opening campfire of the L&V Games, and the Closing Fire of the summer.

The Council Ring has a tradition of burning a 'time capsule' containing the summer's record of important people, events, and moments at the Closing Fire, then digging it up to read at the following year's Opening Fire. This tradition is believed to be very old, possibly dating to the 1920s or 1930s.

The Council Ring is large enough to seat the entire camp (200+ people) on log benches made from trees from the site, set in three rows around a large central fire bowl made of stones from the site. The bonfires are massive — sometimes 10-12 feet of firewood stacked, with flames reaching 15-20 feet high. The area above the fire pit is kept clear of tree branches.

The section system at Camp Kanawana remained essentially the same from the informant's era (1980s-2000s) through to the present day, confirming the 1959 section names (Pioneers, Woodsmen, Coureurs de Bois, Pathfinders) have remained in continuous use for over 60 years.

Morgan M. Carter, identified by oral history as Camp Kanawana director in 2001-2002, is a Montreal-based architect who co-founded Atelier Schleiss Carter in 2018 with Matthieu Schleiss. His firm bio states he worked 'extensively in the non-profit sector for agencies including the YMCA and Canada World Youth' prior to architecture, and has served on the Board of Directors of YMCA Kanawana. He is adjunct faculty at McGill University (since 2011) and Université de Montréal (since 2013), and has also taught at Dalhousie, Harvard, and Carleton. Registered with the Ordre des Architectes du Québec since 2022.

Jay Netherwood (Camp Kanawana director 1986-1987, brother of Bruce Netherwood) has no discoverable online presence beyond a Facebook profile at facebook.com/jaynetherwood. No biographical information was found across 10+ web searches.

Joanna Hode (Camp Kanawana director 1995-2000) has no discoverable online presence under any tested spelling (Hode, Houde, Hod). The surname 'Hode' is extremely rare in Quebec; 'Houde' is the common Quebec form. 16 web searches returned zero results. The 'AA' middle initials may help disambiguate if the correct surname spelling is confirmed.

Peter Gilling Goddard (August 13, 1953 - October 15, 2016) is CONFIRMED as the Peter Goddard who served at Camp Kanawana (director, early-to-mid 1980s). Identification upgraded from 'possible match' to confirmed based on a condolence message on his obituary explicitly mentioning 'Kamp Kanawana' (insider spelling).

Magloire Pagé (1826-1901) was a pioneer settler of Saint-Sauveur-des-Monts. He was part of the 10th generation of the Pagé family since their arrival in New France. He married Adéline Beauchamp (1830-1898) on July 28, 1851, in Saint-Jérôme. In the 1885 census, the couple owned lot 43 in the concession of côte Saint-Elmire, Saint-Sauveur.

Magloire Pagé fils (b. 1853, Saint-Sauveur), son of Magloire Pagé and Adéline Beauchamp, acquired the paternal land in 1874 and married Olivine Desjardins on August 3, 1875. Olivine died at age 54 on June 20, 1904, and was buried in the Saint-Sauveur cemetery. Their known children include Léonie Pagé (1882-1941) and Édouard Pagé (b. March 30, 1893).

Édouard Pagé (b. March 30, 1893, Saint-Sauveur), son of Magloire Pagé fils and Olivine Desjardins, began an apprenticeship in baking in 1910 under Ubald Gauthier on Drolet Street, Montreal. In 1912, baker Camille Gauvreau ceded his Saint-Sauveur bakery to his son Ovila, who rented it to Édouard Pagé. Pagé acquired the business in 1914. The bakery (Boulangerie Pagé) has operated continuously at 7 avenue de l'Église since 1903 (when Gauvreau founded it). In 1963, Édouard sold the business to his sons Bernard and Philippe Pagé.

Édouard Pagé served as president of the Saint-Sauveur School Commission (Commission scolaire). His efforts led to the construction of a boys' school that was blessed on January 9, 1949, and named École Saint-Édouard in his honor. The school retained this name until 1995.

Télesphore Pagé, the youngest son of Magloire Pagé fils, married on May 27, 1925, inherited the family land, and settled there with his wife Clarilda Dagenais (1901-1995). The old Pagé farmhouse faced the mountains near Saint-Sauveur.

In 1957, Mickey Stein was staying in the old Pagé family farmhouse near Saint-Sauveur when he observed the mountain opposite and conceived the idea for the Mont Habitant ski resort. With associates Stephen and Stanley Vineberg, Stein developed the mountain, hiring designer Sel Hannah; Mont Habitant opened for the 1958-59 winter season.

The Pagé family genealogy in Saint-Sauveur spans at least four generations: (1) Magloire Pagé père (1826-1901), married Adéline Beauchamp 1851; (2) Magloire Pagé fils (b. 1853), married Olivine Desjardins 1875; (3) children including Léonie (1882-1941), Édouard (b. 1893), and Télesphore (youngest son, married 1925); (4) Édouard's sons Bernard and Philippe (took over bakery 1963). The family owned land on lot 43, côte Saint-Elmire, and 'Domaine-Pagé' is a named locality in Saint-Sauveur whose toponymic origin the Commission de toponymie has not formally determined.

The first bakery in Saint-Sauveur was established in 1897 (not 1903) by Camille Gauvreau, who purchased land from notary Malo. It was later known as the 'Ancienne boulangerie Gauvreau' and is listed in the Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec (ID 206587). The building is at 7 avenue de l'Église, the same location as Boulangerie Pagé. The '1903' date sometimes cited may refer to a different milestone or error; Gauvreau established it in 1897 and Édouard Pagé took it over in 1912-1914.

The YMCA 'Torch Ceremony for World Friendship' originated at a 1926 international YMCA conference where representatives from 52 nations gathered to discuss YMCA involvement in post-WWI peace-building. On the final night, they lit a 'Fire of Friendship' and senior leaders passed torches to the younger generation, who declared in their own languages: 'We leave this fire with a vision of a great Christian fellowship, conscious of difference but resolved to love.' One torch was housed at the Greater Des Moines Y Camp for 99 years. YMCA Camp Fuller (Providence) held a 'World-Wide Friendship' ceremony in 1932 where boys carved sticks with friends' autographs and pledged friendship. Kanawana's 1935 'Torch Ceremony for World Friendship' was part of this YMCA-wide interwar peace tradition.

Dr. James Orbinski is described as 'the 15th recipient' of the Pip Award on the YMCA Quebec press release (2024). With 12 documented recipients through 2018 and Orbinski as the 15th in 2024, exactly 3 awards were given in the 2019-2023 period, while 2 years had no award (likely 2020 and 2021 due to COVID). The 2010 gap is confirmed by numbering: Mosher was the 8th recipient in 2015, meaning one skip year in 2007-2014, which is 2010.

Stuart McLean attended Lower Canada College for high school before becoming a counsellor at Camp Kanawana in 1969. Both institutions use the motto 'Non Nobis Solum.' McLean is the only documented individual known to have attended both LCC and Kanawana, making him a confirmed personal bridge between the two institutions. However, no documented evidence exists of a deliberate motto adoption pathway from LCC to Kanawana.

M.H. Penton authored 'Non Nobis Solum: The History of Lower Canada College' (1972), a history of the school that may contain references to YMCA or camp connections. The book is listed on Internet Archive but has not been accessed. LCC founder Charles Sanderson Fosbery adopted 'Non Nobis Solum' from his family crest when the school opened in 1909.

A silent 1960s film of Camp Kanawana showing swimming and diving scenes is available on YouTube (title: 'YMCA: Kamp Kanawana (no sound)', ID: ZrUuQ1SU7q8). This is distinct from the 1993 Cathy Reeves documentary. The footage appears to be from the YMCA of Montreal archival collection.

The Clivus Multrum composting toilet system at Camp Kanawana was installed circa 2006-2007 as part of the 'virage vert' (green shift) that began in 2006. Two new green sanitary installations were tested during the summers of 2007 and 2008. Grand Portage cabin was demolished around 2006 to make way for the new washroom buildings housing the system. A TELUS sponsorship in 2010 supported continued green shift work.

The Camp Oolahwan property at 54 Chemin d'Entrelacs, Sainte-Marguerite-du-Lac-Masson was sold after the camp's 2005 closure. It was purchased by Louis Pratt in partnership with Louis Nault. The site became Érablière Ste-Marguerite (sugar shack) and Aventure Oolahwan (outdoor activities). A luxury vacation cottage development called Club Lac Walfred was built on the broader property by Habitations Germat / Timber Block Homes circa 2015.

Surviving traces of Camp Oolahwan at the former site include a hiking trail, bird feeder, volleyball court, and the main building with cafeteria. The Association du Lac Walfred (homeowners association for the cottage development) adopted an owl logo in memory of Camp Oolahwan's own owl logo.

YWCA Camp Hochelaga in Vermont is described as 'the last residential YWCA summer camp,' suggesting that Camp Oolahwan's 2005 closure was part of a broader YWCA trend of exiting residential camp operations. No YWCA public source states a specific reason for Oolahwan's closure.

Camp Otoreke closed in 1982. The YMCA sold the property in 1987. After closure, the three-island site's current status is unknown. The camp had operated for nearly 90 years of continuous use (1894-1982).

William Henry Ball graduated from the International YMCA Training School (now Springfield College) in the class of 1891, alongside James Naismith (inventor of basketball) and Amos Alonzo Stagg. Ball was a founding editor of 'The Triangle' (Physical Department publication) with Stagg and Luther H. Gulick. He worked at YMCAs in Yonkers NY, Prospect Park Brooklyn, Springfield MA, and Detroit. In 1910, he launched the national YMCA swimming instruction campaign. From 1911 to 1924, he served as Secretary to the YMCA International Committee in New York City. He returned to Springfield College to teach (1927-1930) and died December 17, 1955.

Whether William Henry Ball (Springfield College 1891, died 1955) is the same person as 'Billy' Ball who founded Camp Jubilee in 1894 at the Montreal YMCA remains unconfirmed. The timeline is plausible: Ball graduated in 1891 and could have been posted to Montreal by 1894. His known career positions (Yonkers, Brooklyn, Springfield, Detroit, then YMCA International Committee 1911-1924) do not include Montreal, but a Montreal posting between 1891 and his other documented positions has not been ruled out. The Springfield College finding aid (MS 527) may contain biographical details that confirm or deny the Montreal connection.

The C-Vert environmental leadership program was launched in 2005, initially in the Mercier-Hochelaga-Maisonneuve neighbourhood of Montreal. By the 2020s it operates throughout Quebec, engaging 120 teens per summer in sustainable development projects. The Port of Montreal supports the program as part of its community investment policy.
Hedley S. Dimock's full name was Hedley Seldon Dimock (not Sidgwick or Sidgmore as sometimes conjectured). His obituary appeared in the Oakland Tribune, October 5, 1958.

Hedley G. Dimock's full name was Hedley Gardner Dimock. Born 1928. Per Open Library and Internet Archive author records. He published 'Group development' through Sir George Williams University (1966).
In 1961, Hedley G. Dimock held a dual role as Coordinator of Staff Development and Training for the Montreal YMCA, and Lecturer in Group Development at Sir George Williams University.

Camp Oolahwan closure details: a 2007 blog post ('Blue Skies Today') states the camp 'closed in 2004, a victim of rising costs and changing times.' The YWCA website says 1917-2005. The discrepancy likely reflects last camp season (summer 2004) vs property disposal date (2005).
Camp Oolahwan property was 345 acres with a private lake, sold for $1.47 million to developers who subdivided it into building lots.
Camp Oolahwan was located approximately 100 km north of Montreal. Geographic coordinates: 46.0501°N, 74.0659°W, elevation 369m (GeoNames feature ID 5914501).

The YWCA Montreal 150-year timeline (2025) states Camp Oolahwan opened in 1915, while the camp's dedicated YWCA page and the 2017 centennial consistently use 1917. Mary Edgar served as Director of Camp Oolahwan from 1915 to 1919. The camp may have had a precursor or trial season in 1915 before formal establishment on Lake Walfred in 1917.

The Summer Space Day Camp (successor to Camp Oolahwan) served girls ages 10 to 13, with programming including dance, circus, theatre, music, yoga, and kickboxing. Workshops focused on countering violence and early sexualization. The program was discontinued circa June 2020.
CBC Radio 'All in a Weekend' Montreal aired an 11-minute 46-second audio segment about the Camp Oolahwan centennial anniversary (2017).
Commemorative poster titled 'Kanawana: 100 years of spirit and leadership' was produced in 1994 for the camp's centennial. Held in Concordia Archives P0145/12B04 (Communications sub-sub-series).
A Kanawana alumni newsletter called 'The Look Out' was published in 1994, Vol. 1, No. 3, likely launched for the centennial. Held in Concordia Archives P0145/12B04.

The 1993 documentary 'Kamp Kanawana: The Experience that Lasts a Lifetime' was produced by Laurentien Productions for the Montreal YMCA, directed by Cathy Reeves. 9 minutes, colour VHS (1996 release). Features the song 'On My Way to Kanawana' by Richard 'Itch' Kerr. An access copy exists on YouTube (ID: _bznoSFg3MU).

Camp Kanawana anniversary pattern: 95th reunion April 7, 1989 (with '95 years of sharing' promotional materials); centennial 1994 (commemorative poster produced); 120th reunion September 5, 2014 at Victoria Hall, Montreal; 125th anniversary summer 2019 'Family, Alumni, and Friends Weekend' at camp.
A silent 1960s film of Camp Kanawana exists on YouTube (ID: ZrUuQ1SU7q8), titled 'YMCA: Kamp Kanawana (no sound).'

The original 1917 Camp Oolahwan building is still standing and is used as the sugar shack for Érablière Ste-Marguerite. Louis Pratt and Louis Nault invested over $1.5 million in maple syrup equipment. The syrup production project opened mid-February 2019, operating seasonally Feb 15 through end of April.

The YMCA of Montreal had a formal 'Centennial/Expo Project Committee' that produced a 'Summary Historical Statement / resume historique' in 1966. This document is held in Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/1B.
A Young Adult Centennial Conference was held at Camp Otoreke, July 8-15, 1967. Records are in Concordia Archives P0145/14D10.

Chris Adam received the Governor General's Meritorious Service Medal (Civil Division) for creating a culture of sustainability and promoting well-being at Dawson College. He introduced the 'Living Campus' concept that made Dawson College a model of sustainability.
Chris Adam holds a Master's degree in Education and has three years of experience in wildlife and fish management. He is also director of Cadameco Consultants Inc.

The 1980 'Chris Adams of Vanier' who created Camp Kanawana's Nature Awareness program is very likely the same person as Chris Adam, the 2017 Pip Award recipient. Both are from Vanier/Dawson College area, both have wildlife/nature expertise, and the surname difference is a common transcription variant. This identification resolves the open question in environmental-history.md.

Lac de la Montagne Noire (RSVL station 0391A) is monitored by Quebec's Réseau de surveillance volontaire des lacs. In 2021, water transparency was 6.2 metres (3 Secchi disk readings), classifying the lake as oligotrophic (very clear water). This is NOT the same lake as Lac Kanawana — Lac de la Montagne Noire is in Lantier/Val-des-Lacs/Saint-Donat, while Lac Kanawana is near Saint-Sauveur. No RSVL monitoring data was found for Lac Kanawana specifically.

The motto 'Each for all — all for each' is also the motto of Camp Becket (Becket-Chimney Corners YMCA, founded 1903 in Massachusetts), established under director Henry Gibson (1904-1927). Camp Becket has eight core mottos. This suggests the English-language motto may have been a shared YMCA camping tradition rather than unique to Kanawana. Camp Kanawana's 1922 brochure documents 'Each for all and all for each' as its motto; the camp later adopted 'Non Nobis Solum' (Cicero) at an unknown date.
Harold Herbert Potter (1914-2004) worked as a camp counsellor at YMCA Kamp Kanawana during summers in the 1930s while attending Sir George Williams College (B.A. 1935-1939)
Harold H. Potter was the first Canadian-born Black sociologist hired by a Canadian post-secondary institution, appointed lecturer in Sociology at Sir George Williams College in 1947
Harold H. Potter grew up in Little Burgundy, Montreal's working-class English-speaking Black community. His parents were émigrés from British Guiana.
Harold H. Potter was editor of The Georgian, the student newspaper of Sir George Williams College, in 1938-39. Mordecai Richler held the same position a decade later.
The graphic novel 'Jane, le renard et moi' (Jane, the Fox and Me) by Fanny Britt and Isabelle Arsenault (2012/2013) is set partly at Camp Kanawana, depicting a school class trip to the camp

'Jane, le renard et moi' won the Governor General's Literary Award for Children's Illustration (French), the Joe Shuster Award (Writer and Artist), and was named a New York Times Best Illustrated Children's Book

Camp Ouareau was founded in 1922 by Mabel C. Jamieson and Ferna G. Halliday, both school teachers. It is one of the two oldest girls-only camps still active in Canada, located at Notre-Dame-de-la-Merci on Lac Ouareau.
The Canadian Camping Association was founded on May 20, 1936 at the Central Y.M.C.A. in Toronto, with Taylor Statten as its first president
Taylor Statten was a Boer War veteran who became YMCA Boys' Work Secretary in 1906. He founded Camp Ahmek in 1921 and served as both CCA president (1936) and ACA president (1942).

Edgar Munroe Robinson (1867-1951) was YMCA International Committee Boys' Work Secretary from 1900. He developed camping programs, father-son programs, and was also the first Executive Director of the Boy Scouts of America (1910).

Hedley S. Dimock was dean of YMCA College (George Williams College) in Chicago. He launched camping character education institutes in 1930 and led philosophical discussions on 'small-group-centered methods' at camp in the 1940s-1950s.

EMSB schools (Vincent Massey Collegiate, JFK High School, École Secondaire Louis Joseph Papineau) send students on overnight camping experiences at Camp YMCA Kanawana, with activities including archery, rock climbing, canoeing, nature interpretation, and woodworking.
Camp Ouareau became bilingual in 1976. Jacqui Raill became director in 1994, having been a counsellor since 1975, bringing a focus on environmentalism and sustainability.

A silent film (no sound) of Kamp Kanawana from the 1960s, showing swimming and diving activities, exists as a YouTube access copy (Concordia Archives P0145-09-0087). URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZrUuQ1SU7q8
On September 5, 2014, Camp YMCA Kanawana alumni (former campers and staff) assembled at Victoria Hall (Westmount) to celebrate the camp's 120th anniversary reunion.
Derek Walsh (ACQ) received the Canadian Camping Association Award of Excellence in 1983. The CCA fonds at Trent University associates him with Kamp Kanawana and YMCA Montreal.

Magloire Pagé married Adéline Beauchamp on July 28, 1851 at Saint-Jérôme. Their son, also Magloire, was born in Saint-Sauveur in 1853 and in 1897 became the village's first baker. The bakery was sold in 1912 to Édouard Pagé; Boulangerie Pagé remains active in Saint-Sauveur today.
Camp Kanawana launched the 'Mountaineer' program as an all-gender tent to provide a safe and welcoming environment for transgender, non-binary, and gender non-conforming campers.
YMCA day camps, holiday camps, and spring break camps will no longer be offered as of fall 2025. The Kanawana summer camp will continue to operate.

Camp B'nai Brith of Montreal was established in 1921 (Mount Royal Lodge of B'nai Brith Canada). First campsite on a farm 64 km from Montreal; moved to current location 1929. Counsellors were McGill student volunteers. Combined Jewish Appeal constituent agency from 1942.

D.A. Budge, as General Secretary of the YMCA of Montreal, directed James Naismith to the YMCA International Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. When Naismith inquired about becoming a YMCA instructor at the Montreal YMCA, Budge told him about the Springfield school. Naismith enrolled there and invented basketball in 1891.

Camp Tamaracouta's main lodge burned down in 2024. Scouts Canada sold the 1,000-acre property in 2025 to entrepreneur Eric Desroches, in partnership with the Nature Conservancy of Canada and the town of Mille-Isles, Quebec. The camp had claimed to be the oldest continuously operating Scout camp in the world.

Camp Tamaracouta was named for the tamarack trees on the property ('couta' reportedly meaning body of water in a First Nations language). It was founded in 1912 with funds provided by Colonel E.A. Whitehead on a former farm belonging to the Dawson family of Mille-Isles. After WWI, it adopted a Hudson's Bay Company theme with campsites named after HBC trading posts.

Camp Massad Montreal, a Hebrew-speaking Jewish summer camp, was founded in 1947 on Lac Quenouille in Sainte-Agathe-des-Monts in the Laurentians. It is shomer Shabbat with kosher kitchen under the Montreal Va'ad Ha'ir. Founded in modern Orthodox practice but welcoming to children from all Jewish backgrounds.

Pripstein's Camp Mishmar was a co-educational summer camp in Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, Quebec, operating from 1941 to 2014. Founded by Chaim Pripstein (also known as Charles Pripstein), a Polish-born Hebrew teacher at United Talmud Torahs who fled Poland before WWII. He acquired land from a local farmer near Saint-Jerome in 1941. At its peak in the 1960s, the camp had 240 campers per summer. It closed in 2014 due to declining enrolment.

La Colonie de vacances Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc, a French-speaking girls-only summer camp, was established in 1926 by Father Adélard Desrosiers in Contrecoeur, Quebec. It is the second-oldest summer camp exclusively for girls still operating in Quebec and French Canada. Incorporated December 22, 1941. Serves low-income families with sliding-scale pricing.

The University of Minnesota Kautz Family YMCA Archives holds a 'YMCA in Canada records' collection containing minutes, reports, yearbooks, and correspondence from the Canadian YMCA pre-1912 period (when Canadian YMCA was governed jointly with US YMCA under the International Committee). Includes records related to youth development programs and camping.

Harry Ballantyne authored 'A Short History of the Canadian Y.M.C.A. 1851-1944,' prepared for the Canadian YMCA Study Committee. A copy is held on the Internet Archive, uploaded by Concordia University Records Management.

A 'Historical Sketch of the YMCA of the City of Montreal' was presented at the YMCA Jubilee Celebration in 1901, covering the YMCA's history from 1851 to 1901. A copy is on the Internet Archive, uploaded by Concordia University Records Management.

A second CFCF radio broadcast about Kamp Kanawana, dated June 10, 1939, is available on the Internet Archive (identifier: 1939-06-10-kamp-kanawana-broadcast-station-cfcf). This is distinct from the June 26, 1941 broadcast already documented. Both were uploaded by Concordia University Records Management from the YMCA of Montreal fonds.

The annual 'games' at Camp Kanawana were inspired by YMCA Camp Pine Crest (Muskoka, Ontario) and have been held every year since approximately 1948. The 78th edition of the games is scheduled for 2025.

YMCA Camp Pine Crest was founded in 1910, is now part of the YMCA of Greater Toronto, and is located on 650 acres of Muskoka wilderness on three lakes. It is one of Canada's earliest overnight camps and focuses on traditional canoe tripping. A history book, 'Lumbermen & Voyageurs: The YMCA Pine Crest Story,' has been published about the camp.

The Pine Crest Games at YMCA Camp Pine Crest are a two-day event held on the last Tuesday and Wednesday of each summer, involving competitions between two teams: the Lumbermen and the Voyageurs. This is the model for Kanawana's L&V Games, confirming the oral history that the tradition originated at Pine Crest.

YMCA Camp Wanakita was founded in 1953 on Koshlong Lake near Haliburton, Ontario, by the YMCA of Hamilton. Keith Smith was the first director, chosen to find a 'Northwoods property.' George Jones and YMCA colleagues chose the Koshlong Lake site. The name 'Wanakita' was derived from Smith's experience at Camp Kitchikewana, where Kitchikewana was home to Wanakita Beach. First season: 373 boys, 38 staff, $18,882 budget. The camp replaced Camp Erie Heights (Lake Erie), itself a replacement for Camp Tekahoinwake (Grand River). Now over 1,000 acres, YMCA Hamilton-Burlington-Brantford.

YMCA Camp Kitchikewana was founded in 1919 on Beausoleil Island in Georgian Bay Islands National Park, Honey Harbour, Ontario. Operated by YMCA of Simcoe/Muskoka. Over 105 years of continuous operation. The camp provided the name origin for Camp Wanakita (from 'Wanakita Beach' at Kitchikewana). Listed alongside Kanawana in OCA 'Y camps' records.

YMCA Hayo-Went-Ha Camps (founded 1904, Central Lake, Michigan) use 'Woodsmen' and 'Voyageurs' as program group names, paralleling the 'Lumbermen vs Voyageurs' tradition at YMCA Camp Pine Crest and Camp Kanawana. This suggests the L&V/Woodsmen-Voyageurs division was a wider YMCA camp pattern, not unique to Pine Crest.

Stuart McLean's personal and literary archive is housed at McMaster University, including manuscripts, correspondence, photographs, fan mail, sound recordings, and set pieces from live Vinyl Cafe performances. This archive is a potential source for Camp Kanawana materials from McLean's five summers (1969-1975).

In the graphic novel 'Jane, le renard et moi' (2012), the protagonist Hélène dreads an English immersion class trip to Camp Kanawana (Lac Kanawana). On the second-to-last evening at camp, while sitting on the porch of her cabin, a fox approaches her — the pivotal encounter of the narrative. The camp's use as an English immersion destination in fiction reflects its real-world role hosting school groups.

Camp YMCA Kanawana's Facebook page (facebook.com/YKanawana) contains a photo album labeled '1987-1994' with historical photographs from that era. The page is active with photos, videos, and reels documenting camp activities.
Camp YMCA Kanawana held an Open House on Sunday, June 14, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Concordia University Archives hold a document titled 'Interpretation of scores for counselors participating in a research project at Kamp Kanawana' dated 1960, held in sub-series P0145/12B. This may be connected to the Hedley Dimock character education research conducted at YMCA camps in the mid-twentieth century.

Audrey Dowse is a Camp Administrator Hall of Fame inductee (nominated 2022), recognized for her work with Camp YMCA Kanawana and YMCA Day Camps. She is listed on campadmin.org alongside camp administrators from YMCA camps across North America.

Camp YMCA Kanawana hosted an Alumni, Family & Friends Weekend on September 7-9, 2018. The Pip Award is presented at this annual alumni weekend. This confirms the event is an annual tradition, not only held for milestone anniversaries.

The Pine Crest Games at YMCA Camp Pine Crest have been held since 1940, making them one of the oldest continuous camp competition traditions in the YMCA system. The two-day event occurs on the last Tuesday and Wednesday of each summer. Staff and campers are randomly assigned to teams each year.

Marie-Pierre Lacasse holds the title 'Executive Camp Director' (directeur principal) of Camp YMCA Kanawana as of 2024. She is listed on the YMCA Quebec management team page and on LinkedIn as Directeur principal at Les YMCA du Québec.

The municipality of Mille-Isles, where Camp Kanawana is located, was officially created on July 1, 1855, after detaching from the parish of Saint-Jérôme. It is named after the Mille-Isles Seigneury, originally granted in 1683 to Michel-Sidrac Dugué de Boisbriand (governor of Montreal 1670). Early settlement in the area dates to the 1830s.

The Laurentian mountains northwest of Montreal are within the traditional territory of the Anishinaabe (Algonquin) peoples. Unlike most of Ontario and the Prairies, Algonquin territory in this region has never been covered by a land-sharing treaty.

The Pip Award is presented twice each year: first at camp during the summer (e.g., Carol Skinner on July 7; Marina Sharpe on August 2), and then again at the annual Alumni and Friends weekend in September. This dual presentation format is documented in YMCA Quebec press releases for the 2016 and 2018 awards.

The 2026 Camp Kanawana program 'Explorers Pioneers' serves girls and non-binary campers aged 11-12. Campers spend most days in the regular residential camp program while also preparing for a 3-4 day camping trip at Papineau-Labelle Wildlife Reserve, combining canoeing and hiking components.

The 2026 Camp Kanawana program 'Adventurers Pathfinders' serves girls and non-binary campers aged 13-16 with a 4-6 day introductory canoe trip in La Vérendrye Wildlife Reserve (flat water) or on Quebec/Ontario rivers (white water). This mirrors the 'Adventurers Coureurs des Bois' program for boys and non-binary campers.

The 2026 Camp Kanawana summer season runs from June 22 to August 14, with four 12-day sessions: June 22-July 3, July 6-17, July 20-31, and August 3-14. The 6-day Woodsmen program includes a trip to Sommet Saint-Sauveur water park (weather permitting).

The 109-page university paper 'Mary S. Edgar's Contribution to the Canadian Camping Movement' in the Sundridge-Strong Digital Collection was authored by Marilee C. Tisdall and dated 1978. The appendix is missing. Tisdall received the ICC (International Camping Congress) award from the CCA in 1983.

Mary Susanne Edgar (May 23, 1889 – September 17, 1973) was born in Sundridge, Ontario. She graduated from the National Training School of the YWCA in New York City in 1915. From 1912-1914 she did First National Girls' Work for the YWCA in Canada. From 1915-1919 she was Girls' Work Secretary at YWCA Montreal and Director of Camp Oolahwan in the Laurentians.

Mary Edgar's papers are held at Queen's University Archives (primary holding). Trent University Archives holds photocopies as fonds 82-010 (15 cm, 1920-1970). SFU Digitized Collections hold Mary S. Edgar Papers (CPR-1-58). The book 'Legacy to a Camper: The Story of Mary S. Edgar' by Jocelyn Palm was published by the Canadian Camping Association in 1982.

The Quebec Camping Association fonds (85-013) at Trent University Archives contains 90 cm of textual records in 3 boxes, dated 1948-1982. Contents include correspondence, minutes of meetings, camp visitation reports, historical background papers from the standards committee, provincial board reports, and files from Miss F.M. Kelly. Most records are in French.

The QCA fonds (85-013) at Trent contains camp visitation reports covering 1962-1968, 1968-1971, and 1972-1978. Series 7 contains Provincial Standards Committee / Comité Provincial des Normes files (Miss F.M. Kelly). The OCA fonds accession 88-006 (Boxes 41-42) also contains QCA English Section materials: minutes, reports, correspondence, constitution (1972-1979).

The Association des camps du Québec (ACQ) was founded in 1961. The QCA (formed 1937 as a CCA provincial unit) and the ACQ appear to be the same organizational lineage under English/French naming. Camp YMCA Kanawana is described as 'a founding member of the Association des camps du Québec.'

BAnQ numérique contains at least 38 digitized newspaper issues referencing Kanawana, across 8 newspapers: The Westmount Examiner (12 issues, 1935-2003), Le Petit Journal (10 issues, 1937-1999), Le Devoir (8 issues, 1989-2019), La Presse (2 issues), Le Droit (2 issues), Le Soleil (1 issue), The Sherbrooke Record (1 issue), The Huntingdon Gleaner (2 issues).
In 1937, the St-Jean Ambulance Association sent a qualified instructor to Camp Kanawana starting July 1 for a first aid course, as reported in Le Droit (Ottawa) on June 25, 1937.
A 'Mr. Buckley' had 'many years experience in camping, both at Kanawana and at other camps in Canada and the United States,' as reported in The Westmount Examiner, March 29, 1935.

In 1962, the YMCA planned 'bigger and better' citizenship training and educational programs for youth and young adults at Kamp Kanawana, its eight city branches, and Sir George Williams University, as reported in The Westmount Examiner, November 16, 1962.

In summer 1971, Camp Kanawana in Saint-Sauveur hosted 'Noosphere,' an international development education simulation for approximately 100 young Canadians aged 16-19, organized by Perspective-Jeunesse, as reported in Le Soleil, July 7, 1971.
In 1976, Lovell's Montreal City Directory listed 'Kamp Kanawana' at 1441 Drummond, Montreal, H3G 1WS, telephone 849-5331. A second listing appeared in Chateauguay with telephone 692-2801.

Le Devoir covered Camp Kanawana during its 1994 centennial year in at least 3 issues: January 15, July 6, and October 24, 1994. Full article texts are on BAnQ numérique but require in-person or card-holder access.

On May 16, 2023, the superintendent's house at Camp YMCA Kanawana was destroyed by fire. The isolated building on Montée Sainte-Elmire in the Spring Valley sector was a total loss. No one was inside. 25 firefighters from Saint-Sauveur, Morin-Heights, and Sainte-Anne-des-Lacs responded. Other buildings were unaffected. Cause undetermined.
Y camp counselors received three-day leader training at Camp Kanawana, as reported in The Sherbrooke Record, July 21, 1972.

The YMCA Montreal annual report for 1966-67 is digitized on Internet Archive (identifier: sgw-ymca-annual-report-1966-67). It is the only YMCA Montreal annual report from the 1940s-1960s known to be digitized. Other digitized reports are from 1856, 1876, 1889-1890, 1891-1892, and 1993.

Ross Bannerman directed Camp Pascobac (1951, recruited by Nelson McEwen) and Camp Stephens in Winnipeg (1956). He authored 'Report on Kamp Kanawana' (1969) held at Concordia Archives 12B01. He had a YMCA International Branch file (c.1968-1970) at Concordia and later became CEO of the Montreal YMCA in the late 1970s.

Concordia Archives sub-series 12B01 holds Kamp Kanawana general administration records including: season reports, committee minutes, camp director correspondence, Dave Twynam correspondence. Sub-series 12B04 holds brochures from 1950, 1959, 1960s, 1964, 1965. Sub-series 14D03 contains the YMCA Montreal annual reports. Sub-series 14D10 contains Nelson McEwen correspondence (1941-1945).
A 'Kanawana Reminiscence (of 1948)' by Ben T. Hannah (written 1989) is held at Concordia Archives, sub-series 12B01. Hannah was a camper or staff member in 1948.

The University of Minnesota Kautz Family YMCA Archives holds 'YMCA in Canada records, 1851-1989' which includes records from the Montreal YMCA era when Canadian national administrative headquarters were located in Montreal (before formation of the National Council of YMCAs of Canada in 1912).

Peter Gilling Goddard (August 13, 1953 - October 15, 2016) is confirmed as the Peter Goddard who served at Camp Kanawana. A condolence message on his obituary states: 'I knew Peter years ago at Kamp Kanawana. I remember a warm-hearted and very kind man.' The use of insider spelling 'Kamp' strengthens the identification.

Peter Gilling Goddard was born August 13, 1953, the third son of Elizabeth Anne Goddard (nee Macdonald) and Raymond Gilling Goddard of Smiths Falls, Ontario. Siblings: John, Allan, David, Jennifer, Barbara, and Kathy.

Peter Goddard died suddenly on October 15, 2016 (age 63) while walking Shaw Woods trails with the Mississippi Valley Field Naturalists and his brother Allan. Funeral at C.R. Gamble Funeral Home, Almonte, Ontario; memorial November 26, 2016 at First Unitarian Congregation of Ottawa.

Peter Goddard served Boy Scouts of Canada for 40+ years (teaching, instruction, leading, managing). He worked at the Bill Mason Center as instructor and leader of outdoor activities, and at the Rideau Valley Conservation Authority in outdoor field management and instructing, running summer camp programs at Baxter Conservation Area. He recently retired before his death.
Peter Goddard's father Raymond Gilling Goddard (September 2, 1921 - May 13, 2013) was a WWII veteran (First Canadian Infantry) and graduate of McGill and Bishop's Universities.

Philip Mortimer Caddell was born July 7, 1913 in Brantford, Ontario, Canada, and died July 24, 2004 in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada (age 91). His parents were Captain William Persse Caddell and Florence May Ogden. He had an older brother Shirley Lee Forsythe Caddell (born November 1911).

Philip 'Pip' Caddell was born in Canada (Brantford, Ontario) but raised in Scotland; he returned to Canada as a teenager. He married Elga Ramsey in 1945. Elga (born 1917) was a devout Anglican associated with St. Philip's in Montreal West.

Philip 'Pip' Caddell's employer was a local brewer. He attended the 1936 Montreal Maroons vs Detroit Red Wings six-overtime playoff game (settled by Mud Bruneteau) and the 1935 Maroons Stanley Cup win. His spoken story 'The Black Horse' — about helping his employer honour a commitment to reward Maroons captain Hooley Smith with a Percheron horse — was transcribed from memory by his son Andrew and published posthumously in 'The Goal.'

James Lawrence Caddell was born March 16, 1973 in Montreal. His mother was Norma Lewis, a journalist and communications lecturer at Dawson College who covered John Lennon's 'bed-in' for peace for the Montreal Gazette in 1969. Andrew Caddell was one of her former students.

James Caddell graduated from Cortland High School near Syracuse, NY in 1991. He moved to Montreal and attended Dawson College, then enrolled at McGill University in North American studies before switching to political science and history (BA ~1997). In summer 1997 he was a Normandy Foundation Scholar (six-week tour of European battlefields: Waterloo, Somme, D-Day Normandy).

James Caddell earned an MA in War Studies from Royal Military College, Kingston (1998-2000, as a civilian student). At RMC he met Tara Newell (MA in Public Administration at Queen's); they recognized each other from McGill where James had worked part-time for the Student Society and Tara had signed his paycheques as Student Society president.

James Caddell joined the Royal Canadian Hussars reserve while at Dawson/McGill. In 1995 he took a year off, trained at CFB Valcartier, and deployed to Bosnia: Rotation 5 of Operation Cavalier, May-October 1995, serving in CANBAT 2 (Canadian Battle Group 2), part of UNPROFOR, as a Cougar driver in 42 Troop of 'D' Squadron of the 12e Régiment blindé du Canada. He was awarded the Peacekeeping Service Medal and UNPROFOR Medal.

James Caddell died October 16, 2005 in Tupiza, Bolivia (age 32) of pulmonary edema caused by altitude sickness. He had suffered altitude sickness on Mount Everest 9 months earlier above 5,000m. Tupiza is below 3,000m; no one in the hotel or local hospital recognized the symptoms or had oxygen. His wife Tara Newell was beside him.

James and Tara Caddell's world trip started June 2004. Itinerary: crossed Australia, toured Hanoi and Angkor Wat, humanitarian work in East Timor and Indonesia, 2 months as CMAT volunteer at orphanage in Kannyakumari district (Tamil Nadu, India) working with children orphaned by the 2004 tsunami, trekked in Nepal, toured Gallipoli and Jerusalem, dined in Provence, learned Spanish in Buenos Aires and Santiago, arrived by bus in Bolivia.

Tara Newell (wife of James Caddell) founded the James Caddell Memorial Foundation providing educational opportunities for marginalized girls in India. She spent 16 years with MSF (Médecins Sans Frontières), including Emergency Coordinator deployed to Syria, culminating as MSF's Representative to the United Nations. As of August 2025, she is Chief Programs Officer (VP) at CARE Canada.

Andrew Caddell married Elaine Feldman; children: James (1973-2005), Emily, and Jack. He is a double graduate of Carleton University, Ottawa, with an MA in Journalism (2002, thesis: 'Like Moths to a Flame: the news media's influence on the United Nations and the specialized agencies').

Andrew Caddell's career: broadcast journalist (Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec City, Calgary, St. John's, 1975-1981), political advisor (1980-1986), Director of Communications to Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador, Town Councillor Montreal West (1989-1993, Public Security), served with WHO Geneva and UNICEF in Macedonia and Bangladesh, foreign service officer at Global Affairs Canada for 15 years (last role: Senior Policy Advisor, North America Policy and Relations — Mexico), retired GAC July 2017.

Andrew Caddell's current roles include: weekly columnist for The Hill Times (Ottawa), frequent guest on CJAD Radio (Montreal), Town Councillor of Kamouraska Quebec, President of the Task Force on Linguistic Policy, Fellow of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute and Environics Institute, Principal of QIT Canada Inc. (Emergency Management software), and Advisor to the Montreal Irish Monument Foundation.

'The Goal: Stories about Our National Passion' by Andrew Caddell and Dave Stubbs (Deux Voiliers Publishing, 2015; revised/expanded edition 2017) contains Philip 'Pip' Caddell's posthumous spoken story 'The Black Horse' — a secondary source for Pip's biography and Montreal hockey culture of the 1930s.

Nelson McEwen, born c.1897 in Charlottetown, PEI, was hired in 1919 (age 22) as Assistant Boys Work Secretary at Winnipeg YMCA. He personally directed Camp Stephens in Winnipeg from 1924-1927, then was recruited to Montreal YMCA as Boys Work Secretary, where he directed Camp Kanawana c.1927-1947. This extends his documented Kanawana tenure from the previously known 1930-1931 to a ~20-year period.

Nelson McEwen co-founded the Canadian Camping Association with Taylor Statten, serving as Secretary while Statten was President. Note: CCA was formally founded in 1936 at Central YMCA Toronto; McEwen may have been involved in the 1946 reorganization/national assemblies rather than the 1936 founding.
Nelson McEwen developed the Hi-Y program to 'massive size' in Montreal and conducted two National Assemblies of Hi-Y at Geneva Park in 1940 and 1946.

In 1947, Nelson McEwen left Montreal to accept the position of General Secretary of the Saint John YMCA (New Brunswick). At Saint John he recruited Ross Bannerman, Lloyd and Niles Ring, and Doug Allen to YMCA careers.

Camp Becsies was located on Lac des Becs-scie, a lake in Saint-Sauveur (83%) and Mille-Isles (17%), in the same municipality as Camp Kanawana. The lake has a total area of 0.5 km², approximately 2.2 km long, 155-340m wide. It is likely one of the 'three private lakes' on or adjacent to Kanawana property.

Camp Becsies served campers from the Montreal Protestant Orphans' Home in 1934 and 1936. In the 1960-1971 period, Camp Becsies was repurposed for family camping (family camping brochure c.1962, administrative records 1960-1971). Photographs of Camp Becsies exist in the Concordia archives.

Camp Dorval (P0145/12E, 1926-1928, 0.5cm records) was a short-lived YMCA day camp in Dorval, Quebec (West Island of Montreal). Only 0.5cm of archival records survive for its three years of operation, suggesting a small operation.

Camp Thunderbird (P0145/12I) and the Wilderness Survival Camp (P0145/12J) are YMCA Montreal camps listed in the Concordia Archives. CORRECTED 2026-07-09: a direct fetch of the Concordia finding aid found a specific dated item, "Camp Thunderbird - brochure, correspondence, reports, publicity. -- 1942-1943" (Box HA2316) -- dating Camp Thunderbird to the early 1940s, not "the mid-1970s" as this fact previously speculated. The Wilderness Survival Camp's dating is confirmed and sharpened by finding-aid items: "Wilderness camp director's report" (1973), "Wilderness camping programs-brochures" (1973-1974), "Program planning 1974-75 -- Survival camp" (1974), and "Wilderness survival camp" (1975) -- a precise 1973-1975 operating window. The 1974 'Report of the Staff Task Group on Outdoor Education in the Montreal YMCA' and 1975 'Proposed Hike and Trip Camp' remain plausible context for the Wilderness Survival Camp's origin specifically, not Thunderbird's. No gender assignment is stated in either finding aid.
Camp Perrot (P0145/12G) was a boys' camp operated by Montreal YMCA. A document 'Comparison of Two Boys Camps operated by Montreal YMCA' compares Camp Perrot and Kamp Kanawana from c.1945-1946.

Gabor Ivan Zinner wrote an MA thesis at McGill University (Political Science, 1973) titled 'Noosphere - an experiment in simulation.' This almost certainly documents the Noosphere international development simulation held at Camp Kanawana in summer 1971. Available at https://escholarship.mcgill.ca/concern/theses/6w924d11w

The Noosphere simulation (1971) was modeled on a 'Third World Village' organized in Winnipeg the previous year (1970). It was the first time such an experience was attempted in Quebec. An 'education committee in Montreal with members from various development organizations' established the project.
A second newspaper article about the Noosphere simulation appeared in Montreal-matin on August 24, 1971 (BAnQ: https://numerique.banq.qc.ca/patrimoine/details/52327/4512657).
Gabor Ivan Zinner, author of the 1973 McGill thesis on Noosphere, is now a lawyer in Calgary, Alberta (Zinner Law Office, 100-1100 8 Ave SW). He practices civil litigation and commercial law.

Camp Kanawana held an 'Opening Campfire 2020' as a Facebook Live video, confirming the campfire/council ring tradition was active as recently as 2020 during COVID restrictions. URL: https://www.facebook.com/YKanawana/videos/opening-campfire-2020/1432885173577431/
Camp Kanawana has 4,416 photos on Flickr (flickr.com/photos/kanawana/) and an active Instagram account (@ymcakanawana, 1,835 followers, 573 posts as of June 2026).

The 1974-1975 Camp Kanawana director (who worked alongside Stuart McLean as assistant director) is confirmed NOT to be A. Ross Seaman (left for Dawson College 1974), NOT Dave Twynam (does not appear until at least 1976), and NOT Ross Bannerman (his 1969 report suggests an earlier role). The anonymous commenter who identified himself as this director on Westmount Magazine in 2017 was young enough to sublet McLean's Dorchester flat.

James Caddell was Senior Program Manager at Human Resources Development Canada before his world trip. After moving to Ottawa (~2000), he switched to the 2nd Intelligence Platoon of the Royal Canadian Hussars and received the Queen's Jubilee Medal from his new regiment.

James Caddell's memorial service was held in Ottawa on November 5, 2005. Obituaries were published in the Globe and Mail and Ottawa Citizen. A BillionGraves entry exists under the name 'Lawrence James Caddell.' A Wikipedia article on James Caddell exists.
Andrew Caddell's siblings/half-siblings of James include Emily Caddell and Jack Caddell (from Andrew's marriage to Elaine Feldman). Andrew's Twitter/X handle is @pipson52.
Ross Bannerman established the St. James YMCA branch in Winnipeg (date unspecified, between 1951 and 1956).

Derek Walsh search (32+ queries, 5 surfaces) returned zero new biographical information. He remains biographically opaque. The CCA fonds at Trent University and Concordia YMCA fonds are the only remaining leads requiring physical archive access.

The Pip Award recipients for 2019-2023 cannot be identified through publicly accessible web sources. 42+ queries across 8+ surfaces yielded zero results. The 2019 recipient's title begins with 'Dr.' per Andrew Caddell's LinkedIn. No YMCA Quebec press releases were published for any award 2019-2023.

Nelson McEwen died in 1956 while still in active YMCA service. He was serving as the first Metropolitan General Secretary of the Winnipeg YMCA at the time of his death, a position he accepted in 1951 after serving as General Secretary of the Saint John YMCA (1947-1951).

Nelson McEwen's full career timeline: born c.1897 Charlottetown, PEI; hired 1919 (age 22) as Assistant Boys Work Secretary, Winnipeg YMCA; directed Camp Stephens 1924-1927; recruited to Montreal YMCA as Boys Work Secretary c.1927; directed Camp Kanawana c.1927-1947; General Secretary, Saint John YMCA 1947-1951; first Metropolitan General Secretary, Winnipeg YMCA 1951-1956; died 1956 in active service.

Nelson McEwen founded the 'Order of the Triangle' at Camp Stephens, Winnipeg, during his tenure there (c.1919-1927). Through this program he recruited young men including Mitchel Sharp and Bill Master to YMCA service.

At the Saint John YMCA (1947-1951), Nelson McEwen recruited Ross Bannerman, Lloyd and Niles Ring, and Doug Allen to YMCA careers. This confirms the connection chain: McEwen recruited Bannerman at Saint John, Bannerman later directed Camp Pascobac (1951) and Camp Stephens (1956), then authored the 1969 Report on Kamp Kanawana.

The Camp Stephens Alumni blog states McEwen 'founded the Canadian Camping Association in 1946 with his good friend Taylor Statten.' The official CCA records show the CCA was founded on May 20, 1936, with Statten as president and Dr. George S. Patterson as secretary. McEwen's role may relate to a 1946 reorganization or national assembly rather than the original 1936 founding. The discrepancy between 1936 (CCA official) and 1946 (Camp Stephens blog) is unresolved.

Doug McEwen served as director of Camp Stephens from 1966-1970 and as President of the Canadian Camping Association from 1967-1969. He is listed in the CCA fonds at Trent University Archives as associated with 'YMCA Camp Wa-Sa-Ah-Dun, St. Catharines, Ontario.' His relationship to Nelson McEwen (possible son) is suggested by context but not confirmed.

The McMorris thesis documents Nelson McEwen as camp director in 1930-1931 only. The Camp Stephens Alumni blog documents him as Boys Work Secretary of the Montreal YMCA from c.1927 to 1947, directing Camp Kanawana throughout. The discrepancy is likely explained by McEwen holding an administrative title (Boys Work Secretary) while operational camp directors (Camp Chief / Director) such as Greig Macdiarmid (1935-1938) reported to him. McMorris may document only the years McEwen personally served as on-site camp director.

Concordia Archives sub-series 14D10 contains 'National Council Boys' Work Secretary, Nelson McEwen — E. M. Nelson Correspondence, 1941-1945.' This confirms McEwen's National Council role and his concurrent connection to the Montreal YMCA during wartime.

Nelson McEwen's deep biographical research (20+ web searches across 8+ surfaces) yielded no obituary text, no photograph, no birth/death exact dates, and no family details beyond what the Camp Stephens Alumni blog provides. Find A Grave has no matching record. Winnipeg Free Press historical archives not accessible online. Further research requires: (1) Winnipeg Free Press microfiche for 1956 obituary, (2) PEI vital statistics for birth record, (3) Concordia Archives 14D10 correspondence for biographical details.
Kate Taylor's camp alias/nickname at Kanawana is 'Wawa'.
Kate Taylor holds an Honours BA in Psychology from Trent University (Peterborough, Ontario).
Kate Taylor was previously Camp Director at Camp Ta-Wa-Si Inc. (Johnston's Point, Northumberland Strait, New Brunswick), a camp founded in 1940.

Kate Taylor led the introduction of a gender-expansive tent option at Camp Kanawana — a co-ed sleeping arrangement open to transgender, non-binary, and gender-questioning campers, or anyone who prefers it.

Kate Taylor appeared on three camping industry podcasts: Go Camp Pro 'Beyond Camp' #18 (Social Media Advocacy), CampHacker #147 (Summer Self-Care for Camp Directors), and Camp Code #95 (How to Combat Learning Loss in Your Staff Team).
Kate Taylor also served as Consultant & Graphic Designer at Stephane Richard Development Consulting (concurrent or sequential with Kanawana directorship).
Marie-Pierre Lacasse holds a BA in Leisure Sciences from Concordia University (2004-2006) and also studied at Universite Laval.
Marie-Pierre Lacasse is certified as a Leave No Trace Master Educator, Wilderness First Responder (WFR), and Red Cross First Aid Monitor.

Marie-Pierre Lacasse's career before Kanawana included: Wilderness Safety Systems (Asst Director, 2007-2012), Camp Boisjoly (DG, 2011-2014), Camp Odyssee/Minogami (Director, 2014-2015), Camp Portneuf (DG, 2015-2018), and roles at Loisirs Saint-Sacrement, Domaine du Lac bleu, and Unite de loisir et de sport de la Capitale-Nationale.

Marie-Pierre Lacasse launched the first ADHD-adapted summer camp in the greater Quebec City region at Camp Portneuf in 2018, collaborating with Lyne Guillemette of the Panda Association. The ADHD groups had 1 monitor per 3 youth (vs. 1:5 regular) and included psychoeducators.

Marie-Pierre Lacasse launched 'Aventure a Kanawana' (Kanawana Adventure) day camp in summer 2024 — an English-immersion day camp for ages 5-12, maximum capacity 48 children, with shuttle service from Saint-Sauveur. It is the first day camp program in Kanawana's 130-year history.

Lac Kanawana has RSVL monitoring station number 573, with monitoring data since at least 2013. Precise physical data: surface area 0.2388 km2, maximum depth 12.4 m, volume 1,273,000 m3, altitude 318.4 m, watershed area 5.17 km2, drainage ratio 22.00.
The camp beach is listed on Swim Guide (ID 5490) and Great Lakes Guide as 'Plage du camp Kanawana YMCA camp Beach', indicating formal water quality monitoring for swimming safety.
Lac Kanawana is in the Riviere du Nord watershed; the associated watershed organization is ABRINORD (Organisme de bassin versant de la riviere du Nord).

Philip D. Fagans (spelled 'Fas-ana' in 1918 Gazette, likely OCR error) was Seton's Executive Secretary of the Woodcraft League of America, headquartered at 13 West 29th St, New York City. Before that, he was a YMCA camp director at Trenton NJ and West Side YMCA Camp NYC, and later founded Greenkill Camp in Kingston NY.
