The 1962 Kamp Kanawana map (viewed directly, McMorris thesis Figure 2.6, same P145/12B07 folder) uses a numbered legend: 1 Craftshop, 2 Lodge, 3 Long House, 4 Dining Hall, 5 Business Office, 6 Chief's Cabin, 7 Pump House, 8 Windward Ho!, 9 Sanctan. It also labels Lac des Becsies, Round Lake, Lake Wilson, Lake Kanawana, Snowshoe Lake (a lake name not otherwise documented in this KB), Farewell Rock, Parliament Rock, Frog Bay, Chapel, Baseball Field, Indian Council Ring, Look Out, Sandy Beach, Cougars and Pioneers/Woodsmen/Coureurs des Bois/Pathfinders section clusters, a sailboat icon, and a trail to Saint-Sauveur. Golf Course and Lacrosse Field, both present on the 1928 map, are absent from the 1962 map -- narrowing the golf course's decommissioning window to sometime between 1928 and 1962.

Concordia Archives P145/12B03's finding aid (Box HA2694) itemizes several architectural drawings/blueprints not previously catalogued in this KB: 'Sleeping cabins, Kamp Kanawana' (pencil architect's drawing, 1940), 'Eight-boy Cabin' (Boy Scouts of America Engineering Service blueprint, 1945), and 'Proposed craft shop Kamp Kanawana' (blueprint, 1952) -- the last predating the 1960 Millen Memorial Craft Shop dedication (f_1788) by 8 years, suggesting either a distinct earlier proposal or a multi-year planning process for the same building. Box HA2313 separately holds a dining/kitchen pavilion blueprint and letter (1919), ice-house/cold-storage blueprints (c.1929), 1950s water-filtration-system blueprints, and undated architectural drawings for the Lodge and the boat dock.

Concordia Archives P145/12B03, Box HA2342, lists an item 'Map of Camp Agaming. -- 1929' alongside three undated (1960s) colour photos of Kanawana in the same folder. 'Camp Agaming' does not appear anywhere else in this KB or in general web search -- it's unclear whether this is a mislabeled/alternate name for a Kanawana-related site or a genuinely distinct camp filed in the same folder by association. Flagged as an unresolved lead, not investigated further this session.

Olivier Charron (b. Nov 4, 1830, Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, Laval; d. Nov 15, 1902, age 72) became owner of lot number 280 "located at Lac Kanawana" in 1887 -- seven years before the YMCA's 1894 founding of Camp Kanawana (then Camp Jubilee, at a different lake). He married Arthémise Bouchard in 1851. This is a distinct pre-camp landowner from the Pagé family (lot 43, côte Saint-Elmire), documented on the same municipal pioneer-families page but not previously extracted from it.

The Répertoire du patrimoine culturel du Québec (Quebec government cultural heritage registry), in its group entry for the YMCA (id 8364), states verbatim: "le camp Kanawana en 1894. Ce dernier permet aux enfants de s'éloigner de l'air pollué de la ville" -- an official government source directly naming and dating Camp Kanawana's 1894 founding as the YMCA's first vacation camp located outside the city.

"Live a lot" is a song traditionally sung at the closing ceremony of every session at Camp Kanawana, performed (per a YouTube video titled "Live a lot- Camp YMCA Kanawana") by then-Camp Director Sean Day.

Camp YMCA Kanawana issued an official statement/video, "Camp YMCA Kanawana Stands with Trans Campers," on its Facebook page, committing to pronoun accommodation, equitable and safe sleeping arrangements regardless of sex assigned at birth, and staff education on trans-youth issues. The exact date of the post could not be confirmed from the fetch.

"Journée plein air" (Outdoor Day) is an annual event hosted at Camp YMCA Kanawana, a partnership between the Ville de Saint-Sauveur and the Club Optimiste de la Vallée de Saint-Sauveur. The 2023 edition was held Sunday, August 27, 2023, offering guided hiking, archery, fishing, free canoe/kayak/paddleboard use, rock climbing, and beach access, with a free shuttle from Mont-Habitant (no on-site parking). The event historically focused on trout fishing and has expanded in scope since approximately 2022.
entities: Club Optimiste de la Vallée de Saint-Sauveur

facts.claim: "Companion" is a current Camp YMCA Kanawana staff role providing one-on-one inclusion support: the Companion supervises one assigned camper with special needs all day (meals, activities, personal care), sleeps in that camper's cabin/tent, and plans activities with them across the four 12-day sessions. The role requires French plus intermediate English, First Aid/CPR certification, and a clean criminal record check.

A job listing titled "Director, Outdoor Education Centre Kanawana" was found on Glassdoor, indicating a distinct off-season directorship title for Kanawana's Outdoor Education Centre operation, separate from the summer camp on-site Director role documented in directors-index.md. The direct page fetch returned a 403 error; the title is confirmed only via a search-result snippet, not the full listing text, and should be treated as an unverified lead pending independent corroboration.

Grace McMorris, author of the 2023 Concordia MA thesis on Kamp Kanawana, was listed as a "recent graduate" panelist with affiliation "Historica Canada" (Canada's national heritage/public-history organization) at a Concordia History Department careers event, "Where Will Your History MA Take You?", held March 25, 2024. No further post-graduate career detail is given.

Camp Kanawana has a review listing on CampRatingz.com with 9 anonymous user-submitted reviews spanning 2007-2014, averaging 3.8/5. The platform's existence and aggregate rating are noted here as stated fact; the substance of individual anonymous reviews (including one unverified 2012 allegation of institutional safety lapses) is NOT integrated as fact and is instead flagged for human review -- see priorities.json (p_194).

Camp YMCA Kanawana requires every camper and their parent/guardian to read and sign a formal bilingual "Serment du campeur / Camper's Oath," tied explicitly to the camp motto "Non Nobis Solum" ("Not for Ourselves alone"). The 2010 and 2013 versions are nearly word-for-word identical. The oath's promises are: Respect the natural environment that makes camp so beautiful; Treat all campers and staff with respect and courtesy; Use appropriate language; Respect other's belongings; Respect all safety regulations implemented by Kanawana staff during activities on camp and on canoe trip expeditions; Not use or possess alcohol or illegal substances during my stay at camp or a canoe trip expedition; Not use tobacco during my stay at camp or a canoe trip expedition off property; Contribute to the camp community through happiness, enthusiasm and humour. The signed copy is kept on file at the camp office.

Rob Braide, President of Standard Broadcasting Corporation and of Montreal radio stations CHOM, MIX 96, and CJAD, was a Camp Kanawana camper for 9 summers. In 1967, at age 14, he and 6 other boys plus a counsellor undertook a week-long, 150-mile canoe trip from Camp Kanawana in Saint-Sauveur to Ottawa, re-tracing the historic east-west fur-trade route between Deep River and Ottawa, facing rapids, high waves, and long portages. His testimonial was published in a 2007 Camp YMCA Kanawana recruitment document, "Reportage vécu."

A 2006 Camp YMCA Kanawana staff application form lists "sean.day@ymcamontreal.qc.ca" as its contact email, confirming Sean Day held a staff or administrative role at Kanawana by 2006. This does not by itself establish that he held the Director title that year -- it is contextual evidence, not a resolution, for conflict c_017 (Sean Day's documented directorship start, disputed between 2005 and 2008).

The 2005 English-language Camp YMCA Kanawana Parent Handbook (recovered from the predecessor ymcakanawana.com domain via Wayback) carries the document-author metadata "aboyer" -- a plausible but unconfirmed reference to Arleen Boyer, the camp's Executive Director 1995-2000 (see directors-index.md). The document postdates her documented tenure by roughly five years, so this is a lead rather than a confirmation: she may have continued authoring administrative templates informally, or the metadata may simply be inherited from an older template file.

As of June 16, 2026, ymcaquebec.org hosts a new authoritative current-year parent preparation guide ("Camp-Kanawana-GUIDE-Parent-EN_2026.pdf" / "-FR_2026.pdf"), superseding both the January 2026 and 2025 versions previously cached. It follows the same 43-page structure as the 2025 guide, with the canoe-trip complement embedded in the same PDF (pages 29+) rather than as a separate document. Not yet re-extracted in full for content changes.

The YMCA of Montreal's 1890-91 Annual Report (presented May 28, 1891) announces securing "the services of Mr. W. H. Ball as Physical Director. Mr. Ball is a graduate of the Springfield School... commences his work with us first of September next." The same report separately identifies him as "Mr. W.H. Ball, jr., of Yonkers, N.Y." -- indicating he came to Montreal from Yonkers, New York.

W. H. Ball is confirmed as the YMCA of Montreal's Physical Director in every annual report checked from 1892-93 through 1900, a consecutive run spanning the 1894 founding of Camp Jubilee (the original Camp Kanawana).

The YMCA of Montreal's 1902 Annual Report states: "Mr. W. H. Ball, the Association's first Physical Director, who rendered such helpful service during the past ten years... resigned and accepted a similar position with the Prospect Park Branch of the Brooklyn Association. He was succeeded by Mr. J. E. Merritt." This confirms a roughly ten-year Montreal tenure (September 1891 to 1901 or 1902).

Lovell's Montreal Directory, 1893-94, independently corroborates W.H. Ball's YMCA role via a non-YMCA-produced source: an institutional listing reads "YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION, D.A. Budge, general secretary; T.D. Patton, asst secretary; W. H. Ball, physical director, Dorchester cor Dominion Sq," and a separate residential street-directory line reads "Ball W. H., physical director Y.M.C.A."

Two caveats qualify the identification of "Billy Ball" with W.H. Ball, Physical Director: (1) no period document found uses the nickname "Billy" -- he is always referred to as "W. H. Ball" or "Mr. Ball" in contemporary sources; "Billy Ball" appears only in modern (21st-century) secondary sources such as the YMCA Quebec website and QAHN. (2) No period document explicitly states Ball personally led the 1894 boys' camp trip -- the YMCA of Montreal's 1894-95 annual report's Physical Department section (his department) describing the first Summer Camp is unsigned, a separate Junior Department camp committee in that era is credited to volunteer chairman John W. Ross, and the 1895-96 Summer Camp writeup is signed by Wm. Tees, Chairman -- neither names Ball specifically.

A self-published alumni blog, "Camp Otoreke Blog" (established 2005 by former staff, low reliability -- single uncorroborated source with anonymous/pseudonymous commenters), suggests the site is still informally called "Otoreke Island" and was privately owned by multiple co-owners by 2008 (a commenter identifying as "Michael Evans" states he was "one of the current owners of Otoreke Island" and hosted a 2005 reunion there). A separate 2005 commenter ("Finn Sander") describes the camp buildings as having suffered "years of neglect, invasive foliage, cyclic freezing and thawing, pervasive humidity, and attendant mould and rot" by that year -- i.e., abandoned/derelict rather than redeveloped. No official toponym search (Quebec's Commission de toponymie) confirms "Otoreke Island" as a recognized place name.

The same low-reliability, single-source "Camp Otoreke Blog" (see f_1834) posts a staff roster from a commenter ("Howard Duncan"): Ron and Valma Huppfield ran the camp during WWII; Rev. and Mrs. McGerrigle were directors afterward; Colin and Mrs. Mackay succeeded the McGerrigles as directors in the early 1960s. These names do NOT appear elsewhere in this KB and have no independent corroboration -- flagged explicitly for verification (YMCA annual reports, obituaries) before any standalone biography stub is created, per CLAUDE.md's formal-RALPH requirement for people stubs.

Re-mining the already-cited BaladoDecouverte heritage-tour source (previously used only for the 1897/two-islands/80-campers claims) surfaces unextracted detail: a local entrepreneur named Victor Bergeron was hired to build a two-story log cabin able to house 25 young men, and the early Camp Jubilee/Otoreke operation purchased staples "from the Bergin and Corbeil General Store."

Concordia University Archives sub-series P0145/12C (Camp Otoreke) is organized into seven sub-sub-series: 12C01 (General administration), 12C02 (Financial administration), 12C03 (Land/facilities/equipment/supplies), 12C04 (Communications), 12C05 (Staff/counsellors), 12C06 (Campers), 12C07 (Program). The finding aid confirms the existence -- but not the content -- of 1982 revenue/expenditure and tax-status records within 12C02, suggesting Camp Otoreke's closure-year finances were documented, though the documents themselves are not available online.

Two open ambiguities in the Concordia finding aid for Camp Otoreke-related material: (1) two separate 1967 catalog entries -- "Report of the Boys' and Girls' Camping Committee to the Metropolitan Planning and Development Committee of the YMCA of Montreal" (Box HA1881) and "Camp Otoreke report -- Planning and Development" (Box HA2367) -- may be the same document cross-referenced or two distinct related documents. (2) W.E. Cushing's 1943 manuscript appears under two variant titles/locations: "Early Days at Lake St. Joseph" (Box HA1881) versus the previously-cited "Historical sketches -- Lake St. Joseph" (Box HA2307) -- possibly the same manuscript catalogued twice, or two distinct short pieces. Neither ambiguity is resolvable online; both require a physical Concordia Archives visit.

The YMCA of Montreal's 1930 Annual Report (covering the 1929 season) describes the new equipment on "Lac Becscies" as furthered by building a wharf, a new dining pavilion, four new tent floors, and a well, explicitly stating: "This camp will form a valuable annex to the main camp for 'peak' periods and also for overnight and short term out-trips." This reframes Camp Becsies, at least in its origin, as Kanawana's own overflow/annex infrastructure rather than an independently operated camp.

The Montreal Protestant Orphans' Home was given free use of the YMCA's Lac Becscies equipment for four consecutive seasons -- 1933, 1934, 1935, and 1936 -- per the YMCA of Montreal Annual Reports for 1934, 1935, 1936, and 1937 respectively, each using near-identical wording ("given the free use of our auxiliary camp equipment," or in 1937, "again given, free of charge, the use of our property on Lake Bec-scies, for which their Board has expressed generous appreciation"). This refines the previously documented "1934 and 1936" claim to all four consecutive years.

The YMCA of Montreal's 1937 Annual Report names W.J.G. Macdiarmid as the Kanawana Camp Director in the same passage documenting that year's (1936 season's) Protestant Orphans' Home free-use-of-Becscies arrangement. This independently corroborates the already-documented director in directors-index.md (Greig / W.J.G. Macdiarmid, Camp Chief 1935-1938+). The 1934 Annual Report separately names W.H. Spearman as Kanawana's Camp Director for the 1933 season.

The YMCA of Montreal's 1930 Annual Report records a $201.00 surplus applied against $2,258.00 in capital expenditure "on the Becscies extension and the new craft shop" for the 1929 season (a combined figure, not broken out separately). The same report states a group of businessmen from the Westmount Branch underwrote the expense of twelve boys from the Protestant Orphans' Home to attend as regular Kanawana campers that season -- a separate sponsorship channel, distinct from the later equipment-loan arrangement at Becscies.

A systematic check of YMCA of Montreal Annual Reports for every year from 1938 through 1962 (21+ consecutive years) found zero mentions of "Becscies," "Becsies," "Becs-Scie," or the Protestant Orphans' Home camp arrangement -- confirming the 1936 end-date of the documented arrangement but leaving the reason for the subsequent gap (until Camp Becsies' 1960 resumption) undocumented. Notably, Kanawana itself recorded its highest attendance to that point in the 1937-38 season (407 boys, 1,442 camper-weeks, "necessary to refuse registration for periods in July"), arguing against a simple Depression-driven cost-cutting explanation for the Becsies arrangement's end, though this doesn't rule out reasons specific to the Orphans' Home side.

Camp Amy Molson, founded May 23, 1944 by the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent Society specifically as a dedicated summer camp for children from foster homes/orphanages (58 campers, 5 counsellors in its first season), is a plausible but unconfirmed contributing thread to the Camp Becsies 1936-1960 gap. It does not cleanly explain the gap: a 7-8 year unexplained span remains (1936 to 1944), and the Ladies' Benevolent Society and the Protestant Orphans' Home were still separate organizations at that date (they merged c.1946-1947, see f_1845).

The Montreal Protestant Orphans' Home was founded in 1822 as the Protestant Orphan Asylum, built a permanent home in 1849 on St. Catherine St. near Drummond, moved to Summerhill/Cote-des-Neiges in 1894, and merged with the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent Society around 1946 or 1947 (sources disagree on the exact year) to form the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent and Protestant Orphans' Society, later known as Summerhill Homes. Retrieved only via search-result summaries -- direct fetch of the source page returned HTTP 503 twice -- so this should be independently re-verified, especially the exact merger year, before being treated as fully confident.

The Woodcraft League of America (the national woodcraft-movement organization Kanawana chartered a tribe in circa 1922) grew to roughly 5,000 members at its peak in the 1920s-30s, declined during the WWII-era shift toward industrialization and Cold War militarism, and dissolved entirely in 1946 after founder Ernest Thompson Seton's death, when his family declined to keep the organization running. This is general/national context, not a Kanawana-specific charter-lapse date.

Grace McMorris's thesis (re-mined via a direct full-PDF extraction) quotes Kanawana's own 1925 season report stating the Woodcraft League program was "easily adapted to camp" (thesis p.58) -- a verbatim primary-source quote not previously captured in the KB.

The "Kanawana Outing Club" (previously known only from a felt badge reading "KANAWANA OUTING CLUB" around a YMCA triangle logo) is confirmed via direct fetches of the Concordia finding aid (sub-sub-series 12B03, 12B04, and 12B07) as a distinct WINTER-season hiking/trail program, with its own trail system ("Kanawana Outing Club trails"), its own promotional poster and artwork/printing plate, running at least from the 1970s ([197-]) through 1979 per the archivist's own bracketed annotation on the 12B07 item -- separate from the main summer honour-award badge system.

The Concordia finding aid (sub-sub-series 12B07, Program) lists earlier winter-camping precedents than the "1970s" window currently attributed to Winter Outdoor Family Camping: a "Winter ski camp" (1945-1947) and a one-off "Winter camp" (January 28-29, 1961). Whether either is the same program as the later Winter Outdoor Family Camping or Winter Kanawana Outing Club is not confirmed -- flagged as a plausible link, not a confirmed identity.

The Concordia finding aid (sub-series 12B01, General Administration) lists a "Working paper on year-round use" dated 1969, showing the YMCA was formally studying year-round use of the Kanawana site 27 years before the 1996 year-round residential programming launch already documented in this KB. This directly precedes, and may help explain, the camp's 1994-95 leadership restructuring into a year-round Executive Director plus a three-season on-site Camp Director.

Grace McMorris's thesis (re-mined via a direct full-PDF extraction) explicitly declines to cover how Kanawana's coeducational programming -- including how the L&V Games' masculine team structure (Lumbermen and Voyageurs) adapted for girls after 1968 -- worked in practice: "A study of co-ed camps, or even of Kanawana's co-ed programming, is beyond the scope of my research since I am focusing on the kinds of masculine ideals that were being promoted by Kanawana..." (thesis, scope statement) and, in her conclusion: "This would have had a dramatic effect on the camp dynamic. How did the camp's mission and programming change to reflect the presence of girls and women at camp?... the development of femininity at and through summer camp is another area of research I am most interested in." This documents the open question as a genuine, acknowledged gap in the existing academic literature on Kanawana, not merely an unresearched item for this project.

The Concordia finding aid for Camp Dorval (sub-series 12E) lists specific items "Camp Dorval director's report" (1926) and "Report on Camp Dorval season 1928" (Box HA1894), plus photographs (Box HA2318) -- consistent with, and slightly more granular than, the already-documented 1926-1928 operating window. No gender assignment is stated in the finding aid.

Mary Susannah Edgar's biography, per the Trent University Archives finding aid for her fonds: parents Joseph Edgar and Mary Little; educated at Sundridge Public School, Barrie High School, Havergal Ladies College (Toronto), University of Chicago extension courses, and Teachers College, Columbia University; graduated the YWCA National Training School, New York City, 1915. She held a YWCA 'First National Girls' Work' role from 1912 to 1914 -- predating her 1915-1919 Montreal/Oolahwan period. In 1920 she undertook a four-month YWCA volunteer posting in Japan, and that same year purchased the Lake Bernard property -- two years before Glen Bernard Camp opened in 1922, refining the previously-recorded chronology.

Mary Edgar wrote four books, not one as previously recorded: Wood-fire and Candlelight (1945), Under Open Skies (1956), The Christmas Wreath of Verse (1967), and Once There Was a Camper (1970). She collaborated with Canadian Girls in Training, Girl Guides of Canada, the Canadian Camping Association, and the Ontario Camping Association.

Grace McMorris's thesis (full-text extraction) states that visits between Kanawana and its girls'-camp neighbours were not a one-off: 'in the 1940s Kanawana occasionally hosted visitors from... Camp Oolahwan... and from the Junior League Camp.' The exact date of the already-documented cocoa/'Indians' greeting event is now pinned to the 'Intermediate Section Log, 17 July 1946' (YMCA of Montreal fonds, P145/12B07).

A previously undocumented girls' camp, the Junior League (of Montreal) Camp -- serving the Griffintown Girls Club, opened 1921, a 'fresh-air' camp funded by galas/social events for underprivileged children -- also had contact with Kanawana. McMorris's thesis cites the 'Intermediate Section Report, 5 July 1943,' recording that some Kanawana counsellors snuck off to the Junior League camp to meet women counsellors there -- a distinct, dated cross-camp social contact.

A 1970s photograph from Camp Oolahwan itself (Figure 2.9 in McMorris's thesis) shows girls in 'Indian' costumes -- direct evidence that Oolahwan practiced its own 'playing Indian' tradition, paralleling Kanawana's. A separate undated Camp Oolahwan newspaper advertisement (Figure 1.4) exists in the Y des femmes Montreal collection.

Library and Archives Canada's 'Montreal Young Women's Christian Association fonds' catalog description (not yet accessed/extracted) lists a dedicated series: 'Camp Oolahwan committee minutes, reports and training programmes, 1916-1974,' plus Committee minutes (1910-1973), Finance (1918-1975), Reports (1877-1972), and photographs (1937-1973). This is a strong new lead for Camp Oolahwan's capacity, age range, and post-Halliday directors -- see priorities.json for the future ingestion item.

The Junior League of Montreal was founded in 1912; its summer camp (the one that had contact with Kanawana) was founded in 1921, financed partly via a 1930-31 campaign that also funded a Griffintown dental clinic and hospital canteens. Per the McCord Stewart Museum's own fonds description, the camp welcomed 300+ girls per year by the early 1960s (roughly 12,000 girls total), and 'today, Camp Amy Molson carries on its mission.' A 1956 Maclean's article states that as of that year, 'for thirty-six years' the League had given nearly 400 underprivileged girls a three-week vacation at a Laurentians camp, with the Montreal branch then the oldest in Canada (511 members).

The YMCA of Montreal's 1994 Annual Report (English and French editions) states under 'Kamp Kanawana': 'This was Kanawana's 100th year of operation. As part of the centennial celebration, an Alumni reunion was held during Labor Day weekend attracting over 200 past campers and staff.' This directly answers how the camp's 1994 centennial was marked: an alumni reunion, Labor Day weekend, 200+ attendees.
The same 1994 Annual Report also records: camper registration reached 101% of capacity, camper return rate was 70%, and there were 40 subsidized campers (a 10% increase over 1993).

A 'Kanawana calendar 1993/94' is held in Concordia Archives Box HA1874 (same box as The Look Out, Vol. 1 #3), per the Concordia finding aid -- a previously uncatalogued item in this KB, adjacent to the newsletter.

The 1989 French YMCA of Montreal Annual Report describes a separate, earlier institutional anniversary: the 'Centenary of YMCA Camping in Canada' (1889-1989), marking 100 years since Big Cove (Halifax YMCA, 1889) -- NOT Kanawana's own centennial. Kanawana and 28 other YMCA camps participated via a relay campfire: ashes from a fire lit at Big Cove were distributed to every YMCA camp, each burning a campfire for 29 hours (one hour per camp) comparing songs/legends/customs, culminating in a time capsule (camper signatures plus campfire ashes) buried at the October Canadian Camping Association congress. This event is easily confused with the 1994 Kanawana-specific centennial and with an April 7, 1989 '95 years of sharing' Kanawana reunion (the same year, a different event) -- flagged for careful disambiguation.
entities: Centenary of YMCA Camping in Canada

facts.claim: The 1989 French Annual Report documents a five-year facility 'rajeunissement' (rejuvenation) campaign at Kamp Kanawana totaling $250,000, underway as of 1989; Kamp Kanawana facilities/equipment renewal was one of ten designated targets in the YMCA Montreal Foundation's endowment/planned-giving initiative.

The 1988-89 Kamp Kanawana Committee, per the 1989 French Annual Report, comprised Andre Herard, Chris Adam, Keith Farquharson, Paul Cappelli, Derek Walsh, Tom Snabl, Bruce Netherwood (YMCA), Maureen McBride, Jay Netherwood (YMCA), and Bill Pigott (YMCA) -- confirming Derek Walsh's Kanawana committee involvement in this era, corroborating his separately-known 1983 CCA Award of Excellence.

The 1990 Annual Report lists 'Netherwood, Bruce (Director, Kamp Kanawana)' and separately 'Netherwood, Jay (Supervisor, Kamp Kanawana)' -- showing Jay Netherwood remained on staff in a supervisory role after handing the Director title to his brother Bruce, refining the existing directorship timeline. The same report describes a five-year strategic-planning process (begun circa 1990) covering building strategies for the Downtown YMCA and Kamp Kanawana, as well as the Du Parc YMCA.

The YMCA of Montreal's 1971-72 Annual Report states: 'A ski tow has been installed there to broaden the scope of winter programming' -- the earliest documented step toward Kanawana's Winter Outdoor Family Camping program, one year before the fuller description below.

The 1972-73 Annual Report precisely dates the Winter Outdoor Family Camping program: 'A ski lift has already been installed there, two slopes have been groomed for downhill runs and miles of trails marked for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Emphasis this past winter was on providing families with opportunities to participate together in outdoor recreation. Courses of instruction were carried on for all ages, and a babysitting service enabled parents with toddlers to take part in activities.' This replaces the previous broad dating of 'the 1970s' with a precise winter 1972-73 description.

Further institutional-history data points from the annual reports: the 1974-75 report records 475 campers, the 'second highest registration in 25 years' despite a national decline in resident camping; the 1976-77 report documents the 'commencement of the planning process for new facilities at Kamp Kanawana'; the 1980-81 report records over 750 children at Kanawana.

The 1996 Annual Report states: 'This was the first time that programs were offered to groups other than summer campers. A group of 50 Korean students... participated in traditional camp activities for four days, sleeping in tents, cooking on open fires and integrating with the campers.' This documents a genuine 1996 'first,' but describes an in-season (summer) international-student visit, not a winter/off-season residential stay -- it corroborates 1996 as a diversification milestone but does not by itself confirm the separately-sourced claim that year-round RESIDENTIAL programming began that year; the two claims may be related but are not shown to be the same thing.

A systematic check of every YMCA of Montreal Annual Report from 1980 through 1988 (8 consecutive years) found no mention of 'outing club,' 'winter,' or 'ski' in the Kanawana section -- the Kanawana Outing Club's exact wind-down date after 1979 remains a confirmed dead end for this surface.

The well-known songwriter Richard Kerr (Barry Manilow's co-writer) has no documented connection to YMCA camp songs or 'On My Way to Kanawana,' per Wikipedia and SecondHandSongs. The KB's 'Richard "Itch" Kerr' (the actual Kanawana camp-song composer and 2007 Pip Award recipient) is very likely a distinct, non-notable person -- this identity question remains open, not resolved in favour of the famous songwriter.

Two documented sources disagree on institutional continuity for Montreal's mid-century girls'/underprivileged-children's summer camps: the McCord Stewart Museum's own Junior League of Montreal fonds (P685) description states 'today, Camp Amy Molson carries on its mission' -- implying Camp Amy Molson is a successor to the Junior League's 1921 camp. But Camp Amy Molson's own official history states it was founded May 23, 1944 by the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent and Protestant Orphans' Society (not the Junior League), with 58 campers in its first season. See conflict c_018 -- flagged for human/editorial review, not resolved by the 'oral history yields to documents' policy since both sides are documented institutional sources, not an oral-history-vs-document case.
entities: Montreal Ladies' Benevolent and Protestant Orphans' Society

facts.claim: A full-text search of Grace McMorris's thesis (129-page PDF, re-extracted directly) found zero matches for 'McConnell' anywhere in the document, and exactly two matches for 'Wilson' -- both trivial, simply listing 'Lake Kanawana and Lake Wilson' as the camp's two swimming/canoeing lakes with no discussion of naming origin, donation, or any connection to a person named Wilson. This resolves the McMorris-thesis question for both j-w-mcconnell.md and lake-wilson.md: the thesis is not a source for either question and can be marked exhausted.

Three more official Quebec 'Lac Wilson' toponymy entries were found beyond the one already known (Sainte-Lucie-des-Laurentides): Brownsburg-Chatham (fiche 451695) -- named for a family who owned the land in the early 20th century, who also built a dam on Reardon Creek to create the lake; Saint-Theophile (fiche 67250) -- named for a man named Wilson who reportedly built a fishing camp there; and Grenville-sur-la-Rouge (fiche 67246), origin undetermined. 3 of 4 documented Quebec 'Lac Wilson' toponyms are named for a landowner/settler named Wilson (one involving a dam, like the camp's own Lake Wilson) -- this pattern evidence mildly favours the pre-existing-settler-family hypothesis over the McConnell-son hypothesis for the camp's own Lake Wilson naming, though it does not prove it.

Wilson Griffith McConnell (b. March 3, 1908, d. January 12, 1966), per a Concordia AccessToMemory finding-aid search snippet, managed St. Lawrence Sugar and was a jazz enthusiast/collector of recordings and equipment. No mention of Camp Kanawana, the YMCA, or Lake Wilson appears in the visible finding-aid description. Obtained only via search-engine snippet, not a full-text confirmation.

Concordia's public finding-aid summary page confirms exact box locations, but not content, for the three manuscripts most likely to discuss Lake Wilson's naming: Ralph Dawson's 'History of Kamp Kanawana' (1933, Box HA2307); R.L. Charlton's 'Notes re Early Days of YMCA Camps at Lake St. Joseph and Kanawana' (1943, also catalogued as 'Early Days of YMCA Camps,' attributed to 'R.H. Charlton' in one listing, Box HA1881); and W.E. Cushing's 'Historical sketches - Lake St. Joseph' / 'Early Days at Lake St. Joseph' (1943, Box HA1881). No secondary source anywhere reproduces or summarizes their content regarding the lake name -- confirmed dead end for content without physical archive access.

The two 1961 Dimock 'studies' are unpublished internal YMCA/camp administrative research reports, not journal articles, per the Concordia finding aid: both titled documents sit in Box HA2323 of the YMCA of Montreal fonds, alongside 'Interpretation of Score for Counselors Participating in the Research Project at Kamp Kanawana' (1960) and 1961 opinion/attitude questionnaires and score sheets. A previously undocumented THIRD report extends Dimock's Kanawana-linked research to 1970: 'Research on the Selection and Training of Camp Leaders' (1970), also in Box HA2323. Related preliminary materials sit in Box HA2317: 'Camp Leadership Project Interim Report' (1959), an application questionnaire (1960), and 'Montreal YMCA 1960 Research Project - Study Group One/Two' plus '1960 YMCA Camping Research Project' folders 1-7 (1960-1961). This explains why no journal-publication citation exists in JSTOR, Google Scholar, HathiTrust, or ERIC (all checked, all null) -- the material was never published outside internal YMCA administrative channels.

A full-text search of Grace McMorris's thesis (129-page PDF) found zero matches for 'Dimock' anywhere in the document -- the thesis, though already cited in hedley-dimock.md, does not cover Dimock's counsellor-research studies at all.

The American Camp Association's Hedley S. Dimock Award recipient list is extended, per direct WebFetch of each year's ACA press release: 2022 Simone Gamble (NY & NJ) and Tracey Gaslin PhD (Ohio); 2023 Matt Buczek (NY & NJ) and Rachel Fendell Satinsky (Keystone); 2024 Elisa Spungen Bildner and Robert Bildner, Foundation for Jewish Camp (NY/NJ); 2025 Bashier Kayou (New England) and Bethany Uhl MD (Ohio); 2026 John Hamilton (Heart of the South) and Chris T. Rehs-Dupin (NY/NJ).

The 2015 Hedley S. Dimock Award recipients were, per a search-snippet only (the direct ACA page returned 403): Ellen S. Gannett, M.Ed. and Lance Ozier, Ed.D. -- medium confidence, not independently re-verified via a direct primary-source fetch. The 2019, 2020, and 2021 recipients remain unresolved: two specific 2019 claims found via search ('Florida Youth Conservation Centers Network' and 'David Bryfman') could not be adjudicated against any primary source and should NOT be treated as confirmed.

Two specific claimed identities for the 2019 Camp YMCA Kanawana Pip Alumni Award recipient were investigated and explicitly DEBUNKED, not merely unconfirmed: 'Dr. Amy Ornstein' is a pediatrics faculty member at Dalhousie University (Halifax) specializing in child-maltreatment pediatrics, with no connection whatsoever to Camp Kanawana, YMCA Quebec, or Montreal found in any source. 'David Bryfman' is CEO of The Jewish Education Project (New York); no source connects him to the Pip Award or Camp Kanawana. Both names appear to be search-engine confabulation/conflation (likely with the separately-unverified 2019 ACA Dimock Award claims). Neither should be added to the KB as the 2019 recipient. The 2019-2023 Pip Award recipient gap otherwise remains unresolved after an additional ~20 queries across new surfaces (YMCA Quebec newsroom, Facebook, LinkedIn, Wayback Machine, archive.ph, PressReader, newspapers.com) -- genuinely exhausted for agent-accessible web research.

The Ontario Camping Association's 1940 Kanawana file sits in Box 1, Folder 5 of the 'Camp Brochures and Photographs' series (OCA fonds 72-007, Trent University Archives), alphabetically between 'Glen Mohr' and 'Kiawa.' No content description is available online beyond this single-line catalog entry -- confirms this is a genuine physical-archive-access requirement, not an online research gap.

A previously unflagged Concordia Archives sub-series, P0145/12B05 ('Staff and Counsellors'), exists specifically for Kamp Kanawana staff/counsellor records -- potentially relevant to the still-unresolved question of whether any McGill Camping School (1937-1940) staff also worked at Kanawana, though its contents are not visible online. No named individual was found on both sides of that connection after this session's additional targeted search.

YMCA Camp Pine Crest (Muskoka, Ontario), whose Lumbermen-and-Voyageur tradition Kanawana borrowed in 1947, itself had roots in the Broadview Boys' Institute camping tradition dating to 1896; the Broadview Boys' Institute (Toronto) amalgamated with the Toronto YMCA in 1910 to become the Broadview YMCA, which opened Pine Crest that same year. However, the Pine Crest Games themselves are independently confirmed (per the YMCA of Greater Toronto's own history page and blog) to have begun in 1940 -- so the 1896 Broadview root is institutional/camp lineage, not evidence that the L&V-style competition itself predates 1940, only seven years before Kanawana adopted it.

CORRECTION: Camp Hayo-Went-Ha's 'Woodsmen' and 'Voyageurs' are NOT a Color-War-style competing team pair, contrary to a prior inference in this KB implying a parallel structure. Direct fetches of both program pages show Woodsmen is a younger-boys' in-camp-activities program level ('Fun is the focus... enjoy the many in-camp activities') and Voyageurs is an older-campers' canoe-expedition program level (an AuSable River trip) -- neither page describes any team rivalry or scoring against the other. The naming parallel to Kanawana's sections is coincidental in format, not evidence of a shared competitive tradition.

The broader 'Color War' genre (of which Kanawana's Lumbermen-vs-Voyageurs is a Canadian/YMCA/frontier-themed regional variant) is documented by historian Leslie Paris (UBC) as originating with 'Red and Gray Week' in 1916 at Schroon Lake Camp, a Jewish boys' camp in the Adirondacks, becoming a widespread American camp staple by the 1920s. This places Kanawana/Pine Crest's L&V tradition as a regional YMCA branch of an already-established American genre, not a novel invention.

The modern Kanawana canoe-tripping program for ages 13-16 is itself branded 'Voyageurs' (per the current YMCA Quebec website), including a flat-water option in La Verendrye Wildlife Reserve alongside whitewater options (Coulonge, Dumoine, Noire rivers) -- a separate naming use from the historical L&V Games team of the same name. This resolves the open question about a La Verendrye/L&V connection as 'no direct institutional link found -- likely thematic naming coincidence' between two distinct camp institutions (the historical L&V team vs. the modern canoe-trip program tier), rather than the L&V Games tradition literally expanding into a canoe-trip program.

Derek Walsh's biography remains genuinely exhausted online (9 additional queries this session across web search, obituary databases, LinkedIn, BAnQ, and alumni searches -- zero new facts, reconfirming an existing 32+-query dead end). However, new corroborating context was found: Walsh is named on the 1988-89 Kamp Kanawana Committee (see f_1866), extending his documented Kanawana institutional involvement well beyond his 1974-75 camp directorship and 1983 CCA Award of Excellence.

A systematic search for additional notable Camp Kanawana alumni beyond current documentation (18 distinct queries across 7 surfaces: Google web, LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Newspapers.com, Wikipedia, Google Books) found no previously undocumented, independently-notable/public alumni. Every query returned either already-documented figures (McLean, Mosher, Cleghorn, Orbinski, Sharpe, Adam, etc.) or generic camp marketing/program pages -- confirms the existing notable-alumni.md article has genuinely saturated the easily-discoverable public web for this topic.

The McMaster University Stuart McLean fonds finding aid (full 983-line text retrieved via direct fetch, superseding the previously partial/summarized access) lists Box 60, F.16 (Series 4, Vinyl Cafe studio/tour shows, Season 10, 2004-2005): 'Kamp Kanawana - 10.26, n.d.' -- a specific numbered show file explicitly titled 'Kamp Kanawana,' likely corresponding to the already-documented 2005 Kanawana return-visit recording, now with a specific box location and show number.

The same finding aid lists Box 53, F.25 (Series 4, Season 2, 1995-96): 'Vinyl Cafe Show 2.10 Camp - Not Published, n.d.' -- confirming the exact box and season/show number for the already-known unpublished 'Camp' script, and establishing it as a distinct, earlier file (~10 years before) from the 'Kamp Kanawana' 10.26 file above -- two separate camp-themed show files exist. Box 37, F.13 (Series 2, manuscripts for Home from the Vinyl Cafe, 1998) is confirmed as the exact box for the already-known '[Summer Camp]' typescript file (drafts of 'Camp' and 'Letter Home,' with a Meg Masters note dated May 8, 1998).

New, previously undocumented items in the McMaster Stuart McLean fonds: Box 90, F.6 (Series 7, Personal ephemera, 1971-1975) -- 'Address lists and phone number lists, various, including Camp Kanawana, Sir George Williams University and other lists, 1971-1975'; Box 92, F.3 (Series 7, [1970s]) -- 'Dried flowers from Camp Kanawana'; Box 92, F.4 -- 'Kamp Kanawana decals (2)'; Box 92, F.10 (Series 7/8, I.D. and membership cards) includes a 'YMCA Temporary membership card, 1969' -- from the exact year McLean began at Kanawana.

Box 1, F.8 of the McMaster Stuart McLean fonds (Series 1, Correspondence, general 'Y' correspondents) lists a file simply titled 'YMCA, 1976' -- one year after McLean's last documented camp summer (1975). Content not accessible online.

Series 6 (Events, speeches, conferences), F.16 of the McMaster Stuart McLean fonds lists: 'YMCA NAYDO Conference on Philanthropy, Montreal, April 9-12, 2008. Keynote Speaker name tag and cards.' NAYDO is the North American YMCA Development Organization. This documents McLean as a keynote speaker at a YMCA philanthropy conference in Montreal in April 2008, roughly a year before his 2009 Pip Award -- plausible institutional-tie evidence, though web searches for independent corroboration of this specific conference/speaker pairing returned null (archival-only, single-source).

Box 76 ('Tour Shows with No Dates'), F.5 of the McMaster Stuart McLean fonds lists an undated file: 'YMCA Speech, n.d.' -- a strong but unconfirmed candidate to be, or contain, the source material for the 'speech to YMCA camp directors' quoted in the John Island Alumni Newsletter (Spring 2012), an open question in stuart-mclean.md. Flagged as a lead requiring in-person/archival-request follow-up, not a confirmed match. A separate item, Box 90, F.4, 'Canoeing Instructor School, 1974,' is plausibly (but not explicitly labeled Kanawana-)connected to McLean's camp canoeing-instructor role in the same era.

The McMaster Stuart McLean fonds' Series 9 (Photographs, Box 97) photo inventory was read in full and confirmed to contain NO camp/Kanawana-tagged photographs -- a genuine null result answering part of the 'Images' open question in kanawana-in-media.md.

Stuart McLean's oft-quoted line -- 'It was the first place, as a young person, that I felt I could contribute to the greater good' -- was originally said in a CBC Montreal Radio Noon interview, per OurKids.net's own framing ('in an interview with CBC Montreal's Radio Noon two years ago'), not solely in the OurKids piece itself. This adds provenance detail to an already-known quote (medium confidence -- secondary reporting of the interview, not the interview itself).

The 1960s silent Kanawana film (Concordia P0145-09-0087), already cited in kanawana-in-media.md without a direct URL, is confirmed via direct fetch to be hosted at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZrUuQ1SU7q8, titled 'YMCA: Kamp Kanawana (no sound),' uploaded 2022-06-21 by 'Concordia University Records Management & Archives,' description: 'Various scenes from Kamp Kanawana from the 1960s, including swimming and diving.'

Concordia Archives sub-series P0145/13E (Expo 1967/Canadian Centennial) lists an item, 'Expo 67-canoe tripping program. -- 1964' (Box HA1930) -- showing canoe-trip/Expo-67 planning was underway three years ahead of the Centennial. Does not name Kanawana explicitly; a lead, not a confirmed Kanawana-Expo67 connection.

A Quebec genealogy database shows a 1970 Napierville marriage record for a Yves St-Pierre to Lucette Gregoire, matching the wife's name in the already-cited 2020 Montreal obituary of a Yves St-Pierre (age 76 at death). This is weak, corroborating-only evidence that does not establish any YMCA/Kanawana/camp-counsellor connection -- the identification of this Yves St-Pierre as the 1967 CCA Centenary Journey trip leader remains unestablished.

Concordia Archives sub-sub-series 12B01 (item list for 1966-1968) and 12B04 (Communications, 1913-2003) were confirmed, via direct finding-aid fetch, to contain no file, report, or item referencing the 1967 CCA Centenary Journey trip, a Yves St-Pierre trip report, or a 'Planning and Development (1967)' report -- ruling out these two specific locations as the source of the missing participant-roster material.

The Georgian, Sir George Williams University's student newspaper, is digitized on Internet Archive (200+ individual issues, vol. 1-33, covering 1936-37 and 1962-70), part of a larger 2,100+ issue digitization project by Concordia University Records Management and Archives completed circa November 2021. The Georgian merged with Loyola News in 1980 to form The Link. Not yet searched for Kanawana mentions -- archive.org's search API does not perform true full-text OCR search (see f_1904).

The McGill Daily and Le Delit are fully digitized on Internet Archive as the 'McGill Student Publications Collection' (9,868 issues, 1911-2001), OCR-searchable in principle. A methodological test found that archive.org's advancedsearch.php 'text:' field does NOT perform true full-text OCR search across these collections: a positive-control query for a guaranteed-present term ('computer riot,' referencing SGW's well-documented 1969 Computer Riot, extensively covered by the Georgian) also returned zero results via this API. Properly searching either collection for 'Kanawana' requires a human using the real browser-based search-inside feature, issue by issue -- flagged as a methodology note for future research sessions, not a content-based null result.

Lac Landron (associated with a 1962-63 YMCA canoe-trip base-camp lease) is a real, documented lake located in the unorganized territory of Lac-Lenotre, MRC La Vallee-de-la-Gatineau, Outaouais region, inside the Zec Capitachouane -- east of, and administratively adjacent to (not inside), La Verendrye Wildlife Reserve proper. Its main watercourse is the South Channel of the Ottawa River. The toponym was officially registered December 5, 1968 by Quebec's Commission de toponymie, named after Pierre Landron (attempted a brick factory at the Saint-Charles River in 1688).

La Verendrye Wildlife Reserve was established in 1939 as the 'Reserve de la Route Mont-Laurier-Senneterre' (anticipating a road connecting Mont-Laurier to Abitibi); it was converted to a park and renamed in 1950 to mark the bicentennial of explorer La Verendrye's 1749 death; it is now a 'reserve faunique' administered by SEPAQ.

From 1993, canoe-camping within the Reserve La Verendrye was managed by the Federation quebecoise du canot-camping (FQCC, later Canot Kayak Quebec) in partnership with SEPAQ; around 2022, SEPAQ took over full/sole management. Current official Kanawana Voyageurs canoe-trip program pages make no reference to Lac Landron or any private base camp, and the camp's own official history pages omit the Lac Landron/La Verendrye base-camp narrative entirely. This is strong circumstantial (not direct documentary) evidence that the YMCA's 1962-63 Lac Landron lease has lapsed or been discontinued -- no source states this outright.

No source (Camp Ouareau's own history/Wikipedia, the McMorris thesis, or Trent University's Ontario Camps Association finding aid) documents any direct visit or contact between Camp Ouareau and Camp Kanawana -- the connection between the two camps remains personnel-network-only (via Ferna Halliday's shared YWCA/YMCA ties), not an institutional/inter-camp-visit one. Separately, the Mabel/Mable Jamieson title dispute (whether she held a formal 'secretary general of the YMCA of Montreal' title) remains unresolved: Trent's Ontario Camps Association fonds finding aid contains one incidental photo caption naming her among OCA social circles, but no source anywhere gives her an explicit title beyond Camp Ouareau's own (self-reported) history page.

Walter Edgar Cushing (b. May 19, 1870, Montreal), per the full-text-read 1905-1969 Cushing genealogy supplement, was 'a local public accountant, and an active social worker... At times he was a vice-president and director of the Y.M.C.A., a director of the Boys' Home of Montreal, a member of the Boys' Farm and Training School at Shawbridge and the Daily Bible Schools.' He died January 13, 1935. This independently corroborates a real, substantial YMCA governance role for Walter Edgar Cushing (age 22 in 1892, a plausible candidate for the 'Lemuel Cushing' 1892 Lake St. Joseph trip). However, it also directly CONTRADICTS this KB's existing identification of 'W.E. Cushing' (author of the 1943 'Historical sketches -- Lake St. Joseph' manuscript held in Concordia Archives) as this same Walter Edgar Cushing, since he died eight years before that manuscript's 1943 date. This identification needs correction or re-examination -- either the Concordia archive's '1943' filing date reflects a later transcription of earlier notes, or the 1943 'W.E. Cushing' is a different person.

A full-text search of both the McMorris thesis (129 pages) and the complete 1905-1969 Cushing genealogy supplement (240 pages) found zero mentions of 'Cushing' or '1892' in either document (except the one Walter Edgar Cushing biographical entry, f_1909, which does not mention 1892 or camping). This is a meaningful negative finding: the most rigorous available secondary sources on both Kanawana's history and the Cushing family do not repeat or corroborate the QAHN's 'Lemuel Cushing led the 1892 trip' claim. Concordia's own sub-series 12L finding aid (camper/visitor lists 1893-1897, 1904, 1908) also names no Cushing among its listed individuals.

Harold Beveridge Cushing died October 31, 1947 (married Jessie Alice Barnard November 8, 1915, in Niagara Falls, NY), per the full-text-read 1905-1969 Cushing genealogy supplement -- consistent with, and corroborating, his being alive and available to advise during Kanawana's 1946 polio outbreak.
D.A. Budge's exact death date is confirmed, via direct raw fetch of the McGill Archival Collections Catalogue page, as February 13, 1933, in Montreal.

Concordia Archives sub-series 13D (Memorials, tributes, testimonials, honours), Box HA2330, holds 'research reports on D.A. Budge' as part of Joyce Oliver's 1939-40 'Book of Remembrance and History' project (approximately 50 biographical subjects researched for a YMCA commemorative history). Contents not yet read -- a concrete additional archival lead for closing D.A. Budge's remaining biographical open questions.

No obituary, FindAGrave entry, or FamilySearch profile for A. Ross Seaman (died 1987) was located despite an exhaustive search. The Vankleek Hill newspaper 'The Review' (archived from 1893) very likely carries an October/November 1987 obituary, but its own online archive is not full-text searchable and standard obituary aggregators don't cover it -- this requires a paid GenealogyBank-style subscription search or direct contact with the newspaper or Hillcrest Funeral Home (Vankleek Hill), not further web queries. Separately, no name for Seaman's successor as Kanawana director beyond the already-known Ross Bannerman (1969) was found -- Concordia's own finding aid lists a run of unattributed 'Director's Annual Reports' (1970-1975) whose authors are not given in the online finding aid.

The McMorris thesis cites Kanawana's invitation of girls (ages 10-12) to camp for the first time in 1968 to the 'One-hundred and seventeenth Annual Report 1968' (YMCA of Montreal fonds, Annual Reports, P145/02D) -- a more specific citation than previously recorded in this KB for the already-documented 1968 coeducation date.

Taylor Statten's full biography, per a full-text read of Donald Burry's 1985 MA thesis 'A History of the Taylor Statten Camps' (University of Saskatchewan): full birth name Emerson Taylor Israel Statten; born July 12, 1882, in his grandfather's exchange hotel in Springfield (now Erindale), Ontario; parents John Marr Statten and Eleanor Elmina (nee Taylor) Statten; eldest of four children (sister Bolina 'Bay,' b. 1884; brothers Waldemar 'Waldie,' b. 1887, and Lincoln, b. 1889). Joined the YMCA in 1902 via J. Howard Crocker's Leaders' Corps (Toronto Central YMCA); became full-time Secretary of Boys' Work of the Toronto Central YMCA on May 1, 1905, holding the post until 1911 (refines the previous 'around 1905-1906' dating). Prior to founding Ahmek, Statten ran a camp called 'Camp Tuxis,' which closed in August 1920, the same year he began planning the private camp on Canoe Lake that became Ahmek (1921). He died in his sleep on Thursday, November 1, 1956, after a day working in the garden at Little Wapomeo, per a Statten-family Christmas letter reproduced in the thesis.

The underlying full-length biography behind most Taylor Statten scholarship is identified: C.A.M. Edwards (Charles Austin McNally Edwards), 'Taylor Statten: A Biography,' foreword by J. Alex Edmison, Ryerson Press, Toronto, 1960, 161pp. Confirmed via multiple used-book-retailer listings (Google Books, Amazon, AbeBooks, Biblio) but NOT digitized anywhere -- checked HathiTrust and Internet Archive directly, neither holds it.

A full-text grep of Donald Burry's 178-page 1985 thesis on the Taylor Statten Camps found zero mentions of 'Kanawana' and zero mentions of 'Naismith' anywhere in the document -- this source does not address whether Taylor Statten ever visited Camp Kanawana, despite being the most detailed available biography drawing on direct 1984 family interviews.

Donald Burry's 1985 thesis contains an internal three-way disagreement on the Ontario Camping Association's founding date, distinct from this KB's existing citation (the OCA's own website, giving 1933): citing a 1984 personal interview with camping historian Mary Northway, Burry states OCA founders (including Statten) organized in 1930, with Statten becoming the OCA's first President only in 1938, succeeding A.L. Cochrane's 'Original Honorary President' role. Citing an undated Charles Plewman tribute essay, Burry separately records that Statten 'became the first President... in 1933' -- but Burry himself appends '(sic)' to this claim, signalling his own doubt. This is a genuine multi-source disagreement (OCA website vs. Northway-via-Burry vs. Plewman-via-Burry), none of which is oral history, requiring human/editorial review rather than the 'oral history yields to documents' policy.

Terry Mosher's parents were Jack and Norma Mosher, per a 2015 interview: 'My parents... always tried to get me out of the city for a period of time during summers and sent me to a series of camps, Kanawana being my favourite.' He attended Victoria School, King's School, and Westmount Junior High during his Montreal years (age 7-14), living in a converted-garage coach house in an alleyway between Lincoln Avenue and Saint-Luc (now de Maisonneuve), between Fort and Chomedey near the old Forum, with painter John Little (his godfather) as downstairs neighbour. He said in 2015: 'I remember the layout of the camp surprisingly well -- and I haven't been back since 1954! I am told that it has hardly changed.'

The 2015 Pip Alumni Award ceremony for Terry Mosher was held Saturday, August 8, 2015 -- not August 3 as stated in the already-cited YMCA Quebec newsroom page, which appears to contain a transcription error. Two independent sources (a 2015-08-01 Suburban blog post and a second, differently-URLed YMCA Quebec newsroom page) both state 'August 8,' and a day-of-week check confirms August 3, 2015 was a Monday while August 8, 2015 was a Saturday -- consistent with both correcting sources describing a Saturday camp event.

A full raw fetch (not just a search-engine snippet) of Concordia's finding aid for sub-sub-series 12B01 confirms exactly one Dave Twynam entry exists: 'Camp director Dave Twynam-correspondence. -- 1979' (Box HA2054) -- no separate 1976 entry exists anywhere in the list, further corroborating the already-resolved conflict c_007 in favour of 1979.

A previously undocumented Twynam/Johnston publication: Twynam, G.D., & Johnston, M. (2004), 'Changes in host community reactions to a special sporting event,' Current Issues in Tourism, 7(3), 242-261 -- a longitudinal study of Thunder Bay resident reactions to the 1995 Nordic World Ski Championships, alongside his already-known Scott Tournament of Hearts and Scouts Jamboree studies.

A third independent research pass on Joanna Hoad's post-Lower Canada College life and pre-Kanawana history (21 queries across WebSearch, WebFetch, Facebook, ZoomInfo, genealogy sites, and a direct Wayback Machine CDX query) found zero new facts, confirming the two prior exhausted passes (2026-07-05, 2026-07-07). The Wayback CDX query for lcc.ca confirms only the three already-cited captures (2001 staff profile, 2004 staff photo, 2007 gallery caption) exist anywhere matching 'hoad.' Recommend treating this as genuinely exhausted for RESEARCH purposes; a VERIFY task (cross-checking existing citations/dates/names) toward R3-verified status is achievable without further research, since R3-verified does not require resolving the two remaining 'Important' open questions (departure date, post-LCC life) -- those can legitimately remain open.

Grace McMorris's thesis (Figure 2.1 caption, p.60) directly reproduces a photograph of the Kanawana totem pole, captioned 'Totem pole at Kanawana circa 1970s.' McMorris's own footnote states: 'It is unclear if this is the same totem pole [as the one erected in 1927 by Harold Cross], however, since the photograph was taken in the 1970s.' This is the primary academic source directly addressing the totem pole's continued existence into the 1970s, now read directly rather than cited secondarily.

The same thesis (p.68) states the 1962 Kanawana map labels 'Indian' three times: 'the Indians and Settlers teepee, the Indian Council Ring, and the Indian Grave. The Council Ring was always marked by a drawing of a totem pole' -- confirming the 'Indian Council Ring' name and totem-pole iconography persisted at least through 1962. A separate reflective passage (p.112) about the camping movement's reconciliation dilemma in general terms ('It is not enough to cover up the murals and take the totem poles down') is rhetorical/general, NOT a specific claim that Kanawana itself removed its poles -- should not be read as evidence of removal.

The camp's current official facilities page lists 'fire bowls for campfires and cookouts' among current amenities, but does not use the name 'Council Ring' or mention totem poles -- inconclusive (promotional copy is not exhaustive) rather than evidence of removal. The camp's own curated history timeline (1894, 1910, 1947, 1968, 2022, 2025 milestones) omits the Council Ring/totem-pole tradition entirely -- a notable absence from the camp's own public-facing narrative, though not proof the site no longer exists.

YMCA Canada's own institutional history states: '1912 - Formation of National Federation: A national Federation is created to unify local YMCAs and provide leadership and coordination across the country.' A naming discrepancy is unresolved: a 1972 Concordia-catalogued report uses the name 'National Council YMCAs of Canada' instead of 'Federation' -- the exact relationship/renaming between these two national-body names is not reconciled.

Concordia's finding aid for YMCA of Montreal fonds sub-series 12A extends the previously-documented camping governance chronology into the early 1980s: 'Camping and Outdoor Education Branch of Management minutes, 1975-1978'; a 'Special Intercommittee Task Force on Camping, 1981-1982'; a 'Comite du service des camps / Camping Services Committee, 1981-1982'; and 'YMCA Canada -- Resident Camp Statistics 1984-1988' (compiled 1989). A governance-title gap still remains between 1982 and the 2004 'Regional Director of Camps' title (1983-2003 remains open).

The YMCA of Montreal moved from Dominion Square to a new building on Drummond Street in 1912 (cost $540,206); a 12-storey annex was added 1930-31; Sir George Williams University students used the building's chapel, gym, and pool until the 1970s. 'The YMCA occupied the building until it was demolished in 2002.'

On October 11, 2023, YMCA Quebec's own newsroom announced intent to sell the (rebuilt) downtown Montreal YMCA building on Drummond/Stanley streets, citing reduced post-COVID membership revenue, aging-infrastructure costs, and only one-third of the building being used for programming; existing tenants (a language school with ~3,400 students, TeenZone with ~650 participants, and homelessness/reentry services) were to continue 'until 2025.'

Concordia's static finding-aid page for sub-sub-series 12B04 (Communications) gives the exact catalog entry for the 'On My Way to Kanawana' recording: 'On My Way to Kanawana. Song composed and performed by Richard Itch Kerr. CD. 4'30. - nd.' (Box HA2559, P145/SR0001). The item is undated in the finding aid itself; no lyrics, transcription, or streamable/digitized copy exists online.

Concordia's static finding-aid page for sub-sub-series 12B07 (Program), Box HA2315, lists 'Song sheets, skits' (1925, 1927), 'Kanawana song books, Canadian YMCA song book' (1941-1945), 'KK pageant scripts' (1931-1932), and 'Fire of Friendship, Kanawana show' (1939) -- all folder-level descriptions only, with no individual song titles or ceremony scripts itemized online.

YMCA Camp Pine Crest (Muskoka, Ontario) has run a two-day 'Lumbermen vs. Voyageurs' color-war competition, 'The Pine Crest Games,' every year since 1940, using an axe (Lumbermen) and paddle (Voyageurs) as team symbols -- a striking naming parallel to Kanawana's 'L&V Games' (Lumberman/Voyageur) worth investigating as a possible shared-origin or common-inspiration lead. A centennial book, 'Lumbermen & Voyageurs: The YMCA Pine Crest Story,' exists but its contents could not be retrieved online (repeated HTTP 429 rate-limiting on the shop page; no WorldCat/review record with cheer text).

Concordia's static finding-aid page for sub-sub-series 12B04 (Communications), Box HA1874, itemizes individual Kanawana camp brochures by year: 1950, 1959, [1960s], 1964, 1965, [1968?], [197-], 1978, 1982, 1983, and 1997. None are digitized online; the same box holds the full 1932-1940 run of 'The Green Triangle' newsletter as a single undifferentiated entry (individual issue dates not itemized in the public finding aid).

The McMorris 2023 thesis, citing Concordia P145/12B07 ('Fire of Friendship — Kanawana Show'), notes the Fire of Friendship service's suggested programme was designed to be used 'at the end of a Boy Scout day' -- indicating the programme text was adapted directly from Boy Scout ceremonial material rather than composed originally for Kanawana.

Concordia's finding aid for sub-series 12L (Camp Jubilee/Lac St-Joseph), Box HA2312, lists a 'Director's report (1908)' -- a single, specific dated record from the middle of the undocumented 1901-1923 gap between directors John Roy and Philip Paterson. This item is not currently digitized and would very likely name whoever was director in 1908 if physically consulted.

QAHN's article on the camp's founding treats Lemuel Cushing's 1892 Lake St-Joseph trip and the YMCA's 1893-94 opening of Camp Jubilee as two separate, non-linked mentions, with no stated causal or organizational relationship between them; the article does not mention Billy Ball at all. This confirms the relationship between the two events is genuinely undocumented in this source, not merely under-researched.

Concordia's finding aid references a 'Permanent Camp Committee' with minute and correspondence files spanning 1895-96, 1899-1901, 1908, 1911-1926, and 1921 -- a previously unexplored archival lead covering most of the period Ralph Dawson may have been active, and a plausible venue for his role at the camp to be documented.

Télesphore Pagé (the family member who married Clarilda/Claire-Ida Dagenais in 1925) lived 1895-1961, per 'Hommage à Télesphore Pagé,' La Mémoire de la Vallée de Saint-Sauveur, bulletin de la SHGPH, no. 81, hiver 1999 -- confirming he was alive through the 1960 'Pagé farm' purchase and died the following year, consistent with (but not proof of) his being the seller.

CORRECTION 2026-07-09 (supersedes f_1518): the person born April 1908 who attended école du Grand-Ruisseau, worked in logging camps, was hired by Auguste Dionne, married Marguerite Amyot in 1935, and opened a grocery store on rue de la Gare in Saint-Sauveur is not a second 'Télesphore Pagé' -- a direct re-read of the full raw vss.ca pioneer-families page text identifies this person as Télesphore Léonard (1908-1997), son of Joseph-Vital Léonard and Léonie Pagé (1882-1941, daughter of Magloire Pagé père). He is a Pagé descendant through the female line, surnamed Léonard, not a Pagé. Every biographical detail (birth month/year, the grocery, rue de la Gare) matches exactly between the two article sections, indicating f_1518 conflated adjacent entries on the source page during an earlier extraction pass.

A direct full-text read of the McMorris 2023 thesis found exactly two acreage figures, neither for the Saint-Sauveur Kanawana site: the original Camp Jubilee/Lake St-Joseph island property was 33 acres, bought from the government in 1898 for $1/acre (citing Cross, One Hundred Years, p.189); and the 1950s Voyageurs de la Vérendrye program used a 25-acre lease on Lac Landron in La Vérendrye Park. The thesis's own passages on 1928-1962 property growth (Lake Becsies, the Pagé farm) give no acreage figure for either transaction -- confirming this is a genuine absence in the primary academic source, not an extraction gap.

Wikimapia's entry for Kamp Kanawana independently states the camp is '455 acres' in phrasing near-identical to promotional language elsewhere ('pristine wilderness just outside St-Sauveur des Monts, one hour north of Montreal'), differing from the YMCA's own current claim of 550 acres. The page's content could not be directly fetched or dated to confirm whether this reflects an older survey, a scraping/copy error, or genuine change; the discrepancy remains unresolved.

Batshaw Centres' institutional history pages for Camp Weredale and Youth Horizons make zero mention of the YMCA, Kanawana, or any two-site plan -- the Weredale institutional history is told entirely independent of any YMCA connection, ruling this source out as an explanation for why the Kanawana-Weredale two-site plan was abandoned.

The City of Saint-Sauveur's draft Plan d'urbanisme (March 2024) states directly: 'Avec ses grands espaces naturels, le camp Kanawana présente également une valeur environnementale méritant d'être reconnue au sein de la présente planification' -- a dated (2024) municipal document explicitly naming Kanawana's environmental value, though it stops short of conferring any formal legal designation.

Saint-Sauveur's zoning regulation (Règlement 222-2008, consolidated) defines an 'Affectation récréative et de conservation (RC)' land-use category whose stated purpose names a vacation camp ('camp de vacances') as an example qualifying use, alongside trails and outdoor recreation with minimal development. A zone code 'RC 123' appears near a reference to a road on côte Sainte-Elmire (the camp's address), but the camp parcel's actual zone designation could not be confirmed from the extracted text, since zone boundary maps are graphical, not text-searchable.

Concordia's finding aid for sub-sub-series 12B01 (Kamp Kanawana General Administration) lists an item titled 'Proposed wildlife sanctuary, bird and game sanctuary — 1847, 1954-1960' -- a previously undocumented lead. Whether this proposal concerned the camp property itself, was ever enacted, or relates to a different YMCA holding is undetermined without physical examination of the folder.

A Montreal Gazette clipping titled 'Summer Camps – Kanawana,' dated April 18, 1974, exists on Newspapers.com -- a concrete, dated lead that could plausibly describe the camp's section structure mid-way through its 1968-early 1980s coeducational transition, potentially bearing on when section names were reassigned along gender lines. The clipping is paywalled (HTTP 403 to automated fetch) and requires the operator's own Newspapers.com public-access account to read.

The 'Rangers' section name is entirely absent from the McMorris 2023 thesis, which exhaustively covers Kanawana's primary sources from 1894-1967 and documents the 1959 renaming's four core section names (Pioneers, Woodsmen, Coureurs de Bois, Pathfinders) in detail -- confirming Rangers was not one of the 1959-renaming names. Combined with the KB's existing 1955 'Rangers' plaque (the earliest dated Rangers artifact), this indicates Rangers already existed as an established, separately-named program by 1955, four years before the 1959 core-section renaming -- refining the article's prior framing of Rangers as introduced 'beyond' 1959 to instead predating it. Trailblazers and Foresters remain undated; neither appears in the McMorris thesis, any pre-1980s cached primary source checked, or anywhere beyond current (2026) YMCA program pages.

Robert 'Rob' Braide was born April 4, 1953, in Montreal, and grew up in Westmount, attending Westmount High and Dawson College before five years at Carleton University's Faculty of Music (electronic/computer composition), which he left to take CHOM's all-night show in September 1977. His career spanned CHOM (DJ, then Music Director, then Program Director, 1977-mid-1980s), CKGM programming (1981), General Manager of CJAD/FM96 (renamed Mix 96) under Standard Broadcasting from June 1987, Astral Media Group VP (branding/communications/industry relations, post-2008 Standard Radio acquisition, laid off January 2009 in a 23-position restructuring), and later VP of content/regulatory affairs at Stingray Digital, retiring around age 58. He now runs a consulting firm, Braide Media, and was inducted into the CAB Hall of Fame (November 2009) and the Canadian Music and Broadcasting Hall of Fame. He has served on numerous community boards (Montreal Board of Trade, Palais des Congrès, Saidye Bronfman Centre, St. Mary's Hospital, Montreal Children's Hospital, Les Amis de la Montagne, Montreal Jubilation Gospel Choir, Trevor Williams Kids Foundation, Quebec Community Groups Network) and chaired Calgary's Studio Bell/National Music Centre.

Rob Braide is stated to have chaired the YMCA's Kamp Kanawana Capital Campaign, per History of Canadian Broadcasting's biography page -- a direct institutional tie to Kanawana beyond being a camper alumnus. No specific year(s) are given for this chairmanship.

Ian Braide and Vicki Braide (Kanawana campers/CITs, 2000-2007 and 2000 respectively) are grandchildren of David Ian William Braide (1928-2018), a Montreal businessman with a 36-year career at Canadian Industries Limited, via his son Robbie David Braide. David Ian William Braide's obituary states he held YMCA board roles including 'the Montreal and Westmount YMCAs' -- a separate, real YMCA connection in this Braide lineage. No source found directly links this family to Robert 'Rob' Braide the broadcaster (b. 1953); despite the rare surname and shared Westmount/YMCA milieu, a family relationship between the two Braide lines remains unconfirmed by any source found.

At YMCA Camp Manitou-Lin (Grand Rapids, Michigan area, an unrelated YMCA camp), 'Uncle Bob' Augustine held the title Resident Director in 1931, then was promoted to Camp Director from 1932-1948 -- suggesting that in at least one other YMCA camping context, 'Resident Director' functioned as a subordinate/on-site precursor rank to 'Camp Director,' not a co-equal or administratively separate role. This is offered as a circumstantial cross-camp comparison for Kanawana's 1942 two-tier Resident Director/Camp Director structure (Edgar Smee/R.H. Hanagan), not a confirmed answer -- no YMCA of Montreal-specific policy document defining the two titles was found.

An 18-query, 4-surface sweep found no source naming a specific pedagogical framework (place-based education, bioregionalism, forest-school pedagogy) as influencing Kanawana's environmental programming. The closest adjacent finding is a 2009 description of a mandatory 'tournée verte' (green tour) covering the camp's ecological infrastructure, built into every stay -- a described practice, not an attributed theory. Chris Adam's 'Nature as Mentor' philosophy is documented as his own Dawson College/Earthvalues Institute brand, connected to Kanawana only biographically (he is a Pip Award-winning alumnus), not as an adopted camp curriculum.

Direct GBIF and iNaturalist API queries confirm real, geotagged citizen-science observations exist at 'Ch du Lac-Kanawana, St-Sauveur' -- amphibians (Pickerel Frog, American Toad, Green Frog), mammals (beaver, fisher), insects, and plants, dated June 2026. These are informal, individual app-user observations, not an institutional survey; no eBird hotspot exists under the Kanawana name and no formal biodiversity inventory or bioblitz involving the camp was found.

Concordia's static finding-aid page for sub-series 12F (Camp Weredale), Box HA1894, documents a real, signed 1979 lease agreement between the Weredale Foundation and the Montreal YMCA, plus continuing joint files -- 'Weredale Foundation/YMCA' (1980-1981), 'Comité Weredale' (1981-1982), a day-camp program proposal (1980), and a 'YMCA staff cottage rental' (1981). This contradicts the wiki's prior framing of the Kanawana-Weredale two-site plan as simply proposed then abandoned: a genuine multi-year operational relationship existed from at least 1979 to c.1982. The reason the arrangement eventually ended remains undocumented online.

Youth Horizons was formed in 1977 (from Allancroft Centre, Summerhill Homes, Weredale House, and Mount Bruno Girls Cottage School), confirmed via direct raw-HTML fetch of Batshaw Centres' own timeline page, cross-corroborated on two further pages of the same site. A previously-circulating '1973' date was traced to a misreading of an adjacent, unrelated timeline entry ('Ville Marie Social Services is formed,' 1973) -- a confirmed misreading, not a genuine source conflict.

A full-text search of the complete McMorris 2023 thesis (covering 1894-1967) found zero occurrences of 'Weredale' anywhere. A direct raw-HTML check of the Frank Crabbe memorial blog post (a first-hand account of the Weredale/Camp Lewis milieu, 1961-65) likewise contains zero mention of Kanawana. No shared staff, programming, or organizational practice between Camp Weredale and Camp Kanawana during 1934-1977 has been found in any source checked -- this remains a confirmed dead end for online research.

The YMCA of Montreal fonds' full 125-page master finding-aid PDF is directly downloadable via curl (unlike the bot-walled AtoM catalog interface) and readable via pdftotext -- a superior, reusable research tool. It confirms sub-sub-series 12B05 (Staff and counsellors) is explicitly access-restricted, explaining why static finding-aid pages for 12B02/05/06 consistently 404 while 12B01/03/04/07 work.

The same master finding-aid PDF's item-level list (sub-series 09 moving images, 11 sound recordings) surfaces several previously uncatalogued Kanawana-specific audiovisual items: 'Camp Kanawana: Boating and Water Sports All Summer Long' (16mm, ~8 min); 'News Documents and Kamp Kanawana' (VHS, 15 min); a French and an English 'Kamp Kanawana' PSA (December 1988 and March 1987, 1 min each); a 'Kamp Kanawana' audio reel (undated); a 1969 promotional audio tape; an August 24, 1962 audio interview with a 'Woodsman' section member; a 'Homesick tape' (undated); and a 1963 audio recording titled 'What is God? / Interview of Kamp Kanawana campers and staff.' Only catalog metadata was retrieved, not transcripts or audio itself.

The wiki's sources-index.md previously listed '12G | Camp Perrot' as if it were a standalone, described archival sub-series. The finding aid's own descriptive body has no 12G entry at all -- it jumps directly from 12F (Weredale) to 12H (Ski lodge). Camp Perrot material exists only as comparison documents within 12A, consistent with existing KB facts; this is a genuine cataloguing gap in Concordia's own finding aid, not a wiki error, and was independently corroborated by a separate research pass on the same day.

BAnQ numérique's search and article-detail pages are blocked at every level tested by a Radware 'perfdrive.com' bot-validation redirect (confirmed on multiple distinct URLs) -- a more specific characterization than the KB's prior generic '403' note. No new Kanawana newspaper hits were found; every article surfaced by site-restricted search was already in the KB. Notably, no 'Montreal Star' + 'Kanawana' hit surfaced anywhere despite the Star's 1869-1979 run being partly digitized -- unclear whether this reflects a genuine absence or incomplete BAnQ digitization of that title.

The Ballantyne 1944 history's full cached text (38,099 characters) was directly re-grepped for 'camp', 'Laurentian', 'Saint-Sauveur', 'St. Joseph', 'Ball', 'Cushing', and 'Kanawana' -- zero mentions of any of these beyond a generic national camping statistic already in the KB (5,835 boys / 95,360 camper-days in 1942). This independently reconfirms the source is a genuine dead end for Kanawana-specific content, not merely under-searched.
