The YMCAs of Quebec 2022 impact report records that the association 'reopened Camp YMCA Kanawana after two years of closures' -- corroborating the two lost summers of 2020 and 2021 from the association's own reporting.

CAUTION ON A NUMBER: the 2022 impact report states 'Close to 300 campers, including Ukrainian refugees, had a memorable summer in our day camps and at Camp YMCA Kanawana.' This is the FINANCIALLY-ASSISTED subset across day camps AND Kanawana combined -- the preceding sentence is about financial assistance -- and is NOT a Kanawana attendance figure. It must not be added to or netted against the 655. The substantive fact is that the camp took in children displaced by the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

The YMCAs of Quebec 2024 impact report marks the 130th anniversary of Camp Kanawana and the launch of 'Adventure at Kanawana', a DAY-CAMP format run on the Saint-Sauveur site -- distinct from the residential camp and from the YMCA Concordia science, engineering and fine-arts camps.

During the 2020 closed summer the YMCA ran a virtual campfire singalong with the Camp YMCA Kanawana team as part of a fundraiser that raised $81,520, with donations doubled by the Trottier Family Foundation. The same report lists Sean Day as Regional Camp Director.

THE 1894 FOUNDING IS DOCUMENTED CONTEMPORANEOUSLY. The YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1894-95 states in its Junior Department section: "We are able to report the holding of our first Summer Camp, which was in every way a decided success, and will become an established item in our prospectus. This Camp was composed of 23 workers and boys." The statistical summary confirms "Attendance at Summer Camp ... 23". The preceding 1893-94 report contains NO mention of a lake, lease, fishing rights or Ste-Agathe -- a null result confirming 1894 as the first year.

CRITICAL NULL: the YMCA of Montreal annual reports NEVER call any camp "Camp Jubilee." Every pre-1921 report was searched. "Jubilee" appears only in the YMCA-worldwide sense -- the 1893-94 report's "This is the Jubilee Year in the history of the Young Men's Christian Association" (the 1844-1894 golden jubilee) and the 1894-95 report's "The World's Jubilee Convention, London, Eng., June 6-10, 1894." That the association's first boys' camp began in the YMCA's Jubilee Year is a real coincidence, but the association's own records do not make the connection or use the name. This wiki uses "Camp Jubilee" throughout and should attribute it to whichever source actually supplies it.

The 1894 camp ran as TWO PARALLEL STREAMS on one leased lake. The 1894-95 report's Junior Department section reports the first boys' camp (23 workers and boys); its Physical Department section separately records "The Association has leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a lake near St. Agathe... Last year 53 members took advantage of this privilege" -- adult/senior members. From 1896 the reports state the split explicitly (28 junior, 40 senior). INFERENCE, labelled: only the Junior line becomes Kanawana; the Senior line stays on Lac St. Joseph and becomes Camp Otoreke.

The first Summer Camp committee, named in the 1894-95 annual report's officers list: "Summer Camp. John W. Ross, Chairman. E. J. Coyle. R. L. Charlton." John W. Ross recurs as camp chairman for roughly thirty years and later becomes Association President and Honorary President. By 1896 a "PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE" exists: John W. Ross (chairman), Jas. Wilson, W. E. Cushing, R. B. Ross Jr. -- putting W. E. Cushing on the camp committee from 1896.

KANAWANA'S FIRST SEASON IS SUMMER 1910, announced in the forward tense in the 1910 annual report: "A new site has been secured for the Boys' Camp on Lake Kanawana, near Shawbridge, in the Laurentian Mountains... a summer vacation camp for boys, from July 1st to August 15th. They will have accommodation for 70 boys. This camp will be under the charge of Mr. W. J. Holliday, of the Central Branch. The Summer Camp at Lac St. Joseph will have renewed equipment, and will be given over entirely to the senior members." Two internal confirmations: the 1931 report says the camp "HAS BEEN IN OPERATION FOR TWENTY-ONE YEARS IN ITS PRESENT LOCATION" (of the 1930 season) and the 1939 report calls 1938 "The twenty-ninth season at Camp Kanawana" -- both giving 1910.

NAMES FILLING THE 1902-1920 DIRECTORIAL GAP, from the annual reports (season years): 1908 Junior Camp under W. J. Holliday; 1910 Kanawana opens under W. J. HOLLIDAY of Central Branch; 1913 "in charge of Messrs. D. J. EVANS, HAROLD CROSS, and H. A. LORDLY for successive portions of the season"; 1915 T. HICKS MILLER (Physical Director, Westmount) in July and JOHN McKINNON (Boys' Work Secretary, Central) in August; 1916 "Mr. MacKinnon acted as Leader throughout"; 1917 supervised by J. G. MacKINNON with Jos. DALLEY and John BRADFORD; 1918 John MacKinnon to 3 August, G. D. BRANDON relieving to 17 August; 1919 "Mr. MacKinnon has been appointed Director for this season". NOTE the 1913 entry: Harold Cross running part of the 1913 season predates by a decade the c.1925-1928 directorship the wiki records for him.

THE ASSOCIATION RAN TWO COMPETING ANNIVERSARY CLOCKS, which explains two long-standing confusions in this wiki. A "camping since 1894" clock is used in the reports of 1946 ("the 52nd for boys arranged by the Montreal Association"), 1948 (54th), 1949 (55th), 1966-67 (73rd year), 1967 (74th), 1968 (75th anniversary), 1977-78 and 2005-06. A "Kanawana site since 1910" clock is used in 1931 ("TWENTY-ONE YEARS IN ITS PRESENT LOCATION"), 1939 (29th season), 1984 ("its 75th year of service") and 1985 ("for the past 75 years"). CONSEQUENCES: the 75th anniversary was celebrated TWICE, in 1968 and again in 1984; and the 1993 report announces the camp "celebrating its 100th anniversary this year" while the 1994 report says "This was Kanawana's 100th year of operation" -- two centennials, one from each clock.

The earliest founding-date claims in the annual reports are UNRELIABLE and conflict with the contemporaneous record: the 1931 report says "IN 1898, OR FORTY YEARS AGO, THE FIRST BOYS CAMP OF THE ASSOCIATION WAS OPENED AT LAC ST. JOSEPH"; the 1932 and 1933 reports date Lac St. Joseph activity to 1891/92; the 1954 and 1955 reports say "the site of the first Y.M.C.A. camp established in 1892"; the 1953 and 1965 reports say 1893. All postdate the events by three to four decades and conflict with the 1894-95 report's own first-person "our first Summer Camp". The corpus also holds a document titled "1900-12-10 seventh annual report of the current camp committee" -- 7th annual in 1900 gives 1894.

The scarlet fever outbreak that quarantined Kamp Kanawana for about four weeks is recorded in the YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1941: "a mild case of scarlet fever developed, followed by two others, so that the camp had to be quarantined for about four weeks." DATE UNRESOLVED BY ONE YEAR: the wiki dated it 1941 from McMorris, but the association's fiscal year then ended 31 March, so the 1941 REPORT describes the summer of 1940. Three cases and four weeks match McMorris's "full month" closely enough to be the same event, but a different source-dating on her side, or two outbreaks in consecutive years, cannot be excluded without reading her citation. Same one-year offset class as the Council Ring rebuild (recorded 1929, actually 1928).

CORRECTION TO THE POLIO RECORD: the 1947 annual report (1946 season) does NOT state that polio cases occurred at camp. It says "The polio epidemic affected attendance for the last half of the season, although most doctors advised parents that conditions at camp were more favorable for children than were those in the city" -- i.e. the city-wide Montreal epidemic as an attendance depressant. The six-case figure this project holds comes from the McMorris thesis, which remains its sole source. The annual report corroborates the YEAR and the ATTENDANCE EFFECT, not the case count.

The camp's water supply failed in 1932: "PROBABLY THE MOST SERIOUS PROBLEM THE CAMP IS FACING AT THE PRESENT TIME IS THAT OF AN ADEQUATE WATER SUPPLY. THE FACT THAT BOTH WELLS PRESENTLY BEING USED WERE DRY DURING THE PAST SEASON LEADS ONE TO BELIEVE THAT IT IS SURFACE WATER WHICH IS BEING USED." Resolved the following year -- the 1934 report records "two new wells were sunk."

NULL RESULTS ACROSS ALL 114 ANNUAL REPORTS MENTIONING KANAWANA: no fire, no storm destruction, and no death at camp is reported in any of them. The 1969 camper drowning appears ONLY in the Kanawana season report, not the annual report (whose sole 1969 Kanawana passage is an attendance line, and which returns zero hits for regret/sorrow/died/death/accident/tragic/drown). The 1976 viral meningitis outbreak likewise appears only in the camp's own director's report. Two apparent hits are false positives: a 1938 "two or three drownings" line concerns a city branch waterfront, and a 1962 "water pollution cancelled swimming" line concerns the Ile Perrot day camp.
NULL: Camp Weredale and Camp Ouareau appear NOWHERE in any of the 114 YMCA of Montreal annual reports that mention Kanawana.

Camp Otoreke is explicitly identified by the association as Kanawana's ORIGINAL SITE, not a separate camp: the 1965 annual report states "The Otoreke site, near St. Adolphe d'Howard, has been owned by the YMCA since 1893 and is the original location of Kamp Kanawana." The 1910 split was a division of one institution -- boys to the new Lake Kanawana site, men remaining on Lac St. Joseph, which became Otoreke. Per CLAUDE.md's hub-and-spoke rule this makes Otoreke, and likewise Bec-scies and Perrot, core site/ rather than connections/related-camps/. Camp Tamaracouta (Boy Scouts) is the genuine related-camps candidate -- the 1964 report records 120 acres acquired "in cooperation with the Boy Scouts Association Camp Tamaracouta. This move now joins the two camp properties."

THE FISCAL CONVENTION OF THE YMCA OF MONTREAL ANNUAL REPORTS, needed to date anything drawn from them. Reports up to and including 1925 cover a year ending 30 APRIL. The 1926 report covers an ELEVEN-MONTH transitional period ending 31 March 1926 (its own table says 'BRANCHES, ELEVEN MONTHS PERIOD ENDING MARCH 31st, 1926'). Reports from 1926 through 1950 cover a year ending 31 MARCH. From 1951 the fiscal period is the CALENDAR YEAR, decided explicitly: 'It was decided ... that effective January 1st, 1951, the fiscal period should accord with the calendar year.' CONSEQUENCE: for every report up to 1950, report YYYY describes the summer of YYYY-1, and any month named in it falls in the twelve months BEFORE the March/April year end. NOTE the refinement: the April-to-March change happens at the 1926 report, not the 1927 report.

DATE CORRECTION: W. J. G. Macdiarmid was appointed to succeed J. G. MacKinnon temporarily as Executive Secretary on 15 SEPTEMBER 1927, not 1928. greig-macdiarmid.md carried 1928. The report recording it is the 1928 one, whose fiscal year ends 31 March 1928 -- it cannot contain a September 1928 event. Found by the p_257 fiscal-convention audit.

DATE CORRECTION: Macdiarmid 'entered the Secretaryship' during the eleven months from May 1925 to March 1926, not in '1926' flat. The 1926 report covers that transitional eleven-month period. Recorded as 1925-26.

DATE PRECISION: the 1937 Annual Report covers the fiscal year ending 31 March 1937 and therefore describes the 1936 SEASON. greig-macdiarmid.md said its Protestant Orphans' Home passage documented 'that year's' arrangement, which read as 1937 and contradicted camp-becsies.md, which correctly assigns the 1937 report to the 1936 season. Both articles now agree.

AUDITED CLEAN by the p_257 fiscal-convention sweep: camp-becsies.md ('the 1934, 1935, 1936 and 1937 Annual Reports, covering the 1933, 1934, 1935 and 1936 seasons respectively'); council-ring.md's 1928 rebuild; the directors-index rows for 1913, 1915 and 1918; w-h-spearman.md's 1934/1933 and 1935/1934 pairings, its 1 September 1929 appointment, its 31 March 1949 promotion and its 31 May 1954 retirement. Two FORWARD-LOOKING exceptions are correct as written and must not be 'corrected': the 1910 report announcing Kanawana's first season for the coming summer of 1910, and the 1946 report announcing Macdiarmid's Toronto move as taking effect the following 1 September.

THE ASSOCIATION CALLS W. J. HOLLIDAY "THE FIRST CAMP DIRECTOR" IN ITS OWN WORDS. The 1931 Annual Report, describing the camp's twenty-first-anniversary event for the 1930 season: "W. J. HOLLIDAY, THE FIRST CAMP DIRECTOR, DELIVERED AN INSPIRING ADDRESS, AND MR. GNAEDINGER, THE FORMER PRESIDENT OF THE COMMITTEE, GAVE A TALK REMINISCENT OF THE DAYS WHEN A CAMP OF THIRTY-FIVE BOYS WAS CONSIDERED LARGE." This independently corroborates the 1910 report's forward-tense announcement putting Holliday in charge of the new Lake Kanawana site, and settles that he is regarded by the association as Kanawana's first director. Found incidentally during the p_260 verification pass, not by the sweep that established the 1910 announcement.

THE M. E. WILLIAMS CUPS -- a previously undocumented Kanawana competition, with its own winners roll 1917-1922, thirty years before the L&V trophy. The Gas Bag "Extra, Vol. 13 No. 1" (1923) asks "Which branch will win the M. E. Williams cups?" and prints a two-column WINNERS table for Aquatics and Athletics. It was an INTER-BRANCH competition (North Branch, Central, Westmount), not the intra-camp two-team format the L&V Games later used.

The M. E. Williams cups winners roll as printed in the 1923 Gas Bag Extra, with the ditto marks read as repeats -- AN INFERENCE, since the OCR renders them as garbage characters ("sf", "s", "ce", "ef", "es") rather than legible ditto marks. AQUATICS: 1917 North Branch, 1918 [ditto], 1919 [ditto], 1920 Central, 1921 Westmount, 1922 [ditto]. ATHLETICS: 1917 Westmount, 1918 Central, 1919 [ditto], 1920 [ditto], 1921 Westmount, 1922 [ditto]. The positions of the named entries are certain; the repeats are not, and a page image would settle them.

THE KANAWANA FEE WAS $8.50 PER WEEK IN 1923, extending the documented fee series back four years from the 1927-1929 figures. The 1923 Gas Bag Extra: "The cost is $8.50 per week. This includes one return trip from Montreal to Camp." So the fee was UNCHANGED across at least 1923-1929, through a period when the annual reports repeatedly note it was deliberately below every other permanent camp "to keep the cost within reach of the average home."

Visitor charges at Kanawana in 1923, from the Gas Bag Extra: 50 cents per night, 50 cents per meal, and $1.50 each way for the rig to Piedmont. The Camp Management "prefers to know in advance if visitors are expected."

R. L. CHARLTON WAS ACTIVE AT KANAWANA IN 1923, not only in the founding era and the 1943 manuscript: the 1923 Gas Bag Extra reports "Mr. R. L. Charlton reports that he hopes to complete arrangements for a Senior Log Cabin. On rainy nights the Cabin, with a roaring fire throwing out its warmth and comfort, will be more than welcome." Charlton sat on the first Summer Camp committee in 1894 and wrote the "Notes re Early Days" manuscript in 1943 -- this places him still working on camp buildings nearly thirty years after the founding.

NULL RESULT (p_246): only TWO Gas Bag items exist in the digitized YMCA of Montreal fonds -- the issue of 1 September 1923 and the "Extra, Vol. 13 No. 1" of 1923. RESOLUTION (c_024, operator, 2026-08-14): the 1919 memoir's Lac la Croix passage records a SITE-SELECTION SEQUENCE, not a rival account of where the 1894 season was held. The syndicate decided to locate the first camp at Lac la Croix; the first group went out in 1894; a better location was found 'just a little further on'; property with fishing privileges was secured at Lac St. Joseph. Lake Saint-Joseph stands as the 1894 camp site; Lac la Croix is recorded as the site originally selected and abandoned.

CORROBORATION of the 1919 memoir's reliability: the memoir says property 'with fishing privileges' was secured at Lac St. Joseph, and the YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1894-95 -- written within a year of the events -- says the Association 'has leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a lake near St. Agathe'. Two independent documents twenty-five years apart describe the same transaction in the same terms.

ATTRIBUTION CAUTION: the August 1919 'Brief Autobiographical Sketch of Association Career' is NOT by W. H. (Billy) Ball. Ball appears in it in the third person as a fellow member of the founding syndicate ('a small group composed of W. H. Ball, John W. Ross, Will Wilson, myself and others'). The author is the man who became the third General Secretary of the Winnipeg YMCA in June 1894.

NULL/SCOPE RESULT (p_255): the phrase 'Camp Jubilee' appears in exactly ONE of the 634 digitized text items in the YMCA of Montreal fonds -- the 1988 retrospective report 'Kanawana... A Place to Grow'. Every other corpus use of 'Jubilee' is the YMCA movement's own jubilee sense (the 1844-1894 World's Jubilee Convention; Montreal's own 1851-1901 jubilee celebrated June 1901). No contemporaneous 1894-1910 document in the corpus calls the camp 'Camp Jubilee'.

The 1988 report 'Kanawana... A Place to Grow' is the source of the 'Camp Jubilee' name in this wiki's chain, and its 1894 entry is demonstrably unreliable in detail: it states 'Three islands were purchased on Lake St. Joseph' in 1894 with '20 participants'. The contemporaneous 1894-95 report says the land and fishing rights were LEASED from the Government, and gives 23 workers and boys; the 1902 report records that three islands in Lac St. Joseph were sold by public auction on 26 November 1901, the Committee purchasing one small island adjoining 'our present island' for $50.

The 1988 report also states that in 1910 'Camp Jubilee was renamed Camp Otoreke' -- making Otoreke, not Jubilee, the name with contemporaneous documentary support for the original site. The earliest Otoreke attestation in the corpus is the 1921-22 Annual Report: 'CAMP OTOREKE -- The Camp for men was again conducted during the months of July and August', carried as a budget line separate from Kamp Kanawana.

What the YMCA of Montreal actually called the original camp, contemporaneously and consistently, was descriptive rather than a proper name: a standing committee simply titled 'Summer Camp' (chaired by John W. Ross, in the Committees for 1895-96 list); 'the summer camp at Ste. Agathe' (1895-96); 'the Summer Camp at Lake St. Joseph' (1897-98); 'THE ASSOCIATION SUMMER CAMP, LAKE ST. JOSEPH' (1899); 'SUMMER CAMP, ST. AGATHE' (1902); 'The Camp at Lac St. Joseph, Ste. Agathe' (1903).

EARLIEST RECORDED REFERENCE to the original camp location: the YMCA of Montreal Annual Report for 1894-95, Physical Department section -- 'The Association has leased land from the Government and the fishing rights of a lake near St. Agathe, and purpose using it as a summer camp for our members.' The LAKE IS NOT NAMED. The earliest naming of the lake in the corpus is the following year's 1895-96 report: 'In July and August the Association carries on a camp at Lac St. Joseph, near St. Agathe, for the use of the members on their vacation.'

MATERIAL QUALIFICATION to the p_255 'Camp Jubilee' null: while the name appears in only one of the 634 digitized corpus items, it IS the name used by CONCORDIA'S OWN ARCHIVAL DESCRIPTION of the YMCA of Montreal fonds -- sub-series 'P0145/12L - Lac St-Joseph/Camp Jubilee', and a series description reading 'Season reports of the Junior Camp (Camp Jubilee/Otoreke)'. QAHN uses it too: 'That camp, called Camp Jubilee after the fiftieth anniversary of the YMCA'. So the name is the received archival and heritage-sector name for the site, not a wiki invention -- it simply has no attestation in the association's own 1894-1909 records.

The camp's two in-house histories do NOT use the name 'Camp Jubilee' either. The 1935 'A History of Kamp Kanawana' does not contain the word; the 1951 'Kamp Kanawana History' says only that 'After much searching a site was chosen on Lac St. Joseph at Ste Adolphe de Howard' -- wording which is itself consistent with the Lac la Croix site-selection sequence recorded in the 1919 memoir. || CORRECTION 2026-09-02: this fact previously rendered the 1951 quotation as 'at Ste [Agathe]', with Agathe supplied in brackets. The document does not say Agathe. It says 'Ste Adolphe de Howard' -- Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard -- and mentions Sainte-Agathe separately and earlier, as the REGION toured in spring 1893 before a site was picked. The bracket inverted the document's own distinction between where they looked and where they landed, and it pointed away from Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, which is exactly where QAHN places Camp Jubilee. Found on the first end-to-end read of the full cached text.

QAHN dates the renaming of Camp Jubilee to Camp Otoreke to 1909; the camp's own 1988 retrospective dates it to 1910. Both postdate the events by decades and neither is corroborated by a contemporaneous document; the earliest corpus attestation of 'Otoreke' is the 1921-22 Annual Report.

EDITORIAL DECISION (p_255, operator, 2026-08-14): the wiki KEEPS the name 'Camp Jubilee' for the 1894-1909 camp, with a stated explanation that it is the archival name (Concordia's fonds description and QAHN) rather than the association's own, which called the place descriptively -- a committee titled 'Summer Camp', then 'the Summer Camp at Lake St. Joseph'. Rationale: it is the name a researcher uses against the Concordia finding aid, so dropping it would cut the wiki off from its own source record.

The QAHN photograph 'Camp Otoreke (YMCA Camp), Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard, 1944' is an old photographic postcard whose verso, transcribed by QAHN, reads: 'Camp Otoreke. 3 August 44. I am having a grand time here. This is a picture of our new lodge. We eat upstairs, also have parties there. Downstairs are the shower and changing rooms. The weather so far has been perfect. We went on a 15 mile paddle yesterday for a swim in the falls and a picnic supper... Love Betty.' So by August 1944 Otoreke had a NEW LODGE with an upstairs dining and function room and downstairs showers and changing rooms, and its campers took fifteen-mile paddles.

QAHN's historical note on the Otoreke photograph, credited to the Concordia University Archives, records the site's post-1910 career: after the YMCA's main camping program moved to Kanawana in 1910, Otoreke 'operated variously as a camp for men over 18, for women and men over 18, for married couples, and for low-income families. It was sold in 1987.' It also describes the site as 'several islands plus a landing area on the mainland'.

CORROBORATION, NOT A NEW CONFLICT (p_263): QAHN, citing the Concordia University Archives, says the original Montreal YMCA camp 'began operation in 1893'. The wiki's own framing already treats 1893 as documented precursor activity and 1894 as the first camp proper, on the strength of the contemporaneous 1894-95 report's 'our first Summer Camp'. THE 1918 SEASON IN DETAIL, from the Gazette of 27 July 1918 (recovered via Google Books after newspapers.com blocked access): 'At the Y.M.C.A. boys' camp at Kanawana there are now about 90 boys whose ages range from 12 to 17 years.' The boys 'sleep under canvas' and are 'wakened at [6].30 a.m. by a bugle', a welcome summons because it means 'the morning dip, which is preceded by physical exercises'. 'Nearly all the boys can swim, and many become expert oarsmen -- twelve rowboats and six canoes are at their disposal.' Meals were 'served in the dining pavilion'.

TWO NEW 1918 STAFF NAMES from the same Gazette report: 'the camp cook is Mr. Harry Smith, from the Montreal High School, and being well acquainted with boys' appetites, the campers never have to go short'; and 'Lessons in basketry and woodwork are given by Mr. Robert Spinney'. Woodcraft was 'one of the special features of this year's camp', with 'long rambles... giving the boys a chance to study nature'. Neither man is otherwise known to this project.

THE 1974 SEASON, from the Gazette summer-camp feature of 18 April 1974 (recovered via Google Books): Kanawana is listed under 'RESIDENTIAL CAMPS - CO-ED' and 'was billed as Quebec's oldest boys' camp until sister campers invaded four years ago'. That summer '90 boys and 90 girls' were expected. Facilities: 'canoes, sailboats, handicraft shop'. Location 'just outside St. Sauveur'. The stated rationale for coeducation, quoted from a YMCA public relations manager: 'We went co-ed in response to requests from parents who wanted their daughters to have the same opportunities as their sons.' And a striking demographic figure: 'French campers constitute 30 per cent of the Kanawana population.'

DOES NOT REOPEN THE COEDUCATION DATE. The 1974 Gazette's 'sister campers invaded four years ago' would put coeducation at about 1970, but the date is settled at 1968 on three independent traces: the camp's own 1988 report ('1968 Kamp Kanawana admits female campers for the first time. 66 girls registered'), the annual-report camper-weeks tables where bracketed girl-camper figures first appear in the 1968 column, and the 1970 season report calling that summer the camp's 'third year as a coeducational camp'. A newspaper feature's round 'four years ago' is loose journalism against a hard enrolment figure. Recorded so the settled question is not reopened by a later pass.

The 1988 Kanawana Camping Task Force chronology records, for 1964: "The Y purchases 120 acres of land south of Lac Wilson which connects Kamp Kanawana to Camp Tamaracouta. A portion of this is sold to the Boy Scouts of Canada." The same chronology records a second 1964 purchase: "The Y purchases the Page's property. This land is the entrance to Kanawana and contains the Farm house and the Block house." This is the first documented statement that Kanawana's property was made physically contiguous with Camp Tamaracouta, and that part of the acquired land passed to the Boy Scouts rather than remaining with the Y.

The 1988 Task Force report gives the only itemised property breakdown in the record, attributed to "a report submitted to the Y from Royal/Lepage in 1989": Land 455 acres; Lac Kanawana 60 acres; Lac Wilson 17 acres; Lac Rond 5 acres; TOTAL 537 acres. The report states in the same paragraph: "There was no record found that showed the Kanawana site has ever been surveyed." The report adds that the property "completely encompasses three lakes: Kanawana, Wilson, and Rond, and touches the tip of Lac Spring," and that the 455 acres are "mostly hilly, rolling terrain" with facilities on "a thin strip of land north of Lac Kanawana."

The figure "Between 1,000-1,500 acres" in the 1988 Task Force report is NOT a statement of Kanawana's size. It appears under a "SITE / Size:" heading in a specification for a hypothetical REPLACEMENT property, written in support of the Task Force's recommendations that the Board consider "A) The sale of the Kanawana site; B) The purchase of a new site." The adjacent criteria are prospective, not descriptive -- "Undeveloped, wooded area that contains 2-3 lakes"; "Adjacent to a national or provincial park"; "Preferably near downhill ski area"; "Facilities be developed on northern shore" -- and the report's costing section budgets "Land Cost 1,000 acres @ $1,000" for the purchase. Neither the sale nor the new site took place. This passage is a documented trap: read out of context it would appear to corroborate the 1974 Gazette's 1,200-acre figure, and it does not.

Six independently cached documents spanning 1964-1970 state Kanawana's size as roughly 1,000 acres, establishing that the large figure was the camp's own settled self-description for at least that period rather than a one-off error: the 1964 Kamp Kanawana annual report ("over approximately 1,000 acres"); the SGW YMCA annual report 1964 ("1,000 acres"); a YMCA news release of 13 May 1969 ("it covers more than 1,000 acres"); the 1969 Kamp Kanawana annual report ("We occupy 1000 acres of valuable land"); and the 1970 Kamp Kanawana annual report ("a small area of our 1,000 acres"). The series begins in the same year as the 120-acre purchase that connected the property to Camp Tamaracouta.

Camp Kanawana cancelled its residential season for a second consecutive summer in 2021, and the decision reached camp families in the last week of April 2021: 'This week, the family learned Kanawana is pulling the plug on camp for a second consecutive summer due to COVID-19.' The article is by Jessica Wong, CBC News, posted 29 April 2021 -- a month before the 28 May 2021 CBC report that Quebec sleepaway camps had been given a greenlight 'too late'.

IDENTIFICATION NOT ESTABLISHED (2026-08-25 RALPH loop, p_272): whether the Gaetane Verna named as a former Kanawana counsellor and section leader is the internationally known curator of the same name is SUPPORTED BY FOUR CONVERGING ATTRIBUTES but confirmed by no source. FOR: (1) the name is rare and matches exactly; (2) CBC says she grew up in Quebec, and the curator was raised in Montreal after her family moved to Canada from Kinshasa when she was two; (3) CBC says she was 'now based in Toronto' in April 2021, and the curator directed The Power Plant in Toronto from 2012 until her 2022 move to the Wexner Center; (4) the curator holds a bachelor's degree in management and international business from Concordia University, Montreal -- the institution descended from the Sir George Williams YMCA, the same institutional lineage that supplied Kanawana staff. AGAINST: no source of any kind connects the curator to Kanawana, to the YMCA, or to summer camp; her professional profiles carry no such mention. UNRESOLVED AND UNREADABLE: a Toronto Life feature is reported by search engines to give her daughters' ages as six and ten, which if paired with the reported October 2015 publication date would NOT match CBC's April 2021 description (elder daughter plus a 15-year-old), but WOULD match it if the piece dates from her 2012 appointment. The article could not be read through any route tried -- WebFetch 403, curl 403, Wayback egress blocked, archive.today connection reset, text proxy served a Cloudflare challenge -- so neither the ages nor the date is established and this line of evidence is unusable, not merely inconclusive.

Concordia's finding aid for P145/12C01 (Camp Otoreke general administration) lists a file titled "Evaluation, recommendations re Camp Otoreke as a mixed [gender] camp. - 1936." The YMCA of Montreal was therefore formally evaluating mixed-gender camping at one of its own camps in 1936 -- twenty-nine years before the 1965 Kanawana director's report that recommended coeducation and was declined, and thirty-two years before Kanawana admitted girls in 1968. The file's CONTENTS are not established by the finding aid; what is established is that the evaluation existed and is dated 1936.

P145/12H is a whole sub-series titled "Ski lodge" documenting YMCA of Montreal winter operations at the Otoreke site, 1929-1959: "Ski lodge-H. C. Cross' file. - 1929-1946"; "Memorandum proposing ski club. - 1941"; "Correspondence, memoranda, reports on ski facilities. - 1946-1950"; "Purchase by YMCA of Christieville property. - 1948-1951"; "What the Otoreke Ski Lodge Committee wants in facilities at the Mainland Inn. - [195-]"; "Otoreke ski lodge-1954-1955 report"; "Ski lodge 1955-1956"; "Christieville ski lodge correspondence. - 1959"; plus ski lodge photographs. This is documentary evidence for a sustained winter programme -- the 'Winter Programming (if evidence found)' article CLAUDE.md Phase 2 section 8 lists as conditional. It also gives Harold C. Cross a named archival file spanning 1929-1946.

P145/12B07 (Kamp Kanawana - Program) lists the camp's own culture files, several earlier than anything this wiki currently cites: "Place mat or paper napkin with artwork and menu. Kanawana campers reunion. - 1913" -- material culture from the camp's fourth year at Saint-Sauveur; "Badges. 9 award ribbons glued on poster-size paper for display. - [192-] or [193-]"; "Song sheets, skits. - 1925, 1927"; "KK pageant scripts. - 1931-1932"; "Water safety training; drills; pageants. - 1931"; "Canoe care, water safety. - 1933"; and "Firelighting ceremony. - 1936" -- a dated document for the Council Ring tradition.

P145/13B (Anniversaries) holds a file group headed "World Y 50th Jubilee, Montreal Y 50th" containing "Jubilees. - 1893, 1894, 1901", alongside "42nd anniversary-order of service. - 1894" and "Observance of 50th anniversary-YMCA of Montreal. - 1901". This is the documentary context for the name Camp Jubilee: the camp was founded in 1894, in the same years the world YMCA movement and the Montreal association were marking jubilees. The finding aid does not connect the files to the camp, and no such connection is asserted here -- but this is the archival series in which a connection, if documented anywhere, would sit.

P145/12N04 is a sub-sub-series for the Quebec Camping Association / Association des camps du Quebec, holding "Constitution et reglements-Association des Camps du Quebec. - 1979", "Annuaire 1979, liste des membres. - 1979", a "Special general meeting. - October 25, 1979", and 1978-1980 publications. This is the resolution route for the unverified claim at f_2215 that Kanawana was 'a founding member of the ACQ': a 1979 constitution and a 1979 membership list, held in the YMCA of Montreal's own fonds, would show whether the association dates from that year and whether the YMCA was in at the start. Sibling sub-sub-series cover the American Camping Association (12N01, records 1937-1959) and the Canadian Camping Association (12N02, records 1936-1951, including "Meetings-notices, agendas, minutes, correspondence. - 1936-1939" from the CCA's founding period).

CORRECTION TO f_2263. Concordia's static-HTML mirror is a strict SUBSET of the archive's own finding aid, not a substitute for it. The authoritative document -- 'Finding Aid - YMCA of Montreal Fonds (P0145)', 125 pages, generated 24 November 2023 -- describes 15 series and 173 sub-series/sub-sub-series units. The mirror carries 95. Every mirror page corresponds to a unit in the finding aid (no mirror page is absent from it), but 78 units have NO mirror page at all. The gaps the mirror walk confirmed as 'genuine 404s' -- 12B02, 12B05, 12B06, 12C06, 14D01, 14D02, 14D11, and the parent sub-series 12B, 12C, 12G, 12N, 14D -- are real archival units that simply were never given a mirror page. THREE KANAWANA SUB-SUB-SERIES HAVE NO MIRROR PAGE and had never been seen by this project: P0145/12B02 Financial administration; P0145/12B05 Staff, counsellors; and P0145/12B06 Campers. The last is the camp's own records of its campers. The full Kanawana sub-series is therefore 12B01 General administration, 12B02 Financial administration, 12B03 Land/facilities/equipment/supplies, 12B04 Communications, 12B05 Staff/counsellors, 12B06 Campers, 12B07 Program -- of which this project had only 12B01, 12B03, 12B04 and 12B07.

The finding aid's physical description of P0145/12B (Kamp Kanawana) records what the archive physically holds for the camp: "7.72 m of textual records / graphic materials (photographs, artwork) / OBJECTS (T-SHIRTS, BADGES, RIBBONS, PENNANTS) / cartographic records (maps) / architectural and technical drawings / sound recordings (audiocassettes) / MOVING IMAGES (FILM REELS, VIDEOCASSETTES) / other materials". CLAUDE.md Phase 2 section 4 sets 'Merchandise and paraphernalia' as a research target to be pursued through eBay, Etsy and collectibles databases; the camp's own badges, ribbons, pennants and t-shirts are held in the institutional archive, along with film reels and audiocassettes.

The finding aid gives the complete camping-series structure, including three sub-series with no mirror page: P0145/12G Camp Perrot, P0145/12B Kamp Kanawana and P0145/12C Camp Otoreke as parent units, plus P0145/12N Camping associations. It also confirms two names in the archive's own words: P0145/12K is "Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye" and P0145/12L is "Lake St-Joseph/Camp Jubilee" -- the institution's own catalogue pairing the original site with the Jubilee name. P0145/12N03 is titled "Quebec Section, Canadian Camping Association", distinct from 12N04 "Quebec Camping Association/Association des camps du Quebec".

Concordia's archives have been posting digitized YMCA films to YouTube, and at least one Kanawana-relevant item is not yet in this wiki: "Canoe Trips" (YouTube cP_V1Fn2kUQ), whose archival description reads "P0145-09-0066 : Promotional video for the canoe trips organized by the YMCA of Montreal. Date of production is unknown, no sound." It was uploaded on 13 February 2026 -- i.e. the digitization programme is active and the catalogue changes. A second candidate, "Voyageurs (1963)" (YouTube 95NB-6BE3mM), is very likely P0145/12K 'Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye' material but its archival description could NOT be read -- YouTube returned HTTP 429 on repeated attempts -- so it is recorded here as an unverified lead, not a fact.
