ACCESS MECHANISM FOR THE ATOM CATALOGUE (researched 2026-08-25). The block is AtoM's built-in JavaScript Challenge, a standard feature of the software, not a Concordia-specific control. Its 'test_headless' setting is what refuses automated clients. It was introduced in response to administrators reporting AI bot traffic causing high CPU load on archival servers. The same software ships the remedy: 'endpoint_exceptions' (documented as 'useful for API endpoints that should not be challenged, such as AtoM's Rest API'), plus 'cidr_exceptions', 'network_user_agent_exceptions', 'asn_exceptions' and 'country_exceptions'. Separately, AtoM's REST API requires a key, and 'Only an administrator has the proper permissions to generate an API Key'. The named person at Concordia is JOHN RICHAN, Interim Director and University Archivist, who is also separately listed as Digital Archivist -- the only person holding both the archival authority and the systems role. Requests go to archives@concordia.ca, which targets a five-working-day response. Caveat: it is the Archives & Special Collections SHARED catalogue, jointly with Library Special Collections, so the sysadmin may sit with the Library.

CONSTRAINT ON P0145/12B06 'CAMPERS'. Concordia RMA states on its Reading Room page that "in compliance with the Act Respecting Documents Held by Public Bodies and the Protection of Personal Information, documents containing personal information cannot" be released, and that "requests may be refused if they contravene the Privacy Act". Camper records are personal information about identifiable and frequently living individuals, so 12B06 should NOT be expected to be released; the realistic asks are aggregate or structural (enrolment totals, section organisation), plus 12B05 staff rosters and 12B02 financial records. This aligns with CLAUDE.md's own standing rule against extracting personal information about living private individuals. Reproduction fees for scholarly use are scanning-only: low-resolution scans $10.00/image for 0-50, $7.50 for 51-100, $5.00 for 101+; high-resolution $15.00/$11.50/$7.50; audiovisual $1.00/minute. Unflashed digital photography in the Reading Room is free -- for a Montreal-based researcher the cheapest route to bulk material. Appointment required; Mon-Thu 9:00-11:30 and 1:30-4:00, Faubourg Building FG A112, 1250 Guy.

THE FINDING AID CARRIES ITEM-LEVEL AV RECORDS -- 611 'Item' entries in all, and the Kanawana audio holdings are the single richest unexploited seam found to date. Quarter-inch audio reels in P0145/11: P0145-11-0180 'Kamp Kanawana'; P0145-11-0190 'Kanawana promotional tape'; P0145-11-0191 'Pathfinder evaluation'; P0145-11-0193 'Kamp Kanawana - Interview with Woodsman', dated 24 August 1962; P0145-11-0194 'Homesick tape'; and P0145-11-0197 'What is God? / Interview of Kamp Kanawana campers and staff', 1963. Also P0145-11-0002, 'On my way to Kanawana', a 4-minute CD from 2001, 'Words and music by Richard Itch Kerr and used for the YMCA Montreal 150 years'. Two of these are DATED ORAL RECORDINGS OF CAMPERS AND STAFF from 1962 and 1963 -- primary voice material from the period this wiki documents almost entirely through paper.

P0145-11-0191 is an audio reel titled 'Pathfinder evaluation'. This bears directly on a standing open question in coeducation-gender.md: the 1965 'Pathfinder program Summer Summary' is ambiguous because 'Pathfinders' was introduced at Kanawana in 1959 as a BOYS' section name for ages 14-15, and was only later reassigned to the senior girls' section. An evaluation recording could settle which programme is meant. The item is undated in the finding aid; the immediately adjacent untitled item P0145-11-0192 carries the dates 1969 and 1964, which brackets the neighbourhood but does not date the reel itself.

Moving-image items for the camp, with reference codes: P0145-09-0012 'Camp Kanawana: Boating and Water Sports All Summer Long' (inter-titled silent footage, digitized 2003-01-16); P0145-09-0035 the 1993 Cathy Reeves documentary; P0145-09-0057 'News Documents and Kamp Kanawana'; P0145-09-0066 'Canoe Trips'; P0145-09-0088 'Kamp Kanawana' [ca. 196-], a 16 mm reel, no sound, 'Various scenes from Kamp Kanawana, including swimming and diving', access copy created 2003-01-30; P0145-09-0135 'Message d'interet public: - Kamp Kanawana', 6 December 1988, a French public-service announcement; and P0145-09-0136 'Kamp Kanawana', March 1987, noted as the English version. The 1987/1988 pair is a bilingual PSA campaign the wiki does not record at all.

Item-level photograph descriptions for the camp, all b&w prints unless noted: 'Several tents on camp site' and 'Seven swimmers with life saver' and 'Man getting ready to dive in lake' [193-?]; 'Entrance to site made of logs' [194-?]; 'Several people on waterfront or bathing with lifeguard' [195-?]; 'YMCA Kamp Kanawana Hospital -- Boy lying in bed with nurse by his side' [195-?]; 'Staff group photo' [196-?]; and two colour prints [198-?], 'Colorful cabin with totem in wood' and 'Two people pointing at a Kamp Kanawana map on exterior wall of a cabin'. For Otoreke: 'Cafeteria full of people eating' [194-?]; 'Group photo in stairs or balcony of the camp building' [195-?]; and a dated 1944 print, 'To Chapel Island, Kamp Otoreke -- Group of people on a log bridge on their way to Chapel Island'.

The finding aid's scope note for P0145/12B dates the Kanawana sub-series 'nd, [190-]-2003' -- beginning in the 1900s decade, before the 1910 purchase of the Saint-Sauveur site -- and lists its contents as 'directors' reports, annual reports, correspondence, CAMPER APPLICATIONS, blueprints, maps, photographs, publicity brochures and films, t-shirts, badges, ribbons, pennants, and other materials'. The presence of camper applications confirms why 12B06 'Campers' is likely restricted under privacy law (f_2271). The scope note also shows how the two Concordia surfaces relate: each sub-series entry carries a 'Finding aids: Box listings:' line pointing at the concordia.ca static mirror page, so the PDF supplies series descriptions and item-level AV records while the mirror supplies the file-and-box listings beneath them. They are complementary layers, not rival copies -- which is why both were needed.

CAMP LIGHTHALL IS THE JUNIOR LEAGUE CAMP -- an INFERENCE, not a stated fact, and recorded as such. No document says so in terms. The convergence: the Junior League Camp was founded by 'Miss L[i]ght-hall of Montreal, on family property near St. Marguerites' (Agnes Knox Mutchler, its director, Canadian Camping June 1949); the Junior League of Montreal's own fonds description dates the camp's founding to 1921; the name 'Junior League Camp' last appears in Canadian Camping in June 1967; and in the January 1975 and January 1976 Quebec directories 'CAMP LIGHTHALL' -- organizational, girls, St-Sauveur-des-Monts, 150 girls aged 6-14, $75.00/12 days -- stands where it used to be. The rename is bounded to between June 1967 and c. 1972 (the Trent CCA portrait series). There is no Lighthall toponym in Quebec, so the name is the family's.

THE GREEN TRIANGLE MENTIONS THE JUNIOR LEAGUE CAMP IN AT LEAST ELEVEN ISSUES, 1932-1940, which upgrades this wiki's previous 'visited on occasion' to a sustained neighbourly relationship. Two entries are operational rather than social. 29 July 1938, over the signature 'Chief' (the camp director): 'Our camp doctor is dividing his time between Kanawana and the Junior League.' And 1 July 1939: 'Three carloads of Staff members drove to the Junior League Camp last Tuesday night, to visit the christening of two beautiful new buildings with Ginger Ale. They were welcomed by Mrs. Perrault, Chairman of the Building Committee, and Mrs. Bert Hough, the Camp Director...' -- which names two Junior League Camp officers for 1939 and dates two new buildings to June 1939. The remaining mentions are boys'-camp humour about hikes to the girls' camp, including a spoof advice column signed 'A Junior League Girl' (13 Aug 1932) and verse about 'Junior League land' (13 Aug 1936).

MARGARET SEAMAN'S IDENTITY AND CAREER CONFIRMED. Canadian Camping, June 1967, p. 125, profiling the Montreal YMCA's Director of Camping: 'Mrs. Seaman, also a keen camper, has directed Camp Perrot (girls' section), Camp Chapleau of the Old Brewery Mission and the Junior League Camp of Montreal.' This closes an identification a-ross-seaman.md had explicitly flagged as unconfirmed -- that the 'Margaret Seaman' who directed Camp Perrot's girls' section in 1952 was A. Ross Seaman's wife -- by attributing that directorship to Mrs. Seaman directly. It also establishes a camp-directing career of her own across three unrelated organizations (YMCA, Old Brewery Mission, Junior League of Montreal), and means the Kanawana-Junior League connection ran through a person as well as through geography.

THE 'YO TRIUMPHY' CHEER WAS ALREADY 'FORMER' BY JULY 1938. The Green Triangle of 9 July 1938 reprints it: "The following is a FORMER Kanawana yell, which is very effective when shouted rapidly...-Let's all try to learn it:-- / Yo triumphy, yo triumphy, (sung slowly) / Hobben slobben rebeqca le-am, / De whoop, de whoop, de shol-de-vere, / De boom de rye, de hi-de-pock, / Hoonica heenica, whack-de-whack, / Hoh dob de bowl de barra, / Con slob de hol dobra, / KANAWANA...rah!" This is an independent second witness to a text previously known only from the 1922 brochure, and the readings differ throughout, so neither is authoritative. It also dates the cheer's obsolescence: campers were still singing it in 1933 (f_0xxx, Green Triangle 29 July 1933) and by July 1938 it had to be taught back to them. The 1938 printing adds a performance instruction the brochure lacks -- the opening line is marked '(sung slowly)' while the whole is 'shouted rapidly'.

TWO CEREMONIES DESCRIBED IN PERFORMANCE, where the Concordia finding aid holds only catalogue titles. (1) Green Triangle, 2 June 1938: "The Fire of Friendship in the centre of the council ring was kindled by the torches of campers representing the Spirits of Work, Play, Co-operation and the True Spirit of Kanawana in a very impressive ritual. The serious part of the programme was followed by several rollicking songs led by Chief and Norm Wallace. Following the singing of 'Abide With Me' the campers slowly wended their ways through the trail to their respective tents." Three of the four torch-bearing Spirits restate the YMCA developmental scheme, with the camp's own spirit added. (2) Green Triangle, 21 July 1940, on the firelighting: "around the rocks, an Indian brave came into view; he prayed to WAKONDA to light the fire. Suddenly with a bright blue flash and a great hissing sound, the fire flared up." The same deity name closes the c.1925-27 Council Ring script, so the invocation persisted at least fifteen years; the blue flash and hissing indicate a chemical accelerant.

THREE CORPUS-WIDE NULLS, established against verified full text of all 38 digitized Green Triangle issues (2026-08-25) rather than against a search index: (1) 'Chopsy' and 'Cropsy' appear NOWHERE in the camp's own newspaper across its entire 1932-1940 run; (2) no explanation of the name 'Kanawana' appears anywhere; (3) neither 'Non Nobis Solum' nor 'Each for all and all for each' appears anywhere -- the motto is absent from the camp's own paper throughout the 1930s, which bears on when it was adopted. METHOD NOTE, because the first attempt failed silently: Internet Archive stores these under human-readable filenames ('The Green Triangle - 1939-07-22_djvu.txt'), so a conventional <identifier>_djvu.txt fetch returns a styled 404 -- six of which came back byte-identical at 137,595 bytes, which is what exposed them. A first verification control then demanded each issue's own year appear in its text and falsely rejected twelve real issues, including 1938-07-29, whose masthead OCR reads 'Saturday, Juiy 83, 195'. The OCR of this 1930s mimeograph is heavily degraded and any search across it must assume so.

SMALLER FINDS FROM THE FULL GREEN TRIANGLE READ, 2026-08-25. (a) CAMPER SELF-GOVERNMENT: the 9 July 1938 issue reports 'OFFICERS OF CAMP COUNCIL ELECTED. At a meeting of the all camp council, the following were elected to office: President: Norm Wallace. Vice-President: Ken Smith. Secretary: Ian Fraser. Dater: Benny Leslie.' -- an elected all-camp council this wiki does not document. (b) The 23 July 1932 issue is THE FIRST ISSUE, opening with a signed editorial from the 'Chief' on 'Camp Spirit': 'It is the thing that welds us together... It grows around the Camp Fire as we sing our camp songs, as we swing along the roads on our hikes, shoulder to shoulder.' (c) 4 August 1935: 'Last Sunday morning Mr. H. J. Cross, a former Kanawana Chief, addressed the camp assembled in chapel' -- placing Harold Cross as a FORMER Chief by 1935. (d) 6 August 1932 carries a signed piece by 'Graig MacDermaid' (Greig Macdiarmid). (e) 21 July 1940 names 'The Kanawana Pump-House Boys, Bruce Johnson, George Blackburn, Ed Smee, and Fred Weiner' playing mouth-organ, and announces 'the Kanawana Circus'. (f) 13 August 1932 records hikers passing "D'Arcy McGee Camp" and giving 'the Kanawana Yell'; 30 July 1932 has Otoreke 'playing baseball against Camp Kinkora'. Neither neighbouring camp is documented in this wiki.

GREIG MACDIARMID'S POST-MONTREAL CAREER AND DEATH, from his Canadian Camping obituary (Vol. 15 No. 1, December 1962, p. 17), headed "In Memoriam: J. G. 'Greig' Macdiarmid, May 21st, 1962": "Camping, in Canada, lost a knowledgeable and ardent supporter with the sudden death, in May, of Greig Macdiarmid, GENERAL SECRETARY OF THE TORONTO YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION. A former director of Camp Kanawana, he served the Y's in Montreal and Toronto and during World War II was SENIOR OFFICER OVERSEAS of Canadian YMCA War Services. His interest and enthusiasm was a key factor in the expansion of CAMP PINE CREST, NORVAL, WANGOMA and the development of TWENTY-THREE YMCA DAY CAMPS in the Toronto area. He set the stage for the Y's co-operation in the operation of Camp Illahee for medically handicapped children." He therefore rose from Executive Secretary of Toronto CENTRAL YMCA (1946) to General Secretary of the Toronto association, and died suddenly on 21 May 1962. NOTE THE PINE CREST ADJACENCY: this wiki records Camp Pine Crest as the source of the Lumbermen-versus-Voyageurs competition Kanawana adopted in 1947, and the man who expanded Pine Crest was Kanawana's own former Camp Chief. No source connects the two facts causally; they are recorded as adjacent, not as a chain.

A. ROSS SEAMAN, FULL BIOGRAPHY, from his Canadian Camping profile as President of the Quebec Camping Association (Vol. 19 No. 4, June 1967, p. 125): born and educated in Montreal; B.A. from Sir George Williams University; MASTER OF EDUCATION FROM SPRINGFIELD COLLEGE; "he really began his career AT THE AGE OF 10 when he attended Camp Kanawana as a camper", working up from C.I.T. to Director; first YMCA post 1945 as Community Secretary at the Point St. Charles Branch; then Executive Secretary of the Lachine Branch; then Metropolitan Programme Secretary and Director of Camping. In 1967 he directed both Kanawana and 'Les Voyageurs', described as "a pioneer wilderness camp for teen agers". HIS WIFE'S MAIDEN NAME IS BRADLEY: "Mr. Seaman married Margaret Bradley and has three children, Derek, aged 16, Suzanne, aged 14 and Dawn aged 3." That dates the children's births to approximately 1951, 1953 and 1964.

ROY LOCKE: MIDDLE INITIAL, QCA PRESIDENCY, AND THE KANAWANA MANUAL OF OPERATIONS. Canadian Camping, April 1952: "Roy D. Locke director of Y.M.C. Kamp Kanawana is president of the Quebec Camping Association" -- settling the middle initial as D and making the 1950 'Roy N. Locke' a transcription error. December 1953: "Roy Locke in Montreal, who, in addition to the Metropolitan Boys Work job, takes over Camp Kanawana and the planning for Camp Perrot. Roy has something which is of interest to all camp people in Canada, and that is A BOOK HE IS DEVELOPING ON THE TOTAL CAMP OPERATION." June 1953 describes what is almost certainly that book -- the KANAWANA MANUAL OF OPERATIONS, written because "a change in the camp director may lead to inefficiency and needless friction": four sections (programme, administration, buildings and equipment, general) containing a statement of objectives "such as emphasis on simple living in the out-of-doors, Christian motivation", sample hike and canoe-trip menus, "a seven page outline 'Things a new staff member needs to know about Kanawana'", per-position staff duties, and the canoeing, rowing, sailing and swimming tests. NO COPY IS KNOWN TO SURVIVE in this project's sources.

KANAWANA IN THE QUEBEC CAMP DIRECTORIES, 1975 AND 1976. Both list the camp as "KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA)" under ORGANIZATIONAL RESIDENTIAL -- CO-ED, director DEREK V. WALSH, address P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts / 1441 Drummond St., Montreal. 1975: 90 boys and 90 girls aged 8-15; activities tripping, swimming, sailing, arts and crafts, C.I.T. programme. 1976: 98 boys and 91 girls aged 8-15; four two-week sessions from 28 June to 26 August; $210.00 for two weeks, $190 each additional two weeks; activities tripping, canoeing, ORIENTEERING, arts and crafts, sailing. 'Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye' is listed SEPARATELY in 1975 -- also under Walsh, c/o Kamp Kanawana, 15 boys and 5 girls aged 13-17, wilderness/canoe trips/fishing/campcraft -- and is merged into the Kanawana line by 1976 as "KANAWANA (1894) -- Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye". These are the first per-session fee and per-gender enrolment figures this wiki holds for the 1970s.

THREE FURTHER KANAWANA APPEARANCES IN CANADIAN CAMPING. (a) June 1950 carries a first-person wartime memoir: a wounded soldier in a Canadian Army Hospital at Caserta, Italy recognises the writer -- "John Kidd... Kidd... I know now... Kamp Kanavana... 1934" -- and the passage lists what the camp meant in memory: "Cool blue waters, green hills, boats, THE CHUTE, CIRCUS DAY, campfires, the kid looking for a piece of shore-line, THE HIKE OVER TO THE DANCE AT MAROIS, CHEF WATSON grumbling with a twinkle in his eyes." The soldier says "Kanawana helped me to straighten out my thinking about people, about life." (John Kidd also appears in the Green Triangle of 17 October 1936.) (b) Summer 1983: "A special public thanks goes to PETER GODDARD and the staff of Kamp Kanawana in Montreal for accepting the tremendous task of mailing to every camp" -- 6,500 National Camping Day posters distributed across Canada from Kanawana. (c) Winter 1988: a French-language article on acid rain, "L'Etranger", by JAY NETHERWOOD, Camp Kanawana. CORRECTION 2026-08-25: an earlier version of this fact called Jay Netherwood 'a name this wiki does not hold'. That was wrong -- he is documented as Director 1986-1989 in the Montreal YMCA Metropolitan Staff rosters, authored the Kamp Kanawana Director's Report 1987, and continued as 'Supervisor, Kamp Kanawana' in 1990. The error came from a grep for 'Netherwood' that stopped at Bruce. What the 1988 article adds is not his existence but his authorship: a signed French-language piece on acid rain, published nationally while he was director -- the only known writing by him outside internal YMCA reports, and evidence for the camp's environmental turn a generation before the 2006 'green shift'.
facts.correction: Corrected 2026-08-25 on operator notice: Jay Netherwood was already documented (director 1986-1989).

facts.claim: THE 1949 ORIGINS PASSAGE, and a caution about it. Canadian Camping Vol. 1 No. 3 (June 1949), in Agnes Knox Mutchler's 'Quebec Camps': "The date and origin of many of the early camps is even now clouded in antiquity. Certainly a boys' camp sponsored by the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal in 1893 and called OTOREKE was among the earliest. KANAWANA, at present directed by Roy Locke, Vice-President of the Quebec Section, HAD A MYSTERIOUS BIRTH about this time under the same sponsorship." This is a 1949 secondary account by a neighbouring camp's director, not a Montreal YMCA record, and it disagrees with this wiki's documented sequence (Camp Jubilee founded 1894 at Lake Saint-Joseph, renamed Otoreke in 1909, Kanawana established at Saint-Sauveur in 1910). It is recorded as evidence of what the camping movement BELIEVED in 1949 -- including that Kanawana's own origins were already considered obscure -- and NOT as a competing chronology. It does not reopen the founding date. Note also that 'Camp Jubilee' appears NOWHERE in the 164-issue run.

ORAL HISTORY (M. Aronson, 2026-08-25): Jay Netherwood was Kanawana's director in 1985 AND 1986. This does not conflict with the documented record, it fills a hole in it. The Metropolitan Staff rosters document Netherwood as Director from FY1986 onward, and document Peter Goddard at both ends of his tenure (signing a newsletter as Director on 15 November 1982, and named Director in the FY1986 roster) -- but directors-index.md states plainly that '1983-1985 is bracketed between those two points, not stated'. The operator's 1985 therefore lands in a span NO DOCUMENT COVERS. Under the standing directive of 2026-07-07, oral history yields to documented sources only where the two directly conflict; an undocumented span is not resolved by that rule and remains open. Recorded as an unconfirmed oral-history datapoint narrowing the Goddard-to-Netherwood handover, NOT as a correction to Goddard's bracketed 1982-1986.

THE FIRST MONTREAL BOYS' CAMP, 1891, AND ITS IMMEDIATE END. From the August 1919 'Brief Autobiographical Sketch of Association Career' (author unidentified, p_236), a first-hand account: "During the vacation period of 1891 I returned to Montreal and took out to JONES' ISLAND, about 40 miles north-west of Montreal in the Ottawa River, THE FIRST MONTREAL BOYS' CAMP. A very unfortunate circumstance occurred THE FIRST DAY we were under canvas. A lad named DAVID LOUDEN while out swimming got beyond his depth and was drowned. Louden came from one of the finest homes in Montreal. On the arrival of help the next day THE CAMP WAS BROKEN UP AND THE SITE WAS NEVER AGAIN USED FOR THIS PURPOSE." This is three years before Camp Jubilee and at a site this wiki does not otherwise document. It also reframes the 1892 planning committee (Ross, Cushing, Wilson, Patton, Ball) as a SECOND attempt: the memoirist moves straight from Louden's death to forming the syndicate that chose Lac la Croix and then Lac St-Joseph. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: this passage sits one paragraph ABOVE the Lac la Croix passage already quoted in founding-1894.md, in a document this project had already read and extracted from -- an overlooked passage in a known source, not a new source.

BILL BOURNE, KANAWANA LEADER, DROWNED 30 JUNE 1933. The Green Triangle of 8 July 1933, in the Chief's own season-opening column: "It was with great sadness that we learned this week of Bill Bourne's drowning in Brome Lake, on Friday June 30th while attempting to save the life of his friend. As a camp we cannot but feel sensitive of the loss of perhaps THE FINEST LEADER WE HAVE EVER KNOWN. Those boys who were fortunate enough to be in his tent last year and all others who came into contact with Bill will never forget his example." He died away from camp, at Brome Lake in the Eastern Townships, days before the 1933 season opened, and in a rescue attempt. Not previously documented in this wiki.

p_245 RESULT -- GENUINE NULL. Only ONE issue of 'The Lookout', the Kamp Kanawana Alumni Committee's newsletter, is digitized on Internet Archive: Vol. 1 No. 3 (1993), identifier the-lookout-vol-1-no-3, uploaded by archives@concordia.ca into the ymca-montreal-fonds collection under subject 'The Lookout'. Three independent queries (identifier wildcard, subject facet, and free text) all return exactly one item. Issues 1 and 2 and any 1994 centennial issue are NOT online and must be requested from Concordia. SEPARATELY, the enumeration established the shape of the parent collection: ymca-montreal-fonds holds 1,037 items, of which this project holds 634. The 403 not held are NOT unread documents -- a 12-item random sample returned mediatype 'image' with JPEG and no text layer in every case. They are digitized PHOTOGRAPHS. Only THREE mention Kanawana, all titled 'Team Building - Kamp Kanawana 1/2 - 2001': P0145-02-3264, P0145-02-3294 and P0145-02-3335. The remaining camp-tagged images are day-camp and generic-camp subjects from the 1980s and 2001.

p_248 RESULT -- NOT ESTABLISHED, and the search is recorded rather than the answer. The 1969 camper drowning is attested ONLY by the Kamp Kanawana annual report 1969, under HEALTH AND SAFETY: "The tragic drowing of one of our campers this Summer has forced us to look at our standards in the whole area of camping. We are convinced that, especially in terms of aquatics, hiking and tripping, both our training and standards are of the highest possible quality." No name, no date, no location within the season. A full-text search of all 634 documents in this project's YMCA of Montreal corpus for 'drow*' returns every other drowning in the association's records -- David Louden 1891, Bill Bourne 1933, the 1893-94 and 1905 member obituary lists, the 1938 waterfront note -- but NOTHING further on 1969. Open-web search returns nothing. The remaining routes are the Montreal Gazette and Montreal Star for summer 1969, Quebec coroner records, and Concordia's physical holdings. HANDLE WITH CARE: a child's death, with family very possibly living. Establish the facts before deciding anything about publication, and decide that with the operator.

p_236 ANSWERED: the author of the August 1919 'Brief Autobiographical Sketch of Association Career' is T. DUNCAN PATTON, one of the five men on the fall-1892 committee appointed to plan Camp Jubilee. The signature is illegible in the OCR, but the memoir identifies itself twice in the body -- 'Shortly before Christmas MRS. PATTON and I journeyed eastward' (Dec 1901) and 'During all of our residence in India MRS. PATTON suffered much' -- and records that a Lake of the Woods island was named 'Patton'. It also rules out W. H. Ball as author: the writer lists 'W. H. Ball, John W. Ross, Will Wilson, MYSELF and others', placing Ball beside him. Every p_236 constraint matches: Montreal YMCA from 1883, Assistant Secretary from 1 Sept 1888 at $40/month, graduated 1892, membership and finances at Dominion Square, third General Secretary of the Winnipeg YMCA from June 1894 succeeding Herbert Gill (first was C. M. Copeland), Area Supervisor for Military District No. 10 1916-1918. The identification was available inside a document this project had already read and extracted from.

T. DUNCAN PATTON'S CAREER, from his own 1919 memoir, read in full. Montreal: walked into the YMCA on Victoria Square in 1883 'a gauky country lad... seeking for a boarding house', met by D. A. Budge; distributed Gospel-meeting invitation cards 'on the street corners and in the saloons'; helped originate the Sunday night Strangers' Tea; apprenticed to the machinist trade then worked at Drysdale & Co's Book Store; ENLISTED WITH THE MONTREAL GARRISON ARTILLERY FOR THE RIEL REBELLION IN 1885, three months' service reaching Long Lake, Sask. At Springfield in the fall of 1891 he PLAYED RIGHT GUARD ON AMOS ALONZO STAGG'S FOOTBALL TEAM AND 'CAPTAINED ONE SIDE OF THE INITIAL BASKET-BALL GAME UNDER THE DIRECTION OF DR. JAMES NAISMITH'. Winnipeg 1894-1901 (third General Secretary; brought D. L. Moody to the city in 1897; Portage Avenue building opened 1 Jan 1901 at $100,000). CAMP STEPHENS: first visited the Lake of the Woods islands July 1894, 'and from that date on camps were promoted and held annually'; five islands, ~27 acres, passed to the Winnipeg YMCA in 1907; one island named 'Patton' for him. Calcutta 1902-1905, Acting General Secretary ~18 months, toured Asian Associations at John R. Mott's request. Ottawa 1905-1910: ran THE FIRST 'WHIRLWIND' FUNDRAISING CAMPAIGN CONDUCTED IN CANADA (March 1906, $200,000 in ten days) and moved the Ottawa boys' camp to Lac d'Or beyond Renfrew. Winnipeg again from 1910; resigned September 1915 'because of the attitude of some of the Directors'; Military YMCA work from 1 October 1915; Area Supervisor for Military District No. 10 from May 1916; in the 1918 Dominion campaign raised $508,709 against a $175,000 allotment in Saskatchewan.

CONFIRMED INDEPENDENTLY: T. Duncan Patton -- one of the five men on the fall-1892 committee appointed to plan Camp Jubilee -- was ONE OF THE TWO CAPTAINS IN THE FIRST GAME OF BASKETBALL EVER PLAYED, 21 December 1891 at the International YMCA Training School, Springfield, under James Naismith. His own 1919 memoir says 'I captained one side of the initial basket-ball game under the direction of Dr. James Naismith', and that self-report is corroborated by two sources independent of him: 'Thomas Duncan Patton' appears in the documented roster of the eighteen original players, and Library and Archives Canada describes him as 'originally from Montreal... one of the two team captains selected by Naismith for the first game', one of four Canadians in that class besides Naismith. TEXTUAL WRINKLE RECORDED, NOT SMOOTHED: the First Team account names the captains as 'T. B. Patten and C. B. Libby' against its own roster of 'Thomas Duncan Patton' and 'Eugene Samuel Libby' -- both captain names garbled the same way, with the memoir supplying the first-person tiebreaker. NOTE ALSO that a SECOND member of the 1892 committee, W. H. Ball, graduated Springfield in the class of 1891 alongside Naismith and Stagg -- two of the five camp planners were at Springfield in Naismith's orbit.

THOMAS DUNCAN PATTON: FULL NAME, DATES AND POST-1919 CAREER. Born 15 APRIL 1865 in DANVILLE, Estrie region, Quebec; died 1 APRIL 1944 in TORONTO, aged 78. The 'T.' is THOMAS. Graduated the International YMCA Training School (Springfield) in 1892. His career continued well past his 1919 memoir: National Territorial Secretary, Winnipeg 1920-22; Territorial Secretary, Toronto 1922-26; organizer for the Ontario Prohibition Union 1926-27; Executive Secretary of Dixon Hall, Toronto 1927-32; Treasurer of the Christian Social Council of Canada 1932-41. DATING CAUTION: the same source gives '1892-1894 Assistant Secretary, Montreal' and '1892-1901 General Secretary, Winnipeg', overlapping ranges that cannot both be right. Patton's own memoir is specific and internally consistent -- Assistant Secretary in Montreal from 1 September 1888, Dominion Square membership and finances after his 1892 graduation, Winnipeg from June 1894 succeeding Herbert Gill as third Secretary -- and is preferred for those dates.

PATTON AND NAISMITH LEFT MONTREAL FOR SPRINGFIELD TOGETHER -- documented contemporaneously by the YMCA of Montreal's own annual report for 1889-90, in consecutive sentences: "We have also to announce that MR. T. DUNCAN PATTON, who has been a faithful assistant during the past two years, LEAVES IN SEPTEMBER TO ENTER FOR A YEAR'S COURSE AT SPRINGFIELD. He will carry with him the best wishes of all the members for his future success. ... MR. JAMES NAISMITH, B.A., OF McGILL, ALSO EXPECTS TO GO TO SPRINGFIELD IN SEPTEMBER." This is an institutional record written at the time, a year before the first basketball game, and is the strongest corroboration of Patton's 1919 memoir. The same run of reports tracks him further: the 1892-93 staff list gives 'D. A. Budge, General Secretary; T. Duncan Patton, Assistant Secretary; ... W. H. Ball, Physical Director' -- Patton and Ball on the same staff two years before the first camp season; the 1893-94 report records that 'Mr. T. Duncan Patton, FOR SIX YEARS associated in the work here, has accepted the Secretaryship of the Winnipeg Association, and will enter upon his duties July 1st' -- 'six years' counting back to 1888 and confirming the memoir against the player-exhibit's '1892-1894'; and in 1897-98 Montreal resolved to telegraph him at Winnipeg congratulating him on their Building movement. ONE SMALL UNRESOLVED DETAIL: the report says July 1st, the memoir says June.

NULL RESULT, checked 2026-08-25: David Louden's 1891 drowning at Jones' Island is NOT recorded in the YMCA of Montreal annual reports. A search across the 1889-1899 reports in this project's corpus for 'louden|lowden|loudon' returns only 'Lowden, J. R.', a subscriber, in the 1895-96, 1897-98 and 1899 donor lists -- a different person. Neither 'Jones' Island' nor the 1891 camp is mentioned anywhere in those reports. The association's only published account of the episode remains Patton's own 1919 memoir. Note the contrast with the 1893-94 report, which DOES list members who died that year including two drownings -- so the association did print such notices when it chose to. A Montreal newspaper of summer 1891 remains the route.

ROY D. LOCKE'S STANDING IN THE CANADIAN CAMPING MOVEMENT, dated from the complete Canadian Camping run: June 1949 'Kanawana, at present directed by Roy Locke, VICE-PRESIDENT of the Quebec Section'; February 1951 programme-committee chairman as 'Roy D. Locke, PRESIDENT of the Quebec Association'; April 1952 'Roy D. Locke director of Y.M.C. Kamp Kanawana is president of the Quebec Camping Association'; April 1954 listed as Quebec PAST PRESIDENT and 'Boys' Work Secretary, Metropolitan YMCA Montreal'; June 1954 'Past President of the Q.C.A.' giving a conference speech. He also sat on a February 1951 national committee alongside Mary Edgar (founder of Camp Oolahwan), Agnes Mutchler (Junior League Camp) and CCA president Kenneth Murray. His 1953 'A Manual of Operations' article is bylined 'Roy D. Locke, EXECUTIVE SECRETARY: BOYS' CAMPING, MONTREAL Y.M.C.A.' and was still carried in the magazine's cumulative subject index printed in December 1963. SEPARATE, UNVERIFIED LEAD: the 1978 Kamp Kanawana director's report thanks 'the Town of Montreal West and MAYOR ROY LOCKE for the loan of water meters this summer'. Locke moved to the Westmount Branch in September 1954 and was on Metropolitan Staff in 1986, so the name, place and period fit -- but no document links the mayor to the YMCA and the identification is NOT asserted.

MURRAY B. SHANTZ ENTERED THE YMCA PROFESSION AS A MONTREAL TRAINEE. The 1943 annual report records that 'Murray Shantz, George Barker, Gordon Patrick and Lloyd Welton complete their TRAINING FELLOWSHIPS' under the association's policy 'of providing Training Fellowships to young men looking to the Assn. secretaryship as a career' -- eleven years before Montreal appointed him to camping. He also sat on the association's Boys' Camping Committee: the 1958 Camp Perrot annual report lists 'Murray B. Shantz' alongside Hedley Dimock, George Clouston, O. N. H. Owens and Dr. Preston Robb, so his camping involvement extended beyond Kanawana. And he was still a known name to the camp in 1993, appearing as 'Murry Shantz' in the alumni roll printed in The Lookout. The 1959 report's 'Murray G. Shantz' is a transcription slip; every other appearance gives B.

GEOFF ANDERSON, EARLIER TRACE -- A LEAD, NOT A FINDING. The YMCA of Montreal's 1962 annual report names 'Geoff Anderson' in its 'YMCA International' section, in a passage about a WORLD SERVICE FELLOWSHIP student from SIR GEORGE WILLIAMS UNIVERSITY who 'spent his summer' with a work camp 'at the refugee camp in' LEBANON, noting it was 'the second year that a student from' the university had been placed. THE OCR OF THIS PAGE IS BADLY INTERLEAVED -- columns are scrambled -- so the association of the name with the fellowship is legible but the sentence structure is not. On the most natural reading Anderson was that student, which would place him at Sir George Williams and in Lebanon in summer 1962, six years before he appears running youth work at West Island's North Shore Centre in Pierrefonds. The page needs re-reading from the scan rather than the OCR before anything is asserted.

JAMES H. TURNER'S PRE-KANAWANA POSTINGS, and confirmation that he was the ON-SITE director. 1967 annual report: 'J. Turner, Youth Secretary, International Branch to Assistant Secretary, Lachine-Dorval Branch'. November 1968 staff newsletter: a Youth-and-Industry pilot backed by 'five major companies and Chateauguay school officials' was 'conceived by JIM TURNER, THE BRANCH'S EXECUTIVE SECRETARY, who will also serve as co-ordinator' -- designed 'to give students an in-depth look at industry... tour plants, meet face-to-face with all levels of management'. September 1969: on the West Island / Lachine-Dorval amalgamation he became 'associate executive, with special responsibility for staff supervision and North Shore area development'. The news release of 29 January 1970, headed 'TURNER TO KANAWANA', then states he 'will be the ON-SITE DIRECTOR AND HEAD OF PROGRAM at Kamp Kanawana this summer... best known for his innovative approach to activities for school-age youngsters'; the French edition gives 'directeur et chef des programmes'. This settles the two-tier question for his tenure in the association's own words: Turner on site, Roy Locke over the Camping Branch above him.

LEO J. ROBITAILLE RAN THE 1973 SEASON HANDS-ON -- an inference from three documents, stated as such. His Director's Report of 17 August 1973 is written in the first person of someone making operational decisions (recommendations to 'send at least two more people to the Canadian Canoe School', 'have less C.I.T.s in camp', and 'get a doctor... in the infirmary. With Medicare this is quite feasible at no cost to us') and names no on-site director above or below him. Two months later a news release of 26 October 1973 announcing Kanawana's winter season -- 'a lift, three downhill slopes, 20 miles of trails for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, a club house and a baby-sitting service' -- states that 'INSTRUCTIONAL COURSES WILL BE DIRECTED BY LEO ROBITAILLE', and gives a residential contact number for 'Mrs. Elaine Robitaille'. A HANDOVER IS VISIBLE THE NEXT YEAR: the 1973-74 annual report lists the Camping and Outdoor Education Branch executive as 'T. Potts/L. Robitaille', both men named for the same post. DISAMBIGUATION: Georges Robitaille, president of the ACQ's French section in 1976-77 and a Recreation Canada consultant, appears repeatedly in Canadian Camping in these same years and is a DIFFERENT MAN.

THE 1953 KANAWANA MANUAL OF OPERATIONS, fully itemised from Roy D. Locke's own article (Canadian Camping, June 1953, p.15). Four sections. PROGRAM: 'a simple statement of our camp objectives such as emphasis on simple living in the out-of-doors, Christian motivation'; sample menus for hikes and canoe trips; 'a seven page outline "Things a new staff member needs to know about Kanawana". This is very valuable. It eases the orientation period'; detailed duties for each staff person; copies of the canoeing, rowing, sailing and swimming tests. ADMINISTRATION: staff and counsellor remuneration, pre-camp training and evaluation with outlines of existing training courses; a purchasing list naming each company, address, phone and contact; duties for the CITY CAMP OFFICE covering promotion, registration, bills, TRAIN ARRANGEMENTS, refunds, parent contacts and lost-and-found; the camp business office covering food control, inventories, campers' monies and tuck shop; a typical two-week menu; emergency procedures and the operation of the CAMP HOSPITAL. GENERAL: samples of every form -- counsellor contracts, application forms, confidential forms, clothing lists, medical sheets. Locke's framing: 'At the present time in Canada there is no school for Camp Directors... directors of camps develop skill the hard way -- by making mistakes and profiting from them.'

A 1953 KANAWANA BUILDING SURVEY, described by Roy D. Locke: 'A wide variety of buildings and equipment had been erected without a carefully considered plan of development. We had a log cabin painted with whitewash, cabins with painted clapboard, cabins with log slab siding, some with brown stain, some with the bark still on. To bring order to this situation we NUMBERED EACH BUILDING and developed a listing of the material in footing, walls, roof, their colour and their condition. The buildings were divided into three groups, poor condition, good condition, excellent condition. Each building was examined and a detailed recommendation was made as to necessary repairs and changes.' Also recorded: 'THE THIRTY-TWO DIFFERENT LOCKS were changed to a Yale master key system' -- a proxy for the number of lockable structures on site c.1953 -- plus standards for the repair and painting of 'our fleet of boats, canoes, and dinghies', and procedures for fire drill, extinguishers, pumps, refrigeration and the truck. A NUMBERED BUILDING INVENTORY WITH CONDITION GRADES EXISTED IN 1953; no copy is known to survive.

'OUR PROPERTY WAS SURVEYED' -- 1953, and it bears on conflict c_026. Roy D. Locke writes: 'Our property was surveyed and an expert forester employed to give a careful report on our 360 ACRES OF FOREST for purposes of "thinning out" dead trees and replanting areas where necessary.' TWO THINGS FOLLOW. (1) A new figure enters the acreage series: 360 acres OF FOREST in 1953 -- forest cover, not total property, so it is not directly comparable to the 455 land / 537 total of 1989, and it sits sensibly below them. (2) It does NOT contradict the 1988 report's 'There was no record found that showed the Kanawana site has ever been surveyed'. That was a statement about records FOUND IN 1988, not about whether a survey ever happened. Read together they say a survey was done around 1953 and its record was lost within thirty-five years -- which STRENGTHENS the c_026 resolution rather than reopening it, by showing documentary loss was occurring. c_026 stays resolved; this is added as corroborating context. Locke also states plainly, in the same article: 'Our boys' camp was established in 1894. It has been on its present site since 1910.'

NORREY OWENS IS O. N. H. OWENS -- established 2026-08-25 by an office, not a name. The complete Canadian Camping run shows both forms holding the same post in the same association: June 1954, 'THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION... President -- Mr. O. N. H. OWENS' (with Agnes Mutchler as VP and A. Ross Seaman as Conference Chairman); January 1976, the QCA membership roll lists 'Owens, Mr. O.N.H. -- Quebec Camping Association', i.e. a current member in the year the Order of Owens was founded; and March 1977, a conference report naming 'an impressive list of past presidents of Q.C.A. in attendance, namely; NORREY OWENS, Zave Ettinger, Ross Seaman, Bob Jlazanick, Peter van Wagner, Bill McCarthy and Val Willis.' The same-named-son alternative collapses: a son would not appear on the roll of the association's past presidents. His documented service therefore runs 1929-1977, FORTY-EIGHT YEARS, and the 1977 conference is the latest confirmed sighting. STILL UNPROVEN: whether he is the 'OWENS, OWEN NORREYS HARRINGTON' of the LAC First World War file, and his birth and death dates. Also newly recorded: the 1937 annual report credits his Kanawana Committee chairmanship with a season of 310 boys for 1,092 camper-weeks, against 259 boys for 917 weeks the previous year.

p_202 RESULT -- THE KANAWANA FLICKR ACCOUNT CANNOT HOLD THE EARLIEST L&V PHOTOGRAPH, and its catalogue is now recorded. p_207 RESULT -- THE PINE CREST BLOCK WAS TRANSIENT, AND THE PAGE IS NOT WORTH MORE ATTEMPTS. 'Lumbermen & Voyageurs: The YMCA Pine Crest Story' had been recorded twice as HTTP 429 rate-limited and treated as blocked. On 2026-08-25 the shop page returned HTTP 200 and was read in full. It contains ONLY marketing copy -- 'covers 100 years of camping magic... written to commemorate the 100 year anniversary of Camp Pine Crest' -- with no table of contents, no excerpt, no cheer text and no origin story. The book is $25.00 and purchasable. So the 429 was a rate limit, not a wall, and the real obstacle was never the fetch: the contents are simply not published online. Acquisition (purchase or interlibrary loan) is the only route, and it matters more since 2026-08-25, when Greig Macdiarmid -- Kanawana's Camp Chief 1935-1939 -- was found to have driven Camp Pine Crest's expansion as General Secretary of the Toronto YMCA before his death in 1962 (f_2284).

p_196 RESULT -- THE BOOK IS IDENTIFIED BUT NOT DIGITIZED. 'Saint-Sauveur: Son histoire, notre patrimoine' is by LORRAINE DAGENAIS in collaboration with CARMELLE HUPPE, published by the Societe d'histoire et de genealogie des Pays-d'en-Haut in 2019 and since reprinted. It is sold locally in Saint-Sauveur (a RONA Dagenais notice advertises it). No digitized copy or BAnQ online edition was found. It is the cited source for the Olivier Charron pre-camp landowner detail (f_1815) and may carry further pre-camp land history. Acquisition is physical and local -- and the SHGPH is already the target of p_208 (the 'Hommage a Telesphore Page' request), so the two should be one approach to one organisation.

THE MONTREAL BUS PICK-UP POINT MOVED FOR 2026, from Town of Mount Royal to Westmount. The 2025 guide gives it as 'Ecole secondaire Pierre-Laporte : 1101 Rockland Road | Mont-Royal | Quebec | H3P 2X8'. The 2026 guide replaces it: 'Due to circumstances beyond our control, we would like to inform you that the bus meeting point will now be WESTMOUNT HIGH SCHOOL : 4350 Sainte-Catherine Street | Westmount | Quebec | H3Z 1R1. The entrance to the parking lot is on Hillside Lane, and the exit is on Hallowell Avenue.' 'Rockland' appears nowhere in the 2026 guide. Buses leave around 8:30-9:00 a.m. with campers asked to arrive an hour early; a $25 charge applies to any transportation change made 72 hours or less before the first day of a session.

2026 SEASON STRUCTURE AND DATES from the parent guide: four sessions running 22 June to 14 August 2026, with departures and returns at 22 June, 27/28 June, 3 July, 6 July, 17 July, 20 July, 31 July, 3 August and 14 August. OPEN HOUSE: Sunday 14 June 2026, 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Airport transfer by a camp driver costs $96 plus tax each way, $192 return, and camper flights must arrive no earlier than 22 June and depart no later than 14 August -- 'There will be no campers on site prior to June 22nd nor after August 14th.'

TUCK, MERCHANDISE AND A CAMPERSHIP MECHANISM, 2026. 'Every camper at Camp YMCA Kanawana will receive a REUSABLE WATER BOTTLE on their first day at camp, and will be sent home with a T-SHIRT from this season.' Tuck fees are added automatically at registration and cover both items; 'A CANOE PADDLE is included in the Tuck items for campers registered to any Voyageur programs.' Unspent tuck over $10 is refundable only on written request, issued in September -- and, notably, 'All remaining tuck money remains within the YMCA, and goes towards providing services to families with lower incomes, INCLUDING SENDING CAMPERS TO KANAWANA.' Unspent tuck therefore funds camperships. Group photos are taken at the start of each session by a camp photographer and distributed by download link afterwards.

THE 2026 LEADERSHIP TEAM, with one new post. Executive Camp Director MARIE-PIERRE LACASSE (ext. 7); Summer Camp Director JUSTIN CALDWELL (ext. 4); Summer Camp Assistant Director QUINN DURAND (ext. 5); Assistant to the Directors AMY THOMSON (ext. 6) -- all four also in the 2025 guide. The pairing of trips with rentals in one coordinator role is itself notable given the camp's year-round rentals business. CANOE-TRIP PROGRAMME DETAIL, 2026, from the trip complement embedded in the same PDF. Trip staff 'are all aged 18 years old and up and have extensive canoe tripping' experience; participants 'have to demonstrate that they can swim 150 METRES WITHOUT A PFD'. Preparation includes practising packing dry bags and 'a boat trip to Lake Wilson to practice paddling'. Equipment is verified before departure by trip leaders AND campers jointly. 'All our wilderness medicine protocols are reviewed and certified by a doctor to allow our staff to practice wilderness responder treatments.' First-aid kits carry acetaminophen, ibuprofen and a salbutamol inhaler. Transport is by 15-passenger vehicle with a camp-owned trailer for canoes, with a planned stop en route. Trip menus are largely vegetarian: 'Thai coconut curry, chili, Mexican wrap, bean salad, red dhal, pesto pasta, LAZY PIEROGIS, barley soup, vegetarian sloppy joes, General Tao tofu, teriyaki bowl'; trail snacks include 's'mores, cinnamon buns, magic squares, TRIPBROWNIES, caramelized pears/peaches, trip pie, apple crumble'. A programme named 'VOYAGEUR EXTREME' appears.

A PRODUCTION ARTIFACT LEFT IN THE PUBLISHED 2026 GUIDE. Between the staff-contact page and the canoe-trip section, the PDF carries an unremoved French-language instruction to a designer: 'Pourriez-vous creer un bouton << Virtual >> << Virtuel >> dans les tons de bleus pour mettre a droite des cours dans le calendrier? (comme le bouton deferred)'. It concerns a web calendar and has nothing to do with the camp. Recorded because anyone doing full-text search on this PDF will hit it, and because it is evidence the guide is assembled from shared YMCA-wide design assets rather than produced standalone.

THE WORKING CORPUS WAS NOT IN THE REPOSITORY. Discovered 2026-08-25 while running p_231: the 634-document YMCA of Montreal text corpus that this week's work rests on -- the Patton memoir identification, the Owens sweep, the five director drafts, the 1969-drowning sweep -- existed ONLY in the session's ephemeral scratchpad. Just 39 of its 634 files had counterparts anywhere in the repository, and the container is reclaimed after inactivity. The corpus is now copied to sources/cache/ymca-montreal-fonds/ (16 MB, 634 files) and verified after the copy by control terms: 257 files contain 'Kanawana', 73 'Otoreke', 28 'Patton', 24 'Owens' -- matching the pre-copy counts. This was a durability failure, not a research one, and it was invisible to every check the project had: the verify harness audits what the wiki says and what sources record, not whether the underlying text still exists anywhere permanent.

p_231 EXECUTED, AND ITS PREMISE CORRECTED. 566 held corpus items were registered individually in sources.json, taking it from 68 registered of 634 held to all 634. Total source records 1,300 (1,274 unique ids). CRUCIAL DISTINCTION PRESERVED: the 565 newly registered items with text carry read_state 'SKIMMED', not 'extracted', with basis 'full-text-cached-and-keyword-swept-not-read-closely'. The text is held and has been keyword-swept repeatedly, but these items have not been read closely and no fact has been extracted from them individually. Marking them 'extracted' would have inflated the project's read receipts by 565 and defeated the purpose of the field. Dormancy consequently rises to 572 of 1,300 -- an honest number, not a regression.

A FOUNDING-ERA DOCUMENT THAT CANNOT BE READ. 'Seventh Annual Report of the Current Camp Committee', dated 10 December 1900, is digitized in the ymca-montreal-fonds collection (8 pages) but has NO OCR TEXT LAYER -- it is an image-only scan, which is why its cached file is 0 bytes. pdftotext and pdfminer both return nothing and no OCR binary is available in this environment. THE TITLE IS THE FINDING: a SEVENTH annual report in December 1900 counts the series back to 1894, the founding year, meaning the Camp Committee produced annual reports from the beginning. Only two camp-committee reports are digitized at all, both from 1900; the other six are not online. This is a specific, high-value ask -- either an OCR pass on the existing scan or the originals from Concordia.

THE 1900 JUNIOR CAMP REPORT, read in full -- the earliest camp season this project can read at first hand. 'The Junior Camp was held this year from Thursday June 28th to Saturday July 14th. It was a record Camp in point of numbers': 45 BOYS, 6 LEADERS, 17 VISITORS, with 'Mr. Calhoun and Mr. Brown in charge'. Six tents were used 'and some of the boys slept in the house'; tent leaders were 'Messrs. A. Peden, H. Beall, D. McGavin, G. Shaw, W. K. L. Greig and Mr. Brown'. The weather was brutal -- '11 days out of 16 being wet, and consequently it was very hard to keep the boys amused and in control'. Religious observance was heavy: morning and evening prayers daily, three Friday night meetings, and on Sundays 'three services, Bible class and evening song service'. Finances closed at a balance of $5.05, with tea, coffee and spices donated by Mr. Marotte of Marotte Leblanc and Co. The cook 'was only fairly satisfactory and was DISGUSTINGLY DIRTY in his work -- though some excuse is found in the fact that the kitchen is too small'. Eight suggestions went to the PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE, including a mail box and a mail bag for the teamster, fixing a smoking chimney, 'more butter plates and salt cellars', 'a rainbarrel or pump beside the kitchen IN ORDER THAT THE COOK MAY HAVE NO EXCUSE FOR NOT WASHING THE DISHES PROPERLY', a boathouse with rope painters and anchors, rubber sheets for the tents, and 'That an athletic field be procured as soon as possible.' The existence of a standing 'Permanent Camp Committee' in 1900 corroborates the Concordia holding sought under p_209.

WHY THE BUS POINT MOVED IN 2026 -- the chain behind 'circumstances beyond our control'. In late spring 2026, Ecole secondaire Pierre-Laporte (Town of Mount Royal) notified Kanawana that its parking lot could not serve as the Montreal pick-up and drop-off point for the coming summer, because of renovations scheduled late. Kanawana's Executive Camp Director asked Matt Aronson to help secure the Westmount Library parking lot; Aronson judged that lot far too small to handle an entire session's worth of campers, and instead proposed approaching Chris Manitt, a former Camp Kanawana staff member who chairs the governing board of Westmount High School. Manitt obtained permission from the school's principal, and Aronson coordinated with Westmount Public Safety so the pick-up and drop-off would not create unexpected traffic or parking problems. As of the end of summer 2026 the arrangement appeared satisfactory to all parties. This is the operator's own account of events in which he was a participant; no document held here records any of it.

CHRIS MANITT -- a former Camp Kanawana staff member who chairs the governing board of Westmount High School. When this was first recorded the name appeared nowhere else in this KB, this wiki, or the 634-document YMCA of Montreal fonds corpus, and his Kanawana years were unknown; f_2326 (operator recall, same day) places him as a CIT in 1995. ALEX BOLLHORN WAS A CIT IN 1993, named at the foot of column 1 on the 'C.I.T.'s of '93' plaque in the same cohort as Matt Aronson (f_1568). He was the SIBLING of Tiff Bollhorn, a CIT in 1995 and staff in 1997 (f_1614, f_1705); the operator confirms both the relationship and the family spelling, BOLLHORN. The operator himself supplied the correction ('No, it was my memory, you were right'), locating the wrong spelling in his own recall of his sister's name rather than in the agent's reading. STANDING: family spelling BOLLHORN, on the operator's authority and the two clearly legible plaques; the 1993 plaque's paint reads BALLHORN, faintly but independently. Both recorded, neither merged.

It credits 'CIT DIRECT: Maria English', dating it to the 1999-2000 period. f_1618 belongs to a DIFFERENT object (cit-1999-2.jpg), so the KB has been carrying one fact for two boards. A JBC BOARD MADE BY PAINTING OVER AN EARLIER SIGN. assets/images/plaques/junior-boys-councellors-2006.jpg is titled 'The J.B.C. 2x6' -- a joke about the board being a two-by-six -- with headings for S.D., JBC's and JC's and roughly sixteen names beneath them in pencil or thin marker, now faded past recovery. An EARLIER INSCRIPTION shows through the white lettering reading approximately 'THE WOODSMEN 2006'. This is the only documented instance of plaque REUSE in the collection and it bears on dating: on these walls a surface and its text need not be the same age. No fact described this object before the p_291 audit.

AN UNCATALOGUED 2010 BASIN PADDLE. assets/images/plaques/basin-trip-2010.jpg shows a canoe paddle lettered 'Basin '10, Session 1 -- ADVENTURERS EXTREME - LIKE A BOSS', with 'Neato Gang' and 'Sweet Chili Heat!' on the blade and roughly ten names in small script that the available frame (a wide wall shot) cannot resolve. No fact described it before the p_291 audit.

AN UNCATALOGUED AND FULLY LEGIBLE 2002 BOARD. assets/images/plaques/dsc-0554.jpg is a green parallelogram with a white ruled border naming JACQUES HOSSON, CHRISTIAN LEBLANC, ARANTXA GURUTBAY, BRIGID TIERNEY and LAURA HAMILTON. Nothing is missing or illegible and no fact described it before the p_291 audit -- it was simply never read. AN EFFACED KANAWANA BOARD. assets/images/plaques/dsc-0684.jpg shows a dark red board headed KANAWANA in blue with a painted name list beneath it -- perhaps a dozen lines -- weathered to bare traces of pigment in the grain. Nothing is readable. No fact described it before the p_291 audit. Recorded so that its existence, and the fact that it once carried names, is on the record even though its content is probably lost.

THE CAMP'S OWN CAREER LADDER, MEASURED. Cross-referencing all 151 transcribed plaques (p_291) against each other yields 1,493 distinct named individuals, of whom 149 appear on boards in MORE THAN ONE YEAR and 43 can be traced from a junior position (camper, CIT, LIT, JC, Ranger, Voyageur) to a staff-grade title (Counsellor, Tripper, Master, Capitaine, Section Director, Director) on a later board. This wiki has previously described the camper-to-staff progression only through individual careers -- Reiko Webster, David Leduc, Matt Hamerman. It is not anecdotal: it is the ordinary path, documented forty-three times over on the camp's own walls, and it is the strongest available evidence that Kanawana's leadership was grown internally rather than recruited. || COUNT CORRECTED (p_296, 2026-08-28): this fact first said 45. One of those 45, Jeff Ware, qualified only because the index classed the 2009 'WOLF' credit as a staff title. It is not one -- the operator identifies WOLF as a leadership PROGRAMME, the Rangers programme revived in 2001 and renamed later that decade (f_2343) -- so a Wolf on a trip board is a programme participant, like an LIT. Reclassified as leadership-track, and the count is 44. || COUNT CORRECTED AGAIN (2026-08-28): 150/44 became 149/43 when ARIEL MCGEARY and ARIEL MCGEARY HALL were found to be one person split across two rows by a surname variant. That is the hidden-SPLIT failure p_298 anticipates, found on the first close reading of the output rather than by the audit that queued it. Two display errors were fixed in the same pass -- 'Sally Waff' for the confirmed Sally Watt, 'Matt Iviott' for Matt Wiviott. Three errors in one screen of output is the honest measure of what the remaining rows hold, and the conservative merge rules mean the residual risk runs toward SPLITTING one person into two rather than merging two into one: the true traced count is likely a little below 149 and the true progression count a little above 43. || SYSTEMATIC BUG FOUND AND FIXED (2026-08-28): the progression count was 43 and is now 69. The operator noticed his own absence -- Matt Aronson is on the 1993 CIT plaque AND the 2002 staff plaque, an obvious progression that the index did not show. Cause: on the large staff boards the names are recorded under generic column keys (col1..col4), and the index derived a person's role from the KEY rather than from the BOARD, so every name on the Staff of '79, Staff of 1990 and Staff 02 plaques was tagged 'Member' instead of 'Staff'. Roughly 255 staff appearances were silently demoted and any career whose staff rung fell on one of those three boards became invisible. NEWLY VISIBLE AS A RESULT: Julien Tasse (1963 Advance Guard leader to 1990 staff, 27 years), Phil Kaufman (CIT 1992 to staff 2002), Matt Aronson and Steph Hurlburt (CITs 1993 to staff 2002), Dan Aronson (CIT 1995 to staff 2002), Bruce Netherwood (1984 CIT director to 1990 staff), Toby Desjardins, Eric Boghen, Peter Lopata, John Kennedy (CIT 1975 to staff 1979), four of the 1988 Voyageurs on the 1990 staff board, and eleven CITs of 1998-2001 on the Staff 02 board. THE PRIOR CAVEAT WAS TOO SOFT: this fact estimated the true count as 'a little above 43'. It was 38% higher. A classifier that reads structure instead of meaning fails silently and in bulk, and it took a person who knew he belonged on the list to catch it. || FURTHER CORRECTION (2026-08-28): a second systematic split was found when clustering by surname -- the Knights roll's 'Sir'/'Lady' titles were never stripped, so every knight who also appears on another board was indexed as two people. Fixed: traced people 149 -> 155, progressions 69 -> 71. See f_2355. || COUNT NOW 70 (2026-08-28): Julien Tasse was removed after the operator identified him as the camp's caretaker throughout (f_2357) -- he held a staff role on every board he appears on and never progressed into one.

THE FOUR LONGEST DOCUMENTED ASSOCIATIONS ON THE PLAQUE WALL. (1) JULIEN TASSE spans 27 years: named apart between painted arrows as leader on the Advance Guard boards of 1963 and 1964, again on Advance Guard 1986, on the Staff of 1990 plaque, and thanked collectively as 'The Tasse's' on the Staff of '79 board; Yves Tasse appears in 1986 and 1990 beside him. RESOLVED 2026-08-28 (f_2356): the operator states Julien and Yves are FATHER AND SON. Which is which is inferred from the chronology rather than stated -- Julien as the father, a boy on the 1963-64 boards and back as staff by 1986-90, with Yves his son -- and on that reading Julien's own association runs the full 27 years. (2) CHRIS ADAM heads column one of BOTH the Staff of '79 and the Staff of 1990 plaques, an 11-year span his article does not record. (3) PHIL KAUFMAN: CIT 1992, Staff 02 -- 10 years. (4) MATT ARONSON and STEPH HURLBURT are both CITs on the 1993 board and both on the Staff 02 plaque, 9 years apart. || AMPLIFIED (2026-08-28): Julien Tasse's 27 years are explained -- he was the camp's CARETAKER for thirty-odd years and died c.1992-95 (f_2357). His span is continuous employment, not a camper's return, and he is therefore NOT a junior-to-staff progression.

TWO CIT DIRECTORS WERE ON STAFF BEFORE THEY DIRECTED -- previously unrecorded. SOPHIE CAISSE, credited 'director' of the 1993 CIT programme (f_1568), and PAULA CUSSEN, credited 'Director' of the 1995 CIT programme (f_1614), are BOTH named on the Staff of 1990 plaque (f_1704). Neither the directors index nor either article records their 1990 service, because the 1990 plaque's fact carried only 5 of its ~102 names until the p_291 audit. Their directorships were the end of a run at the camp, not the start of one.

ANDREA PAHL: CIT 1993, CIT DIRECTOR 2001 -- a complete eight-year loop. She is named among the 32 CITs on the 'C.I.T.'s of '93' plaque (f_1568) and credited as the director of the 2001 CIT programme on the 'CITs 2001' board (f_1621). The directors index records the 2001 directorship but not the 1993 cohort membership, so the arc has been invisible. It is the same shape as Reiko Webster's documented 1986-CIT-to-1992-CIT-director path, and the p_291 audit adds a middle rung to Webster's too: she is on the Staff of 1990 plaque between the two.

THE 1995 CIT COHORT AS A TRACEABLE GROUP. Of the 29 CITs named on the 'CITS 95' plaque (f_1614), at least TWELVE reappear on the 'Kanawana Staff 97' plaque (f_1705) two summers later: Sarah Addleman Frankel, Avigail Aronoff, Tiff Bollhorn, Laura Davis, Marc Dunn, Adriana Greenblatt, Emily Lecker, Chris Manitt, Jon Mee, Nick Muszynski, Marina Sharpe and Charlie Shulman. Two of them go further: AVIGAIL ARONOFF is a Director of the 2002 LIT programme (f_1650) and on the Staff 02 plaque, and JON MEE is a Tripper on that same 2002 LIT board. Roughly two in five of one CIT year were still on the payroll two years on, and the cohort supplied programme leadership seven years on.

COHORT PERSISTENCE AMONG CAMPERS, NOT ONLY STAFF. Three further groups hold together across years on the boards. (1) All EIGHT campers of the 'We Shower Tent' of 2nd session 2000 (f_1701) reappear later: Annabel Busbridge and Emma Gaudet as 2002 LITs, Sarah Carsley and Stacey Corber as 2001 CITs and on Staff 02, Kim Creton and Jess Dobrinski on the Malibu 2001 trip, Sara Held on Nature Trip 2003 and Malibu 2006, Katie Smith as a 2002 Ranger. (2) FIVE of the eight campers on the 2010 Lookout board (f_1653) -- Christina Kaminski, Manon Griffin, Lily Foris, Emma Copeman, Tessa Dixon -- were together on Adventurer Girls 2008 (f_1592), and four of those five on Roadhouse 2007 (f_1682): the same girls across four years and three boards. (3) SEVEN of the 24 LITs of 2008 (f_1651) are JCs together in 2009 (f_1639): Clare Mintzer, Sybil G-Stock, Kayla Patton, Justin Pulfer, Caroline Di Tommaso, Emily Morgan and Laura Morrison.

SIBLINGS AND FAMILIES ON THE PLAQUE WALL. The boards record several sets, of which one is stated outright and the rest are patterns: BIANCA 'I'M NOT DAPHNE' PUNGARTNIK, LIT on the Roadhouse 2007 board, names her relationship to Daphne Pungartnik, LIT on the Swazi 2007 board, in her own painted nickname -- a camp joke doing the work of a document. ALEX AND TIFF BOLLHORN (CITs 1993 and 1995) are confirmed siblings by the operator. Unstated but recurring across separate boards and years: Katie and Anna Rotman (same 2005 trip); Thomas and Michael Bracken (same 1995 cabin); Emma and Maya Anders; Julie and Zack Brzezinski; Carlos and Belen Azofra; Kenya and Nao Shatani; Theo and Zoe Lerikos; Vicki and Ian Braide, whose surname is that of the notable alumnus Rob Braide; Mark and Craig Gillett, knighted in consecutive years; Ian and Sarah Fincham; George and Howard Burman; Tom and Jan Snabl, thirty-two years apart. NONE of the unstated pairs is asserted as a family relationship; they are recorded as observations for anyone who can confirm them.

THE KNIGHTS OF KANAWANA ROLL, READ AS A WHOLE. The dining-hall roll board records 29 investitures across 13 distinct years between 1980 and 2009 -- an average of about one a year against a camp of several hundred campers a season, which bears out the charter's claim to 'a select group'. SIX OF THE 29 ARE LADIES, two of them among the four inaugural knights of 1980 (Lindsay Kertland, Avril Chaplain); the charter's language is gender-inclusive from the outset and the order appears never to have had a men-only phase, roughly a decade into coeducation. THE ROLL IS ALSO FULL OF GAPS -- nothing for 1983-86, 1989-91, 1995-97, 2000-01 or 2003-07 -- and the board cannot distinguish between three readings: that the order ran continuously and no one met its six challenges in those years, that it lapsed and was revived, or that the board is an incomplete record. The camp's 1988 report stating that all listed programmes including the Knights were 'still in effect' (f_2110) sits against a roll silent from 1989 to 1991, which makes that stretch the sharpest test case. FINALLY, the order honoured CAMPERS and a striking number of them returned as staff -- Denys Lawrence, Lindsay Kertland, the four CITs of 1992-93, Josh Usheroff, Ian Braide -- so the roll functions as an early rung on the camp's documented career ladder (f_2335) rather than as a terminal honour.

THE RANGERS PROGRAMME RAN, LAPSED, WAS REVIVED, WAS RENAMED WOLF, AND LAPSED AGAIN. The operator gives the sequence: the Rangers programme was REVIVED IN 2001, ran under that name, BECAME THE WOLF PROGRAMME later in the 2000s, and then lapsed a second time. The plaque record fits this exactly and could not have been read this way without it -- Rangers boards run 1955 to 1964 (f_1669-f_1676), the camper-weeks tables show Rangers last carrying campers in 1967 (f_1949 and section-names.md), then NOTHING for thirty-four years, then Rangers boards again for 2002, 2003, 2004 and 2005 (f_1677-f_1680), and then in 2009 two trip boards credit a 'WOLF' -- Phil Simon on the Yak Trip (f_1691) and Jeff Ware on Talahassee (f_1711). RANGERS TODAY IS THE ONE-MONTH LIT PROGRAMME, ages 15-16 with DAFA certification from the Conseil quebecois du loisir (f_0465), i.e. the name has returned a second time and now denotes something different again.

TRAILBLAZERS IS THE CIT PROGRAMME RENAMED, AND ITS LINEAGE RUNS BACK TO THAT PROGRAMME'S INCEPTION. The operator states that the traditional full-summer LIT programme IS the CIT programme, continuous from its inception, and is now called TRAILBLAZERS; that the RANGERS name now denotes the separate one-month LIT programme; and that the FORESTER programme, a tripper-training stream for the same cohort, was added only in the past few years. This DATES TWO PROGRAMMES THE WIKI RECORDS AS UNDATED: section-names.md states plainly that 'Trailblazers and Foresters remain entirely undated: neither appears in the McMorris thesis or any pre-1980s primary source checked, only in current (2026) YMCA program pages.' Trailblazers is not undated -- it is the CIT programme under a later name, so its history is the CIT history this project already holds, running from the 1960 CIT plaque (f_1544) forward. Foresters IS genuinely recent. The wiki has been treating one continuous programme as two unrelated ones, an artifact of a name change.

'WOLF' ON THE 2009 TRIP BOARDS IS A PROGRAMME, NOT A JOB -- AN INFERENCE OF MINE, CORRECTED. The p_291 plaque audit found two 2009 boards crediting a 'WOLF' on its own line beneath Counsellor and Tripper (Phil Simon, Yak Trip, f_1691; Jeff Ware, Talahassee, f_1711) and recorded this as 'a third staff role in the 2009 staffing structure'. THAT READING WAS WRONG. The operator identifies Wolf as the Rangers leadership programme under its later name (f_2343), so a Wolf named on a trip board is a PROGRAMME PARTICIPANT attached to that trip -- exactly parallel to 'L.I.T. Daphne Pungartnik' on the Swazi 2007 board (f_1709) and 'Lit Amy D.' on the Basin 2007 board (f_1597), both of which the same audit had already transcribed without drawing the connection. The evidence for the correct reading was in the audit's own records. CONSEQUENCE: the count of documented junior-to-staff progressions in f_2335 falls from 45 to 44, because Jeff Ware qualified only through this misclassification. || PHRASING REFINED (2026-08-28, same day): this fact said Wolf was 'a programme, not a job'. That was too sharp a dichotomy and the operator corrected it -- 'I think that WOLF when written next to a name was a rank/role, like a CIT or LIT'. He is right, and CIT and LIT show why: each names BOTH a programme and the standing a person holds within it, and each appears beside a name on these boards exactly as WOLF does. So a Wolf credit IS a designation attached to a person; what it is not is a STAFF post, which is the reading actually being discarded here. NOTHING ELSE CHANGES: Wolf remains classed as a leadership-track rank alongside CIT, LIT and JC rather than as staff, and the count of documented junior-to-staff progressions in f_2335 stays at 44. Note the operator hedges this one ('I think'), unlike his flat statements on the programme lineage in f_2343, and it is recorded at secondary reliability accordingly.

THE PLAQUES CARRY CAMP CULTURE, NOT ONLY ROSTERS, AND THE EXTRACTION PASS THAT PRODUCED THIS KB'S PLAQUE FACTS RECORDED ONLY THE NAMES. Recovered by the p_291 audit: a ROBERT FROST epigraph on the 1984 CIT board ('We have promises to keep / and miles to go before we sleep -- R.F.'), the only literary quotation in the collection; THIRTEEN CATCHPHRASES filling the centre of the 1985 CIT board ('Somethin' fierce!', 'Woah Bess!', 'Where do you find us? Under C.', 'Dude Monger' and nine more), the richest surviving sample of 1980s camp slang held anywhere in this project; the 1975 CIT board's motto 'WHY CAN'T WE BE FRIENDS?', the title of a War single released that same summer, plus a line naming that cohort's MASCOTS; and a DATED SETLIST on the 2006 Senior Girls board of which 'Tainted Love' and 'Proud Mary' are clearly legible -- pop covers rather than traditional camp songs, and the only documented dated setlist this project holds against a songs article built almost entirely on oral history.

KANAWOODSTOCK WAS A RECURRING MUSIC EVENT, EVIDENCED BY THREE OBJECTS ACROSS ROUGHLY SIXTEEN YEARS: a wooden GUITAR (year painted ambiguously, 1993 or 1995, title and year only), a GUITAR PICK for 2000 naming Justin Francis, Matt Busbridge, Gareth Potter and Alex Bonebakker under a KISS lyric ('I want to rock & roll all nite'), and a real DRUM HEAD still in its hoop for 2009 titled 'Anarchy in the KK' with the A drawn as an anarchy symbol, signed by seven. Each generation named the event with the music of its own moment; the 2009 object is a piece of the festival's own equipment rather than a plaque. Nothing in traditions/ treats Kanawoodstock as a named event.

A THEMED-DAY COMPETITION FORMAT RAN AT KANAWANA AND IS NOT NAMED AS A TRADITION IN THIS WIKI. Four instances: WESTERN DAY 1968 (a shield naming the winning team, the Cowboys); VIKING DAY 1972 (an arrow-shaped board with a longship reading SWEDEN in heavy black across the middle -- a NATIONAL assignment, implying the camp was divided into country teams rather than staging a Viking pageant); a WIZARD OF OZ DAY on a deeply carved, badly weathered board whose year and winning team cannot be read (f_1806); and an Arthurian all-camp day, 'Sir Kay, or Arthur's Lost Knight', run in 1987 and rated by the director as 'slightly less than mediocre'. Separately, the ALL-CAMP GAME was named and commemorated per session: 'Treasure Island KK' for 1st session 1996 on a ship-shaped board, and the 3rd session of 1995 on a bone-shaped board.

RAKU WAS ALMOST CERTAINLY A CAMP DOG. The 3rd-session 1995 all-camp board reads 'We saved Raku and the red-day tuck!' -- opaque on its own -- and the board is CUT IN THE SHAPE OF A BONE, with a red K at one end, a green K at the other, and a PAW PRINT painted beside the lettering (f_1593). The object's form carries the meaning of a sentence that is otherwise a private joke. This KB records no camp animals of any kind, and an animal important enough to build an all-camp game around leaves no other trace in the project.

TWO DECORATIVE TRADITIONS RUN SIDE BY SIDE ON THE PLAQUE WALL, AND NEITHER IS RECORDED IN THIS KB. (1) INDIGENOUS-DERIVED IMAGERY: a 1982 Senior Girls Staff wood slice painted with a large THUNDERBIRD in Pacific-Northwest formline style (ovoids, split-U wing feathers, red-black-white palette, f_1697); the Montreal-to-New-York paddle's stylised mask and sunburst medallion in the same idiom (f_1662); and the 1959 La Verendrye board painted directly onto a MOOSE ANTLER, naming a section 'The Cawasachouanes' (f_1648). wiki/site/indigenous-names-and-land.md exists but holds no fact about the camp's use of such imagery on its own objects -- these are dated, material instances. (2) EUROPEAN FOLK CARVING: against that, a shield-shaped board carries only chip-carved rosettes, scrolled triangular banding and dotted borders in a Scandinavian or Slavic decorative vocabulary (f_1702), and the 1983 Senior Girls Staff pennant is a hand-drawn SIERPINSKI GASKET three or four levels deep (f_1698). The two vocabularies do not mix on any single object.

THE SANCTUM WAS THE SENIOR BOYS SECTION CABIN, IN USE FROM THE MID-1990s UNTIL IT WAS DEMOLISHED IN 2007. This answers the epitaph painted on the 2007 Senior Boys board -- 'May the Sanctum R.I.P.' (f_1688) -- which the plaque audit found and no document held here could explain: the boys were commemorating the demolition of their own cabin in the same season it came down, on the board that names them. IT IS ALSO AN ARCHITECTURAL EXCEPTION. This KB records the camp's Senior sections (Coureurs de Bois, Pathfinders) as housed in PLATFORM TENTS and its Junior sections (Woodsmen, Pioneers) in cabins (f_0452, f_0587, section-names.md). A Senior Boys CABIN therefore ran against the standing accommodation pattern for roughly a decade. The 2007 demolition falls inside the camp's documented 'green shift' revitalisation of 2006-2012; whether it was part of that programme is NOT stated by the operator and is not asserted here.

THE SUEZ BRIDGE CROSSES THE NARROW CHANNEL BETWEEN LAKE KANAWANA AND LAKE WILSON. Named on a 1987 Senior Boys board (f_1687) and otherwise undocumented, it is now located: the operator places it over the narrow canal joining the camp's two main lakes. THAT CHANNEL IS ALREADY IN THIS KB FROM THE OTHER SIDE -- the site article records the two lakes as 'connected by a dam between Lake Kanawana and Lake Wilson that is ceremonially opened at the end of each season', so the bridge, the dam and one of the camp's surviving seasonal rituals all sit at the same point on the property. The 1998 five-kilometre swim ran 'Wilson Falls to Frogs Bog', Lake Wilson to Lake Kanawana (f_1586), which is to say it passed through this channel. The name is a joke on the Suez Canal. Note the Knights of Kanawana charter's fifth challenge asks candidates to contribute 'something of permanence to camp -- a substantial part of a totem pole, or a bridge', so camper-built bridges were an expected thing at Kanawana; whether the Suez Bridge was one is not stated.

RAKU WAS THE DOG OF CAMP DIRECTOR JOANNA A.A. HOAD. This CONFIRMS an inference the plaque audit drew from an object's shape rather than its text: the 3rd-session 1995 all-camp board reads 'We saved Raku and the red-day tuck!', which is opaque on its own, but the board is cut in the shape of a BONE and painted with a PAW PRINT, from which f_2349 concluded Raku was a dog. He was, and he belonged to the on-site Director. THE DATE FITS PRECISELY: Hoad's on-site Directorship ran 1995 to 2000 (f_1730), so the 1995 all-camp game built around rescuing Raku falls in her FIRST season -- the new director's dog, made the object of the whole camp's game. This is the only camp animal recorded anywhere in this project. (The operator gives the surname as 'Hode', which is the spelling this wiki carried before correcting it against Lower Canada College's archived staff records; the corrected form Joanna A.A. Hoad is used here.)

FAMILY GROUPS ON THE PLAQUE WALL, TIERED BY EVIDENCE. Clustering all 1,483 indexed names by surname yields 166 surnames held by more than one person. THREE ARE CONFIRMED: Alex and Tiff BOLLHORN (CITs 1993 and 1995, operator-confirmed siblings); Daphne and Bianca PUNGARTNIK, both LITs in 2007, whose relationship is stated by Bianca's own painted nickname 'i'm not daphne'; and Matt and Dan ARONSON (CITs 1993 and 1995, both on Staff 02), operator-confirmed brothers. TWENTY-SEVEN MORE ARE STRONG -- an uncommon surname shared by people appearing on THE SAME BOARD or in the SAME YEAR, which is what siblings at camp together look like: the three GOUGEONS (Danny, Eric, Jerome, all on Staff '97); Katie and Anna ROTMAN on the same 2005 Swazi trip; Thomas and Michael BRACKEN in the same 1995 cabin; Maria, Sofia and Sole PARDO in 2008; Roma and Joy KOZLOV on the 1972 first all-female canoe trip; Mani and Tony ALONSO, Liliane and Pierre GRAS, and Desmond and Robert PERKINS on the Staff of '79; Doug and Heidi LOERICK and Jubal and Mitch GRAHAM on the Staff of 1990; Ben and Naomi GOLOFF, Keith and Sarah SIMMONS, Robert and Sylvain TESSIER, and Ali and Dave LEDUC on Staff 02; Michael and Stephen COOKSON on Staff '97; Eyal and Misha ARTZY knighted in consecutive years; Mark and Craig GILLETT likewise; Julien and Yves TASSE.
