SIXTY-THREE ARE PLAUSIBLE (uncommon shared surname, overlapping or nearby years) and SEVENTY-THREE ARE WEAK (distant years, or a surname common enough to be coincidence). NO RELATIONSHIP BEYOND THE THREE CONFIRMED IS ASSERTED ANYWHERE IN THIS WIKI; a shared surname is a lead, not a fact. || UPGRADED (2026-08-28): the TASSE pair moves from STRONG to CONFIRMED -- the operator states Julien and Yves are father and son (f_2356). Four confirmed families now: Bollhorn, Pungartnik, Aronson and Tasse, and Tasse is the only one that is a generational rather than a sibling pair.

TWO MORE INDEX BUGS FOUND BY SURNAME CLUSTERING, BOTH THE SAME CLASS AS THE STAFF-COLUMN BUG (f_2335). (1) THE KNIGHTS' TITLES WERE NEVER STRIPPED: the roll paints every entry 'Sir X' or 'Lady X', so 'Sir Denys Lawrence' indexed as a different person from the Denys Lawrence on the Staff of '79 board. Every knight appearing anywhere else was held twice and their career split in half. Fixed; traced people 149 -> 155, junior-to-staff progressions 69 -> 71. (2) THIRTY PAIRS REMAIN THAT ARE PROBABLY ONE PERSON UNDER TWO SPELLINGS -- Walter/Wally Betz, Nandy/Nancy Fletcher, Barb/Barbara Goddard, Jessica/Jess Dicesare, Daniel/Danny Van Gelder, Bradley/Brad Tagieff, Steve/Stephen Reizes, Kaya/Kayla Sabourin among them. They are CANDIDATES FOR HUMAN JUDGEMENT, NOT A MERGE LIST, and two show why: the matcher paired 'David Paltiel' (CIT 1975) with 'Sir Dave Paltiel' (knighted 1982), a merge this project had ALREADY DECLINED on reasoning -- the order honoured campers, so a 1975 CIT knighted seven years later does not fit and a younger sibling is at least as likely -- and it collapsed Elissa Sukosd (2003) with Melissa and Mel Sukosd (2007-08), who are far more likely sisters than one person. An automated similarity test can see neither objection, which is why the pairs are recorded rather than applied.

JULIEN AND YVES TASSE ARE FATHER AND SON, AND THIS RESOLVES THE LONGEST OPEN QUESTION IN THE PLAQUE INDEX. The name Tasse spans 27 years of camp boards -- Julien Tasse set apart between painted arrows as leader on the Advance Guard plaques of 1963 and 1964 (f_1588, f_1589), 'The Tasse's' thanked collectively on the Staff of '79 board (f_1703), Yves and Julien Tasse both named on Advance Guard 1986 (f_1590), and both again on the Staff of 1990 plaque (f_1704). This project had recorded the two possible readings and declined to choose: one man returning across three decades, or two generations sharing a name. THE OPERATOR SETTLES IT AS FATHER AND SON. WHICH IS WHICH IS AN INFERENCE, NOT HIS STATEMENT: the chronology makes Julien the father, and JULIEN TASSE'S OWN CAMP ASSOCIATION RUNS 1963 TO 1990 -- twenty-seven years, the longest single-person span documented anywhere in this collection. The plural in 'The Tasse's' on the 1979 plaque is consistent with a family already at camp in that year. || INFERENCE CORRECTED (2026-08-28, within the hour): this fact first reasoned that Julien was 'a boy on the 1963 and 1964 Advance Guard boards' who returned as an adult. HE WAS NEVER A CAMPER ON THOSE BOARDS. The operator states he was Kanawana's CARETAKER for thirty-odd years (f_2357), so he was already the adult on site in 1963, set apart between painted arrows on the Advance Guard boards because he was leading the section, not because he was its most senior boy. TWO CONSEQUENCES. First, the alternative reading this fact carried -- that Yves might be the father -- is now closed: a caretaker of thirty years present in 1963 is the father. Second, JULIEN TASSE MUST BE REMOVED FROM THE JUNIOR-TO-STAFF PROGRESSION COUNT, since he held a staff role throughout and never progressed into one; that count falls from 71 to 70. The 27-year span stands and is stronger, but it is a span of EMPLOYMENT, not of a camper's return.

JULIEN TASSE WAS KANAWANA'S CARETAKER FOR MORE THAN THIRTY YEARS. He died circa 1992-1995 -- the operator gives a range and it is preserved as a range. This is the single longest documented service by any individual in this project, and it explains a pattern the plaques could show but not account for: Tasse's name appears on camp boards across 27 years (Advance Guard 1963 and 1964, 'The Tasse's' on the Staff of '79, Advance Guard 1986, and the Staff of 1990) not because he was a camper who returned, but because HE LIVED AND WORKED THERE THROUGHOUT. His last surviving plaque appearance, the Staff of 1990, falls within a few years of his death. He is the father of Yves Tasse, who appears on the 1986 and 1990 boards (f_2356).

THE DINING HALL IS TECHNICALLY NAMED SALLE JULIEN TASSE, AND THE NAME NEVER STUCK. After Julien Tasse's death circa 1992-95 the camp formally renamed its dining hall (built 1911) after its caretaker of thirty-odd years; in practice everyone continued to call it the dining hall and the new name did not enter ordinary use. The operator, on site as camper and staff from 1985 to 2002, records both the renaming and its failure to take. THE IRONY IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: the dining hall is the room where Kanawana's plaque wall hangs. Every one of the 151 boards transcribed in the p_291 audit is mounted inside a room named for a man whose own name appears on four of them, and this project read all 151 without knowing whose room it was. The site article records the Dining Hall's construction date and its capacity of over 300, but held no name for it.

E1-REVIEWED IS NOT A RELIABLE STATUS, MEASURED. The p_218 sweep found ten defects in articles already carrying this project's TOP pipeline status, and the p_227 pass that fixed them (2026-08-28) found that SIX HAD ALREADY BEEN QUIETLY FIXED in the interval and FOUR WERE STILL OPEN. The four: directors-index.md's era summary listed 1968 as an open year while its own table gave Seaman as director 1959-1968; the same article carried two incompatible 1951 titles for Nelson McEwen (now conflict c_028); pip-alumni-award.md asserted '12 documented recipients through 2018' where its own table names 11; and section-names.md's research note gave the Trailblazers age as 16 against the camp's own 16-17. THREE OF THE FOUR ARE SELF-CONTRADICTIONS WITHIN A SINGLE FILE -- a claim in prose disagreeing with a table a few lines above it -- which is the class of error a citation check cannot catch, because both halves are properly cited. The lesson is not that these articles were badly made; it is that a status label records when an article was last reviewed, not whether it is currently true, and that the wiki has no mechanism to detect a fact drifting out from under an article that already passed.

THE VERIFY PASS ON THE SIX PLAQUE-AUDIT ARTICLES (2026-09-02, p_291-p_296 output, draft -> R3-verified) FOUND ITS LARGEST DEFECT CLASS TO BE STATED COUNTS DISAGREEING WITH THE DATA BEHIND THEM, NOT UNCITED CLAIMS. multi-year-index.md said '1,493 distinct named individuals, of whom 149 appear in more than one year' where person-index.json holds 1,483 and 155; it said 70 progressions where the index, once the progression test was written down, yields 66; and its table listed 149 rows against a body claiming 155. named-places-and-camp-vocabulary.md carried a progression count of 44. Every one of these numbers was CORRECT WHEN WRITTEN and went stale because a later fix moved the index without moving the article. The mechanical verify harness passed all six articles clean both before and after these corrections, because it checks citation integrity and not whether an article agrees with its own data.

THE DOCUMENTED JUNIOR-TO-STAFF PROGRESSION COUNT FROM THE PLAQUE INDEX IS 66, not the 70 previously published. The figure fell when the test was written down as code (scripts/plaque/build_table.py) instead of applied by eye. Two criteria had been loose. (1) A knighthood was being read as junior standing: Josh Usheroff (Knight 1998, Staff 2002) and Lindsay Kertland (Knight 1980, Staff 1983) were counted on that basis, but Knight, Signatory, Award recipient and Guest are honours or neutral labels that establish nothing about rank. (2) Order was not required: Alex Zannis (Counsellor 2006, Voyageur 2008) and Kertland again (CIT 1985, after her 1983 staff credit) were counted although the staff credit came FIRST. The count of people traced across more than one year is unaffected at 155, and distinct named individuals at 1,483.

EIGHT PEOPLE IN THE PLAQUE INDEX CARRY A STAFF-GRADE ROLE ON AN EARLIER BOARD THAN A JUNIOR ONE: Bruce Netherwood (Director 1984, Member 1986, Staff 1990), Bruce Weihs (Counsellor 1985, Voyageur 1988, Staff 1990), Erin Savage (CIT 2001, Staff 2002, Member 2003), Roxanne Sayegh (CIT 1998, Staff 2002, Member 2003), Jeff Muss (CIT 1982, Staff 1983, Member 1986, Voyageur 1988), Lindsay Kertland (Knight 1980, Staff 1983, CIT 1985), Alex Zannis (Counsellor 2006, Voyageur 2008) and Rob Shackell (Member 2001, Tripper 2005, Voyageur 2008, Tripper 2010). The likeliest explanation for most is that 'Voyageur' and 'Member' are GROUP labels on trip and section boards which list staff alongside campers, so a tripper reads as a camper years after his first tripper credit -- Rob Shackell is the clearest case. The residue after that explanation is where two different people may share a name. Tracked under p_298.

THE 1995 RAKU BOARD IS THE FIRST MATERIAL EVIDENCE OF ANY KIND TOUCHING JOANNA A.A. HOAD'S KANAWANA DATES. Her 1995-2000 on-site directorship is the one span in the directors index that no document has ever corroborated (two full research passes, nine or more surfaces, both spellings). The bone-shaped all-camp-game board for the third session of 1995 reads 'We saved Raku and the red-day tuck!' and Raku is independently identified by the operator as Hoad's dog. This is not proof of her appointment: it is a dated physical object consistent with her being at camp that summer, reached by a different route than the memory it agrees with.

THE 1984 CIT BOARD'S ROBERT FROST EPIGRAPH IS ALTERED, NOT QUOTED. It reads 'We have promises to keep / and miles to go before we sleep -- R.F.'; Frost's 'Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening' reads 'But I have promises to keep, / And miles to go before I sleep.' Both lines are moved into the first person PLURAL. It is the only literary quotation found on any of the 151 Kanawana plaques.

THE KANAWANA SITE ARTICLE CARRIED TWO SOURCE ENTRIES NUMBERED 36 (found 2026-09-02, in an article at E1-reviewed status). The Julien Tasse oral-history entry had been appended with the number of the existing acreage-series entry, making the ^36 marker on the dining-hall line ambiguous between them. Renumbered to 41; the article's Sources header, which read 40, was wrong by one before the fix and is now 42. The mechanical verify harness did not catch it because the harness inspects DRAFT articles only, and this article is E1-reviewed -- the same blind spot f_2359 records from the other direction.

THE SOURCE-NUMBERING BACKLOG (p_302, cleared 2026-09-02) HAD FOUR DISTINCT SHAPES, and only one of them was a typo. (1) HEADER DRIFT, nine articles: sources appended, '*Sources: N*' never updated -- eleven of twelve headers were LOW, which is the signature of appending to a finished article. (2) ENTRIES STRANDED BELOW THE SECTION, three articles: camp-songs-cheers (entry 20), murray-shantz (2-4) and t-duncan-patton (6-9) each had source entries appended AFTER the '## Research Notes' heading, so they were outside the Sources section, invisible to a counter and unreachable by their own ^N markers. (3) BULLETS MIXED WITH NUMBERS, four articles: council-ring, da-budge, lv-games and billy-ball had Sources sections where some entries were bullets and some were numbered, so a printed number no longer matched its position in the list -- council-ring's header even documented the mess ('bullet/label-style source list, not numbered') instead of fixing it, and said 3 where the article had 11. (4) ORPHAN LABELS: ^mc in lv-games and ^cr in council-ring were label markers with no definition or a definition inside a bullet. Every one predates 2026-09-02 and none was visible while checks A1 and G ran on drafts only.

ONE QAHN ARTICLE ON THE YMCA CAMP AT SAINT-ADOLPHE-D'HOWARD IS HELD IN sources.json UNDER THREE SEPARATE IDS: src_qahn_howard (12 facts, 1 wiki article), src_qahn_ymca_camp (3 facts) and src_qahn_ymca_camp_saint_adolphe (1 fact). All three records describe the same piece -- Camp Jubilee and Camp Otoreke at Saint-Adolphe-d'Howard. A fourth id, src_qahn_kanawana, was cited in t-duncan-patton.md and exists in no record at all; it has been repointed to src_qahn_howard, the id with the most use. This is the same defect as check K's twenty duplicated source_ids but reached from the other direction: there the ID is shared by different records, here different IDs are shared by one source.

THE INTERNAL-CONSISTENCY CHECK (p_301, built 2026-09-02, scripts/verify/consistency.py) HAS TWO HALVES BECAUSE THE DEFECT HAS TWO SHAPES. DERIVED: a number in prose against a value computed from a data file -- these need a hand-written registry, since no parser can know that 'distinct named individuals' means len(person-index.json); the registry also reports when a guarded sentence is REWORDED, because a rule that silently stops matching leaves the number unchecked. TABLE: a stated count against the rows of a table in the same file -- general, no registry needed, and the shape of three of the four live defects p_227 found (f_2359). The check reproduces both classes on demand: reverting multi-year-index.md to its stale 1,493/149 and pip-alumni-award.md to '11 documented recipients' makes it fail, restoring them makes it pass. ITS FIRST THREE HITS WERE ALL FALSE POSITIVES, which is how a check gets switched off, so it now discounts placeholder table rows (pip-alumni-award's 2010 'No documented recipient' row means thirteen rows document twelve recipients), rejects ratio phrasings ('three names OF roughly one hundred'), and permits a deliberate mismatch only through a '<!-- count-ok: reason -->' comment, which forces the reason to be written down.

SIXTEEN OF THE SEVENTY-EIGHT ENTRIES IN THE PLAQUE INDEX'S CURATED ALIAS LIST COULD NEVER MATCH ANYTHING (found 2026-09-02, p_298). The list records deliberate 'these two spellings are one person' decisions, but its keys are written the way a person writes names -- 'j.m. sotiran', "andrew 'hippo' elridge", 'julien tasse' with the accent, 'jen kauf[man]' -- while norm() stripped periods, accents, quoted nicknames and bracketed completions BEFORE performing the lookup. One entry in five was silently doing nothing. Three of the near-miss pairs the project was holding for human judgement (J.M. Sotiran/Sotiron, Nandy/Nancy Fletcher, Andrew Eldridge/Elridge) had therefore already been decided and the decision had never taken effect. Fixed by shaping the alias keys through the same normaliser as the names they are matched against, with a collision check. Seven names merged; distinct names 1,483 -> 1,476, traced people 155 -> 159, progressions 66 -> 69. The traced count went UP because some merges joined two single-year people into one person with two years.

THE NEAR-MISS NAME PAIRS IN THE PLAQUE INDEX ARE NOW GENERATED AND EVIDENCED RATHER THAN LISTED (scripts/plaque/candidate_pairs.py, kb/plaque-audit/candidate-pairs.json). 39 pairs. Three mechanical tests are applied. CO-OCCURRENCE -- both spellings on the same board would mean two people, since a roster does not list one person twice -- rules out NONE of them: every near-miss pair sits on different boards, including the four that share a year. ATTESTED ELSEWHERE separates four: 'Buppy Warren', 'Shaun Leggett', 'Simon Heller' and 'Sir Adrian Di Giovanni' each appear in the KB or wiki from non-plaque sources while their counterpart appears nowhere else. LOW-CONFIDENCE READING separates two: the audit itself flagged 'Nikki Bohbot' and 'Simon Hiller' as uncertain while not flagging their counterparts. SIMON HELLER / SIMON HILLER CARRIES BOTH SIGNALS and would give Staff 1990 -> CIT Director 1993 -> CIT Director 1995. The remaining 33 have no mechanical evidence either way. NOTE ON THE ATTESTATION TEST: its first version counted the whole of facts.json and found nothing, because p_292 folded the plaque transcriptions into the fact claims -- a test whose corpus contains the thing it is testing always passes.

THE 1951 KAMP KANAWANA HISTORY STATES THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME 'LAKE WILSON' OUTRIGHT: "A short time later Mr. J. W. McConnell purchased the land around Lake Desjardins. This he presented to the Y.M.C.A., and the lake was renamed 'Lake Wilson' after Mr. McConnell's son." (OCR reads 'ren-owned' for 'renamed' and 'sone' for 'son'; the scan renders terminal periods as 'e'.) This is a primary in-house camp document, and it confirms BOTH halves of what the wiki held as unverified: the oral-history claim that the lake was formerly Lac Desjardins and was renamed after McConnell bought and donated it, AND the McConnell-son hypothesis that lake-wilson.md called 'plausible but unverified'. The article's Open Question 1 was rated CRITICAL and named the 1933 Dawson history and 1943 Charlton account as 'the most likely sources, but confirmed archive-only', while this document sat in the KB marked extracted.

LAKE KANAWANA WAS FORMERLY LAKE ST. LOUIS. The 1951 camp history says the 1910 site-search committee 'explored the country and Lake St. Louis, the present site, was located', and then, after the naming decision: 'The name of the lake was also [changed] from Ste Louis to Lake Kanawana.' The lake took the camp's name, not the reverse. This appears nowhere else in this project -- the strings 'St. Louis' and 'Saint-Louis' occur in no wiki article.

THE 1910 SITE SEARCH, AS THE CAMP TOLD IT IN 1951: 'Early in 1910 a Committee under the Chairmanship of Mr. R. L. Charlton was constituted to look for a new site for the boys' camp' -- constituted because 'it was recognized by Association leaders that one camp could not house both boys and young men.' The committee was Charlton with 'Messrs. R. B. Ross Jr., and L. Cushing'. 'During the late winter months of 1910' they went to the Laurentians, 'arrived at St. Sauveur and commenced to walk at night over the hills to Lac Marois. Running into a rain and snow storm the Committee lost its way and stayed overnight at a farmhouse. The next day the country was explored and Lake St. Louis, the present site, was located.' The document credits them with 'great foresight' for 'suggesting the purchase of all the shore line on the lake'. NOTE FOR THE CUSHING DISAMBIGUATION: this document names TWO different Cushings in two different decades -- 'W. E. Cushing' on the 1892 founding committee and 'L. Cushing' on the 1910 site committee.

CAMP ATTENDANCE IN 1900, from the 1951 camp history: 'During the summer of 1900 the attendance was thirty-seven boys and seventy-two young men. The dining marquee had been replaced by a log cabin and kitchen at a cost of $700.00.' Young men outnumbered boys nearly two to one -- which is the stated reason a separate boys' camp was sought a decade later ('one camp could not house both boys and young men'). Neither figure appears anywhere else in this project.

THE FIRST CAMP'S EQUIPMENT, 1894, per the 1951 history: 'The equipment consisted of six tents - a marquee for a dining tent - all cooking was done over an open fire.' The same document describes the 1893 reconnaissance party as '"Gentlemen Adventurers" [who] toured the country over "Corduroy" roads in buckboards and thoroughly investigated the lakes and islands by boat', and gives the property extent as of 1951: 'all of Lakes Kanawana, Wilson, and Round Lake, plus a sizeable part of the shoreline on Lake [Becsiee -- OCR uncertain, possibly Becasse].'

A SOURCE MARKED 'extracted' HAD NEVER BEEN READ END TO END. The 1951 'Kamp Kanawana History' carried read_state 'extracted' with basis 'derived:cited-by-fact' and no cache_path: nine facts quoted passages from it, and on that basis it counted as read. Reading the whole 6,476-character text on 2026-09-02 -- prompted by the operator asking what it says -- produced four new facts (f_2371 to f_2375) and one correction (f_2180). One of the new facts answers an Open Question that lake-wilson.md rated CRITICAL and described as depending on two archive-only documents. THE PATTERN: 'extracted' means somebody took what they went looking for. It does not mean anybody read the document. read_state_basis 'derived:cited-by-fact' should be treated as UNREAD for any question the extracting pass was not asking.

SIX CAMPERS AND ONE STAFF MEMBER NAMED IN THE 1935 CHRONICLE, none previously in this knowledge base. JULY BEST-CAMPER SHIELDS: 'Bob Bennet, Senior, John [surname illegible in the OCR], and Bryce Chatam, Juniors, and Junior Taylor, Juvenile, were awarded shields as the best Campers in their section for the month of July.' ALL-CAMP REGATTA AGGREGATE WINNERS: 'Bob Bennet was Senior aggregate man, Bryce Chatam Junior, and Harold Meyer Juvenile.' Bennet and Chatam therefore each won twice. BOATING CARNIVAL: 'a House of Parliament was removed from the hill and DOUG MACDONALD felt much better' -- an outhouse prank, the chronicle declining to say more ('the matter is far too delicate'). STAFF CHANGE, last week of July: the camp lost its Junior Director 'in exchange for WILF BUCKLEY'. The August shield winners are in the document but their names are lost to the scan ('with receiving the Senior shield, the Junior, and the Juvenile' -- three names dropped out of the OCR).

FIRST CALIBRATION OF THE FULL RE-READ (p_304). The 1935 'History of Kamp Kanawana' -- 4,928 characters, 38 facts already citing it -- turns out to have been mined THOROUGHLY: almost every event, visitor and date in it was already extracted. So the failure is NOT that sources went unread across the board. Two things were missed, and they are the same two things: NAMES and NUMBERS. Six named individuals (f_2377) were dropped while the events around them were kept -- 'Best camper shields were awarded at Kanawana in 1935' recorded the ritual and discarded the people, which is exactly the failure the plaque audit found on painted boards. And a dollar figure was recorded as $5 where the document says $55. THE RE-READ SHOULD THEREFORE HUNT NAMES, NUMBERS AND EXACT QUOTED WORDING, not events -- the events are largely in.

THE CONCORDIA FINDING AID LISTS 'WINTER SKI CAMP RECORDS -- 1945-1947' UNDER KAMP KANAWANA'S OWN PROGRAM SUB-SUB-SERIES (P0145/12B07). This is twenty-five years earlier than anything in winter-programming.md, which states the camp 'was a summer-only operation for most of its history, but beginning in the 1970s it expanded into winter programming' and dates the earliest documented step to a 1971-72 ski tow. A finding-aid title proves the RECORDS exist and are filed as Kanawana program material; it does not by itself prove the programme ran on the Kanawana site, and the records themselves have not been read. But 'summer-only until the 1970s' cannot stand as written while a 1945-1947 winter ski camp file sits in the camp's own program series.

THREE ARCHIVE ITEMS NAMED IN THE CONCORDIA FINDING AID AND NOWHERE IN THIS PROJECT. (1) 'Kamp Kanawana: Report of First Year of Camp -- 1910' (P0145/12B01) -- the camp's own report on its first season at the Saint-Sauveur site, the single most direct document on the founding of the present camp. (2) "Certain Experiences in Attempting to Accomplish Democratic Program Building" -- 1927 (P0145/12B07), a programme-philosophy document from the Harold Cross era. (3) 'Kanawana [Winter] Outing Club -- [197-]-1979', filed alongside 'Winter ski camp records -- 1945-1947'. Also worth restating because it is the largest single body of camper names in the archive: SIX MICROFICHES, 'Junior Camp Opening Roster', 1924-1939 -- sixteen consecutive years of rosters, filed in 12B01.

'CAMP BECSIES' IS A REAL YMCA OF MONTREAL CAMP, with its own sub-series P0145/12D in the Concordia fonds, alongside Otoreke (12C), Dorval (12E), Weredale (12F), Perrot (12G), Thunderbird (12I) and the Wilderness Survival Camp (12J). This settles an OCR uncertainty in the 1951 camp history, which gives the camp's extent as 'all of Lakes Kanawana, Wilson, and Round Lake, plus a sizeable part of the shoreline on Lake [Becsiee]' -- the scan's 'Becsiee' is Becsies. Kanawana's property therefore touched a lake that gave its name to another YMCA camp. This project has no article on Camp Becsies and one passing mention.

THE SOURCES ARE ALREADY OCR'd. NOBODY WIRED A QUARTER OF THEM UP. Measured 2026-09-02 in answer to the operator's question about whether re-reading would require fresh OCR: sources/cache held 904 non-empty text files, 40.3 MB, roughly 10 million tokens of already-extracted text. Only 604 of those files were pointed at by a source record. THREE HUNDRED FILES -- 25.8 MB, about 6.5 million tokens -- belonged to no record at all, so no step of this pipeline could see them, cite them, or count them as unread. The largest block by far is CANADIAN CAMPING MAGAZINE: 164 issues spanning 1949 to 1988, fully OCR'd on disk, against 18 source records for the entire run and only 10 of those carrying a cache_path. Next: 57 files in the YMCA of Montreal fonds folder including the 1921, 1922 and 1923 camp brochures, the 1939 and 1941 CFCF radio broadcasts, Kanawana annual and director's reports for 1964-66 and 1969-79, twenty-four SGW YMCA annual reports from 1889 to 1996, the 1901 historical sketch and the 1873 YMCA history. Then 29 web-page caches including a 4.9 MB YMCA newsletter run and Gazette newspaper captures of 533 KB (1897) and 754 KB (1918). All 251 non-duplicate files are now catalogued with read_state 'unread'.

THE GREEN TRIANGLE CORPUS IS CACHED TWICE, byte for byte, under sources/cache/green-triangle/ and sources/cache/ymca-montreal-fonds/. Thirty-eight issues appear in both folders with identical checksums; sources.json points at the fonds copies, so the other 38 looked like uncatalogued material and are not. Forty-nine such byte-identical duplicates were skipped when the orphan files were catalogued. This is why the orphan count is 251 new records and not 300 files -- a raw file count would have overstated the backlog by a fifth.

THE FIRST SAMPLE FROM AN UNMINED SOURCE SUPPORTS THE OPERATOR'S PREDICTION, against the earlier calibration from two well-picked-over documents (f_2378). The first 1,200 characters of one Green Triangle issue -- 30 July 1932 -- name fifteen people: an editorial staff of Harvey Marshall, Jack Millar, Herb Furness, Bill Bourne, Preston Robb, Keith Bowen, Hugh R[?]key, Rob Gibson and Geo. Brugman; a poem signed Max Ford, 1932; departing staff Mr. Buckley (Junior Director for July), Dr. Courville, and leaders Alex Ross and Scotty Kiell; and arriving staff Mr. McDermit and Dr. Colb[?]azer. ELEVEN OF THE THIRTEEN CHECKED APPEAR NOWHERE in this knowledge base or wiki. Note also that 'Mr. Buckley, Junior Director for the month of July' in 1932 is very probably the 'Wilf Buckley' the 1935 chronicle records arriving as Junior Director three years later -- a person visible only because two documents were read closely.

THE FOUR SECTION DIRECTORS OF 1964, none previously in this knowledge base, all school teachers by profession: STANLEY WASILEWSKI, Pathfinder section, completing his FIFTH year as a section director at Kanawana (so from 1960); KENNETH FELLOWS, Coureurs de Bois, second year; DAVE CADDELL, Woodsmen, first year; BOB DRUMMOND, Pioneer, first year. The report also names the camp's four sections in 1964 as Pathfinder, Coureurs de Bois, Woodsmen and Pioneer, and describes the camp's governing body as 'the Council (section directors, the assistant director and the director)', which met regularly to train, assess and plan.

BEN T. HANNAN WAS ASSISTANT CAMP DIRECTOR OF KANAWANA IN 1964, his fifth year in that post and his FIFTEENTH on the Kanawana staff -- so continuously from about 1949. The 1964 report devotes a full paragraph to him: 'a unique and outstanding contribution... a warm outgoing personality and an ability to help that has endeared him to all... A school teacher by vocation, a Kanawanian by avocation.' He also gave the commentary at the camp's parent meetings. NOTE ON SPELLING AND IDENTITY: the Concordia finding aid lists 'Kanawana Reminiscence (of 1948), by Ben T. Hannah -- 1989', one letter different, and consistent with a staff career beginning in the late 1940s. This project also holds an article at people/rh-hanagan.md; whether these are one person, two, or three has not been tested.

JULIEN TASSE IS NAMED THREE TIMES IN THE 1964 KANAWANA ANNUAL REPORT AS THE CAMP'S CARETAKER, doing the work himself: he installed the flush systems in the Pioneer Section and Staff toilets ('The actual installation was done by the camp caretaker, Julien Tasse'), and he rebuilt the Junior Wharf, which had been raised on the ice that winter, its main supports separated and beams rotted ('This was a major job, but the cost was minimum, Julien Tasse doing the work'). THE REPORT ALSO DOCUMENTS HIS FAMILY AND HIS HOUSING: 'As the Tasse family has increased, there are four children as well as Mr. & Mrs. Tasse the present home is completely inadequate.' An addition of a 20 x 20 kitchen and another bedroom plus an adequate furnace was costed at about $3,800, to be built by 'Julien and his assistant'. THIS DISPROVES A CENTRAL CLAIM OF people/julien-tasse.md, which stated that no document from the camp or the YMCA of Montreal named him at all and that everything known rested on four painted boards and one person's memory.

THE UNDATED PATHFINDER SECTION PADDLE IS ALMOST CERTAINLY FROM 1964. The plaque audit recorded a Pathfinder paddle carrying, beside its roster, a column of six ORIGINS -- Australia, England, Holland, Cape Breton, France, Virginia -- with the names themselves abraded past reading, and named-places-and-camp-vocabulary.md carries it as an open question ('undated... which era of the camp do they belong to?'). The 1964 annual report describes exactly this: 'In one section alone six different countries were represented on the staff, one from Holland, one from Poland, three from England, one from France, one from Australia and of course from Canada', and separately that staff came 'from as far east in Canada as Cape Breton Island to Toronto in the west and as far south as Virginia in the United States.' Australia, England, Holland, France, Cape Breton and Virginia are the paddle's six. Stanley Wasilewski was Pathfinder section director in 1964. The report adds that three of the English staff 'came to Canada on a student chartered plane and stayed nine weeks in camp before making a tour of parts of Canada and the United States.'

KANAWANA'S 1964 SEASON IN NUMBERS, from its own annual report -- the seventy-first season, the camp dating itself from 1894. 535 boys attended. About two thirds stayed two weeks, 131 stayed four weeks, 12 stayed six weeks and 20 stayed the entire season. Camp population at peak was about 390 people, with roughly 300 fed daily. Thirty-one counsellors, average age 19.8 years, up 1.2 years on 1962; eighteen (60%) were university students and three were graduates; average salary $173 against a range of $100 to $280, with six over $200; nine had been Kanawana counsellors before. The camp missed its budget of 1,530 camper weeks and ran a deficit; about 50% of campers returned each year, so roughly 250 new campers had to be recruited annually to make budget.

KANAWANA BOUGHT ABOUT 120 ACRES AT THE SOUTH END OF LAKE WILSON IN 1964, AND ONE LOT JOINTLY WITH THE BOY SCOUTS. The annual report: part of lot 215 and lots 216 and 217, Parish of St. Sauveur, 'acquired to protect Lake Wilson'. LOT 215 WAS PURCHASED IN CO-OPERATION WITH THE BOY SCOUT ASSOCIATION, CAMP TAMARACOUTA, and 'the acquisition of this lot joins the property of the two camps'. Lots 216 and 217 were bought outright to stop a proposed summer colony of some 200 lots, whose developer held enough land at the outlet of Lake Wilson to offer water rights on the lake to purchasers; two lots of 100 x 50 feet had already been sold and the camp was trying to buy those back. After the purchase 'the Kanawana property now extends over approximately 1,000 acres.'

CAMPER ORIGINS AT KANAWANA IN 1964, from the annual report: campers came from the Bahamas and the U.S.A.; two boys from Japan whose fathers were posted to Montreal with I.C.A.O. (the International Civil Aviation Organization); and one from Haiti 'his father being the commander of the army of that country'. The Japanese boys' counsellor was from Malaysia and spoke four eastern languages, none of them Japanese. The report notes an increasing number of French campers 'many of whom are sent to Kanawana to learn English', and 'many new Canadian boys at the camp from such countries as Hungary, Holland, Germany, France and Italy.' It also records, as an institutional observation, that the opening of a new YMHA camp had made no difference to the number of Jewish boys attending.

KANAWANA'S 1964 PROMOTION PROGRAMME, in detail the wiki has for no other year. A new folder covering Kanawana, Les Voyageurs, Training Camp and Family Camp plus brief information on Otoreke and the Branch Day Camps; 6,500 distributed by mail and through YMCA branches. Information notebooks for each branch office secretary. A write-up and advertisement in the Montreal Star's camping supplement in late May. Advertisements in eight local papers: the Westmount Examiner, Verdun Guardian, NDG Monitor, Montreal West News, Cote St. Luc News, Lachine Messenger, Lakeshore News and Town of Mount Royal Post. DONALD MCKAY worked on promotion through the branches for about six weeks. A television interview on CFCF's 'Like Young' programme gave two Voyageurs about three minutes on air. Radio station CJAD carried spot announcements worth $1,360 as a community service, and the Director gave two half-hour interviews with DORIS CLARK on her CJAD afternoon show, on the value of camping rather than on Kanawana itself. Crests and a cartoon map of the camp property were sent to each camper on registration. A camp reunion was held in January. Five parent meetings ran monthly from February to June, with slides and a commentary by Ben Hannan; three visiting days drew about 150 visitors.

KANAWANA PLANT AND INFRASTRUCTURE IN 1964, from the annual report. All camp toilets became flush that year, the last two units costing about $1,000. A new compressor replaced a fridge unit installed some fifteen years earlier, and there was no food spoilage that season. Ice had undermined the cement deck at the west end of the senior swimming wharf to the point where the high dive was in danger of collapsing; holes were punched in the decking and six tons of concrete poured. The filtration plant, installed about fifteen years earlier and never overhauled, was passing sand by the closing weeks. A new electric chlorinator was installed. Both 200-gallon galvanized hot-water storage tanks were failing. Tents were upgraded from 12 x 14 wall tents to 16 x 14, requiring larger platforms at negligible extra cost. FRANK NOBBS drew the plan for the proposed addition to the Caretaker's House. A wash house with propane instant heaters was recommended for the Pioneer and Woodsmen sections at about $1,000, because the camp's only showers drew hot water from the kitchen supply and could be used just at certain hours.

KANAWANA'S GOVERNANCE AND MONEY IN 1964: seven members of the Camp Committee visited during the summer; ROY LOCKE and DON DEWAR made a two-day visit and spoke with staff. AL DICKINSON was Financial Secretary of the Montreal YMCA and had met the camp about its finances that year; the report recommends the camp committee take the question to the Metropolitan Property & Finance Committee 'in order that the camps may embark upon a realistic policy for financing the operations.' The report recommends a permanent business manager covering three operations -- Kamp Kanawana, Family Camp and Les Voyageurs -- after two years of unsatisfactory seasonal appointments, and a $5.00 per week fee increase for 1965. The National Employment Service told the camp it could not find a second cook willing to work for $30 a week and that $50 to $70 would be needed.

KANAWANA PROPOSED CO-EDUCATIONAL CAMPING IN ITS 1965 ANNUAL REPORT, two years before the pilot this wiki dates to 1967-1970. The report recommends 'that the Camp Committee give consideration to the setting-up of a pilot project in co-ed camping at Kanawana for the 1966 season', and specifies it: run it in the WOODSMEN SECTION (ten and eleven year olds), add one unit (possibly a tent) to make eight units, four of boys and four of girls; staff accommodation is already adequate; the toilet building needs only 'a partition and a doorway'; and a wash house with showers for the girls would cost no more than $300 or $400. It also records the earlier step: under the chairmanship of KEITH FARQUHARSON a committee had surveyed the YMCA constituency on interest in camping for girls and got 'a very large and positive response', and recommended a girls' camp to the Metropolitan Board of Directors, which agreed there was interest but said it 'could not be contemplated at that time because of other items that had to take priority'. The report's argument: 'Children today, in practically all instances, take part in co-ed activities in the Montreal YMCA and camping need not be an exception.'

KANAWANA RAN A FIVE-AND-A-HALF-DAY T-GROUP LABORATORY TRAINING PROGRAMME FOR ITS STAFF IN 1965, the first year it did so, lengthening pre-camp training from one week to two and starting on 13 June. Two days of general orientation, then the laboratory week, then a second week of camping skills. FOUR SENIOR MONTREAL YMCA STAFF SERVED AS TRAINERS: TED LOWE, Public Relations Secretary; BRUCE McFARLANE, Executive Director of the Verdun-LaSalle Branch; RAY ROUSE, Executive Secretary of the Northmount Branch; and RIX ROGERS, Co-ordinator of Staff Development. The director calls the impact 'startling' and frames the season as the start of 'a whole new era of camping both in concept and in program'. This sits directly alongside Hedley Dimock's counsellor-attitude studies conducted at Kanawana in 1960-61 and held in the Concordia fonds, and is the same human-relations training tradition.

THE KANAWANA-TAMARACOUTA TRAIL WAS OPENED IN THE SEVENTH WEEK OF THE 1965 SEASON, a year after the two camps jointly bought the lot that joined their properties. The 1965 annual report: the trail 'was officially opened by the "Factor" of Tamaracouta and the "Chief" of Kanawana with campers and staff from both camps in attendance', followed by a day in which both camps 'met at the end of Lake Wilson, pitched camp and for a day joined in a program together'. Both camps recommended it become an annual feature. Neither the trail nor the joint programme appears anywhere else in this project.

THE KANAWANA CAMP BELL WAS CRACKED IN 1965. A camper went missing briefly and the camp followed its practice of tolling the bell continuously as a directional signal for both the boy and the search party; to make the job easier the staff member responsible struck the bell repeatedly with a hatchet instead of using the clapper. The child was never more than fifteen or twenty feet from his cabin. Director A. Ross Seaman treats the crack as an omen in the report: 'This bell which has signalled camp time for many, many years was damaged in the performance of its duty... the era that was signalled for so long by this old bell may well have drawn to a close.' The practice of tolling the bell for a lost camper is itself recorded nowhere else in this project.

MRS. TASSE WAS PAID CAMP STAFF ALONGSIDE HER HUSBAND. The 1965 annual report, crediting the caretaker for the plant's condition -- '22,000 board feet of lumber was cut at camp last winter, as well as approximately 100 cords of firewood, which would tell any Camp Committee member that Julien Tasse was hard at work last winter' -- continues: 'He was assisted by Mrs. Tasse who does the camp laundry during the summer, as well as taking care of the feeding of the advance party for the period of six weeks before camp opens.' The same report repeats 1964's recommendation in stronger terms: 'More adequate housing for the camp caretaker and his family is imperative and pressing and should receive immediate attention.'

KANAWANA'S 1965 SEASON WAS ITS WORST REGISTRATION IN MANY YEARS: about 1,200 camper weeks against a budget of 1,500. The annual report lists six causes without ranking them: three consecutive poor summers, especially in August, felt by many camps in the area; the fee increase; the growth of family camping; summer school taking boys who had done poorly in the school year, cancelling 'a fair number of applications'; the average length of stay shortening year on year; and, stated plainly, 'that Kamp Kanawana is not seen as a status camp and with the fee being charged today - by paying a very little more the youngster can be sent to one of the status private camps.' MOREY CROSS led the Camp Committee's promotion effort and GAVIN TURLEY, a YMCA Fellowship Student, was hired part-time as promotion officer and Business Manager on a minimum two-year basis. Seven Fellowship Students were on the 1965 staff, most in senior roles.

RANGERS WAS A CAMPER SECTION AT KANAWANA IN THE 1950s AND 60s, carrying its own line in the camp's ten-year statistical summary. The 1965 annual report's 'Camper Weeks by Sections' table runs Pioneer, Woodsmen, Coureurs de Bois, Pathfinders and RANGERS, with Rangers far smaller than the others -- on the order of 16 camper weeks in 1955, about 130 in 1957 and 118 in 1958 (figures partly OCR-damaged) against roughly 380-400 each for the four main sections. Rangers is absent from the 1964 report's four-section structure. CORRECTION TO MY OWN FIRST DRAFT OF THIS FACT: I recorded this as new. It is not. section-names.md already carries camper-week tables giving Rangers from at least 1955 to a last cohort in 1967, drawn from other annual reports. What the 1965 report adds is a second independent attestation, the per-section magnitudes for 1955-58, and the fact that Rangers had already dropped out of the section structure the 1964 director described.

THE GOLDEN ARROW'S FIRST RECIPIENT, 1965. The award was instituted that summer, given 'at the discretion of the staff to any boy in camp who shows extraordinary personal achievement during his stay... not a popularity poll but an award that is given on recommendation only.' The 1965 annual report presents it to a camper it names only as Gordon, a foster child who was almost totally blind, with some vision in one eye and able to read a little through very thick lenses. At camp he learned to go off the high dive -- 'a real achievement when you can't see where the water is' -- and earned his 'C' canoeist, the report noting that 'nobody made the test any easier for Gordon. He had to measure up to the standard of fully sighted boys.' The report also records the swimming programme's first stage as marked by a 'red disc'.

KANAWANA OFFICE AND PLANT NOTES, 1965. MRS. OLGA HALL joined as Office Secretary in the spring, succeeding MRS. DUFFY who left to have a family; during that year's mail strike she telephoned every parent whose son had written, so letters could be collected by hand and replies carried up to camp. Two skilled chefs worked together for the first time in many years after the Camp Committee raised the assistant's pay, and new white plastic dishes with a blue border from the Cyanamid Company of Canada replaced the worn set. Five new tents were bought and platforms enlarged from 12 x 14 to 14 x 16 in the Coureurs de Bois and Pathfinder sections. A CAMP PLANT MANUAL was being developed with photographs, building dimensions, fixed contents and per-building maintenance charts, to be kept current by the Business Manager. The report thanks the N.D.G. Y's Men's Club, the Westmount Branch YMCA, the Westmount Police Department, Mr. Romeo Lafleur and the Montreal YMCA staff. Signed by A. Ross Seaman, Director.

THE 1966 KANAWANA ANNUAL REPORT IS WRITTEN ALMOST ENTIRELY IN STATISTICS, and this project had extracted two facts from it. PRE-SEASON: 916 staff man-hours on promotion plus unrecorded branch hours; 3,855 phone conversations between camp staff and parents; 9,000 folders and flyers distributed; 608 parent-hours at information meetings; 16 committee members giving 137 man-hours; 335 hours interviewing prospective staff and 195 pieces of recruiting correspondence; sixty staff hired by 1 June; 4,848 man-hours preparing the camp; $14,319 spent on supplies by 1 June; $2,195 for the advance guard's food and wages; income at 1 June of $34,990; a $5,000 opening food order. Staff training totalled 6,150 man-hours and concluded 24 June, of which professional YMCA staff contributed 173 hours of HUMAN RELATIONS TRAINING -- the T-Group method introduced in 1965, continuing. On 25 June six buses and trucks travelled 720 miles to bring 134 campers to opening day.

WHAT A KANAWANA SEASON CONSUMED AND PRODUCED, 1966, from the annual report. FOOD: 43,908 meals eaten in camp and 5,678 more prepared, cooked and eaten on the trail; 10,000 quarts of milk; 5,610 pounds of meat; 3,485 loaves of bread; 131,724 dishes washed with 280 pounds of detergent; 40 cords of hardwood burned by the hot water boiler. PROGRAMME HOURS: 723 on the archery range; 13,040 in the craft shop and on the nature trails; 4,410 of swim instruction; 6,920 in canoe instruction and trips; 631 waterfront tests passed; 23 canoe trips of two to five days; 918 camper-days on hikes; 2,174 counsellor-hours of lifeguard duty; 4,832 training hours in the Training Camp. The camp truck drove 14,237 miles, an average of 237 a day. Campers and staff between them lost only 62 hospitalized days, 'without doubt the best record in the past eight years'. The tuck shop sold 256 paddles and, as 'an innovation', 480 gallons -- 7,680 cups -- of orange and grape drink. The business office handled 12,632 pieces of mail.

KANAWANA STAFF WERE PAID 27.1 CENTS AN HOUR IN 1966, and the report says so itself, with an exclamation mark and a question mark: '51 program and administrative staff members worked a total of 65,382 hours this past Summer for a total payroll of $17,660, providing an average hourly wage of 27.1 cents per hour?!' Ten senior supervisory staff gave 704 hours of intensive supervision; senior policy and training meetings took 380 man-hours; committee members spent 153 man-hours at camp. The whole season came to 111,614 man-hours against a budget of $65,000. Quebec had no general minimum wage covering this work at the time; the figure is recorded here as the camp's own accounting, not as a legal comparison.

THE 1966 REPORT CARRIES A TEN-YEAR STATISTICAL SUMMARY, 1956-1966, that this project has never used: camper weeks by section (Pioneer, Woodsmen, Coureurs de Bois, Pathfinders, Rangers) year by year; campers by single year of age from 7 to 17; length of stay by bracket; NUMBER OF CAMPERS BY RELIGION with columns for Protestant, Roman Catholic, Jewish, Buddhist, Hindu and not reported (1956: 1,134 Protestant, 170 Roman Catholic, 320 Jewish; 1958: 1,203 / 184 / 236; 1960: 1,079 / 258 / 248; 1961: 963 / 266 / 280 -- a Protestant share falling steadily while Roman Catholic and Jewish shares rise); counsellor ages by single year; numbers of programme and non-programme staff, junior counsellors and counsellors-in-training; and the percentage of counsellors who were college men. It also carries a GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION OF CAMPERS for 1965 and 1966 by Montreal district and suburb -- Ile Perrot, Senneville, Baie d'Urfe, Beaurepaire, Beaconsfield, Pointe Claire, Valois, Dorval, Lachine, Ville St. Pierre, St. Laurent, Ahuntsic and Cartierville, N.D.G./Montreal West/Hampstead, Cote St. Luc, Westmount, Snowdon, Central, Outremont, North End, Rosemount, T.M.R., Rosemere, Roxboro, Dollard des Ormeaux, Pierrefonds, South Shore, Verdun-LaSalle, Hudson, Sherbrooke, Chomedey, Fabreville, Montreal East, Ville d'Anjou, Arvida -- plus Ontario, New Brunswick, and 'others from small towns in Quebec and U.S.A. (Campership Fund)'. The OCR of the tables is damaged and individual figures need checking against the scan, but the structure and many values are legible.

KANAWANA'S 1966 REPORT NAMES ITS OWN PLANT AS OBSOLETE, in a line set apart on the page: 'All this and much, much more - with a plant designed and constructed to 1940 specifications - for youth designed and educated for the space-plus age.' The same report records that LAURENTIAN LANDSCAPE built the first phase of a new camp playing field that year, and that 'time just ran out before the rifle range could be built this year'. Thirty loads of sand and gravel went into the road and beaches. The camp 'assisted the local municipality and school board to the tune of $3,037.08' -- a payment in lieu or a direct contribution, the report does not say which.

THE 1966 REPORT CALLS THE SEASON 'THE SEVENTY-THIRD YEAR OF CONTINUOUS OPERATION' and, separately, 'the Seventy-third year of Y.M.C.A. camping for boys in Montreal'. Counting back from 1966 that puts year one at 1894, matching the 1964 report's 'seventy-first season... established in 1894'. Both are explicit institutional claims of unbroken operation from 1894, made by the camp about itself, and they should be weighed against this wiki's treatment of the postwar and interwar gaps in its own records: an absence of surviving documents is not the same as an interruption in operation, and the camp did not think it had been interrupted. The report also credits SHAUN ERB and HARLEY SMITH by name for their contribution to the season, thanks the Westmount Branch YMCA for the use of its building as 'the Montreal Terminal for camper transportation', and thanks the Westmount Police Department for co-operation on change-over days. Signed A. Ross Seaman, Director.

THE KANAWANA CIT PROGRAMME WENT CO-ED IN 1969 AND STOPPED BEING WORK-LEARNING IN THE SAME YEAR -- 'two major innovations' by the director's own account. There were TWELVE MALE AND FOUR FEMALE CITs, with a male AND a female CIT director; most were sixteen. The programme 'was freed of its traditional work-learning aspect and was given the freedom to spend its time learning the various skills required to be a camp staff person. This meant that they no longer were involved in such tasks as waiting on tables.' The cohort SET UP THEIR OWN CAMP ON LAKE WILSON and 'built a small model camp from scratch... an Adirondack shelter for sleeping, a shelter for dining, fireplace, etc, and did a tremendous job.' Five problems are recorded frankly, including that 'the abilities, physical strength and interests of males and females are different and this led to conflict between the groups', that the CIT 'sits in a difficult position - neither staff nor camper', and that the traditional shortage of Junior Counsellor places meant the camp would struggle to place all its qualified CITs the following year.

OUTSIDE GROUPS AND CAMPERSHIPS AT KANAWANA IN 1969, from the director's report. Groups using the property that year included 'the Rhodes students from England, a Kairos group, several troops of Scouts and Cubs and a variety of YMCA groups', plus overnight use of the campsites by the Westmount and N.D.G. day camps. On camperships: 'Westmount Rotary and the St. Nicholas Men's Club both sponsored large groups of campers. Altogether Kamp Kanawana provided 125 WEEKS OF CAMPERSHIPS at no cost to the agency or group.' This is the earliest itemised account of third-party use of the Kanawana site in this knowledge base, and it predates by decades the wiki's framing of outside-group use as a green-shift-era development.

KANAWANA HAD A HORSEBACK RIDING PROGRAMME AND STABLES BY 1969, two years earlier than the Concordia finding aid's 'Horseback riding program - 1971'. The 1969 director's report: 'The horseback riding again this year was one of the most popular programs we offered' -- 'again' placing it in 1968 at the latest. The instructor was a woman ('The instructor did all she could to make sure that each camper got an opportunity to spend time around and on the horses'), and 'several of our senior campers took it as their special program to spend as much of their time as possible helping around the stables.' The director recommends it 'deserves a major emphasis in our future planning'. The same report records that A BUS WAS ADDED TO THE CAMP that year, giving 'a high degree of flexibility in planning the out-of-camp trips', with groups travelling up to 130 miles.

KANAWANA'S 1969 DIRECTOR ARGUED THE CAMP WAS WASTING ITS OWN LAND. Geoff Anderson: 'We occupy 1000 acres of valuable land which will be under increasing pressure as the surge of population continues. We use only a very small portion of this land and it is a luxury that we will soon not be able to justify either on social or economic grounds... Basically, Kamp Kanawana is in use only 1/6th of the year. We must make plans to develop a much greater use of our property year round.' He also names the plant problems: 'an old and inadequate dining hall and kitchen, lack of program space and facilities, lack of storage'. The 1966 report had already called the plant '1940 specifications... for youth designed and educated for the space-plus age'. Year-round use of the site, which this wiki treats as a 1990s and green-shift development, was being argued for inside the camp in 1969. The report also records the season's programme vocabulary: individual activities, cabin group activities, WIDE GAMES ('capture the flag, Indians and Settlers') and total camp activities ('Lumbermen and Voyageurs, Viking Funeral').

1970 WAS KANAWANA'S FIRST SEASON HOSTING CHILDREN WITH CYSTIC FIBROSIS. The annual report devotes a section to it: 'This was our first experience with C.F. campers at our Camp... There were seven in total (3 girls and 4 boys) and although only three stayed for the whole month - and cried because they had to go home - the other four were normal campers but two weeks was long enough for them.' Two went on overnight trips, one returning to camp before bedtime for his therapy; another, aged ten, 'swam two miles for his double black cord'. JOHN HARRIES and the camp nurse briefed the staff on what C.F. was and how to work with the campers, and the nurse 'worked extra duty because of her interest in the campers and her concern for our Cystic Fibrosis campers'. The report is critical of the C.F. Association itself -- 'no clearing house... everyone did pretty well what they wanted when they wanted' -- and asks that the arrangement be fully subsidised in future. Two camp doctors served that summer.

THE 1970 REPORT IS THE FULLEST ACCOUNT OF EARLY COEDUCATION AT KANAWANA IN THIS PROJECT, and it calls 1970 'Kamp Kanawana's third year as a coeducational camp' -- putting the first at 1968, consistent with the 1988 report. The director distinguishes the words: 'The key to a successful operation this year was not coed camping but a coeducational experience. Our goal was the education and development of a better understanding and acceptance of the opposite sex.' Roughly 40% of the overall programme was co-ed and most of it fell in the 13-16 age range; the two sections were physically separated but 'seemed to act and react as one section most of the time (ie Pathfinder yell in the dining hall)'. The most striking passage is about canoe trips: 'Here the campers became individuals and worked together to help each other... There were no mother or father roles played (ie boys gathering wood while the girls cooked). Each person shared the responsibility and the dialogue around the fire at night took on extra significance. School, sex, the world, war, ecology, sing songs, etc., were all part of the campfires.' The report also records, without alarm, that 'some campers had feelings of attraction to others and walking her home after an evening program was common.'

BECSIES AND PAGE'S ARE AREAS OF THE KANAWANA PROPERTY, not only the name of another camp. The 1970 report, discussing rentals: 'There should be a special area (ie Becsies or Page's) with its own eating, etc., facilities.' And, on unauthorised visitors: young people aged sixteen to thirty 'appear at camp - at various parts of the camp - looking for a place to swim, crash, or just get away from it! This group frequented Becsies this Summer. At the point of writing a young couple are located at Wilson. Today there are many young people on the move and in most cases with nowhere to go. We should consider opening Becsies for use by these youth.' A YMCA camp in 1970 proposing to open part of its property to transient young people is a piece of social history this project has nothing else on, and it also gives Becsies a location on Kanawana land rather than only a sub-series in an archive.

FOURTEEN GROUPS RENTED OR USED KAMP KANAWANA IN 1970, listed in the annual report: the Downtown YMCA Aquadyne Club; Mary Queen of Peace Cubs; St. Barnabas Cubs and Scouts; Sunnybrook Cubs; Beaconsfield High School; Outreach Services for Downtown (Metro), Verdun-LaSalle and Westmount; the Westmount and N.D.G. day camps; the W. H. RHODES CANADA EDUCATIONAL TRUSTS; the Boys Brigade of Montreal; the Westmount Project; the N.D.G. Community Services Project; the Integrated Media Workshop; and University Settlement. The director wants rentals put on a proper footing -- 'better facilities, a list of conditions for rentals, and a full-time employee on site to relate to the groups', plus 'a true costing of what it costs to have groups use our facilities'. Together with the 1969 list this makes third-party use of the site a documented feature of the camp from the late 1960s, decades before the wiki's green-shift framing of it.
entities: W. H. Rhodes Canada Educational Trusts

facts.claim: KANAWANA'S KITCHEN WAS CATERED OUT FOR THE FIRST TIME IN 1970, to a firm the report calls Industrial Caterers: 'The food services at camp this year were catered for the first time. The food, service and rapport with the kitchen was excellent this year. Our chef not only prepared top quality meals but personally got involved in our program - a Western style cook-out, received a pie in the face.' OTHER 1970 OPERATING FACTS: only 26 of the previous year's 60 staff returned, and just one to the same senior post; registration reached 1,442 camper weeks after a slow start; the new brochure went to over 30,000 homes with 'drench mailings' in eight communities; pre-camp training ran two weeks with sensitivity training threaded through rather than timetabled, supported by five YMCA staff and one person from C.I.P.; the Training Camp ran co-ed all summer with twelve males and four females, a female Junior Counsellor Director and a male CIT Director. The camp's washing machines broke for nearly three weeks, and staff and parents complained of a 'smell' -- 'our facilities (ie septic tanks and kitchen sewage disposal area) are inadequate for the size and type (coed) of camp we operate. Most parts of our facilities are too small (Q.C.A. standards for tent space), unsafe (rocks in the ball field), or unhealthy.' JULIEN TASSE is named again: he 'once again did a fantastic job holding the camp together with chewing gum, etc.'

KANAWANA'S DIRECTOR PROPOSED IN 1971 THAT THE CAMP LEAVE SAINT-SAUVEUR. His report's 'major recommendations' are four: (1) 'Kanawana program should focus specifically on hikes and canoe trips', cutting all other programme staff and equipment and cooking every meal out; (2) 'KANAWANA SHOULD MOVE THIS ASPECT OF ITS OPERATION 50-100 MILES FURTHER NORTH TO A SMALLER BASE CAMP SITE - buildings and program areas are no longer needed. The hiking areas around St. Sauveur are rapidly disappearing and our canoe trips are venturing this far north at the present moment'; (3) raise the minimum camper age to at least ten, leaving younger children to linked day camps; (4) keep 'Kanawana's present property... for experimental programs or rentals', with the budget surplus coming from rentals rather than the camp, and time freed for 'major renovations (i.e. rebuilding, winterizing, etc.)'. He adds that the Becsies property 'is over-run by locals and wandering youth. It should become a hostel in the north, or better, to sell it now and use the proceeds to equip our hikes and trips' -- and repeats the sale recommendation twice more. His premise: 'We began as a tripping camp and since then have continued to add to it. We are now at the extreme where we must concentrate on all the other program areas to the decline of our tripping quality... we have the experience, knowledge and understanding to operate the best tripping camp in Quebec if not in Canada.' Nothing in this wiki records that the camp's own director once proposed relocating it.

KANAWANA'S 1971 REGISTRATION, SPLIT BY SEX -- the earliest such split in this knowledge base. BOYS: 743 camper weeks, 284 campers. GIRLS: 504 camper weeks, 197 campers. Girls were therefore about 41% of campers in the camp's fourth co-educational season, and stayed slightly less long on average (2.56 weeks against 2.62). The same report records that the riding programme was recommended for DISCONTINUATION as 'too expensive... for Kanawana at the present time', despite going 'extremely well' with trail rides, lunch rides and overnight trips for which 'special stalls were built at two locations on camp property'; and that Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye had its FIRST PERIOD CANCELLED that year, freeing its Park trippers to strengthen the camp's own hike and trip department.

THE KANAWANA TRAINING CAMP WAS RESTRUCTURED IN 1971 TO ABOLISH THE CIT / JUNIOR COUNSELLOR DISTINCTION: 'Basically we did away with the Counsellor-in-Training and Junior Counsellor concept and called all those involved Junior Counsellors.' The programme was opened to enquirers who 'seemed like good prospects' for a one-month term, with a two-month term offered to known or outstanding candidates. The first month ran five days of skill sessions, five on a canoe trip or hike, four free, one working in section and one preparing with section staff, then a fortnight working in sections 'with same status as counsellors (except no swimming on hikes unless another counsellor was on hand)'; the second month reversed the emphasis. The director recommends the Training Camp 'pay full fees' and asks whether it should stay part of Kanawana at all or run as a separate leadership training programme for day-camp and resident-camp staff. This is a documented interruption in the CIT line that section-names.md and cit-lit-program.md treat as continuous from its inception.

KANAWANA'S 1971 PROMOTION AND THE FIRST PROPOSAL FOR AN ALUMNI ASSOCIATION. Promotion began the previous December with Christmas cards to all campers. 'Drench mailings' totalling 17,881 brochures and application forms went to named West Island and South Shore communities with counts per area -- Beaconsfield and Beaurepaire 4,547; Candiac 1,059; Brossard 2,810; Lachine West 2,741; Montreal West, N.D.G. 2,537; Hudson, Hudson Heights and R.R. #1 2,050; Como, Ste Anne de Bellevue, Senneville, Ste Marie Road, Baie d'Urfe 2,137 -- with a further 2,292 to YMCA branches, the Business Men's Club, 1969 and 1970 campers, Downtown Boys, Metro Board members and 'Northeastern U.S. Ys', and West Island Branch mailings to Cedar Park Heights, Lakeside Heights, Valois, Central Pointe Claire and Lakeside. A camper and staff reunion at the Westmount Branch on Sunday 16 May drew about 100 campers. TED PARKS, who edited the Montreal Star's 'Travelogue' section, gave Kanawana 'a very good write-up' on 1 May. THE REPORT RECOMMENDS 'the development of a double K double A group (KAMP KANAWANA ALUMNI ASSOCIATION)' for public relations and financial support -- the earliest proposal for an alumni body in this knowledge base, two decades before The Lookout alumni newsletter of 1993-94.

CONDITIONS AT KANAWANA IN 1971, from the director's report. NO DOCTOR IN RESIDENCE that year -- the nurse carried the load, and sick campers, 'sometimes 8 at one time', had to be driven to the doctor in St. Sauveur, with the standing decision of whether to wait for consulting hours there or drive on to St. Jerome or Montreal. 'After many futile attempts to secure permission to install a washing machine at camp we finally placed a second-hand wringer machine for the benefit of the staff. Until that time the staff had to travel to St. Sauveur to do their laundry.' The ball fields were 'still very dangerous with unlevel ground and large boulders protruding at irregular intervals', and staff levelled some of them by hand in their free time during pre-camp. JULIEN TASSE is named for the fourth consecutive report: the stables 'were placed in excellent condition due to the work of Julien Tasse during pre-camp'. Camper projects that summer included building bridges, clearing new and old trails, SOUNDING THE LAKE, survival hikes and candle-making. Pre-camp sent the two senior sections, male and female, separately on the PRESTON-SIMON TRIP. McGill University donated dehydrated food to the tripping programme. Staff reported feeling 'intrusion' from visiting lay resource people and the director warns of 'a growing split between the lay and staff groups'.

DEREK WALSH'S FIRST SEASON ON THE KANAWANA STAFF WAS 1973, THE YEAR BEFORE HIS DIRECTORSHIP, and he had been a camper there long before. Leo J. Robitaille's 1973 report: 'The design and co-ordination of program was excellently handled by DEREK WALSH as was his supervision and operation of the camp in my absence. Derek had been a camper at Kanawana many years ago but was a newcomer on staff. In spite of this, his many years of experience in other camps in many capacities from camper, through C.I.T. to camp director plus his open personality made him well accepted by even the most senior of our staff.' Robitaille also records that Walsh put in 'many weeks of his own time... at the office and at home prior to camp'. This makes Walsh a camper-to-director progression across a gap of many years and several other camps, and dates his arrival on staff one year earlier than the directors index has it.

THE 1973 KANAWANA STAFF, NAMED BY DEPARTMENT in Robitaille's report -- almost none of them previously in this knowledge base. SECTION DIRECTORS: four that year in place of two plus four head counsellors, 'a much better system'; the junior camp's were EVA MENZAK and BOB FYFE. HIKE AND TRIP: PERRY OLSHANSKY in his third year (senior counsellor, then section director, now Hike and Trip director), sent to the CANADIAN CANOE SCHOOL before camp where he took his Instructor's Certificate; Robitaille credits him with having 'pulled Kanawana back up to being one of the top camps in the country in terms of tripping, canoeing and camp craft'. AQUATICS: WENDELL WHITE (senior) and JANE BANNERMAN, both certified nationally in life-saving and swim instruction; White ran two Bronze courses for CITs and staff and a Royal Life Saving Society examiner came in to test them. SAILING: DAVE BENNET relating solely to sailing, with ERIC SMART of the Board of Management preparing the equipment and spending two weeks of his own vacation at camp training staff. ARTS AND CRAFTS: JAN CHARTRAND, with MOEZ SHABUDIN named for his artistry. BUSINESS OFFICE: CATHY BANNERMAN, who also co-ordinated the CITs. INFIRMARY: the hired nurse withdrew before the season, and the post was covered by a fourth-year medical student to 1 July, then KATHY MacLELLAN (the previous year's nursing assistant), then MRS. LESLIE BLISS, R.N., who had been Associate Business Manager the year before. OFFICE: MRS. OLGA HALL, whose 'continued loyalty over the years' had by then spanned 'four different Camp Directors'.

KANAWANA HAD A FOURTEEN-BOAT SAILING FLEET BY 1973: seven 'Snarks', two 'Cadets', four two-man 'Arrows' new that year, and a 'Szabo' donated by Eric Smart of the Board of Management -- 'there were days this summer when almost all were out on the lake'. The masts of the new Arrows kept bending and the dealer replaced them, blaming badly tempered originals. The same season PERRY OLSHANSKY led an EXPLORATORY CANOE TRIP 'down Thirty-one Mile Lake through to Lake Pensichangan via some other small lakes... south of Maniwaki and east of the Gatineau', from which 'have been developed a number of alternative routes for a variety of age and skill groups' with easier drop-offs and pick-ups than the camp's traditional routes. This is a documented expansion of Kanawana's tripping geography that the wiki's canoe-trip coverage does not hold.

THE CIT PROGRAMME WAS RESTRUCTURED AGAIN IN 1973, its third design in five years: 'Instead of being a separate section, they were integrated and trained on-the-job in all areas of camp.' Robitaille reports it 'quite successful in its first year' and contrasts it bluntly with the previous summer, when CITs 'were considered parasites who were only evident in the staff lounge and who consumed everything in sight at staff snack (summer of 72)'. His recommendation for 1974 is nonetheless to 'have less C.I.T.s in camp'. Taken with 1969 (co-ed, work-learning dropped) and 1971 (CIT and Junior Counsellor titles merged), this is a programme redesigned three times in five years -- against a wiki treatment of the CIT line as continuous from its inception.

KANAWANA'S CATERER CHANGED HANDS IN 1973 AND THE FOOD GOT WORSE. Robitaille: 'the meals were not nearly as consistently good as in previous years with INDUSTRIAL CATERERS. The firm changed names this year having been bought out by J. A. HUBERT AND SONS and they may have occasioned a change in policies.' The chef's supervisor, MR. TIMMINS, had previously visited weekly and came twice all season; the chef was absent more often; and the kitchen boys were hired by the chef in COWANSVILLE while being carried on the camp's payroll, which Robitaille believes diluted responsibility for supervising them. His recommendations: hire the kitchen boys from the Montreal office at the same time as the rest of the staff so they share the orientation, and 'spell out more clearly the chef's responsibility in the contract with whichever catering firm is dealt with'. Also from 1973: PRE-PRE-CAMP sessions were held in town on organisation, programme, first aid, psychology and naturelore, with BARRY BURROUGHS of St. John Ambulance, DR. GEORGE MAGER, a psychologist specialising in children and youth, and LES BORZORMENY, a biology teacher at Lindsay Place High School; Burroughs and Mager came free of charge. ROSS BANNERMAN gave a talk remembered as 'a high point of training camp'. The one consistently negative response was to a simulation game called 'STAR POWER' run by the YMCA's International Program Department, which staff found 'totally irrelevant... and only served to disrupt the unity which was forming amongst the staff'. JULIEN TASSE and his crew are credited for a fifth consecutive report.

KANAWANA'S 1974 REGISTRATION, BROKEN OUT BY SECTION AND SESSION -- the most granular attendance table this project holds for the 1970s. Camper weeks: JUNIOR GIRLS 44/72/48/64 = 228; JUNIOR BOYS 70/102/98/102 = 372; SENIOR GIRLS 72/94/80/70 = 316; SENIOR BOYS 68/94/92/94 = 348. Session totals 254, 362, 318, 330; grand total 1,264 camper weeks. Girls were 544 of 1,264 camper weeks, about 43%, up from 40% in 1971. A ten-year survey completed that year showed 1974 had the HIGHEST PERCENTAGE OF RETURNING CAMPERS IN A DECADE at 45.2% and the HIGHEST AVERAGE STAY at 2.9 weeks. Staff returnees were 72%. The report calls 1974 'the eighty-first year of Kamp Kanawana', again counting from 1894.

STUART McLEAN WAS A KANAWANA SECTION DIRECTOR IN 1971 AND ON STAFF FOR SEVERAL YEARS BEFORE THAT, per the 1974 director's report: 'The program was expertly handled by Stuart McLean. He was a Section Director in 71 and had been on staff for several years before that.' McLean was Assistant Kamp Director in 1974 and the director hoped he would return in 1975. This pushes the start of McLean's Kanawana staff career earlier than the 1969 date this wiki carries, and documents a section-director year the wiki does not record. The same report names the FOUR 1974 SECTION DIRECTORS -- EVA MENZAK, KERRY FINUCAN, KATHY MACLEAN and BOB FYFE -- and PAT MORROW of the Westmount Y's leader corps as head of the CIT programme, whose cohort took a bronze lifesaving course (all but two passing), a six-day canoe trip with Perry Olshansky, and a four-day theory session in which 'they planned Camp C.I.T. in detail'.

SENIOR CAMPERS BUILT AN OUTDOOR SAUNA ACROSS THE LAKE AT KANAWANA IN 1974, and repainted the Lodge. The director's report: 'We saw a group of senior kampers design and repaint the Lodge as well as the oldest senior boys building a terrific outdoor sauna across the lake. My thanks to the two staff involved JON GRIER and BILL FLASCHNER respectively for their enthusiasm and encouragement of these two projects.' Neither the sauna nor the practice of campers taking on camp improvements as programme appears in this project's site record. The same season ran 'each and every one of the 100 plus trips', including 'our first hike along the Aderandack Trail' -- the Adirondack Trail, apparently new to the camp that year -- under Hike and Trip Director PERRY OLSHANSKY in his second year in the post.

KANAWANA WAS ACCREDITED BY THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION AND INSPECTED ANNUALLY. The 1974 report: 'The Quebec Camping Association's representative, DR. ROBERT WILKINSON, again visited us this summer for their annual visit. Implementing most of the recommendations from last year's Q.C.A. visit, the kamp was in excellent order and should be, in my opinion, reaccredited with the Q.C.A.' Q.C.A. standards are also cited in the 1970 report as the benchmark Kanawana's tent spacing failed. Separately, Kanawana was ONE OF SIX CAMPS whose food service was studied in summer 1974 by three registered public-health nurses for a course at Loyola College, and 'the study indicated that we rated very high as compared to these other camps'. The head chef that year was MRS. MADELEINE WUNDELE; ED NEAL of the Downtown Y handled menus; the business office was run by KATHY MOFFAT; four different registered nurses passed through the infirmary, held together by assistant nurse PAM REYNOLDS.

LES VOYAGEURS DE LA VERENDRYE, 1974: three trips -- 2-16 July with 18 participants, 22 July to 5 August with 8, and 22 July to 12 August with 11 -- directed by PAUL MONGRAW, 'again... after a year's absence'. The programme used new GRUMMAN aluminium canoes, 'excellent from every aspect', with the director asking for two more to bring the park fleet to eight. A separate 'WILDERNESS CAMP' also ran in 1974 with fewer campers than the year before, and the director doubts its viability: 'the income generated and the number of participants does not make it very feasible to continue but some study will be required in order to clarify its merits.' Staff were sent that year to the Q.C.A., the Canadian Canoe School and a VERMONT ECOLOGY COURSE, all judged worthwhile. The director closes by naming the two people from his twenty months with the YMCA he 'shall never forget': OLGA HALL and JULIEN TASSE, 'two of the most dedicated and honest people that I have ever worked with' -- Tasse's sixth consecutive appearance in these reports.

KANAWANA TOOK CHILDREN FROM AN ORPHANAGE AND FROM WEREDALE HOUSE IN 1975, and sponsored about twenty-five more. The director's report: 'This summer, we worked with 475 different children. The kampers came from many parts of Canada, the U.S., Europe and even a country that I've never heard of (Abu Dhabi). KANAWANA ACCEPTED CHILDREN FROM AN ORPHANAGE, WEREDALE HOUSE AND ALSO SPONSORED APPROXIMATELY 25 UNDERPRIVILEGED CHILDREN.' This is a direct operational link between Kanawana and Weredale House -- the Montreal boys' home whose own camp, Camp Weredale, this project treats as a separate institution connected to Kanawana only through the 1977-1982 two-site proposal and lease. Registration reached 1,356 camper weeks against a budget of 1,225, up from 1,264 in 1974 and 1,276 in 1973, with the camper returnee rate rising again to 46.8%. Programme staff average age rose to 21.25 from 19; the staff returnee rate was deliberately cut from 72% to 52%, with most new staff hired into senior posts.

KANAWANA'S 1975 INTEREST GROUPS, several of them new and none recorded here before. JAZZ DANCING, 'a new Interest group and was well received thanks to its Instructor, SONIA BARNES'. ORIENTEERING, attempted since 1973 and grown 'very rapidly' under GABY DUGUAY using maps from the MONTREAL ORIENTEERING ASSOCIATION -- 'over 150 different kampers participated and received certificates of participation'. DRAMA, created that year on demand, with about 30 campers preparing and presenting THREE ONE-ACT PLAYS. FOLK GUITAR, popular with a small number. Arts and Crafts under JAN CHARTRAND for a third year. NATURE LORE, of which the director writes: 'Once again, we failed miserably. I am convinced that a very experienced and skilled person is required.' Junior Waterfront ran for a second year under KATIE SHEAHAN. The CIT programme was directed by LYNNE ROBINSON, covering group work, THE HISTORY OF KANAWANA AND THE YMCA, on-the-job experience, a canoe trip and skills. Pre-camp training included a two-day session at the MONT ST. HILAIRE NATURE CONSERVATION CENTRE which 'clearly made an impression on our staff and generated a real concern and awareness for our natural environment'.

KANAWANA WON EXCLUSIVE CANOE-TRIP ACCESS TO PARC JOLIETTE IN 1975. Hike and Trip Director DICK MISCHOOK, recruited that year and bringing route knowledge from POWTER'S CAMP, used Kanawana's own past trip logs with his own to cut the trucking distance needed to reach wilderness, and 'obtained exclusive permission for Kanawana to send canoe trips to Parc Joliette'. The camp's 1975 section directors were JUDY HARPER, SHEILA HAUGHTON, DENIS BASQUILL and JOHN PROCTOR; STUART McLEAN served his second year as Assistant Kamp Director. The Senior Waterfront Director was asked to leave during the fourth session after repeated attempts by the director and McLean to improve his working relationships failed -- recorded here as an institutional fact about the season without the individual's name.

THE GREEN TRIANGLE WAS RUNNING AS KANAWANA'S BI-MONTHLY NEWSPAPER IN 1975, with FOUR ISSUES that year -- a period this project's Green Triangle corpus does not cover, holding issues from 1932-1940 plus 1976 and 1982. The 1975 promotion programme also included: a new brochure covering Kanawana, Les Voyageurs and the CIT programme, 7,000 printed and 3,200 distributed; Kanawana decals with every registered camper's information booklet; Kanawana postcards inserted in one Green Triangle issue; the cartoon camp map 'resurrected'; Christmas cards to former campers of the last three years; A KAMP KANAWANA REUNION IN MARCH ATTENDED BY OVER 200 KANAWANIANS; brochures distributed at Eaton's through the YMCA public relations department; advertisements in the Gazette, the Star and local papers; and a CBC radio interview with the Kanawana director given on behalf of the Quebec Camping Association.

'MEETING THE CHIEF' WAS A CHANGE-OVER RITUAL AT KANAWANA, named in the 1975 director's recommendations: 'Meeting the Chief is very boring for stay-over kampers (and staff). This could be done at the FARMHOUSE next year during our regular change-over procedure.'
