The same list proposes a TWO-YEAR CIT OR LEADER-IN-TRAINING PROGRAMME 'along the lines of the Hamilton Y's Camp Wanakita', because of 'the difficulty we and other camps have in relevant programming with 15 year olds' -- the earliest documented proposal for the two-tier CIT/LIT structure this wiki treats as long-standing. OTHER 1975 SITE FACTS: the Junior Waterfront, the wash areas and the 'carwash' system were replaced, the walk-in fridge rebuilt, and the lodge and staff lounge refinished and painted; the girls' section septic field was flagged as urgent. Exceptionally warm weather dropped the lake about a foot and raised its temperature some five degrees Fahrenheit, driving up the bacteria count and causing 'many colds, sore throats and ear aches'; the nurse was MRS. DIANE GRAY. The head chef was again MRS. MADELINE WUNDELE under ED NEAL of the Downtown Branch. JULIEN TASSE and OLGA HALL are thanked once more -- Tasse's seventh consecutive report.

THE 1976 DIRECTOR'S REPORT CARRIES A COMPLETE KAMP KANAWANA STAFF LIST WITH ROLES -- about eighty-two people, the only full documented staff roster in this knowledge base for any year before the plaque era. The second half of the list survives the OCR with its role column intact and aligned, thirty-seven names to thirty-seven roles: Norman Lipplatt = Kitchen; Kathryn Livingstone = Senior Waterfront Director; Linda Long = Kitchen; Arlen Macfarlane = Truck Driver; Kathryn Maclean = Nurse; Gord MacPherson = Chef; Peter Meadows = Senior Boys Counsellor; Adele McKay = Junior Girls Counsellor; Dick Mischook = Hike & Trip Director; Russell Morley = Kitchen; Gary O'Brien = Truck Driver; David O'Donnell = Sailing Director; Wendy O'Donnel l = Business Office Assistant; Dave Ouellet = Senior Boys Counsellor; David Paltiel = Rover/Counsellor; Catharine Pelletier = Senior Girls Counsellor; Peter Porteous = Rover/Counsellor; Wendy Prince = Arts & Crafts Assistant; Stephen Reizes = Tripping Counsellor; Jeff Roberts = Les Voyageurs Director; Eric Sandmark = Kitchen; Peter Sandmark = Kitchen; Stewart Sandmark = Arts & Crafts Director; Nancy Sawyer = Tripper; Cheryl Scaife = Kitchen; Glenn Shevchenko = Tripper; Robin Siegerman = Senior Girls Counsellor; Abby Simons = Assistant Nurse; Kel th Stuart = Waterfront Auxiliary; Jullen Tassé = Maintenance Supervisor; Yves Tasse = Maintenance; Lisa Taylor = Rover/Counsellor; Diana Townson = Junior Girls Counsellor; Claire Turcot = Senior Girls Counsellor; Barry Vaux = Senior Boys Counsellor; Robert Wiltshire = Senior Boys Section Director; Robert Woodhouse = Les Voyageurs Tripper. The first half of the list preserves the names but its role column is broken across lines by the scan and cannot be aligned safely; those names are: Brian Arbuthnot, Jane Bannerman, John Bannerman, Dents Basqui!|, Steve Bauman, Daniel Beaudette, Seymour Blum, Claude Boucher, Helen Caravolas, Philip Ching, Leonard Chodat, Robert Darker, Stephen Davies, Susan Dean, Karin Deterding, Robert Dewar, Glen Dorey, Jeffrey Dubney, Andy Ellfot, Jenny England, David Erdely, Sandy Farr, Christine Faulkner, Marc Favreau, Kevin Forster, Nancy Fulford, Francine Gagne, Olga Hall, Reed Harris, David Hart, Cathy Hay, Kevin Holgate, Itche Kerr, Jory Kraus, Jacques Labelle, Burke Lawrence, Nancy Lester, Juntor, Juntfor, Juntor, Juntor, Juntor, Juntor, Senlor, Senlor. TWO ENTRIES SETTLE A LONG-RUNNING QUESTION: 'Jullen Tassé -- Maintenance Supervisor' and 'Yves Tasse -- Maintenance'. This is Julien Tasse's JOB TITLE in the camp's own words, and it puts YVES TASSE ON THE PAYROLL IN 1976, ten years before the 1986 Advance Guard board on which this project first found him.

KANAWANA'S 1976 TRIPPING SEASON RANGED FROM THE CAMP PROPERTY TO OTTAWA. The director's report: 'After over 14,000 miles on the Kamp van in 7 weeks, over 85 trips were sent out. These included the local trips on Kamp property to extensive canoe trips in such areas as PAPINEAU-LABELLE PARK, MANEWAN INDIAN RESERVATION, KEMPT LAKE, 31 MILE LAKE, back packing trips to MONT MARCY in Vermont and WAR CANOE TRIPS FROM MONT LAURIER TO OTTAWA and then OTTAWA TO MONTREAL.' The programme was strengthened by canoes and other equipment transferred from the WILDERNESS SURVIVAL CAMP, whose viability the 1974 report had already doubted. DICK MISCHOOK directed Hike and Trip for a second year.

KANAWANA'S SWIM TEAM WON THE 1976 CAMP PEMBINA SWIM MEET against four other camps, coached by assistant director ANDY ELLIOT. The same report notes the season's one disappointment in that department: 'not one of our C.I.T.s completed the Bronze Lifesaving course' -- against 28 of 51 programme staff holding a Royal Life Saving Society bronze medallion or better. NEW INTEREST GROUPS IN 1976: JUDO, led by JEFF DUBNEY, the Westmount Y judo instructor, well received by a small number and needing sixteen mats rather than six to continue; and FOLK DANCING under CLAUDE BOUCHER and FRANCINE GAGNE, in which 'many kampers, particularly the girls, enjoyed learning many old French Canadian dances'. Orienteering continued under ROB DARKER with awards through the summer; drama under STEVE DAVIES and ROBIN SIEGERMAN; archery under KEVIN HOLGATE; naturelore 'improved greatly' under ADELE \'MISTY\' McKAY after years the reports call failures; arts and crafts under STEWART SANDMARK with WENDY PRINCE, covering paddle-making, bird and game carving, furniture, sketching, string art and macrame. Sailing under DAVE O'DONNELL added three more Snarks; canoeing under ROB DEWAR. Staff were sent to the Woodsmanship School and Canoe Tripper's School in Toronto and the Vermont Ecology School.

THE KANAWANA DIRECTOR QUESTIONED THE LUMBERMEN-VOYAGEUR GAMES IN 1976: 'I and some other staff have doubts about the validity of the Lumbermen-Voyageur program. It is a very different style (i.e. ultra competition) of program as compared to the regular Kamp Kanawana programs. It also interfers with the best of the tripping season. Its continuing should be thoroughly discussed and decided this winter.' The same set of reflections asks for 'a group of staff' to make recommendations on how much co-educational programming the camp should run, records that staff struggled with eight-week campers and floats limiting stays to four weeks, and notes that after 'many years of experience with running Kanawana... we have not yet managed to develop a proper file of program resources and ideas.' Registration that year was 1,358 camper weeks against a budget of 1,250, with 480 different children from six provinces and seven countries and more than thirty underprivileged children sponsored by the YMCA; the camper returnee rate slipped to 44.8%, while programme staff averaged 21.6 years with a 63% returnee rate.

KANAWANA BEGAN AN $850,000 TWO-SITE RECONSTRUCTION OF ITSELF IN 1977-78, and this project has no record of it. The 1977 director's report opens: 'This year is a turning point for dear old Kanawana. THE BULLDOZERS HAVE STARTED WORK FOR THE NEW YEAR ROUND SITE. As this is the last year of K.K. as we've known it...' The plan, refined that year by the Branch Building Committee: '1978 will initiate a TWO SITE OPERATION. The present site will have 98 senior kampers while the NEW YEAR ROUND SITE, AT THE WEST END OF LAKE KANAWANA BEYOND FAREWELL ROCK, will house 98 juniors.' Work under way in 1977: 'renovation of block house and farm house; enclosing and renovating the dining hall; relocating tent platforms in the new and old sites; erecting a new shower building in the senior section', with further buildings 'relocated or demolished' over the winter. 'By June 1978 the new site will be in operation with FOUR DOUBLE SELF-CONTAINED LIVING UNITS, SIX TENT PLATFORMS AND A LARGE MULTI-PURPOSE DINING-RECREATION HALL. The project will cost approximately $850,000. We have hired three additional fulltime maintenance people to assist in carrying out of the above work.' A group of staff visited three YMCA year-round camps in the United States that summer 'from an architectual, engineering and program standpoint'. NOTE: this is a DIFFERENT two-site plan from the 1977-1980 Kanawana-Weredale proposal this wiki documents; the two run in the same years and should not be conflated.

THE FARMHOUSE AND BLOCKHOUSE WERE RENOVATED AS PART OF THE 1977-78 YEAR-ROUND PROJECT. the-kanawana-site.md describes them only as they are today -- 'winterized facilities with fully equipped kitchens, living space, bathrooms, showers, and electricity' in Front Camp -- with no date or origin. The 1977 director's report lists 'renovation of block house and farm house' as work in progress that autumn, alongside enclosing the dining hall, and states that the winterised year-round site would be operating by June 1978. The camp's winterised buildings therefore date, at least in their current form, from a deliberate 1977-78 conversion to year-round operation, which is also the earliest concrete step toward the year-round use that the 1969 director had argued for and that this wiki otherwise treats as a 1990s and green-shift development.

THE KANAWANA CAMP DIRECTOR WAS PRESIDENT OF THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION IN 1977. The director's report, thanking camp secretary Olga Hall: 'The extra work related to the building and renovations of K.K. as well as THE CAMP DIRECTOR BEING PRESIDENT OF THE Q.C.A. substantially increased her work load.' The Kanawana director in 1977 was Derek Walsh, per this wiki's directors index (1974 to February 1979). The camp's relationship with the Q.C.A. is documented elsewhere in these reports as annual accreditation inspections; that its own director held the association's presidency is new here, and makes Kanawana a leading rather than merely a member camp in the provincial body.

KANAWANA'S 1977 SEASON: 1,174 camper weeks, a significant decrease the director attributes to a general fall in summer-camp registration that year, but with 414 different children and THE HIGHEST CAMPER RETURNEE RATE IN AT LEAST TEN YEARS at 54.8%, against the previous high of 46.8% in 1975. Programme staff averaged 20.7 years with 66% former Kanawanians; two staff were dismissed during the summer for behavioural reasons. KERRY FINUCAN, a 1974 section director, was Assistant Kamp Director and introduced 'a more flexible and relevant system of interest groups'. Three operational changes are recorded as successes to repeat: buses rented from the Laurentians rather than Montreal, which was cheaper and gave the camp a three-hour break between groups; REVISED POLICIES ON CIGARETTES IN CAMP for both staff and campers, set out in the staff manual and 'well accepted by parents and Kanawanians alike'; and the introduction of HEALTH FOOD AND FRUIT JUICES in the Business Office tuck shop. A Hebertism course was constructed that year. The report also prints a full 1977 staff list of roughly seventy names.

THE 1978 KANAWANA DIRECTOR'S REPORT OPENS WITH A GREETING FROM THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA. Printed above the director's own text, in English and French over the signature 'Pierre Elliott Trudeau, Prime Minister - Premier Ministre': 'I am happy to send my greetings to all Kampers and staff of Kamp Kanawana. Kamp Kanawana provides an opportunity for many young people across Canada to learn about each other's culture in a natural and healthy environment. La dimension internationale qui s'est ajoutee cette annee rehaussera surement l'esprit d'entraide et de cooperation afin de cultiver une jeunesse saine et vigoureuse.' The French half refers to an international dimension 'added this year'. Nothing in this project records a Prime Ministerial greeting to Kanawana, or what the 1978 international dimension was.

WHO CAME TO KANAWANA IN 1978, in the camp's own demographic breakdown -- the most detailed social profile of a Kanawana camper body in this knowledge base. 442 different children made up 1,227 camper weeks, up 9% on 1977 and slightly over the 1,200 budgeted, in what the report calls 'the 85th season'. 'FRENCH POPULATION WAS 27%'. 'Slightly over 33% OF THE KAMPERS WERE FROM SINGLE PARENT HOMES'. 'Almost 5% of our kamper population was from the Laurentian area (St. Jovite, Ste Adele, St. Sauveur, St. Jerome, etc.)' -- local children at a camp founded for Montreal boys. 60% of 1977's campers returned. Campers came from Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Chateauguay, Quebec City, Three Rivers, Hudson, POLAND, New York, Charlottetown, New Jersey, Virginia, North Carolina, Saskatoon, Otterburn, the West Island, the Laurentians, St. Hubert, St. Lazare, Ste Foy, Franklin Centre, TRINIDAD, Valleyfield and Indiana. On discipline: 'seven kampers were sent home during the summer. Four of these were because of drugs, two for cigarette and one due to an injury.'

KANAWANA RAN A CIT EXCHANGE WITH CAMP CONISTON, NEW HAMPSHIRE, IN 1978 -- 'a C.I.T. exchange with the New Hampshire YMCA's Camp Coniston' listed among that programme's highlights, alongside a one-day session with three Mont St. Hilaire naturalists and life-saving courses in which three CITs took Bronze Medallions, seven Life Saving II and two Life Saving I. This is the first inter-camp exchange documented in this project. THE 1978 GROUP-USAGE LIST for the Kanawana site names, under YMCA BRANCHES: International (5 groups), St. Laurent (4), West Island (5) and Operations Management; under SCHOOLS: St. Eustache Elementary, St. Paul's, Victoria, St. Patrick's, LaSalle College, Macdonald High, College de l'Assomption and Vanier College; and under OTHER: Cadets, Mary Queen of Peace Cubs and Scouts, and Resurrection Cubs and Scouts. School use of the site, which this wiki treats as a modern outdoor-education development, was running at eight schools a season by 1978.

THE 1979 DIRECTOR'S REPORT PRINTS THE SAME ROSTER AS THE 'STAFF OF 79' PLAQUE, AND CORRECTS TWENTY-FIVE OF ITS PAINTED NAMES. Setting the typed staff list beside the p_291 transcription of staff-1979.jpg resolves readings the audit could only take phonetically: Allan Iundall is ALLAN GANDALL; Ann Jourdeau is ANN GOURDEAU; Aylene Tickeawin is AYLENE McKEOWN; Bob Bierman is BOB BLUMAN; Carola Hayrey is CAROLA HANEY; Cheryl Scoff is CHERYL SCAIFE; Johanna Gallir is JOHANNA GALLER; John Pisrosaro is JOHN PIEROSARA; Josie Denis is JOSEE DENIS; Jurnette Penwarn is JEANNETTE PENWARN; Karin Reichel is KAREN REICHEL; Kevin Fowler is KEVIN FORSTER; Kevin McIlrath is KEVIN McGRATH; Larry Lacy is LARRY LACEY; Paul Schneiderist is PAUL SCHNEIDEREIT; Pippa Hobbs is PIPPA HOBBES; Renu Cosgrove is RENEE COSGROVE; Robyn Chalmers is ROBYN CHALONER; Steve Weeks is STEPHEN WELLS; Therese Maxim is THERESE MARIN; Yizhi Cagalino is ISABELLA CASALINO; Jeff Lorette is JEFF SURETTE; plus Dave Bennett / David Bennet, Carole Bell / Carol Bell and Jim Pelton / James Pelton. Fifteen names matched outright across the two documents, confirming they describe the same body of people. THIS IS THE FIRST TIME IN THIS PROJECT THAT A PAINTED BOARD HAS BEEN CHECKED AGAINST AN INDEPENDENT WRITTEN ROSTER OF THE SAME YEAR, and it puts a floor under the plaque audit's accuracy: the board's names were readable and the audit read them, but roughly a third came out phonetically wrong, and only a document could say so.

JULIEN TASSE'S JOB TITLE IN 1979 WAS SITE MANAGER, per the staff list in that year's director's report: 'Julian Tasse -- Site Manager'. In 1976 the same list called him Maintenance Supervisor. The 'Staff of 79' plaque records the family collectively as 'The Tasses' with no first name, which is why this project had a plural credit and no post; the typed roster resolves it. Note also the spelling: the camp's own 1979 typist wrote 'Julian', the 1976 typist 'Jullen', the plaques 'Julien'.

KANAWANA'S 1979 SEASON AND THE CHILDREN IT TOOK IN. '441 different kampers and 18 C.I.T.s', 1,375 camper weeks including 132 for the CITs, a returnee rate of 48.80% -- down 7.31 points on 1978. 'KANAWANA ACCEPTED CHILDREN FROM YOUTH HORIZONS, CHILDREN'S MOUNTAIN COTTAGE AND SOME SPONSORED BY THE ROTARY CLUB OF WESTMOUNT' -- continuing the pattern of 1975 (an orphanage and Weredale House) and 1969 (Westmount Rotary and the St. Nicholas Men's Club). The season survived 'two severe rainstorms, a problem with our septic system, problems with our van and trailer and A 10% RETURNEE STAFF' -- staff hiring was still going on six days into pre-camp. KEVIN FORSTER was Assistant Kamp Director. The staff list includes CHRIS ADAM, DENYS LAWRENCE -- knighted into the Order of the Knights of Kanawana the following year -- and DOUG PEETS, the first recipient of the Order of Owens in 1976, now on staff.

THE COUNCIL RING WAS RAZED AND REBUILT IN 1987, answering an open question council-ring.md has carried unanswered ('Does the Council Ring still exist in its 1929 form, or has it been rebuilt since?'). Jay Netherwood's 1987 director's report, under Special Projects: 'A senior boys tent lead by TOBY DESJARDINS spent a week during the fourth session razing and rebuilding a rotting council ring. The new council ring is better designed, larger and more aesthetic.' Toby Desjardins is on the 1984 CIT plaque, so this is a documented camper-to-senior-camper progression as well. The ring standing today is therefore a 1987 structure on the 1922 site, not the 1929 fabric.

CAMPERS REBUILT THE SUEZ BRIDGE IN 1987, answering the open question in named-places-and-camp-vocabulary.md about whether the Suez Bridge was camper-built. The 1987 report: 'The entire senior boys section spent the second and third session rotating their time in RAZING AND RE-BUILDING THE BRIDGE ACROSS THE SUEZ CANAL. Thousands of man hours were used in re-constructing the bridge.' The Knights of Kanawana charter's fifth challenge asks a candidate to contribute 'something of permanence to camp - a substantial part of a totem pole, or a bridge'; here an entire section does it as a work project. The bridge photographed on the 1987 Senior Boys plaque -- 'The Suez Bridge - Senior Boys 87' -- is therefore the board of the section that built it, not merely a section that liked the spot.

KANAWANA'S ENVIRONMENTAL PROGRAMME BEGAN IN 1987, TWO DECADES BEFORE THE GREEN SHIFT. 'For the first time Kanawana hired a nature specialist, CHRIS ADAM, to introduce and develop an environmental program. The results were spectacular... it is socially imperative that we assist in the promotion of environmental literacy.' The nature room held 'at any given time, 75 different species of wildlife found at Kamp Kanawana from ants to meadow voles, from Jaws (our glutinous bullfrog) to Lee (our pet catfish)', and on visitors' days campers took their parents there first 'and they would teach their parents about our fragile world'. The same season the Junior Boys cordoned off a wood thrush nest and replanted an eroded area with a hundred seedlings under rock and leaf litter; the CITs relocated spruce and fir to a depleted part of the Junior Boys section and built a set of stairs and a retaining wall to stop topsoil loss; and Adam closed unnecessary paths that were 'acting as gullies during rainstorms'. CHRIS ADAM IS THE SAME PERSON who appears on the 1979 staff list and who received the Pip Alumni Award in 2017 as Director of the Sustainability Office at Dawson College -- a documented Kanawana career from 1979 counsellor to 1987 first naturalist to a life in environmental education.

KANAWANA KEPT FARM ANIMALS IN 1987 AND JUDGED THE EXPERIMENT A FAILURE. 'Horses, sheep, goats, rabbits and chickens shared their summer with our campers for the first time at Kamp Kanawana.' The purpose was pedagogical: to build responsibility in junior campers by having them care for the animals, and to reduce homesickness, since 'animals are often easier to communicate to than are humans'. It failed for want of a staff member to run it -- 'while the kids visited the animals, the C.I.T.s took care of them' -- and the director recommends scrapping it and instead 'raising grouse for the summer... and release them on the last day of camp'. He credits the nature programme rather than the farm with easing homesickness.

KANAWOODSTOCK WAS RUNNING IN 1987, six years before the earliest surviving object. plaque-culture.md holds three Kanawoodstock objects -- a wooden guitar dated 1993 or 1995, a guitar pick from 2000 and a drum head from 2009 -- and asks whether it was annual or occasional. The 1987 director's report lists it among the season's successes: 'The following are special events or themes that went exceptionally well: GLISSADE D'EAU, KANAWOODSTOCK, SECRET FRIENDS, GREEN TRIANGLE, THE LEGEND OF THE TIPI, KABARETS and THE CHICAGO COFFEE HOUSE.' The same passage records the camp's routine mini-programmes, almost none of which this project holds: 'Pony Express, Monk Meals, Letter Meals, Sneakouts, Twin Meals, Color Meals, Backward Meals, Tacky Meals, Mud Fights, Soap Fights, Record Breaking Day, Killer, Coffee Houses, Kanapyramid and countless other theme and mini-programs... carried out almost daily.' The all-camp days that year were Lumbermen and Voyageur, GREASE DAY, OLYMPIC DAY and 'Sir Kay, or Arthur's Lost Knight' -- of which the director writes 'slightly less than mediocre. Oh well, three out of four aren't bad.' NOTE: 'The Legend of the Tipi' is a named camp legend this project has never recorded.

KANAWANA RECRUITED BRITISH AND IRISH COUNSELLORS THROUGH BUNAC FROM 1987. 'The services of British Universities North American Club (BUNAC) were used for the first time last summer. This non-profit organization interviews 45,000 British university students, then selects 4,000 of the best for North American camps. This year four counsellors - 2 from England, 1 from Wales and 1 from Ireland - were hired. They were fabulous... While it involves hours of paperwork at Immigration and costs more than it does to hire a Canadian, I strongly recommend that this be done again.' This is a formal international recruitment channel, and it materially strengthens the thin evidence base that named-places-and-camp-vocabulary.md records for international staffing -- alongside the 1964 report's six-country section and the Pathfinder paddle it dates.

ACID RAIN WAS KILLING KANAWANA'S MAPLES BY 1987. The director's report, under Repair and Replacement: 'Many of our large maples are dead or dying and the Tasses must cut more down each year. At this rate, in 5-7 years there will be no large trees left and much of the woodsy feeling experienced at Kamp Kanawana will become one replaced by a feeling of camping in a field. While new trees are being planted, this must escalate. Trees which are resistant to acid rain should be identified and planted before next summer. This is essential to any long range thoughts of maintaining a residential camp.' OTHER 1987 SITE AND OPERATIONS FACTS: the Cave, the Hike and Trip equipment room, was stripped, scrubbed, painted and repaired in pre-camp, with new steps built by the packer PETER LOPATA. A new tent platform went up in the girls' section to end the 'nomadic lives' of the female junior counsellors; a road was extended from the Junior parking lot to the canoe dock slip; a removable hanging wall was built behind the workshop. Canvas tents were to be fire-proofed at $40 each across 25 tents. After five years with CLAUDE AND RICHARD CATERERS the food contract moved to the cafeteria service of the Centre-ville Y. 'As per usual JULIEN AND YVES held the camp together' -- both Tasses still on site in 1987, twenty-four years after Julien's first documented board.

THE 1987 REPORT'S SPECIAL THANKS LIST GATHERS FOUR DECADES OF KANAWANA IN ONE PLACE, and several of the names answer questions open elsewhere in this project. It thanks, for donated time or services: CHRIS ADAM; Avenue Video St-Sauveur; Canadian Crossroads International; Paul Capelli; Cap Espace; Roger Cloutier of Metropolitan Tire; KEITH FARQUHARSON -- who chaired the constituency survey on camping for girls recorded in the 1965 report; Ian Greg; Andre Herard; LINDSAY KERTLAND -- Lady Lindsay Kertland of the 1980 Knights roll; Claude Nault of Caterpillar; DAVE PALTIEL -- one of the two candidate identities behind 'Sir Dave Paltiel' on the Knights roll and 'David Paltiel' on the 1975 board and 1976 staff list; ROSS SEAMAN -- camp director 1959-1968; Vivian Turley; DEREK WALSH -- camp director 1974 to February 1979; and the West Island Association for the Handicapped. The director separately thanks CLAUDETTE GRENIER alongside Julien and Yves Tasse. Former directors, former knights and a 1965 committee chair were all still giving time to the camp in 1987.

COUNSELLORS IN TRAINING EXISTED AT KANAWANA BY 1941, NOT THE 1960s. cit-lit-program.md states flatly that 'the Counsellor-in-Training program was introduced at Kanawana in the 1960s' and asks who introduced it. The CFCF radio broadcast of 26 June 1941 has the camp's Chief, HOWIE LANGILLE, describing it as an established category: 'Our youngest group to receive leadership training are known as COUNSELLORS IN TRAINING, and are selected from our most experienced campers. Of course it is the hope and ambition of each of these to become a counsellor after several years of experience and training.' The same passage sets out the whole ladder: 58 counsellors took the training course that year, of whom the Personnel Committee -- chaired by MR. J. W. PERKS, Assistant Superintendent of the Protestant School Board -- selected 45, with a further number taken as Assistant Counsellors, and CITs drawn from the most experienced campers below them. The programme this wiki dates to the 1960s was running at least twenty years earlier.

KANAWANA HOSTED THIRTY OR MORE WARTIME EVACUEE CHILDREN IN 1941. The Chief, on air: 'It is Kamp Kanawana's privilege this year to have THIRTY OR MORE EVACUEES IN CAMP; BOYS FROM ENGLAND, SCOTLAND AND EUROPEAN COUNTRIES. Kanawana has frequently been referred to as an international boy's camp. The contribution to camp life made by other than Canadian boys at Kanawana has indeed been important throughout the history of the camp.' Nothing in this project records the camp's part in the wartime evacuation of British and European children to Canada. The claim that Kanawana was 'frequently referred to as an international boy's camp' also bears directly on named-places-and-camp-vocabulary.md, which records the documentary evidence for international presence as thin.

KANAWANA'S 1941 SEASON, FROM ITS OWN RADIO BROADCAST OF 26 JUNE. 'The 48TH SEASON of Kamp Kanawana... opens Saturday June 28th' and continued to 23 August -- 1941 minus 47 gives 1894 as season one, matching the 1964, 1966, 1974 and 1978 reports. A staff of 68 was hired; an ADVANCE PARTY OF FOURTEEN COUNSELLORS joined carpenters who had been at work for two months; about a hundred campers arrived in the first group; registrations stood 30% above the same date the previous year and were deliberately restricted 'to prevent overcrowding'. FROM THE 1940 SEASON, cited on air: ninety life-saving awards were won, Royal Life Saving Society and YMCA, including RLSS Silver Medallions and YMCA Senior awards; of 103 non-swimmers, 55 passed swimming tests and FOUR COMPLETED THE 'CROSS THE LAKE SWIM'. Every counsellor was required to hold a life-saving certificate or be able to pass the test, and TEN QUALIFIED LEADERS PATROLLED general swims. The broadcast quotes in full a farewell letter written by two junior counsellors of 1940, signed 'Dave & Don': 'Tomorrow we are leaving dear old Kanawana, leaving behind fond faces, but taking back with us memories that will be cherished... the whispering trees and lapping water ever aid the strengthening of spirit, mind and body, the theme of Kanawana life.'

THE 10 JUNE 1939 CFCF BROADCAST WAS THE THIRD OF A SERIES OF THREE, and it put a camper, a leader and a parent on the air. The two earlier Saturday-evening programmes had featured 'MR. MACDIARMID, the director, and DR. MITCHELL, the medical advisor of Kamp Kanawana'. The third brought in JUNIOR TAYLOR, fourteen, 'a camper for the past four years' -- who says 'I went to camp first in 1935', and who is almost certainly the 'Junior Taylor, Juvenile' awarded a best-camper shield in the 1935 season chronicle; BASIL BURGESS, a third-year McGill student, camper from 1930 and leader for three years, returning for his tenth year; and J. F. CARTIER of the Camp Board, father of a camper named Jimmie. Greig Macdiarmid closed the series as 'chief of the camp'. DETAILS GIVEN ON AIR: the camp opened 24 June 1939 and ran ten weeks to 2 September, for boys aged ten to eighteen; information was available at 'any of the FOURTEEN YMCA BRANCHES in the city' -- double the seven listed in the 1921 brochure -- or by telephoning MArquette 8331. Cartier describes 'a BOARD OF MANAGEMENT OF TWENTY-TWO prominent Montreal Business and Professional men' and announces that 'this year... we have added A NURSE to the staff as a further health measure. The nurse will work closely with the Doctor.' Junior Taylor names the chef: 'CHEF McHARDY did a great job last year, and we're all glad he's coming back again.' Burgess describes the pre-war counsellor training course, which covered 'such things as Understanding Boy Nature and How to lead Hikes': 'If a fellow doesn't take in the training course he has small chance of being accepted.' The camp is twice called 'the Boy's Paradise in the Laurentians'.

THE PROJECT RECORDS EVERYTHING AND EMBARGOES BY METADATA (kb/restricted/, settled 2026-09-03). The operator's principle: 'We're better off having the whole record and selecting from it now than deleting material that ought to just be embargoed and potentially creating holes in the record for future scholarly work that may come to rely on this research' -- and publication policy 'at the wiki UI design level, not here'. So nothing is withheld from kb/facts.json or wiki/; both are working surfaces and both are kept complete. Sensitive material is extracted in full, carries a publication block (status embargoed, register id, review date, stated basis), is written into the article where it belongs inside an <!-- embargo:r_NNNN --> block, and is indexed in kb/restricted/register.jsonl. THE REASON OMISSION WAS REJECTED: a hole in the record is invisible and permanent -- a later researcher cannot distinguish 'the source says nothing' from 'someone decided not to write it down', and neither can a later pass of this project, which is how one document gets read three times to the same dead end. scripts/verify/restricted_guard.py checks the LABELLING, not the content: unlabelled is the failure, not present. It has had three bugs, all failing open, all caught by planting a name rather than by reading the code -- title-case-only matching that missed names written in capitals; two protected surnames left in the stopword list during debugging; and asking whether a name appeared inside a block rather than whether every occurrence was inside one. First entries: r_0001, the 1973 report's staff recommendations, five subjects, written into people/leo-robitaille.md; r_0002, an identification-by-inference risk in the 1975 report. Both review 2055.

Embargoed until review: The 1973 Kanawana director's report ends with named staff recommendations. Leo J. Robitaille writes: 'All 73 staff could be re-hired unconditionally with the following exceptions:' and brackets three names against the note 'Do not re-hire' -- Brenda Tooby, Pierre Parizeau and Pierre Audette. No reason is given for any of the three. He then assesses two others individually. Of Al Mongraw: 'does not work well without supervision and does not supervise people well himself. However, he does have good skills at repairing program equipment (canoes, etc.) and could be specifically given this responsibility and supervised. He tends to put his own needs and pleasure ahead of the camp's interests. Considers himself a power figure amongst the staff and is a great rationalizer.' Of Rick Deterding: 'has good skills but poor attitude when asked to do something he doesn't like such as being a counsellor for junior boys.' Context for a later reader: these are one supervisor's end-of-season judgements of people in their late teens and early twenties, written in an internal document for a hiring committee and never meant to be read outside it. Robitaille's report is otherwise warm about the 1973 staff, and he was himself leaving the Association. Two of the five surnames appear elsewhere in the camp's records in neutral or positive terms: a Deterding is on the 1976 staff list, and a Mongraw -- Paul Mongraw -- directed Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye in 1974 after a year's absence, though whether that is the same person as Al Mongraw is not established.

facts.claim: Embargoed until review: The 1975 Kanawana director's report records a mid-season dismissal without giving the person's name. Of the Senior Waterfront Director the report says he 'was most ineffective in his methods of working with most other staff. The instructions went on but in a very uncomfortable atmosphere. After repeated attemps on my and Stuart's part, we were unable to initiate any improvement and consequently, the Senior Waterfront Director was asked to leave during the fourth session of kamp.' THE NAME IS NOT HELD HERE AND HAS NOT BEEN ESTABLISHED: the 1975 report carries no staff list, unlike 1976, 1977 and 1979, so the post holder would have to be identified from another document. This record exists to mark that the identification is possible and should not be made in the wiki: publishing the passage beside a 1975 staff roster would name him by inference even though neither document does. The institutional fact is published at f_2436 without the name.

facts.claim: DEREK WALSH HELD NATIONAL OFFICE IN CANADIAN CAMPING FOR SEVEN YEARS, OVERLAPPING AND OUTLASTING HIS KANAWANA DIRECTORSHIP -- a career this project had no trace of. The Canadian Camping Association's Certificate of Appreciation, presented to him at the Congress Banquet reception on 29 January 1983, summarises it: the award 'reflects the gratitude of the CCA for Derek's contribution as a PAST PRESIDENT OF THE FORMER ENGLISH SECTION - QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION, in addition to his work as CHAIRMAN OF THE CCA PUBLIC RELATIONS AND PROMOTION COMMITTEE and VICE PRESIDENT OF THE NATIONAL ASSOCIATION FROM 1974-1981. Most recently Derek completed a feasibility study on a proposed magazine.' The magazine's own listings corroborate each step: the October 1976 directory gives 'Quebec Camping Association, Inc. (Eng.), Derek Walsh, President, 2233 Belgrave Avenue, Montreal' -- which independently confirms the 1977 Kanawana director's report noting 'the Camp Director being President of the Q.C.A.'; June 1979 records his installation as CCA Vice-President under President Clifford Labbett; the 1980 committee list puts him on Legislation and on Public Relations and Promotion; December 1980 has him agreeing 'to stay on as the representative of Quebec and Ontario until May, 1981'; and May 1981 records that 'Jane McCutcheon succeeds Derek Walsh as Vice-President of the Central Region'.

DEREK WALSH WROTE A CCA PUBLICATION THAT STAYED IN PRINT FOR YEARS, in both official languages: 'How to Promote Your Camp' and 'Comment promouvoir votre camp vacances', CCA/ACC, 4 pages, 1981, priced at $0.75. It appears in the association's publications catalogue in the 1982 insert and again in the autumn 1984 and autumn 1985 issues, three and four years after publication. He also carried out the CCA's feasibility study on publishing a Canadian camping magazine, reported in 1982 as 'investigating the realities of publishing a Canadian Camping Magazine' and noted as completed by January 1983. A camp director whose own 1977 report worried about promotion was, in the same years, the national association's authority on it.

A DEREK WALSH IS LISTED AT CAMP THUNDERBIRD, VICTORIA, B.C. IN MAY 1979 -- three months after Kanawana's Derek Walsh left the camp -- and the identification is probable but NOT established. The May 1979 Canadian Camping, listing Canadians who led sessions at an international event: 'Derek Walsh (Camp Thunderbird, Victoria, B.C. - Derek was also responsible for the Public Relations aspect of the Canadian involvement).' The public-relations role matches the CCA PR chairmanship our Walsh held, and the date matches his February 1979 departure from Kanawana. AGAINST IT: the December 1980 CCA report calls him 'Derek Walsh of Montreal'. Either he went west and returned, or the association's own copy lagged, or these are two men. NOTE ALSO that the Montreal YMCA operated its own Camp Thunderbird -- sub-series P0145/12I in the Concordia fonds -- which is a different camp from the Victoria one and an easy conflation to make. Recorded as an open identification, not a career move.

A. ROSS SEAMAN'S PROVINCIAL AND NATIONAL OFFICES, from the magazine's officer lists. He was SECRETARY OF THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION from about 1949, and the April 1951 issue records the end of it: 'Ross Seaman, secretary of the QCA for the past two years, has been forced to resign from that position due to his recent appointment to the Lachine YMCA' -- which independently dates his move to the Lachine branch. He was in charge of registration for the National-Quebec Conference held that spring at the Sir Arthur Currie Gymnasium, 475 Pine Avenue West. He is QCA Secretary again in the 1962 and 1963 lists, at 4140 Jean Renou, Lachine. He sits on the CCA's national board as 'Mr. A. Ross Seaman, Que.' through 1966-1968. The winter 1968 issue names him a VICE-PRESIDENT of the Quebec Camping Association under president Mrs. Nicholas D. Demetelin, and separately as 'immediate past president' of the English section. In summer 1973 he led a national workshop on FUNDING which delegates found 'left us the most to grapple with in terms of new information'.

ROY D. LOCKE LED THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION WHILE DIRECTING KANAWANA, and published the camp's method nationally. The June 1949 issue calls him 'Roy Locke, Vice-President of the Quebec Section'; April 1952 gives 'Roy D. Locke director of Y.M.C. Kamp Kanawana is president of the Quebec Camping Association', with the association at 1441 Drummond St., Montreal 25; the April 1954 officer list has him as 'Past President -- Mr. Roy Locke, Boys' Work Secretary, Metropolitan YMCA'. He also sat on the CCA national board in February 1951. HIS JUNE 1953 ARTICLE 'A MANUAL OF OPERATIONS' is indexed in the magazine's own cumulative index and sets out the Kanawana manual in four sections -- programme, administration, buildings and equipment, general -- including 'a seven page outline: Things a new staff member needs to know about Kanawana. This is very valuable. It eases the orientation period.' His argument was institutional memory: 'a change in the camp director may lead to inefficiency and needless friction.' This is the direct ancestor of the Camp Plant Manual the 1965 annual report describes being developed, twelve years later.

THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION REPRESENTATIVE WHO ACCREDITED KANAWANA IS IDENTIFIED. The 1974 Kanawana director's report records 'the Quebec Camping Association's representative, Dr. Robert Wilkinson, again visited us this summer for their annual visit.' The magazine's publications catalogue identifies him: 'Robert E. Wilkinson, Ph.D., of MCGILL UNIVERSITY'S PHYSICAL EDUCATION DEPARTMENT and CAMP NOMININGUE, QUEBEC', author of 'Camps: Their Planning and Management', a standard text covering 'management of human and physical resources... health and safety for campers and staff, legal responsibility, administrative guidelines - for Canada and the U.S.A.' The man inspecting Kanawana for accreditation was the author of the field's Canadian textbook and ran a Quebec camp himself.

THE CANADIAN CAMPING RUN'S VALUE FOR THIS PROJECT IS IN THE ISSUES THAT NEVER MENTION KANAWANA. Measured across all 164 cached issues, 1949-1988: the camp family (Kanawana, Otoreke, Weredale, Becsies) is named just 28 times in 15 issues -- and EVERY ONE OF THOSE 15 ISSUES WAS ALREADY WORKED by an earlier pass, which found the Macdiarmid obituary, the Seaman biography, the 1893 Otoreke dating and Locke's Manual of Operations. That pass was thorough on its own terms. What it could not reach was the other 149 issues, where the camp is never named but its directors are: Derek Walsh appears 24 times, A. Ross Seaman 50, Robert Wilkinson 42, Roy Locke 5, Leo Robitaille 10, none of them beside the word Kanawana. A name-based search finds a camp; it does not find the camp's people doing the rest of their working lives. THE SAME LIMITATION APPLIES TO THIS PASS: it extracted 664 passages from a term list, and a term list can only find what someone thought to look for -- the classifier-reads-structure failure of f_2335 and f_2378 in another form.

The first printed issue of Canadian Camping (Vol. 1 No. 1, February 1949) describes itself on its masthead as "the natural evolution of two years of mimeographed bulletins" -- so the Canadian Camping Association had been publishing a bulletin since about 1947. Quarterly, 25 cents a copy, included in CCA membership.

The Canadian Camping Association executive of February 1949 was half Montreal: President Dais L. Gass, 4870 Cote des Neiges Rd, Montreal; Secretary-Treasurer Hay Finlay, 475 Pine Ave West, Montreal; Honorary President A. L. Cochrane (Toronto); Past President Taylor Statten; Editor Mary S. Edgar; Publishing agent Fred Haiblen. Vice-Presidents were the provincial presidents ex officio.

Hedley S. Dimock wrote the lead article of the first issue of Canadian Camping, "The Magic of Camping," and is described there as Dean of George Williams College, Chicago, and as Canadian-born, in Saskatchewan, with thirty years of camping going back to the Saskatchewan prairie. The same issue reviews his Administration of the Modern Camp (Association Press, 1948) and cites his Camping and Character (1929, with Hendry), Marks of Good Camping (1941), and Talks to Counselors, co-written with Taylor Statten.

The cover photograph of the first issue of Canadian Camping is credited to Arthur Friedman, Montreal, Quebec; and the editor's address to readers names "the vast Laurentian playground of Quebec" as one of the magazine's five constituencies.

The 1949 Ontario Camping Association conference (18-19 February 1949, Central YWCA, 21 McGill St, Toronto) had Hedley S. Dimock and Fritz Redl as key speakers; the 1948 conference drew 280 people plus a separate camper assembly of more than 100 children.

The Canadian Camping Association board met at the Royal York Hotel, Toronto, on 20 February 1949. The Montreal delegation is named in the minutes: Miss Dais L. Gass (President, CCA); Miss Sybil Ross (Secretary); Miss Diana Cumner (President, Quebec Camping Association); Miss Dorothy Percival (Director, Camp Ouareau); Mrs. Mutchler (Secretary, Junior Leagues); Mr. C. A. Wiley (Chairman, Finance Committee).

At its board meeting of 20 February 1949 the Canadian Camping Association resolved to take a part-time office secretary and an office at 1421 Atwater Avenue, Montreal, and to hold its Annual Meeting in Montreal in October 1949, concurrent with the Recreation Congress. The national association's office was therefore in Montreal from 1949.

Ottawa camp leaders met at the Chateau Laurier on 12 March 1949 to organize an Ottawa Regional Section of the Ontario Camping Association. The February 1949 OCA conference drew over 400 enrolled -- the previous issue, written beforehand, had reported 280 at the 1948 conference.

C. T. Sharpe, Assistant Director of Camping for the Ontario Department of Education, outlined provincial financial assistance to agency camps meeting health and low-cost requirements at the 1949 OCA conference -- the Ontario precedent for the kind of government support Quebec camps later sought.

The Canadian Camping Association ran a crest design competition in 1949: India-ink designs, minimum four inches, due 15 September 1949 to Arthur Buckley, Chairman of the Crest Committee, YMCA, Geneva Park P.O., Ontario; $15 and an honorary membership to the winner, plus a scroll to the winner's camp.

Taylor Statten, writing to Canadian Camping from Palm Beach in April 1949, is identified as first President of both the Ontario Camping Association and the Canadian Camping Association. His wife's camp name "Tonakela" appears in the same piece.

"Quebec Camps," by Agnes Knox Mutchler, Director of the Junior League Camp, Montreal (Canadian Camping Vol. 1 No. 3, June 1949, pp. 19-20), states: "Certainly a boys' camp sponsored by the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal in 1893 and called Otoreke was among the earliest. Kanawana, at present directed by Roy Locke, Vice-President of the Quebec Section, had a mysterious birth about this time under the same sponsorship."

A Quebec camping officer writing for the national magazine in June 1949 dated Camp Otoreke to 1893 and called Kanawana's own birth "mysterious" and only "about this time" -- so Kanawana's founding date was already unsettled inside the Quebec camping community forty-five years after the fact. This is evidence about the state of the record, not only about the date.
Roy D. Locke was simultaneously Director of Kamp Kanawana and Vice-President of the Quebec Section of the Canadian Camping Association in June 1949.

Forty-five permanent camps were registered with the Quebec Camping Section in 1949; twenty-nine of them non-profit, split between those funded by public contribution and those whose fees cover operating expenses. Two weeks was the shortest camping experience generally offered by 1949.

Camp Lewis, under Mr. Wylie, took five hundred boys for two weeks or longer each year in 1949, per Agnes Knox Mutchler's survey of Quebec camps. (Almost certainly the C. A. Wiley who chaired the CCA finance committee; the spelling varies.)

The Junior League Camp took one hundred girls for three weeks, three times a summer, in 1949. It was started "more than twenty-five years ago" -- so about 1923 or earlier -- by Miss Lighthall of Montreal, on family property near Ste-Marguerite.
Camp Chapleau, "which is Quebec's Bolton," took mothers and children in 1949 under Director Miss Nan Vail.
Camp Oolahwan (YWCA) "was hewn from the woods in 1919" under Mary Edgar, had its own lake and six hundred acres, and was directed in 1949 by Diana Cumner, President of the Quebec Section.
The Quebec Camping Association "had its origin in the thirties" and was an original member of the Canadian Camping Association, per Agnes Knox Mutchler's 1949 survey.
Registered Quebec camps in 1949 clustered in two areas, the Laurentians and the Eastern Townships; the Quebec Section knew almost nothing of camping along the lower St. Lawrence.

The Quebec Camping Section "has backed the appointment of year-round Directors for non-profit camps" as of 1949, for continuity of programme and winter training -- the policy context for Kanawana's own year-round directorship.

The Quebec Camping Section was pressing camps to winterise for skiing in 1949: "In a Province almost as famous as the Alps for luxury skiing, it seems ridiculous that any camps are closed to ordinary people."

Mr. Al Dodds of the Central Y.M.C.A. was Secretary of the Quebec Section of the Canadian Camping Association in 1949 -- a Montreal Central Y man in a Quebec camping office, alongside Roy Locke as Vice-President.

Agnes Knox Mutchler's 1949 survey of Quebec camps opens with an oral-history lament: the pioneers' stories "are simply amazing ... Some day these stories will be written and may they appear, at least in part, in Canadian Camping." They largely were not.

Quebec camping activity in spring 1949 included a four-evening counsellor training course in March with more than one hundred registered, representing all types of camps; a meeting of ten non-profit camps convened by Miss Sybil Ross of the Social Agencies to discuss costs and relations with the social agencies; and a Spring Conference for Counsellors on 13-14 May 1949.

A National Recreation Forum, "Leisure -- a National Issue," was set for on or about 20 October 1949 in Montreal, sponsored by eight national organizations, replacing the Canadian Recreation Congress; the CCA annual meeting was to sit immediately before or after it.

The first National Camp Directors' Seminar and Workshop was held at Camp Wabi-Kon, Timagami, 6-11 September 1949, $37.50 all in, directed by Charles E. Hendry with resource specialists Hedley S. Dimock and Alan F. Klein. Open to directors in all provinces.

At the Canadian Camping Association annual and board meeting, Chateau Laurier, Ottawa, 11-13 November 1949, an interim executive was elected to serve until the February annual meeting: Anne Vail (President, Montreal); Irwin Haladner (1st Vice-President, Toronto); W. E. (Ted) Yard (2nd Vice-President, Toronto, nominated by BC and Saskatchewan); Agnes Mutchler (Secretary, Montreal, 1445 Crescent St.); Ernest (E. O.) Freedman (Treasurer, Montreal, 10 Ontario St. W.). Past Presidents are listed as Taylor Statten (Toronto) and Dais L. Gass (Montreal).

The December 1949 issue of Canadian Camping gives the CCA National Office address on Coursol Street, Montreal, in two conflicting forms in the same issue: the masthead says 2045 Coursol St. and Anne Vail's own message on p. 12 says 2035 Coursol St. Both are recorded; neither is silently corrected.

The Quebec Section held two meetings in autumn 1949 before the season's camps closed. "The program arranged by Roy Lock[e] was different and stimulating" at the October meeting: short talks by young staff on swimming, canoe trips, religion in camp programs, counsellor personality problems, peculiar camper behaviour and nature experiences. Ruby Smith was Social Convener.

For late 1949 the Quebec Section officers were: Diana Cumner President (Y.W.C.A., 1124 Dorchester St. West, Montreal), Roy Locke Vice-President, Al Dodds Secretary, Ruby Smith Social Convener -- with Vail, Mutchler and Freedman of Montreal simultaneously running the national body.

The Ontario Camping Association minimum standards adopted in 1949, printed in full in Canadian Camping: licence from the Provincial Department of Health; pasteurized milk; weekly hot bath in camps over two weeks; doctor available; resident nurse where over two weeks and over thirty children; staff minimum age seventeen; ratios of one cabin counsellor per six campers under ten and per eight aged ten to seventeen; one lifeguard per ten swimmers; a rest period of not less than one hour daily. Standards committee chaired by John Hoyle.

A. L. Cochrane, CCA Honorary President and Director of Camp Temagami, was given a plaque by Ontario's Attorney-General and Minister of Education, the Hon. Dana Porter, for fifty years directing his camp. He was in his eightieth year, and still annually let himself be thrown off the dock sewn in a sack with a ten-pound stone, hands and feet tied, surfacing inside a minute. The motto on the tablet was Ad Unguem Factus Homo.

Alan Mills, the Montreal folksinger and CBC broadcaster, addressed the Quebec Camping Association on camp music in the winter of 1949-50. The Quebec notes list the Section's monthly meetings that winter: "Dr. Allan Ross speaking on Health, Mr. Allan Mills, the radio singer on Camp Music and Dr. Wilson speaking on Camp generally." A named occasion on which Quebec camp directors were addressed on camp music by a professional folk-song collector, in the same city and association as Kanawana's director.

Associated Screen News Limited, 2000 Northcliffe Avenue, Montreal, advertised to camps in February 1950 "de luxe photographic postcards as sold in leading resorts of Canada ... in lots of 1,000 or more," plus lantern slides, transparencies and murals. A Montreal firm selling camp postcards by the thousand in 1950 is the most likely origin for any surviving Kanawana postcard.

The Quebec Camping Association Annual Spring Conference was set for 31 March - 1 April 1950 at the Sir Arthur Currie Gymnasium, McGill University, jointly with the Eastern Ontario Camping Association; key speaker Catherine Hammett. The QCA address was 1124 Dorchester St. W. Separately the McGill Extension Department gave the Quebec Section a ten-week lecture course that winter; the camping names on it were Anne Vail, Norah Bailey and Dorothy Percival.

The Canadian Camping Association was incorporated by early 1950, a new constitution having been accepted by the Secretary of State for Canada, with the objects printed in full including the power to acquire and dispose of real property. Ten Goals for 1950 are listed, among them a Camp Directory of all Canadian camps in two sections, members and non-members, and a goal to explore having the Dominion government build camps for children in national parks, rentable by agencies.

The Ontario Camping Association research committee bulletin "Know Your Camps" (1950) gives: 114 camps and camp groups in the OCA; 41% private, 49% organization, 10% "special"; boys' camps outnumber girls' two to one; almost as many co-educational camps as girls' camps; twenty-eight camps opened since 1945. It also states that "The first camp in Ontario opened in 1893 and is the Y.M.C.A. Camp On-Da-Da-Waks at Golden Lake, Ontario" -- the same year Mutchler gives for Otoreke, so the YMCA was starting camps in two provinces in one year.

Canadian Camping settled the Vail identification itself in April 1950, p. 18: "Miss Anne Vail, President of the Canadian Camping Association, is Executive Secretary of Iverley Community Centre, Montreal, and Director of Chapleau Camp in the Laurentians. Miss Vail is a graduate of the McGill School of Social Work." So "Miss Nan Vail" of Camp Chapleau (June 1949) and Anne I. Vail, CCA President, are one person.

The Canadian Camping Association board met in Toronto on 12 March 1950, Anne Vail presiding. Committee chairs recorded: Dorothy Percival (Membership), Mary S. Edgar (Magazine), Art Buckley (Public Relations), Rev. John Hoyle (Standards), Keith Cleverdon (Sites Development) -- Cleverdon a civil engineer and camp director who undertook a series on sanitation and site development for the magazine. Alan Klein offered a programme advisory service answering letters at the CCA, 2035 Coursol Street, Montreal.

A Red Cross Water Safety Instructor course was scheduled for Montreal in May 1950 specifically "for Canadian Camping Association" -- the mechanism by which Quebec camp waterfront staff got certified in this period.

Empire Crockery Company, 139 Peter St., Montreal -- wholesale crockery, cutlery, kitchenware and manufacturers of food-serving equipment -- is the first Montreal-based camp supplier to advertise in the Canadian Camping run; the Toronto houses dominate everywhere else.

Ernest A. Chapman, "Skipper," died 12 March 1950, having directed Camp Kagawong for forty-three years with more than six thousand campers; he was a past president of the Ontario Camping Association, and the OCA closing banquet stood in silence that night.

John Fisher devoted a CBC broadcast to camping after speaking at the 1950 OCA conference, standing in for Bernard Mason who withdrew; disk recordings of the fifteen-minute talk were available from the CCA in Montreal. Ontario's Department of Education announced that minimum standards would become a condition of licence from 1951.

Charles E. Hendry, School of Social Work, University of Toronto, published "By Emberglow" in Canadian Camping (April 1950, pp. 12-15), describing a sociometric peer rating of named campers conducted in the summer of 1949: "about one hundred and twenty boys in this camp divided into twenty cabins of six campers each ... each camper was asked to rate each other boy in order of preference," from 1 for best liked to 5 for lowest. An acceptability score was computed, five points per first-place ranking, maximum 25 and minimum 5, and the thirty lowest and thirty highest scorers were compared after nearly two months together.

Hendry's 1949 camp sociometric study found that intelligence, good looks, being an old camper, skill in swimming, sailing, handicraft, riding or canoeing, age, and coming from "a better-to-do family" made no noticeable difference to a boy's popularity: "The boy who was an expert canoeist or who was very good looking was found as frequently among the unpopular as among the popular group." What mattered was "by far the most important thing ... the boy's attitudes and behaviour toward the other campers" -- least liked being "campers who showed off, boasted, bluffed and sought the limelight," then uncooperativeness, then lack of consideration, bullying and quarrelsomeness, then "thinking one is picked on, losing one's temper, carrying grudges and making excuses."

Hendry's "By Emberglow" is a dated, described-in-method account of children being ranked against each other by name at a Canadian camp and published in the national magazine -- the same family of document as the staff and camper assessments at issue in p_307 and p_308, and evidence that the practice was well established a decade before Kanawana's own 1960-61 counsellor research. The camp is unnamed and the researcher is only "a friend of mine"; Hendry was at the University of Toronto School of Social Work, where Mary L. Northway was the country's leading sociometrist, so the study is findable.

The Caserta hospital reminiscence in Canadian Camping (June 1950), already in the KB as part of f_2288, was written by John P. Kidd, identified in the byline as "Executive Director, Canadian Citizenship Council, Ottawa." The article is "Campers Are Citizens" (pp. 8-9), and he writes in the first person as the Kanawana leader the wounded soldier recognised -- "the way some of you leaders helped me." So the 1934 Kanawana staff member is the man who by 1950 ran the national citizenship body.

John P. Kidd's "Campers Are Citizens" (June 1950) sets out a programme for camps as "a laboratory for democracy": that the CCA survey citizenship programming and democratic practice in Canadian camps, institute a national "Know Canada Week" for camps, and arrange a CBC national broadcast originating in a camp with the Prime Minister participating; that individual camps invite MPs, mayors and councillors to be a camper for a day and a night, bring in "the D.P.'s and other new immigrants" as part of programme, use Citizenship Branch filmstrips, and make 1 July more than a sports day.

Nora Bailey, who signed the Quebec notes in June 1950, is identified on p. 7 as "Psychologist and Educational Assistant at the Mental Hygiene Institute, Montreal, and co-owner and co-director of Camp Macaza, P. Quebec." Her article, "Let's Take the Pressure Off," argues camp is first a holiday and a mental-health resource for apartment-dwelling city children.

The Quebec Camping Association Annual Spring Conference of 31 March - 1 April 1950 drew over three hundred attendees from all over Quebec and Eastern Ontario, with representatives from some French camps -- the first note in the run of French-language Quebec camps appearing at the anglophone association's conference. Twenty-five exhibits; chairman Sam Fredman. The Quebec annual meeting in May 1950 was a supper meeting with guest speaker Miss Anne Silver, Executive Director of the Montreal Y.W.C.A.

The Canadian Red Cross ran a Montreal and District refresher course 8-10 May 1950 and an Instructors' Course in Swimming and Water Safety in Montreal in May 1950 "specially prepared to train Swimming Instructors and Waterfront Supervisors for camps and beaches in the Province of Quebec ... in co-operation with the Canadian Camping Association (Quebec Section)." This is the certification pipeline for Quebec camp waterfront staff in 1950.

Canadian Sanitation Company, 804 Jean Talon St. W., Montreal, advertised the "Hygeosan" septic toilet needing neither electricity nor running water, "Installed in many schools, camps and cottages," in June 1950 -- the second Montreal-based camp supplier in the run after Empire Crockery.

R. K. Cleverdon's first Camp Site Development article (June 1950) launched a free mimeographed series mailed from the CCA office in Montreal to paid-up members, twelve titles listed: master plan, water supply, latrines and septic tanks, kitchen waste, low-cost shower unit, kitchen layout, administration centre, camp hospital, waterfront improvement/canoe racks/diving towers, cabin types, tent floors, cost estimation. He gives camp capital cost as $300 to $1,000 per camper in 1950.

The Canadian Camping Association opened its first National Office, in Montreal, in October 1950. Anne Vail's account, headed "EXTRA! Exciting News!": "After exploring all kinds of possibilities ... we finally decided it was time to act, not to plan. In October, we signed the lease... The address is 771 BURNSIDE, Montreal; telephone Harbour 4350." The masthead gives it as Room 221, 771 Burnside Ave.

The furnishing of the CCA's first national office at 771 Burnside, Montreal, is described in detail in December 1950: a rug, a typewriter desk and chair, a borrowed typewriter, a standard lamp and a McCaskel photograph "Marine" from a rummage sale, fifty bricks and boards lent by a camp for a bookcase, tables and chairs on loan from other camps. Agnes Mutchler was appointed part-time Executive Secretary; Dorothy Percival moved the membership files out of her apartment; Ruby Smith took pamphlets and books; Dais Gass convened a committee on office furnishings. Two counsellors were making a wall map of Canada to pin members to.

"International Canoe Trips," submitted by Anne I. Vail for Scotty Brotman, was reported at a Quebec Camping Association meeting on 24 November 1950. For five seasons -- so from 1946 -- Scotty Brotman had led a crew of eight from Montreal to New York by canoe, over four hundred miles in a nineteen-foot canoe. The route: push off from Victoria Pier, Montreal, across the St. Lawrence to St. Lambert; portage by truck to St-Jean to save eighty miles; down the Richelieu to Lake Champlain; Canadian customs at Lacolle, American customs at Rouses Point; the length of Champlain, often in five-foot waves and ship backwash; west from Ticonderoga to Lake George; trucked around Hudson Falls to the Hudson; then down through the locks to New York City. Brotman also ran "his own personal crusade to bring adults in touch with the outdoors."

Two further Montreal camp-supplier addresses appear in December 1950: Foodcraft Laboratories Ltd. at 1462 Bishop Street, Room 15, Montreal as well as Toronto; and Simpson's Special Contract Division listing a Montreal branch.
A. L. Cochrane's Christmas greeting of December 1950 notes that he "began trip-camping with boys in 1900, and since then he has directed Camp Temagami for fifty seasons."

R. K. Cleverdon's second Canadian Camping article (December 1950), on sanitary facilities, is a full technical survey of open pit, pit privy, "bucket a day" semi-septic tank and flush-and-septic systems with 1950 costs: $100-125 for a single semi-septic outfit; $175 for one installed flush toilet; about $350 for a 1,250-gallon two-compartment septic tank; one toilet per ten children and never fewer than two per living area.

"Camps that are Different" (December 1950) surveys Canadian camps for children with disabilities: Merrywood-on-the-Rideau, Blue Mountain and Woodeden (Ontario Society for Crippled Children), Illahee Lodge at Cobourg for children with heart, chest and diabetic conditions (founded 1946, also running three sessions a year for people over sixty), and five CNIB camps across Canada. This is the movement-wide context in which Kanawana's own 1970 cystic-fibrosis campers sat, twenty years earlier.

Roy Locke attended the Canadian Camping Association national board meeting at the YWCA in Montreal on 10 December 1950. The attendance list is printed in full: "Anne Vail, Agnes Mutchler, Dorothy Percival, Dais Gass, Nora Bailey, Ruby Smith, Kenneth Murray, C. A. Wylie, Roy Locke, Sam Freedman, and from Ontario, Mary Edgar, Joyce Bertram and C. T. Sharpe." Out-of-town members had been shown the new Burnside Street headquarters the evening before.

Roy D. Locke is named "president of the Quebec Association" in February 1951 and chaired the programme committee for the Biennial National Conference of the CCA, held jointly with the 1951 Spring Conference of the Quebec and Eastern Ontario Association, 6-8 April 1951, in Montreal at the Grenadier Guards' Armoury, theme "Outdoor Living." Sam Freedman was conference chairman; the CCA annual meeting sat on the Sunday morning, 8 April.

Roy Locke's 1951 conference programme committee introduced a structural innovation: splitting conference topics into three integrated workshops or seminars following each other in logical sequence on campcraft, naturelore and handicrafts, rather than single one-hour sessions. His committee "has already met several times."

Kanawana's director Roy D. Locke went from Vice-President of the Quebec Section (June 1949) to President of the Quebec Association (by February 1951), and personally designed the programme of the national conference in the year the CCA met in Montreal.

Speakers secured for the April 1951 national/Quebec conference in Montreal: "Cap'n Bill" Vinal, Professor of Nature Education, University of Massachusetts (nature-lore); Dr. Carter Storr, co-author of The Canoe and You (campcraft); Dr. Taylor Statten, Jr., Child Psychiatrist, Children's Memorial Hospital, Montreal; Miss Betty Jaques, Art Instructor, Macdonald College (handicrafts); Mrs. Alice Turnham, Assistant Curator, Redpath Museum, McGill (nature-lore).

Dr. Taylor Statten, Jr. was Child Psychiatrist at the Children's Memorial Hospital, Montreal, by February 1951; in the April 1949 issue he had been at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, so he moved to Montreal in the interval.

At a Quebec Section meeting in November 1950, "Mr. Sam Vatcher of the Y.M.C.A. spoke on Indian camp fire ceremonies." A Montreal YMCA man giving the province's camp directors a talk on Indian campfire ceremonial, five months before the national conference, is direct evidence about where the Council Ring material in Quebec YMCA camps came from.

The October 1950 Quebec Section meeting had members from various camps describing their summers -- "a red-letter day at one camp, how another built a summer program around a central theme, religion in camp, how one camp endeavoured to encourage democratic practises" -- unattributed, but one of those camps may well have been Kanawana.
R. K. Cleverdon's "So You're Going to Build" (February 1951) gives minimum floor areas for camp buildings: 40 square feet per camper, 60 per junior staff member, 90 per senior or married staff.

W. E. Yard's February 1951 article on winter camping records the Vancouver YMCA's first winter camp for boys, December 1943, on Hollyburn Ridge -- "The Skyline Camp for Boys," 23 boys and 7 staff, using logging-camp nomenclature (highriggers, sparkchasers, whistlepunks, snag fallers, leaders as "hookers," the director as "the push") -- and the second annual Christmas camp at Camp Pinecrest, December 1950, with 30 people from Toronto Central YMCA.

The venue of the 1951 National-Quebec Conference changed between issues of Canadian Camping: February 1951 announced the Grenadier Guards' Armoury; April 1951 announces, twice and in an advertisement, the Sir Arthur Currie Gymnasium, 475 Pine Avenue West (McGill). Both are recorded; the later notice is the operative one.

Quebec Camping Association programme and officers, 1950-51: programme chairman Winona Wood; a February 1951 meeting given to Arts and Crafts, a workshop "making clay pottery, bamboo flutes, and whittling"; a March panel discussion on "Decentralized Camp Administration"; the QCA Annual Meeting on 17 May 1951 at the YMCA as a supper meeting. Mrs. H. ("Morgie") Morgenstern was elected QCA secretary for the balance of the year on A. Ross Seaman's resignation; Ruby Smith and Lauri Hutchison were reorganising the Quebec membership system; and Ross Seaman ran registration for the national conference even as he left the secretaryship.

The Quebec Camping Association's stated ambition in hosting the 1951 national conference was "to establish a precedent whereby every two years a different province will be host to the rest of Canada at a National Camping Conference."

The Canadian Camping Association crest was adopted in the spring of 1951 -- "Behold Our New Crest!" -- drawn by Mr. D. P. Bromley of Toronto for the Public Relations Committee under Art Buckley, to appear on the new letterhead and membership cards. The magazine does not say whether a 1949 competition entry won or Bromley was commissioned.

The Canadian Campers' Club launched for summer 1951: celluloid pins, twenty-five cents, sold to campers at their own camps, ordered from the CCA office at 771 Burnside Street, Montreal, from early May, with the proceeds going to the CCA. Any Kanawana camper of 1951 could have worn one -- a findable object.

"Coals from a Campfire," a mimeographed collection of campfire stories about "a Very Important Person -- Camp Spirit. Half brownie and half nymph," dedicated to "all those happy souls at Camp Ouareau," was written by Joyce Bertram (Executive Secretary of the OCA, bylined "Camp Ouareau, P.Q.") and sold for 75 cents from 108 Lytton Blvd, Toronto. A named invented camp spirit-figure at a Quebec camp in 1951 -- the closest analogue yet found to the Chopsy legend.

Mary S. Edgar printed a council ring fire invocation in Canadian Camping in April 1951: "O fire of our council ring / Brightly burn before our eyes ... Praise be to Gitche Manitou, Great Spirit of the earth and sky!" -- the kind of text that circulated between camps.

Nora Bailey's "A Light for Your Camp" (April 1951) argues a camp needs "a soul" embodied in a person, and that what adults remember of camp "nearly always centre[s] around a person" -- a statement of the theory of camp leadership current in Quebec at the moment Roy Locke was running both Kanawana and the QCA.

C. H. Irwin of Sherwood Forest Camp catalogued what went wrong on Canadian camp canoe trips in 1951: trips pushed out late in bad weather, canoes separated beyond hailing distance, counsellors leaving campers to go into the village, fires left burning, a boy sent to swim for help in his clothes. He also records, and opposes, the live idea that "it is sissy to take a tent on a canoe-trip."

Nora Bailey died in March 1951, aged 41 (1910-1951), "a few weeks before her article was published," of what she "once called an 'idiot' heart" -- a congenital defect she had endured for years and rarely discussed. Her obituary by Mary L. Northway gives: Havergal College; arts degree, University of Toronto; professional training at the Institute of Child Study, where in 1938 she wrote the first M.A. in psychology based on research in camping, "thus setting a precedent for studies in this area"; camper, counsellor and personnel director at Camp Wapomeo; and in 1948 she joined the Mental Hygiene Institute in Montreal.

In 1939, "rather than being dismayed by her precarious heart condition," Nora Bailey signed on as sailmaker aboard the schooner Yankee and spent eighteen months sailing round the world, minding the skipper's two children, standing watch and scrubbing decks; her letters home were mimeographed and circulated among friends.

In 1949 Nora Bailey and Ruby Smith opened Camp Macaza (spelled "Macuza" in the obituary) in the Laurentians, for young boys and girls -- a coeducational Laurentian camp founded by two women in 1949, sixteen years before Kanawana's 1965 coeducation proposal. It establishes that mixed junior camping already existed in the Laurentians in the late 1940s. Northway quotes Bailey on its programme: "Do you know what these children like doing best of all? They like playing hide-and-seek... One is a child nowadays for such a little while. Let the children have time to be themselves."

The Canadian Campers' Club button was sold at 10 cents in institutional camps and 25 cents in private camps -- the recommendation is explicit, so an institutional camp such as Kanawana would have sold them at a dime. Directors were asked to detach the notice page for the camp board and to "plan some special celebration each month at camp, for which a button is the admission ticket." Ordered from the CCA office, 771 Burnside Ave, Montreal, or after 10 June from Miss Dais Gass, Camp Memphramagog, Mansonville, Quebec; Ontario campers from the OCA or, after 20 June, from Miss Joyce Bertram, Camp Ouareau, Montcalm County, Quebec.
Dais Gass, the CCA's Montreal past-president, ran Camp Memphremagog at Mansonville in the Eastern Townships as of June 1951.

Agnes Mutchler's Executive Secretary's report of June 1951 states that the CCA national office was placed "in Montreal, in the vicinity of the President"; that Quebec "felt no immediate need for quarters but offered to pay for services rendered" while Ontario proposed a joint office; and that the CCA went alone because its functions "were not yet sufficiently defined" and its finances required doing things "even more economically than the Ontario Executive considered a minimum."

The scale of CCA national office work in 1951, per Agnes Mutchler: more than 300 letters per general mailing; fifty board members, so calling a board meeting meant at least a hundred letters, and twice that again when the Queen's meeting was cancelled. Committee chairmen frequently did not reply; some sent tentative resignations; "it was not until March of this year that we had even a nucleus of people who answered letters." Her plea: "nothing could be more valuable to the whole organization at this time than accurate camp directories compiled by each Province."

"Bandy Ball," a new game "introduced at the Quebec Camp Conference" in 1951 -- a large shuttlecock with a 2.5-inch rubber base struck with the open palm -- was sold for $1.00 by Joey Richmond, 399 St. Catherine Street West, Montreal.

The British Columbia camping association is noted in June 1951 as being eleven years old, so founded about 1940, with Phyllis Porter as president and Bishop A. H. Sovereign, retired Bishop of Athabasca, as a pioneer of BC children's camping.

"The Longhouse People," National Film Board, 1951, was pushed to Canadian camps in the winter of 1951-52: "photographed in colour on the Brantford Reserve with the full co-operation of the tribal leaders, and which depicts the life, religious ceremonials, dances, healing ceremonies and tribal councils of these fellow Canadians... This film should be of special interest to Campers." Kanawana has a building called the Longhouse; the film is a dated, findable object with the right name at roughly the right moment, recorded as a candidate rather than as an established origin.

Other films Canadian Camping pointed camps to in December 1951: "Summer is for Kids" (shot at Camp Pinecrest, Toronto YMCA), "Canoe Trip," "Indian Canoe Man," "Portage," and, from the OCA office, "A Camper and His Canoe" and "With Paddle and Pack."

John Hoyle's "A Counsellor-in-Training Programme" (December 1951) sets out a five-year plan at Gay Venture Camp. Ages 14-15: volunteers with leadership potential enrolled in a Leadership Training Plan, meeting three or four times a season with the director, not CITs but "merely senior girls who are seized with the urge to leadership," trained by graded apprenticeship -- the worked example being putting a cabin group to bed, night one observe, night two assist then discuss, nights three and four take charge with the counsellor in the background. Age 16: junior counsellor-in-training, one of four daily periods a discussion-lecture group led by the director using Hoyle's textbook Towards the Understanding of Youth. Age 17: senior CIT, daily discussion on camp philosophy, camper behaviour, story-telling, preparing a service of worship, and camp relationships. Age 18: may be invited back as a cabin counsellor.

John Hoyle wrote in December 1951 that "we are quite alive to the fact that the average eighteen year old girl is not sufficiently emotionally mature to be given full charge of a cabin group... Before too long we hope to raise the minimum age to nineteen." He also insists a CIT is not a "Jo-girl" -- "She is always treated as a leader-in-training" -- and records that a senior staff member had been appointed CIT Advisor and supervisor, and that every two weeks the director received a written report on every CIT from all Section and Activity Heads and spent twenty to thirty minutes with each one going through it.
An obituary in December 1951 for Mrs. Joseph Danson, died 25 October 1951, OCA charter member and director of Camp Winnebagoe, Muskoka, "established in 1933."

A British Columbia camp round-up of December 1951 names Stratford Children's Camp (Roberts Creek); the Zionist Camp at Crescent Beach in its 15th year; Camp Fircom (First United Church, Howe Sound); Moorcroft; and the Children's Jubilee Summer Camp on Burrard Inlet, run since 1935 by the Trade Unions' Fraternal Women's Organization with volunteer leadership and the slogan "Campers to-day, leaders to-morrow."

"Indian Lore and the Council Ring," by W. J. Eastaugh, Superintendent of the Ontario Reformatory and former Personnel Director of Camp Ahmek (Canadian Camping, February 1952, pp. 9-12), makes a historical claim about transmission: "Until a few years ago the Y.M.C.A. was the leader in conducting training courses for counsellors and program men. Indian Lore was almost certain to be included in the courses of instruction offered. Why is it that today, we look in vain for courses in this fascinating work when we scan the curriculum of camp leaders' training courses." So by 1952 an authority states in print that the YMCA had been the principal Canadian trainer in Indian-lore programming and had recently stopped.

Eastaugh's 1952 council-ring site prescription: some outstanding conformation of land -- cliff, bluff, point, boulder field -- "some natural feature that will set that part of camp off by itself and provide opportunity for the development of some legend concerning its history." Fifteen to twenty feet clear between the nearest person and the fire; blankets on rope or poles to close in too-open space; a flat area at least nine feet square at the end opposite the entrance for games; a smooth six-foot log ten inches thick set three feet up on posts for pillow fights. "A common mistake to avoid is that of building too large a fire." Reserve the site exclusively and add decoration year on year -- carved totem poles, rocks painted with Indian designs, the approach trail progressively decorated.

Eastaugh's 1952 order of council-ring ceremony: the Chief (usually the camp director) enters, all stand, he proceeds to the Council Rock and raises his hand; fire lit by friction or by a kerosene-soaked rag in a pail sliding down a wire from a clifftop -- "try to avoid the direct use of matches"; the peace pipe, lit by pretending to scoop an ember, pointed skyward with a prayer to "the Great Spirit, Gitchie Manitou"; then challenges, where a brave stands and calls "O'Chief, O'Chief, O'Chief" and, when pointed to, says "I, [name] from [home town] challenge any member of this Council to [game]"; then Ranger Reports -- prepared accounts of a tracked animal, a strange bird, an incident on a canoe trip; then an Indian dance; then a close, for which Eastaugh recommends Seton's Book of Woodcraft and its account of Hiawatha's departure.

Eastaugh's 1952 council-ring initiation ceremony: the peace pipe passed round the circle in silence, a hatchet buried by the Tribal Chiefs outside the ring, and a treasure box unearthed containing wishes and records left by the previous season's Braves.
