The Chief explains that a young Indian coming of age "spent the night in solitary vigil on a look-out ledge under the stars, and there, after serious meditation, he chose for himself a new name," and may give him the Omaha tribal prayer "Father, a needy one stands before Thee. I who pray am he." It closes: "To your wigwams in silence, and keep that silence unbroken until the dawn." Games named: hand wrestling, leg wrestling, cat on the back fence, Pat and Mike, rooster fight, pillow fight, the water boiling contest, the talk fest, the Blood Brother ceremony, and the naming of the tribes.

Cleverdon's "Backwoodsman's Day" at Camp Kandalore (February 1952) describes an all-camp campcraft competition invented because the campcraft counsellor "complained that the boys didn't have enough opportunity to use their campcraft knowledge in camp." Eight teams of twelve, drawn across prep, junior and senior sections, each under a counsellor captain. Events: water boiling (a No. 10 tin, water to an inch of the top, a teaspoon of soap powder so it boils over visibly, wood only, with no leaves, pine needles or birch bark and birch wood with bark still on disallowed); Kim's Game on twenty common camp tools; canoe portaging race; axe-chopping through a nine-inch poplar marked on skill, safety and time; two juniors crosscutting a ten-inch poplar; a knotting relay tested by a boy leaning back on it; swede-sawing; erecting a tarpaulin-and-canoe trip shelter in four minutes; a pancake contest judged by staff wives; a bed-roll race; and ten minutes to erase all trace of the fire.

A Junior Forest Warden Training Camp at Lighthouse Park, West Vancouver, had taken 2,025 boys aged 10-16 since the war, 250 a year, in an eight-day programme of forestry and conservation, organised twenty-one years earlier -- so about 1931 -- by the BC branch of the Canadian Forestry Association, with a six-clause Junior Forest Warden Pledge printed in full.
Canadian Camping, April 1952: "Roy D. Locke director of Y. M. C. Kamp Kanawana is president of the Quebec Camping Association."

The Quebec Camping Association was run out of the YMCA of Montreal's own headquarters in 1952: "Further information on the Conference is available from either of the above mentioned at 1441 Drummond St., Montreal 25, c/o Quebec Camping Association." The co-chair beside Roy Locke was Fraser Woodhouse of the Montreal Boys Association and director of Camp Lewis, conference chairman.

The QCA 1952 Spring Conference, Montreal, 4-5 April 1952, at the Sir Arthur Currie Memorial Gymnasium, McGill, drew about 300 attending and about 20 exhibiting firms, assembled by a committee chaired by Kanawana's director Roy Locke. Its leaders were Hedley S. Dimock (key speaker, opening banquet address "A Critical Look at Modern Camping," plus three discussion groups on Pre-camp Training, In-camp Supervision and Evaluation); Walter Meyer on song leading; Louis Thomas on Indian lore and crafts; Dr. Carter Storr of Ottawa on campcraft; and Don Rose of the Red Cross with Clair Buckley of the Y.M.C.A. on teaching swimming, water safety and life saving in McGill's new pool.

Walter Meyer, "internationally known song leader," led the singing at the Quebec Camping Association's April 1952 conference and gave three sessions on "Song Leading in Camps"; "Meyer specializes in international folk songs." He is the second named professional song-leader engaged to instruct Quebec camp staff in three years, after Alan Mills in the winter of 1949-50 -- two dated occasions on which Quebec camp people were formally taught songs by named professionals in Montreal.

Louis Thomas led the workshop on Indian Lore and crafts at the Quebec Camping Association's April 1952 conference: "Mr. Thomas is an Iroquois Indian and a leading authority on Indian Lore in this part of the country." A named Haudenosaunee instructor teaching Quebec camp directors and counsellors Indian lore and craft in 1952, in a programme organised by Kanawana's director -- so the Indian-lore material in Quebec camps of this period was not only white-invented Setonian pageantry.

The CCA national office left Montreal for Toronto in 1952. The April 1952 masthead reads "Office: 52 Avenue Road, Toronto." W. E. (Ted) Yard (Central YMCA, 40 College St, Toronto) was elected President at the annual meeting on 1 March 1952 "and it is during this term that C.C.A. office is transferred to Toronto." Anne I. Vail joins the Past Presidents; Joyce Bertram becomes Executive-Secretary of both associations under a cost-sharing arrangement with the OCA; the treasurership is vacant. Vice-presidents: Irwin Haladner (Toronto), F. M. Van Wagner (Montreal), Mrs. I. H. McDonald (Manitoba). Mary L. Northway becomes Assistant Editor. So the CCA's Montreal national office ran from October 1950 to early 1952, about eighteen months.

CCA membership reported at the 1952 annual meeting, by province -- Ontario 110 camps and 44 individuals; Province of Quebec 37 camps and 27 individuals; British Columbia 13 and 3; Manitoba 1 and 18; Prince Edward Island 5 and none; Saskatchewan 2 and 2; Alberta 2 and none; New Brunswick 1 and none; New Jersey (special) 1 individual -- for a total of 171 camps and 95 individuals. Fees to the CCA from provincial associations were cut to $3.50 per camp member and $1.50 per individual. Against Mutchler's 1949 figure of 45 permanent camps registered with the Quebec section, 37 were CCA members in 1952.

The Canadian Camper Button report of 1952: 11,000 purchased, 450 used for advertising, 6,280 orders mailed out, 4,270 on hand; $564.40 cash received and $232.25 receivable; expenses $24.00 and cost of buttons $237.07, for a profit of $535.58. Six thousand went into Canadian camps in the summer of 1951, so surviving examples should exist.

A book review in Canadian Camping (April 1952) of Kenneth E. Kidd's Canadians of Long Ago (Royal Ontario Museum / Longmans, 1951) criticises council-ring practice from inside the movement: "Many camps use council rings and other customs which campers often erroneously accept as being typical of real Indian life... as we adults develop this point of view, we can at least supplement our picturesque 'Indian' ceremonies with an understanding of the real life and thoughts of the Canadians of Long Ago." A dated 1952 statement of the critique, two months after Eastaugh's enthusiastic how-to.

Adele Statten Ebbs (Director, Camp Wapomeo), writing on counsellor meetings in April 1952, gives a time-budget of a camp day: nine or ten hours' sleep, about four hours for three meals, an hour's rest, three hours of routine (rising, flag raising, clean-up, flag lowering, bed) -- twenty hours, "leaving four hours for all the other camp activities." Her list of what belongs in mimeographed "Camp Routines": Fire Precautions, Fire Drill, Meal Hours, Tuck Shop, Mail, Food Parcels, Cash, Days Off, Sunday Suppers (Picnics), Care of Equipment, Laundry, Transportation schedules, Lost and Found, Officer of the Day and Night Watch schedules.

Joyce Bertram, "A Little Nonsense Now and Then" (June 1952), on invented camp characters: "Many camps have imaginary characters which add immeasurably to the spontaneity. The author's youthful days at camp were much enhanced by the presence of 'the camper's best friend, Maude', who had more fun than everyone else at camp put together. At another camp, 'Camp Spirit' is no nebulous thing, always on the side of authority, but is a person, with a distinct personality of his own. Though the embodiment of all the virtues we should like the campers to possess, he is still so impudent and cocky and so irrepressibly cheerful that no camper or counsellor could do without him for a single day." So by 1952 a camp professional treats named, persistent invented camp characters as an ordinary and widespread device.

Other spontaneous camp devices recorded by Joyce Bertram in June 1952: a "doughnut bell" or "watermelon bell" which campers drop everything to run to; being got out of bed to watch northern lights and count shooting stars, or taken in slacks and rubber boots to a spot where fireflies danced; and a party for the Weather Man on the twelfth consecutive day of rain -- the Weather Man in sou'wester with two henchmen, Thunder and Lightning, threatening rain to the end of camp unless the cabins amused him, with a giant barometer shifted through the evening's stunts.

Ted Yard's "Memorable Experiences Leading Towards Spiritual Growth" (June 1952) prints the texts of ceremonies at the Toronto Central YMCA's Camp Pinecrest, including a Voyageur-Lumberman ceremony at sunset: "let us this day drink deep of the beauty in lake and sky and stately pine..." -- the Lumberman entering along the shore in high boots, mackinaw and peak cap with an axe on his shoulder, silhouetted against a giant pine ("craftsman, pioneer, conservationist... a living symbol of Canada's great forest lands"); then the Voyageur paddling into silhouette in buckskin coat and tasselled toque ("explorer, adventurer, master of his craft... and in this beautiful setting he travels with the greatest Sternsman of all time").

Camp Pinecrest's campfire induction ceremony, printed in June 1952, had inductees accept the Pine as a symbol of Strength and Fortitude, of Personal Growth, and of Purity, each with its formula: "as the Pine roots cling to the crevices of solid Muskoka rock to hold firm in all weather, so will we hold firm..."; "as the Pine strives ever upward toward a clear, fresh sky, so will we strive..."; "as the stately Pine draws its life from the fresh Northern air... so will we draw ours from the clean speech, clean sportsmanship, and clear minds..."

Camp Pinecrest ran a widening-friendship-circles device in 1952 in which a boy drops a stone in the lake and, as the rings spread, campers rise to speak for their home countries -- Poland, Holland, Greece, Estonia, Scotland, Australia. A Canadian YMCA camp explicitly programming for displaced-persons and immigrant campers.

Irwin Haladner printed a complete job description for camp medical staff at Camp Wabi-Kon in June 1952 -- "Policies and Responsibilities for the Medical Staff" -- including a confidentiality clause: "All information re patients is strictly confidential and not to be divulged to anyone except the camp director." Also: medical exam of all campers and staff within 48 hours of arrival; a daily log of every examination and treatment "regardless of how trivial"; weekly water samples for analysis; the doctor to leave a note of his whereabouts at the medical lodge at all times, even off duty; one day off a week and no more than one medical staff member away at a time; campers may not visit the medical lodge "either in the medical lodge or on the outside at the windows"; sick counsellors visited by their section heads only; and compulsory letter-writing days for patients, Tuesdays and Thursdays, letters turned over to the office for checking.

John Hoyle's second philosophy article (June 1952) argues against bells, gongs, bugles and sirens ("horror of horrors"), against competition and prizes, for a "choice programme" in which campers elect their own activity each period, for the technique of motivation over instruction, and for renaming "problem children" as "children with problems" ("This is not just a play on words").

Erma Sutcliffe's "Child Art Goes to Camp" (June 1952) attacks camp craft orthodoxy: "Are we going to build totem poles when we are neither British Columbians nor Indians?" and "Why should any child make a billfold when he can buy one gayer and with more gadgets at the nearest five and ten store?"

The Holger Nielsen back-pressure arm-lift method of artificial respiration replaced the Schafer prone-pressure method in 1952, adopted that year by the Red Cross, the YMCA and the Scouts -- so any Kanawana lifesaving instruction dated after 1952 should be the Nielsen method.

The Kawagama Cine-Series: three 16mm colour-and-sound counsellor training films made in the 1951 season at Camp Kawagama, Dorset, Ontario, producer David Palter, director Louis A. A. Shore -- "A-Stencilling We Shall Go," "With Paddle and Pack," and "A Camper and His Canoe," the last of which won the First Award in the Amateur Class of the Canadian Film Awards and the trophy of the Association of Motion Picture Producers and Laboratories of Canada as the best amateur film of 1951.

Camp Tonakela, near Madras, India, run without pay by Wallace Forgie, "well-known right across Canada in Y.M.C.A. and other boys' work fields," was supported by Canadian camps giving a Sunday camp-service offering: 452 girls and 1,721 boys in 28 groups the previous year, all free of charge, plus a free daily meal for nearby village children and, in water famine, the camp's swimming-pool supply given over to human consumption. Twenty-five cents from a Canadian camper fed a camper at Tonakela for a day. The name is glossed as "Others First" in a North-American Indian language and "Not for Self" in an East Indian tongue.

"Music in Camp," by Barbara Cass-Beggs, L.R.A.M., A.R.C.M. (December 1952), described as "former Director of the University Settlement Music School & Music School Camp -- now of the University of Swansea, South Wales," who led the music at Camp Gay Venture in the summer of 1952. Her prescription: one singing period a day for the entire camp, campers and staff together, "for staff cannot help in singing songs if they do not know the songs" -- held indoors and preferably with a piano, after a meal while everyone is still at table. "By the end of a month's camp the campers would have a repertoire of at least 50 good (and new to them) folk songs or rounds." Each session: one or two new songs, a well-known song, something serious, something rowdy, something lively, something quiet, worked with descants, informal harmony, solo-and-chorus and antiphonal singing.

Barbara Cass-Beggs drew a firm distinction between singing and cheering in December 1952: "Shouting is not singing... There are plenty of good opportunities in camp where shouting and cheering, etc., are fine, but don't let's get this confused with singing and sing-songs." She also recommended a pre-camp course for song leaders covering "simply conducting, some knowledge of how to use the voice-range, breathing and diction -- what songs to choose and why, and what song books are the most useful" -- evidence that camp singing in this period was formally taught, not just absorbed.

A camp song printed with its borrowed tune in December 1952, p. 6, headed "What is Camp without Music? John Palmer": a lyric titled "A Camp Song" set to the tune of "I'll See You Again" -- Noel Coward's waltz from Bitter Sweet (1929). "We'll return again, / Whenever Camp fires burn again, / Winters may be long and drear / But we'll be here / When summer calls us. / Days so glad and free / Will always linger in memory; / And whatever we may do, / Lakes and skies of azure blue, / Bring us dreams our whole life through / Of you." Exactly the mechanism behind the Alabama Jubilee finding: a camp lyric written over a popular song of the day and printed for other camps to take up.

Ontario's safety provisions became a condition of the non-profit camp grant in December 1952 (L. B. Smith, Camping Branch, Department of Education), printed in full: a resident staff member holding the Canadian Red Cross Standard Certificate in First Aid or the St John Ambulance Senior certificate; health examination within two weeks before camp; a midday rest of not less than an hour; a hot bath or shower at least weekly for stays of two weeks or more; waterfront supervision by a mature person holding the Bronze Medallion of the Royal Life Saving Society; one lifeguard per ten swimmers free of all other duties; and eleven specific swimming rules including that no one swims alone, a classifying swim test before any free swim, and non-swimmers confined to an enclosed shallow area.

David Palter's double-purpose incinerator, in use at his camp in the summers of 1951 and 1952: a cast cement and rock structure lined with firebrick, six feet high by five by eight, servicing a camp of three hundred people, burning all garbage including tins and bottles three times a day while heating a 500-gallon tank for continuous showers and laundry, with a forty-foot 12-inch stack and an optional forced-draught oil burner that "melts glass bottles and practically vaporizes the tin cans." Roughly one 45-gallon drum of ash a day without the burner, a quarter of that with it.

J. Manning of Camp Tanamakoon described orienteering in December 1952 as "a game which started a few years ago in Sweden," used not for contests but to get campers off the camp grounds; a contest to rediscover Lost Lake led two groups by separate routes to a derelict camp site whose rebuilding became the season's major project.

F. M. Van Wagner is identified in February 1953 as "Director: Camp Nominingue, Faculty Advisor: McGill Outing Club," and is the CCA's Montreal vice-president. He records that "The McGill University Outing Club has been lunching around open fires on their weekly ski tours for the past 15 years" -- so from about 1938 -- "Having found this to be a very simple and pleasant experience on almost any winter day in the Laurentians it was a natural step to sleeping out."

The McGill Outing Club ran three or four one-night "camp-outs" each winter for inexperienced members, four to sixteen men and women, in self-sufficient groups of four or five under an experienced leader. No tent -- each party built a large bough lean-to and thick bough beds on the snow. Preferred conditions: clear, cold, moonlit, zero to 20 degrees Fahrenheit.

Van Wagner's 1953 winter-camping technique, recorded in detail: gather all wood before removing skis; build the fire on a base of green hardwood logs 4-6 inches thick and two feet long, or the snow melts and the fire drops into the hole; in three or four feet of snow "a large hole will be melted clear to the ground." Clothing: medium-weight long wool underwear, smooth-finish wool ski slacks, flannel shirt, medium wool sweater, windbreaker, light and heavy wool socks, inner wool and outer leather mitts, ski cap, plus spare socks, mitts and a sweater. "One of the most important considerations when camping out in cold weather is to keep dry. This usually means avoiding perspiration at all costs"; ski boots go inside the sleeping bag or they freeze. No fires are kept burning at night. Two light down bags beat one heavy one. Snow is used for water, so there is no need to camp near water.

F. M. Van Wagner credited the postwar interest in winter camping to "ski troops of the late war," and predicted in February 1953: "It should not be long before our summer camps discover ways of promoting at least a limited amount of winter camping."

Ontario moved to accredit camps in February 1953 (R. K. Cleverdon, Chairman of the OCA Standards Committee). An October 1952 sub-committee studied how Michigan and California implemented ACA standards -- questionnaire plus inspection, with camps meeting the standard "accredited" and permitted to advertise it. The OCA approved accreditation in principle, to be correlated with the Ontario Government's December 1952 safety provisions, with applications accepted September and October 1953 and accredited camps able to advertise the fact for the 1954 season. The first camp accreditation scheme in Canada.

A. B. Hodgetts of HurOntario Camp published a technical critique of the "J Stroke" in February 1953, arguing against Ron Perry's The Canoe and You that the standard teaching term is itself the source of the commonest paddling faults, and that the true path of the blade is "a flattened out letter C" -- "At our Camp, we actually call this the 'C Stroke'." The live methodological argument among Canadian camp canoeists in 1953.

Grey Owl Indian Craft Co., 1569 Nostrand Ave., Brooklyn 26, N.Y., advertised in Canadian Camping from February 1953: "SUPPLIES FOR ALL INDIAN CRAFTS, KITS, BEADS, FEATHERS, ETC.," free catalogue. A commercial American supplier selling the material culture of camp Indian-lore into Canadian camps.

Dr. W. E. Blatz, Director of the Institute of Child Study, University of Toronto, told the 1953 Ontario Camping Association conference, listing what he would do if he started a camp: "I would not impose Indian rituals on the children. If they want to play Indians that's alright; but simply because the camp director wants to play Indians is no reason for making the children conform to the pattern. It prevents them developing their own imaginative play."

Blatz's other 1953 stipulations for an ideal camp: no campers under seven; activities from what the terrain offers, and city games like baseball excluded; plenty of time to sit and think ("Meditation is a lost art for most adults"); co-education -- "Sex must be taken into account as an important factor in the developing adolescent... my camp would be co-educational, with the boys and girls sharing many interests. Dramatics and dancing especially, would be included"; competition only where a game requires it, with no scores carried forward and no prizes; and no uniforms, badges, gadgets or insignia -- "The child would never be made to feel that he has completed anything." Blatz was arguing for coed camps from a child-development chair twelve years before Kanawana's 1965 coeducation proposal.

Dr. Taylor Statten Jr. told the 1953 OCA conference on emotional readiness that not all children are ready for camp; that a short first year should be lengthened later; that "Children unready to join in camp are the bedwetter, the overweight child, the one with a nervous twitch or physical deformity"; that "Parents make superhuman demands on counselors. A father 'wants his boy to become a man in four weeks of camp.'"; and that "Hate and hostility are hard to accept but are feelings most in need of expression."

Mrs. Gisela Commanda hired Indian regalia to camps, per a notice in Canadian Camping (April 1953): she "has a limited number of men's and women's Indian costumes of buckskin, cloth and velvet, ornamented with beadwork. For Hire. Also war bonnets, medicine man outfits, dancers' feather bustle sets, drums and other Indian equipment; some suitable for special occasions and others of less value which would be just right for Indian program in CAMP." Contact: MElrose 1029, 129 Jameson Avenue, Toronto. She is the same Gisela Commanda, A.R.C.A., who wrote the December 1949 handicrafts article, in which she says she "married an Ojibway Indian and spent many months in the Nippissing Reserve."

Mary L. Northway's "Is the Camp Ready for the Child?" (April 1953) proposes taking the four things camp prospectuses promise -- health, skills, social development, spiritual values -- and assaying an ordinary half-hour, breakfast, to see whether any is actually present. Her aside on camp songs: "'Dear old Pine-Knot -- all its boys are brave and grand -- We love Pine-Knot, dear old Pine-Knot, it's the best, best camp in all the land.' And in this, the children's social development grows towards group belonging, only at the expense of establishing a disillusioned belief of group superiority. A very dangerous attitude indeed."

Dorothy M. Douglas, "Is the Child Ready for Camp?" (April 1953), notes that as OCA secretary she had numerous enquiries from parents whose children were "anywhere from four to seven years of age," and observes that "The incidence of bedwetting in some camps is generally indicative of too stimulating a camp programme, or of a lack of security in the children so affected," and that "On the whole, young campers lose a little weight rather than gaining it in the first year or two at camp."

Ontario stepped back from camp accreditation in 1953. At the OCA annual meeting on 27 February 1953, forty-five members attending, Cleverdon presented the proposed standards and "the concensus of opinion was that the proposed set of standards is a starting point and that the association should continue to work progressively without immediate accreditation for camps at the present time." So the February plan did not proceed as scheduled.
Mary S. Edgar asked to be replaced as Editor of Canadian Camping in 1953 after five years; the executive began seeking a new editor and editorial board.

Continental Casualty Company, Special Risks Division, 1510 Drummond Street, Montreal, advertised campers' medical insurance in April 1953: $1,500 medical expenses per accident, $350 per sickness, $1,500 for polio, $2,500 accidental death -- the period's schedule of what a camper's life and limbs were insured for.

Mrs. Dorothy Douglas at the Institute of Child Study, University of Toronto, accepted in 1953 the Chairmanship of a new Canadian Camping Association committee "whose function it is to develop a Canadian Camp Song Book." A boxed notice on p. 24 of the June 1953 issue reads: "You will receive a letter while you are at camp requesting assistance in securing songs popular at camp. If you have any special song or songs that you would like to see embodied in a Canadian Camp Song Book, please send words and music (if available) to Mrs. D. M. Douglas, 76 Park Ave., Oakville, Ont." So in the summer of 1953 every CCA member camp was written to and asked to send in the songs its campers actually sang, with words and music.

The Tajar appears at two Canadian camps in 1953: at Glen Bernard, Mary Edgar's camp, where the tribute article lists her special occasions as "Pippa day, Blue moon night, Japanese night, Tajar day"; and at the Winnipeg Girl Guides' Caddy Lake camp, where the ground floor of the main building holds "Tagar House, the tuck shop and three hot showers." The Tajar is the creature of The Tajar Tales (Jane Shaw Ward, 1946), out of Camp Tawanka -- a mischievous being, part tiger, part badger, part jaguar. That two Canadian camps a thousand miles apart had built it into their calendar and their buildings by 1953 establishes the genre: named, persistent, invented camp creatures, transmitted between camps in print.

The Quebec conference of 1953 was held jointly with the National Camping Conference, 27-28 March 1953, Sir Arthur Currie Memorial Gymnasium, Montreal, with over 170 attending -- down from about 300 in 1952. Programme: Bob Rourke of Pickering College, "A Target for Camping"; Walter Meyer again on the sing-song and a workshop titled "Song-O-Batics" (three sessions), the third consecutive year a professional song leader was engaged by the Quebec association; Canoe Tripping with Ron Perry; Child Development with Dr. H. Caplan, Dr. A. McLeod and Mr. N. Markus; Crafts with Mr. W. McCurdy; Administration with Irwin Haladner on Food Cost Control and Mr. John Venters on Camp Architecture.

At the 1953 Quebec conference, "After a chicken luncheon Saturday, Mr. Roy Locke, Past President of the Q.C.A., gave an impressive speech entitled 'Dividends of Camping'" -- a Kanawana director's own address, titled, dated and placed.

The QCA annual meeting of mid-May 1953 was held in the new YWCA, main speaker Mrs. Alice Turnham on "Camping, Nature Bound," with Anne Vail closing on "Good Luck, Campers." The Quebec provincial contact for membership was Miss J. Brown, 5056 Western Ave., Montreal.

Mary L. Northway's tribute to Mary S. Edgar, "Woodfire and Candlelight" (June 1953), on her retirement as editor after thirty-three years directing Glen Bernard, names the founding generation: "A. L. Cochrane, 'Ernie' Chapman, Mary Hamilton, Taylor Statten, and Mary S. Edgar... Beyond their own camps, together they originated the Camping Association."

Northway's 1953 tribute tells a story against council-ring hierarchy: the little campers at Glen Bernard, "tired of being braves whose worthiness was often unrecognized at the glories of the Council Ring," formed their own secret tribe of four and elected Mary Edgar its only adult member -- "being slightly confused between Indians and Knights, we made her kneel while we dubbed her on the shoulder and initiated her into the secret tribe of the Kickapoos." Northway's moral: "adjustment can be effected by changing the child or by changing the organization. Camp directors do not as often as they should become the least of the braves in a tribe headed by their youngest campers."

In the war years Mary S. Edgar built a separate camp on her property called Shangri-la, used for English girls and afterwards lent to various organizations -- an Ontario camp built specifically to house British evacuee children, worth setting beside Kanawana's own 1941 wartime evacuees.

From the American Camping Association's Camping at the Mid-Century census, reported in Canadian Camping in June 1953: approximately 12,600 organized camps in the United States in 1951, at least four million campers, three resident camps for every day camp, 93% of organization camps charging under $3 a day against 60% of private camps charging $6-$10, and total organized camp property valued at over $350 million. Canadian Camping also reports a population projection of "up to 40%" more camp-age children within five years.

"Shall We Sing a Song of Camp?" by Dorothy M. Douglas, Chairman of the Canadian Camp Song Book Committee (December 1953), gives the mechanics of the national song collection: "All member camps of the Canadian Camping Association (with the addition of a further group of C.G.I.T. camps reached through the kindness of [the officer] of the C.G.I.T. National [Committee]) were sent a letter and reply form by this Committee early in August [1953]... it is encouraging that camps in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba... Nova Scotia, Quebec (two ...) and Ontario responded at once." Quebec camps replied.

Dorothy Douglas asked camps in 1953 to send "an extra copy of your camp's Song Book or Song Sheet," to star the songs the campers particularly enjoy, and to "indicate those songs whose words and/or music originated at your camp" -- with the promise that "The committee will ask your permission before publishing or using these in any way." So a national collection of Canadian camp song sheets, annotated for local origin, was assembled in the autumn of 1953 at 76 Park Avenue, Oakville, Ontario. She notes girls' camps had outnumbered boys' camps in the returns and appeals for boys' camps to write.

Dorothy Douglas's 1953 comparative notes on camp song variants: of "Land of the Silver Birch" she asks "Do you sing this song at your camp? Can you tell us its origin?" -- so in 1953 the origin was already unknown to the national committee -- and records variants in the wigwam verse across camps: "I'll build my wigwam" / "I'll pitch my wigwam" / "I'll set my wigwam"; "Close by the water's edge" / "Close to the forest edge." She notes westerners pitch, because western wigwams are tents of skins or mats, while some peoples' wigwams are bark huts.

Further camp song variants recorded by Dorothy Douglas in 1953: an action song, "origin unknown to us" -- western sheet "We are the red men, tall and STRAIGHT ... We're the men of the old Hancow ... We CAN fight with sticks and stones"; eastern sheet "tall and QUAINT ... the old Duncow ... We DON'T fight with sticks and stones," with her comment "The difference here is quite significant." A Canoeing Song written to "a graceful waltz tune": "And swiftly, as the heron winging, / Our singing paddles dip by" -- elsewhere zip by, elsewhere slip by. "My Tall Silk Hat" sung to "Funiculi, Funicula." And songs she names as sung at sunset campfires nationwide: Fire's Burning, Taps, and Witchcraft.

Stan Symington, National Boys' Work Secretary of the National Council of YMCAs of Canada, listed the eastern-Canada YMCA camps he visited in 1953 with their directors: Naskapie (Quebec City), new partner Lloyd Elmer, via University of Toronto; Pascobac (Saint John), Bob Butler, from Sir George Williams; Wapomeo (Yarmouth), Nate Bain; Barachois (Sydney), Roy McKeen; Magaguadavic (Fredericton), Bert Messacar; Y's Acres (Moncton), Al Tyler; Sherbrooke (Eastern Townships); Holland Cove (Charlottetown), Ivan Robinson; Big Cove (Halifax), Clare Buckley. The institutional peer group Kanawana sat inside.
entities: National Council of YMCAs of Canada

facts.claim: Cleverdon's Ontario standards survey of June 1953 gives the first hard compliance numbers in the run: 100% of camps used pasteurized milk; 77% tested their water supply at least every two weeks; 63% had hot shower or bathtub facilities for all campers; 90% of those without a resident doctor had one on call; but only 65% insisted on pre-camp medical inspections of staff and campers. A daily rest period was universal. On waterfront, only 75% kept to ten children per lifeguard while more than 80% met the other standards. On staff age: in private camps 30% used 17-year-olds as a minimum but no camp averaged under 19; in agency camps -- Kanawana's category -- one-third used counsellors as young as 15 or 16, and CITs as young as 13, though 80% averaged 17 or more.

Scale figures from the December 1953 editor's preamble: "over five hundred camps in Ontario alone" and "CCA can boast about two hundred and fifty member camps across Canada" -- up from 171 at the 1952 annual meeting.

Eanswythe Flynn became both Executive Secretary of the CCA and Editor of Canadian Camping in late 1953, succeeding Joyce Bertram and Mary S. Edgar. Ted Yard reported an 8,000-mile presidential tour of western camps at which the Alberta Camping Association was formed, acting president Murray Faulkner of the Calgary YMCA; and he noted that in the Ontario association Ruby Smith, Nan Vail, Agnes Mutchler, Ken Murray and Dais Gass had again assumed active executive roles -- the Montreal group of 1950-52 turning up on the Ontario executive.

Alan Klein's "Do Lean Years Lie Ahead?" (December 1953) is the period's clearest statement of the counsellor shortage: camps "once ... attracted University students, graduates and teachers, they now get high school students," and he warns against camps competing on salary. Two anonymous first-person pieces follow -- a first-year counsellor's list of grievances (no in-camp training beyond a daily programme meeting; "Joe-jobs" as a steady diet; unstandardised salaries, one classmate with half the responsibility paid nearly twice as much; and the complaint that CITs' parents are asked to pay half fees while the CIT is on full-time duty most of the day) and a CIT's answer.

Ethel Bebb and Margaret Caesar spent five weeks visiting some fifty private camps in Ontario in 1953 and reported bluntly: "We cannot say that camp procedures in all of the Ontario camps which we visited meet even the minimum standards"; some counsellors "too young in actual years"; equipment not kept and property not attractive; "in a few instances there were discontented faces:-- not only among campers but also staff, which reflects upon top direction." What impressed them most was Canadian tripping programmes -- "the pre-training, the preparation, the tripping equipment, the skilled leadership."

Mary Barker's 1953 YWCA camp survey: nine camps (seven Ontario, two Quebec), 5 to 600 acres, 42 to 150 campers aged 8-16, $14 to $20 a week, two-week average, staff mostly unpaid counsellors aged 15-35 with CITs from 13-17 -- with an eight-millimetre, forty-minute documentary film made of the facilities and lent free to any camp director.

Anne Vail's profile of F. M. Van Wagner, "Among Ourselves" (February 1954): Floyd M. Van Wagner, born Hyde Park, N.Y., raised on a farm; Springfield College 1920, captain of the track team and Eastern Colleges quarter-mile champion, "when Dr. A. S. Lamb secured him for McGill University." At McGill he was coach of the track and basketball teams for more than 25 years, did graduate study at Harvard and McGill, and later gave his time to the School of Physical Education and the direction of recreational activities. His McGill career closed with the 1953-54 season. His wife Catherine was a McGill graduate in Physical Education.

Anne Vail's 1954 profile states of Camp Nominingue: "He was co-founder of this Camp with HAY FINLAY in 1925." Hay Finlay is the CCA Secretary-Treasurer of 1949, at 475 Pine Avenue West, and the KB already holds him as Kanawana's Senior Section director in 1922. So the man who ran Kanawana's senior section in 1922 co-founded Camp Nominingue three years later with McGill's track coach -- a documented link between Kanawana's own staff and the founding of the Laurentian private-camp world.
Camp Nominingue, on Little Lake Nominingue, had 180 acres in 1954, surrounded by large tracts of Crown land "where parties are free to travel," and its campers "have visited over 400 lakes."

Anne Vail's 1954 profile states that F. M. Van Wagner "was a promoter of the Canadian Camping Association, the FIRST PRESIDENT OF THE QUEBEC BRANCH" -- naming the founding president of the Quebec Camping Association, an office Roy Locke of Kanawana held two decades later. He was also Past President of the Quebec Association for Health, Physical Education and Recreation and of the McGill Faculty Club, and a Montreal Rotarian since 1935.

F. M. Van Wagner was faculty adviser to the McGill Outing Club from 1940 and a developer of the McGill Ski School, held each January in the Laurentians, followed by camping courses for men students with canoe trips and ski touring as practical application. He was Director of Canoe Trips at Nominingue for 25 years, handing that to son Charles, a Montreal engineer; son Peter was ski instructor at Banff; and he had twin daughters May and Rachel. His portrait was by Nakash, the Montreal studio.

The Canadian Camp Song Book got its own conference workshop: the CCA/OCA conference programme for 25-27 February 1954, Central YMCA Toronto, lists for Saturday morning "(3) Canadian Camp Song Book. Chairman: Mrs. Dorothy Douglas." So the collection begun in August 1953 was still live and being worked in committee in early 1954.

The CCA/OCA conference of February 1954 split kindred-group luncheons by camp type: Private, Girl Guides, Boy Scouts, Church, YMCA, YWCA, Kiwanis, Day, Agency, Salvation Army -- and on Saturday separately Boys' Private, Girls' Private and Co-educational Private. Anne Vail chaired the Friday dinner; the Saturday dinner address on "Spiritual Values in Camping" was by Rev. Richard Jones, Director of the Canadian Council of Christians and Jews.

National Camp Week, 1-8 May 1954, was declared by the CCA in December 1953 -- and Charles F. Plewman notes that "The British Columbia, Manitoba and Quebec Camping Associations have been successfully promoting a Camp Week for some years back," so a Quebec Camp Week predates the national one. Its five stated purposes include "To encourage parents to urge their boys and girls of seventeen and eighteen to join the camp counselling movement, and to teach them that health, character-building and preparation for leadership are of far greater value than large salaries at that point in their lives."

Lotta Dempsey's "Person to Person" column in the Toronto Globe and Mail of 12 January 1954, reprinted in full in Canadian Camping, gives the public framing of the counsellor shortage: "Time was when university undergraduates, young teachers and senior high school students of mature stature flocked to boys' and girls' camps for summer work. Latterly, the lure of big wages in a variety of jobs, and the kudos attached to work in industry during holiday times ... has taken many former counsellors away from the camps."

Dr. J. Harry Ebbs's "Fatigue -- A Major Health Problem in Camps" (February 1954) gives recommended minimum hours of sleep: 6-8 years, 11 hours; 9-11, 10.5; 12-14, 10; 15-17, 9; staff, at least 8. And a warning for the polio era: "Severe physical fatigue often precedes paralytic polio."

Camp Tonakela's 1953 numbers: 3,004 campers in forty-six groupings -- "we have arrived at the point of optimum usage" -- of whom only 278 were girls; 468 girls from Madras orphanage hostels camped as guests of North American camps; emergency feeding of 100-125 village children daily through the year; gifts of Multi-Purpose Food from the Meals for Millions Foundation, rice, wheat and milk powder from the South India Famine Relief Committee, and 20,000 multi-vitamin pills and ten sacks of beans from Church World Service, cutting camp cost per meal to four and a half cents. Directed by a Canadian since its inception in 1936.

The Quebec Camping Association executive for 1954, printed in full: Past President Mr. Roy Locke, Boys' Work Secretary, Metropolitan YMCA, Montreal; President Miss Ruby Smith, 501 Claremont Avenue, Montreal; Vice-President Mrs. A. Mutchler, 1445 Crescent Street, Montreal 25; Secretary-Treasurer Mr. Ken Murray, 112 Dunrae Avenue, Montreal 16; Social Convener Miss Norma Hall; Membership Miss Jean Brown, 5056 Western Avenue, Montreal. This dates the end of Locke's QCA presidency to the 1953-54 turnover and independently attests his YMCA title that year as Boys' Work Secretary of the Metropolitan YMCA.

The Ontario Camping Association "Business Principles" (Code of Ethics), printed in full in April 1954 alongside John Hoyle's "Camping Ethics," has seven clauses: no soliciting of campers enrolled at another member camp; no engaging of staff already under contract elsewhere; no secret price-cutting or special rates to parents; scholarships to be bona fide and openly stated; references to be given honestly and in confidence; no advertising of activities the camp cannot staff or equip; no misrepresentation of facilities.

A. L. Cochrane's memoir of Ernest Arthur Chapman (April 1954): born Hamilton about 1885; physical instructor at the old Highfield School; physical director of St Andrew's College from 1905 for thirty years; married Leila Kirkbride 1909; founded Camp Kagawong on Balsam Lake "more than forty years ago" (about 1912); charter member of the Ontario Branch of the Royal Life Saving Society 1908, its secretary-treasurer five years and president 1928-34; past president of the OCA; Amateur Canadian Champion in boxing and wrestling at his weight; the Chapman Cup named for him.

Catherine Scholes, "School Camping in Canada" (April 1954), states that as of 1953 only four Ontario schools had pioneered school camping and no other province in Canada had school camps at all: Pickering College, Forest Hill Junior High (which "established co-educational camping"), King George School Guelph, and York Memorial Collegiate. Forest Hill's school camp is a documented Canadian coeducational camping precedent from the early 1950s.

Ivan Eaton, Adult Programme Secretary of the Ottawa YMCA, wrote "Day Camp is Big Business" (April 1954), a day-camp counsellor-training curriculum from inside the Y movement, noting more than thirty day camps in Toronto alone, over 4,000 children, six to eight weeks, more than $40,000 a year. It includes "what about a big totem pole for the council ring?" as a craft suggestion.

Elizabeth Wardley Raymer's April 1954 article on the pre-camp conference includes the instruction to "Review words, and songs which are part of regular camp rituals, so that the new members may learn them" -- evidence that transmitting camp song repertoire to new staff before camp opened was standard practice in the association's recommended training.

Sixty-two Canadians attended the ACA National Conference at the Statler Hotel, New York, in 1954, with about 2,000 delegates. CCA/ACA reciprocity was agreed: mutual national mailing lists, monthly magazine exchange, cross-attendance at each other's regional and national meetings at member rates, each provincial association urged to join its nearest ACA Section, a joint camping recruitment film discussed, and each body to describe itself as "Affiliated with" the other. Named in the negotiation: Hugh Ransom, Catherine Hammett, Cliff Labbett, Ted Yard, Irv Haladner.

The Quebec Camping Association executive of June 1954, "Welcome to a New Executive": Past President Miss Ruby Smith; President Mr. O. N. H. Owens; Vice-President Mrs. Agnes Mutchler; Secretary-Treasurer K. H. Murray; Conference Chairman A. Ross Seaman; Programme Ann Vail; Membership Mrs. S. Corden; Publicity Mr. Tony Shorgan; Social Mrs. S. Keator; Counsellor Training Miss Ruby Smith; Camp Standards F. M. Van Wagner; Song Book Mr. William Hewetson (of the Boy Scouts Association); Day Camping Mr. A. E. Cotton; Camp Directory Miss Dais Gass; Nominating Committee Mrs. D. Judah.

Quebec appointed its own Song Book chairman to feed the national committee -- William Hewetson of the Boy Scouts Association -- and the June 1954 editorial makes the national ask explicit: "If every camp director in our membership would submit even one original song or original verses to an old one, Mrs. Dorothy Douglas, our Song Book Chairman, would be well away to a completed venture." Between the August 1953 circular to every member camp and this, there were two separate solicitations of camp song material with a named Quebec collector in between. If Kanawana submitted anything, it went to Hewetson.

Ruby Smith held a one-year Quebec Camping Association presidency, 1953-54, between Roy Locke's and O. N. H. Owens's, and moved to Past President and Counsellor Training in June 1954. A. Ross Seaman appears as QCA Conference Chairman. F. M. Van Wagner held Camp Standards provincially and was elected a CCA national Vice-President at Kingston the same year. Dais Gass and Anne I. Vail, both of Montreal, are listed on the national masthead as CCA Past Presidents.

The Quebec Camping Association's own annual report of June 1954 records that the 1953 conference ran 27-28 March 1953 with Bob Rourke opening; other leaders Irwin Haladner, Ron Perry, Dr. H. Caplan, John Venters, Walter Meyer, Dr. A. MacLeod, Roy Locke and Nathan Markus; about three hundred people attended, and Mary Edgar was the year's most successful guest speaker. The 1954 annual meeting of 7 May had Dr. Taylor Statten speaking on "The Camper, What is She/He Like?", Dr. Mary Winspear at dinner, and square dancing. The report also notes the QCA ran separate informal gatherings for private-camp people alongside its regular meetings -- a documented agency/private split inside the Quebec association.

A full Personality profile of A. Milks ("Ace," W. A. Milks) of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks by Arnold Fraser, Executive Secretary of High Park YMCA (June 1954): born Eardley, Quebec; attended the Ottawa YMCA camp at Marshall's Bay on the Ottawa River in 1907; the camp moved to Golden Lake, Ontario in 1908 "because there was too much sawdust in the water"; counsellor 1915, Assistant Director 1916 under Charlie Plewman; directed On-Da-Da-Waks every summer 1916-1950 inclusive, 34 years; over 300 boys in 1950. The name means "Men of the Woods." Fraser records that the earliest trace of the camp is a minute of an Ottawa YWCA Board meeting recording a camp held in 1893 on the Ottawa River across from Quyon, Quebec -- one year before Kanawana.

The Alberta Camping Association was formally constituted on 13 February 1954, with minutes printed in full and the executive listed -- so the CCA's provincial structure was still being completed in the mid-1950s, with Quebec and Ontario long established. British Columbia membership for 1953-54: 18 camps, 3 agencies, 23 individuals, 20 students.

Keith Cleverdon's "Some Thoughts on Camp Fire Safety" (June 1954) is the first attempt at a Canadian camp fire-safety standard, written because "so far we have done little to set a standard for the protection of our campers... against damage or destruction from fire": frame buildings 20-40 ft apart; two-storey frame sleeping quarters declared undesirable by fire authorities; 30 square feet per person sleeping, 10 square feet dining; two exits opening outward; fire drill once each camp period.

Kirk Wipper, Director of the Ontario Camp Leadership Centre at Bark Lake, published a waterfront audit checklist in June 1954 with the era's depth standards: beginner 3 to 3.5 ft, intermediate 3.5 to 7 ft, senior over 7 ft; 9 ft under a 1 m board, 12 ft under a 3 m board. Mary M. Porter, formerly Waterfront Director at YWCA Camp Davern, Ottawa, set out a drowning-search drill developed with Don Purdy of the Ottawa Red Cross: the four-minute standard, the shallow-water wading line, the surface-dive line, grappling irons.

The first National YMCA Camp Training Seminar was held at Toronto YMCA's Camp Pine Crest, 23 August - 2 September 1954, during the ninth week of Pine Crest's boys' camp season: ten men and two women, from camps between Saskatoon and Kingston, with Ron Perry from Ottawa as discussion leader. Two days' orientation then seven days and nights working through every phase of camp work, testing each discussion immediately against a real cabin group, interest group, waterfront period or overnight. Jointly sponsored by the Camp Pine Crest Committee of Toronto Central YMCA and the National YMCA Camping and Personnel Committee. Personal evaluation interviews with each participant were conducted by Mr. Stan Symington, Boys' Work Secretary for the National Council of YMCAs.
entities: National Council of YMCAs of Canada

facts.claim: Vernon F. McAdam, author of Twenty Twenty-Minute Talks to Boys (December 1954), "for the past thirty years... has talked to boys. Boys' clubs, Boy Scout Groups, Boys' Brigade, High School, Sunday School, and Camp Weredale have been his interests. Each Sunday found him conducting an undenominational chapel service in which his talk formed the focal point." The book was free on request from Boys' Clubs of Canada, 6 Weredale Park, Montreal 6, Quebec. A named Weredale chapel speaker of thirty years' standing, and a published text of what boys at a Montreal camp were told on Sunday mornings in the early 1950s.

Joyce Bertram came to Camp Ouareau straight from the national office of the CCA: "Miss Joyce Bertram, [CCA's] former Executive Secretary... Director and Owner of Camp Ouareau, in the Laurentians, to succeed Miss Dorothy Percival."

Barbara Cass-Beggs, "Sunday Programmes at Camp" (December 1954), gives a named Canadian camp repertoire: "Summer Is A-Coming In"; a Canadian evening built around a Hudson Bay trading post with fishermen, lumberjacks, "Eskimos and Indians," an old Indian storyteller telling a Gitchi-Manitou legend, closing on "The Huron Carol," with "I'se the B'y That Builds the Boat," "Donkey Riding," "Eskimo Lullaby," "The Indian Birch Bark Canoe," "Les Raftsmen" and "A la claire fontaine"; an "America Sings" evening; and a Highland Ceilidh opening with the cutting of the sod for the turf fire and closing with the smooring of the fire. Her cited source books: Fireside Book of Folk Songs, Fireside Book of American Songs, Oxford Carol Book, Kennedy-Fraser's Songs of the Hebrides, Fowke and Johnston's Folk Songs of Canada, Sing Along the Way, Lift Your Voices.

Kay McClelland, Section Head at Camp Oconto, "With the Tens and Elevens" (December 1954), names a second block of the common Canadian camp repertoire for that age: "The Squid Jiggin' Ground," "The Canadian Boat Song," "Why Can't My Goose," "Little Tommy Tinker," "Indians Are High-Minded," "Peace I Ask of Thee, O River," "Land of the Silver Birch," "As the Shadows," "Taps." She also describes the camp song-writing competition -- each cabin writes a song about its own group or section within a week, presented at a special evening -- one documented mechanism by which camp-original songs came into being. On Indian Lore she records the ten-to-eleven-year-old pow-wow as the age at which it took hold, with campers choosing chiefs and witch doctors and hunting up legends.

Gertrude Evelyn "Dinty" Moore, profiled by Lorne E. Brown (December 1954): Margaret Eaton School graduate; the idea for her camp came from Mary Edgar of Glen Bernard on an evening walk; she opened Moorecroft, the first private girls' camp in British Columbia, in 1934, on 75 acres on Vancouver Island; first President of the BC Camping Association, 1939, and principal author of the BC camping standards later used by the province for licensing.

Ted Yard's "Whoduzit?" job-analysis series began in December 1954 with the Section Director post set out in full: staff training, programme planning, cabin allotments, health check-up, laundry and days-off and night-watch schedules, counsellor appraisal sheets, counsellor letters to parents, daily reports, and the principle that "the Section Director is in effect the Director of a small camp unit."

Canada had exactly two diabetic camps in 1954 -- Illahee Lodge at Cobourg (Kinsmen) and Kiwanis Camp Banting on the Ottawa River at $25 a week -- against twenty-five in the United States. The Ontario Society for Crippled Children ran five camps, Blue Mountain alone taking about 275 children a year under Delwin McLennan.

"A Survey of Junior Camping in Ontario" (February 1955), conducted by the Toronto Nursery Education Association, chaired by Flora Morrison and prepared with the advice of Dr. Mary L. Northway, states in its historical preamble: "In Canada in 1884, the Ottawa Y went camping at Golden Lake and in all probability established the first Canadian camp." This conflicts with the same magazine's December 1954 profile of Ace Milks, which dates the Ottawa camp's earliest trace to an 1893 YWCA board minute and its move to Golden Lake to 1908. Two accounts in the same magazine, three months apart, place the Ottawa Y at Golden Lake twenty-four years apart, and one asserts a Canadian first.

The Ontario Camping Association Minimum Standards for Organized Children's Camps, adopted 5 November 1953 and printed in full in February 1955: camp licensed under the Public Health Act; drinking water approved before opening and tested every two weeks; all milk pasteurized; a hot bath or shower at least weekly; a resident doctor or registered nurse in any camp of more than two weeks with more than 30 campers; health examinations for every camper and every staff member; a mid-day rest of not less than one hour; one lifeguard for every ten persons in the water, free of all other duties; written and posted swimming rules applying to staff and visitors as well as campers, and no one ever to swim alone; swim tests on arrival; a counsellor must be at least seventeen; not less than one cabin counsellor for every eight campers; no staff member engaged until the director has contacted at least one referee, and where the applicant has worked at another camp, a report from that camp on character and suitability; at least one half-day a week entirely free for every staff member. Explicitly not mandatory for OCA membership.
The 1955 Quebec Camping Conference was held at University Settlement, 3553 St. Urbain Street, Montreal, 11-12 March 1955, contact Ken Murray.

C. A. Buckley, Director of Big Cove YMCA Camp out of Halifax, was named CCA representative in the Maritimes in early 1955 and was working to build a camping group there. Jack Pearse was developing the Ottawa area, where "some fifteen or more camps" were outside the association. Ruby Smith, Joyce Bertram and Mary Kirkwood arrived from Montreal over the holidays to visit the national office.

Irwin Haladner's presidential message of February 1955 concedes the CCA's structural weakness plainly: "Most decisions are made by a few officers in the locality of the President," and standing committees "have rarely had the thinking and action from broad representation across the country" -- the national body describing itself as Toronto-centred in 1955.

Canadian canoe standards began in 1955: John Hoyle, National Chairman on Standards, "is now calling together a committee to work on the nucleus of a set of standards based on those in Mr. Ron Perry's book, The Canoe and You." Requests had been "overwhelming." The origin point of national canoe-tripping standards in Canada, from a named book.

The CCA Counsellor Placement Bureau, described in operating detail in February 1955: applicants' cards on file at national office; Toronto-area directors pay $1 to register, out-of-town directors free; $1 per counsellor actually engaged; lists mailed periodically. A documented mechanism by which staff moved between Canadian camps in the 1950s.

Fowke and Johnston's Folk Songs of Canada was reviewed at length in February 1955 with an explicit programme for camps: "Camp songs should be, to a great extent, Canadian in our camps... If our campers were to learn even one of these songs for each week spent in camp, theirs would be a rich heritage." The nationalist argument for the camp repertoire, stated outright.

Arnold Fraser, then of the World Alliance of YMCAs in Geneva, reported in February 1955 on YMCA camping in Belgium: two tent camps, Nieuport-Bains and Han-sur-Lesse, built up over eight postwar seasons from campers "huddled together in empty, badly damaged bunkers left over from Hitler's... Atlantic Wall"; "all the camps are on a co-educational basis"; almost a hundred children of American armed-services personnel camped with Belgian children in 1954. A YMCA camping system running fully coeducational a decade before Kanawana's coeducation question.

Joyce Plumptre Tyrrell's obituary of Fannie L. Case (died 23 January 1955, aged 87) states that Case, from her 1905 camping trips into Algonquin Park with her Rochester students, "founded Northway Lodge as the first girls' camp in Canada." This conflicts with the KB's record that Mary Susannah Edgar "is credited with founding the first girls' summer camp in Canada" (Camp Oolahwan, YWCA, 1917). Northway Lodge, 1905, would predate Oolahwan by twelve years.

Fannie L. Case's obituary (April 1955): daughter of a Methodist minister; Teachers' College, Columbia; fifteen years teaching in Rochester high schools; lectured in the psychology of industrial education at Rochester Institute of Technology; a founder of the Rochester chapter of the Girl Scouts. Northway Lodge had no set rules, no boundaries, no whistles, bells or bugles, and no set religious teaching; after nearly fifty years on one site there were still no large buildings, only log and shingle structures built by the campers, everyone in tents strung along the wooded shore; the programme was a morning work hour (clearing trails, burning slash, repairing boats and structures) and canoe trips through the park as the central feature, everything else improvised by campers. The fullest documented statement in this run of the "pioneer camping" philosophy.

Mary Edgar's "Wood-fire and Candle-light" texts were printed in full in Canadian Camping in April 1955, including "The Camp Hymn": "God who touchest earth with beauty / Make my heart anew..." in all five stanzas, plus "The Sand Man," "The Magic Store," and "For an Outdoor Chapel" -- "presented for your use through the courtesy of Miss Edgar." The single most widely sung Canadian camp hymn of the period was written by a woman who had run a camp in Quebec.

Keith Cleverdon's "A Challenge to All" (April 1955) gives the documentary history of Canadian camp standards: the OCA standards committee met 1947-1950 under John Hoyle; proposals were circulated to the membership, discussed at several open meetings, and voted on at two annual meetings; the standards were revised in 1953 and altered again in 1955. The committee then had thirteen members representing the YMCA, YWCA, Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, church camping, the Crippled Children's Society and Kiwanis. A voluntary accreditation scheme in which 44 camps took part had just been analysed, and the 1953 annual meeting had charged the committee with developing a system of accrediting member camps.

Cleverdon recorded in April 1955 where camp directors pushed back against the proposed standards: showers, water testing, emergency transport and isolation of sick children in the Health section; and counsellor age and ratio in Leadership, because "many camps use a system of staffing in which a number of mature senior members are employed along with younger assistants" -- exactly the CIT/junior counsellor structure Kanawana ran. The counsellor ratio was restated as programme staff (excluding kitchen, maintenance and secretarial) at one to every eight campers, each at least 17.

CCA finances printed in full in April 1955: 1954 revenue $627.90 (membership fees), expenses $863.60, deficit $235.70; net worth at 31 December 1954, $974.83. The national association of Canadian camping was running on under a thousand dollars -- whatever authority the CCA had over camps like Kanawana, it was not financial.

Cornelia Goldsmith, Chief of the Division of Day Care and Foster Homes at the New York City Department of Health, addressed the OCA convention on 4 March 1955 ("Camp Parents: A Problem or a Challenge?"), setting out the pre-camp home conference as accepted practice, with preliminary data gathered from school, physician and parents; end-of-season written reports on each child; and an explicit warning against "heavy and dramatic advertising, glamorized brochures" and "high-powered salesmanship," because "children are not commodities."

Margaret Govan (Director, Camp Onawaw), "The Dutiful Bogey-Man" (April 1955), is a complete campfire story printed with stage directions for localisation built into the text: "(USE TOWN NAMES WHICH THE CAMPERS COME.)" and "(USE THE NAME OF A POPULAR SENIOR.)" A documented instance of the mechanism by which a camp ghost story becomes local property -- a published story explicitly designed to be renamed to the camp telling it.

Camp B'Nai B'Rith, Montreal, appears in Canadian Camping in June 1955: Elliott Larman is bylined "Nature Lore Counsellor, Camp B'Nai B'Rith, Montreal" for a full intermediate-level nature programme -- the Star Gazer shoebox constellation viewer with pricked-paper slides of the five circumpolar constellations; bean-plant tropism experiments; a four-foot terrarium whose campers named theirs "Cibbibba Jungle."

Mrs. A. H. Stoddard, Divisional Commissioner for the Province of Quebec of the Canadian Girl Guides Association, wrote "Nature's Craft Shop" (June 1955), a full illustrated nature-craft method: maple seeds for beaks, spruce cones for bodies, milkweed pods for swans, oak apples for heads, melon seeds for ears; tools a penknife, scissors, awl, pins and Seccotine glue.

Dorothy M. Douglas, CCA Song Book Chairman, wrote "Sing a Song of Canada" (June 1955), a working method for getting Fowke and Johnston's Folk Songs of Canada into a camp's repertoire. She names the songs she expects camps to take up: Bonhomme Bonhomme, Alouette, The Day Columbus Landed Here, The Farmer's Curst Wife, Unfortunate Miss Bailey, The Morning Dew, The Blooming Bright Star of Belle Isle, The False Young Man, and -- "here in print for the first time" -- Ontario's "nostalgic and lovely" Land of the Silver Birch; then Jack Was Every Inch a Sailor, Bonavist' Harbour, Youpe Youpe, Lukey's Boat, I'se the B'y, Red River Valley, We'll Rant and We'll Roar, The Chesapeake and the Shannon, Squid Jiggin' Ground, Donkey Riding, En roulant ma boule, C'est l'aviron, The Raftsmen, Lumber Camp Song, Ye Maidens of Ontario, Strawberry Roan, Old Grandma, Bury Me Out on the Lone Prairie.

Dorothy Douglas's 1955 transmission method for introducing a new song to a camp: gather the campers and counsellors who like singing into an informal group of "pioneers," teach them the song first, then have them sing the verses while the whole camp learns the chorus. A documented mechanism for how a new song entered a camp's repertoire -- and one that predicts exactly the pattern of a camp "having always sung" something introduced deliberately in a given year.

J. H. Ebbs's Golden Anniversary profile of Taylor Statten (June 1955): he became Boys' Work Secretary of Central YMCA Toronto in 1905 and ran his first boys' camp at Lake Couchiching that year; later Provincial and Canadian Boys' Work Secretary; Secretary to the National Boys' Work Board from 1921; "responsible for at least 52 camps conducted by the YMCA"; originated the Canadian Standard Efficiency Training programme for Tuxis boys and Trail Rangers in 1914; leadership training camp for Tuxis leaders at Canoe Lake 1920; Camp Ahmek 1921 with 30 boys; director of character education at Pickering College from 1927; president of the Metropolitan Board of the YMCA from 1940. George Chubb (business manager) and Pete Sauve (head chef) had been with the Statten camps since 1921.

Taylor Statten founded Camp Wapomeo for girls in 1924 under Mrs. Statten, "in spite of warnings that co-educational camping would ruin his original camping venture" -- he built instead a "brother and sister type camp." A documented 1924 warning inside the Canadian camping establishment that coeducational camping would ruin a boys' camp, and a documented result that it did not, forty years before Kanawana faced the same question.

Alan F. Klein, Associate Professor at the University of Toronto School of Social Work, argued in June 1955 that where the association has tried to evaluate pre-camp counsellor training, "the demonstrated results... have been disappointing, to say the least, and yet we persist in relying upon it almost wholly." He attacked the unit/section-head system directly: decentralisation is administratively sound but "supervision is not one of [its advantages] because most of us can not obtain unit heads who are qualified to supervise, either because we can not afford them or because they do not exist." He would employ one senior supervisor charged with staff training and use a senior counsellor merely as unit co-ordinator, and sets out four methods -- role playing, case study, the incident method, and the observation method.

Rev. Wilbur Howard proposed at the 1955 Ontario Camping Conference a four-stage periodisation of Canadian camping -- "the Wild and Woolly Stage," "the Lean Towards Hygiene," "Throw Back or Go Back," and a proposed next phase, "Relax and Think." He argued for married couples as cabin leaders, at least one grandparent on staff, and explicitly for "two or three different races" on staff: "If we're really serious about establishing better relationships with people of other nationalities and races, then we should be practical about it and get other races and nationalities into our camps." And he warned against all-"home-grown" staff -- "then your leadership tends to be in-grown. You need some imports." A dated 1955 statement of racial integration as camp staffing policy from inside the Canadian movement.

Nancy Fairley, Waterfront Director at Camp Tanamakoon, named the era's waterfront motivational apparatus in June 1955: Red Cross Junior-to-Senior Swimmer progression, RLSS Bronze Medallion and Award of Merit, Red Cross Leader's Course for 16- and 17-year-olds, "taxi rides" for beginners given by counsellors and CITs, canoe parades and paddle-pasts with the Director taking the salute, "sailing lunches," "Vagabond Days," a camper-run Yacht Club, and comic regatta events (pyjama, newspaper, candle, potato and balloon swims; obstacle, crab, wash-basin and broom canoe races).

Mary Edgar's "Taps" was printed in full in June 1955, credited in advance to Under Open Skies, "to be published by Clarke Irwin & Co. Ltd. in the autumn of 1955" -- a dated announcement a year before the 1956 publication date the wiki records.

"Ace" Milks died in the summer of 1955, six months after his Personality profile. The obituary notice corrects and extends that profile's career dates: Assistant at the Ottawa YMCA in 1916; the Boys' Secretaryship in 1917; Assistant General Secretary in 1939; retired 1950. Survived by his widow Mrs. Florence C. Milks and two sons, William and John, both of Montreal. "We simply cannot imagine the Ottawa 'Y' without him. Camp On-Da-Da-Waks is a monument to the leadership he gave during his whole life." The magazine notes that Fannie Case was the only other Personality subject to have died -- pinning the "Among Ourselves" series as contemporary testimony about the living.

Ferna Graham Halliday's 1955 profile of Mabel C. Jamieson states that Jamieson, while General Secretary of the Montreal YWCA, "established Camp Oolahwan in the Laurentians for the Montreal YWCA," and that after resigning the Montreal post in 1921 and a trip abroad she "came back in 1922 to organize one of the first private camps for girls in Canada... Camp Ouareau." The wiki credits Oolahwan's 1917 founding to Mary Susanna Edgar, whose directorship ran 1915-1919. Both can be true -- an executive who established the camp and a director who ran it -- but the wiki as written does not make that distinction, and Halliday was a Montreal YWCA secretary of the period and a principal in the Ouareau founding.

Mabel C. Jamieson's 1955 biography: Hamilton-born, Hamilton Collegiate Institute, University of Toronto Philosophy, gold medallist; five years National Secretary for the Women's Student Christian Movement, travelling to Canadian universities coast to coast; five years General Secretary of the Montreal YWCA, where "her initiative was responsible for a fine new building"; "instrumental in inaugurating the School Girl Camps under the leadership of the YWCA" soon after graduating. After Ouareau she founded "The French Colony in the Laurentians" on a bay of Lake Ouareau, for adult men and women, "for the study of French literature and as an effort to foster French conversation and an appreciation of what the French language has to offer in a cultural way," with outstanding French instructors gathered around her. Halliday notes she was "beloved by her campers, staff and French-Canadian neighbours."

Mary Edgar's Under Open Skies was reviewed in December 1955 as published by Clarke, Irwin at $2.50 -- so it appeared in late 1955, not 1956 as the wiki records. The magazine also notes that Woodfire and Candle-Light "is now out of print," and reprints three more poems from it: "Resources," "When You Leave Camp," and "A Legacy to a Camper."

Eanswythe Flynn's December 1955 editorial names a concrete camp failure: "We have before us a first-hand report of a camp 'which sends boys on trips within the first three or four days of camp without any training, and before some of them know how to swim. The staff claims they teach them on the trips.'" She also records the movement's own self-assessment: "Camp staff, in many instances, is still far too young to assume responsibility for the lives of small children."

CCA membership as of 1955 covered Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, plus half a dozen members in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, one in Newfoundland and one in Hawaii. Regionalisation was under way: an Ottawa Area Section of the OCA formed in May 1955 with seventy-two representatives from nineteen camps, and a three-day conference-workshop of forty to fifty Maritime camp people at Lone Cloud Camp, Miller's Lake, Nova Scotia, in June.

A national History of Canadian Camping was commissioned at the CCA Ottawa board meeting of December 1955: "One of the interesting decisions to come out of the Ottawa Board meeting is that concerning a History of Canadian Camping. The plan is to involve as many as possible of our Elder Statesmen in the camping world, by asking them to contribute some of their experiences and other information about their own camp development... One day we will have a documented report." If the CCA solicited written reminiscences from camp directors across Canada in 1956, the returns would be a body of first-person accounts of Canadian camps in the founding generation -- and Kanawana's own director was a QCA past president and CCA member.

A. L. Cochrane, profiled by Jack Passmore in February 1956: born Birmingham, England, 1870; five years in the Grenadier Guards; came to Canada in 1894 -- the year Kanawana was founded; physical training instructor at Upper Canada College for twenty-seven years; first boys' camp on Lake Muskoka in 1900, "generally recorded as the first private camp in Canada"; then in the summer of 1903 the canoe expedition that founded Camp Temagami, from North Bay to Trout Lake, the Mattawa, up the Ottawa portaging around log booms, Lake Temiskaming, the Montreal River, "The Notch," the Matabitchuan, Rabbit and Snake Lakes to the north-east arm of Lake Temagami, blazing a giant pine on the island they chose.

A. L. Cochrane bought the first pair of skis sold in Toronto and pushed skiing at Upper Canada College; introduced the Royal Life Saving Society programme into Canada and was consulted when the Canadian Red Cross added water safety to its peacetime programme about 1946; was appointed Honorary Associate of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem by King Edward VII in 1907; was a founder of the CCA and its Honorary President for years; and was given a memorial plaque by Ontario's Minister of Education Dana Porter for Camp Temagami's fiftieth anniversary in 1949.

A complete camp letter to parents was printed in February 1956 for other camps to copy -- Mr. and Mrs. R. Raymer of Camp Tanamakoon, "We Tried It This Year." Sections on letters (write cheerfully; don't tell her how terribly you miss her; homesickness usually passes in three or four days and "actually parents suffer more than children"), parcels (a long list of what is welcome, an explicit refusal of comic books, love-story and confession magazines, and an emphatic PLEASE DO NOT SEND FOOD, CANDY OR GUM with seven enumerated reasons), visitors (the camp on Standard Time in July and Daylight Time in August; no arrivals or departures between 1.30 and 3.00 because of rest hour; campers may not leave camp with anyone but their own parents without written consent), and telephoning (one line into camp; no calls during rest hour or after 8.30).

The CCA board met at the Ottawa YMCA in December 1955 after an evening meeting of over fifty Ottawa camping people with board members from Toronto and Montreal, and discussed "our units of organization in an effort to find a solution for the problem of distance," appointing a national committee under Ted Yard on small city units. Present from Quebec: Agnes Mutchler, Ken Murray and Nan Vail -- Vail then newly appointed Executive Director of the St. Laurent Neighbourhood Association in Montreal.

Dorothy Douglas's February 1956 review of Mary Edgar's Under Open Skies mentions "the legend shared with Glen Bernard by Dawendine, daughter of a Chief of the Mohawks" as one of the tales in it -- a named Indigenous source for a specific camp legend, and a rare instance of a camp story attributed to a named Indigenous person rather than to generic "Indian lore."

C. R. Blackstock of Camp Mazinaw described the river "pointer" in February 1956: a 24-foot lumbermen's log-drive boat, paddled rather than rowed, carrying eight to ten boys, riggable with a short mast and square sail, used to teach stroke rhythm to a whole group at once and convertible into "a pirate ship, a viking vessel." A distinctly Canadian camp watercraft.

John P. Kidd wrote the editorial of Canadian Camping for April 1956, "Camping and Citizenship" -- the second Kidd item in the run after the 1950 byline identifying him as Executive Director of the Canadian Citizenship Council, which identifies the "John Kidd" recorded as a Kanawana leader in 1934. A camp is "a complete world, a society, a civilization, a community, separate and distinct" -- "a small and more or less homogeneous society, generally with simple but effective organization, and with almost continuous face-to-face relationships, with a minimum of group tensions fortified by history and tradition." On citizenship: "Citizenship isn't just anybody's business; it is everybody's business. Nor can citizenship be taught, like a skill... attitudes, respect for the rights of others, and a sense of individual and group responsibility -- these things can not be taught." He points to ritual, such as flag raising, as one of the ways a camp does this work.

Mary Edgar's "The Camper and the Boogey-Man," printed in April 1956 among poems from Woodfire and Candle-Light, is a rhymed cautionary tale in child dialect: "Onct there was a little camper / An' she wandered out at night; / A great black Boogey catched her / And he dragged her out of sight... / He led her through a fearsome ditch / Down a deep, dark well, / An' made her live with snakes and toads / An' things too bad to tell," ending with an explicit MORAL warning campers not to wander out at night. With Margaret Govan's "The Dutiful Bogey-Man" of April 1955, that is two bogey-man texts in the national camping magazine within twelve months, one explicitly a discipline device and the other explicitly written to be localised with camp names.

The History of Canadian Camping project got named investigators in April 1956: "Investigation by Mrs. David Palter and Mr. Keith Cleverdon into the possibility of compiling a History of Canadian Camping, involving representatives from all provinces, and embracing all of Canada."

Barry Lowes set out Camp New Moon's complete four-year Canadian CIT ladder in April 1956: at 15, campers help put younger groups to bed and lead camp-wide programmes under a senior counsellor -- "These are not duties, they are opportunities. No one must." At 16 they return as CITs, full paying campers, told this is their last summer as a camper, choosing one or two days a week (never more than two) assisting a cabin group from reveille to taps, with an individual programme ensuring two weeks in each of the four units. At 17 the best return as Staff Aids -- no fee, no pay. At 18, Junior Counsellors, in a cabin with a senior counsellor. At 19, Senior Counsellors. He calls it "a farm system" and "a long process, four years... with an immeasurable investment of time, energy and money by the camp."

Barry Lowes documented Camp New Moon's own failed experiments with Staff Aids in April 1956: first housed together (they became "glorified campers"), then rotated every two weeks (good for them, disruptive for campers), finally placed in one cabin group for the whole summer. His framing of the problem: "'He feels that he is too old to be a camper.' How many times have you heard that statement from the parents of 15 and 16-year-olds? If a camper feels that he or she has outgrown camp, then the blame must fall upon us as camp directors."

J. E. Anderson, M.D., "Is There a Doctor in Camp?" (April 1956), gives hard numbers: almost ten percent of Ontario approved camps had no professional medical staff at all; sixty percent employed at least one registered nurse; thirty percent had a resident doctor plus nurses; seventy-nine percent of camps employing a doctor had a capacity over one hundred. He publishes a scoring scheme for how much medical staff a camp needs and a complete camper medical form as used by Camp Kennaway (Boy Scouts Association), plus the practice of a confidential per-camper note to each section leader after the first-day medicals, and the requirement of a legal waiver, filled out before camp, for campers whose religious convictions forbid medical treatment.

"Duel Issues" began in April 1956 as a regular feature edited by Mary Barker, printing two signed opposing arguments. The first: Resolved that campers should wear uniforms. For: uniforms cut lost articles and pilfering, make tidiness enforceable, build esprit de corps, and crucially mean "no cause for the well-to-do girl to outshine her poorer sister."
